Week 2: Cell Biology & Pharmacology / Cell Structure & Organelles

Question 1
A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and a 6-kg weight loss over 3 months. He drank heavily for 20 years but quit last year. He takes no medications. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and his liver is firm and palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated, and CT shows a liver mass. Biopsy shows malignant hepatocytes with several large, prominent nucleoli in each nucleus. Which process is taking place in these structures?
A. rRNA transcription, pre-RNA processing, and ribosome subunit assembly
B. Formation of the basal body
C. Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
D. Degradation of ubiquitin-tagged proteins
E. Beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids
Answer: A. rRNA transcription, pre-RNA processing, and ribosome subunit assembly
Why this is correct: The nucleolus is the site of rRNA transcription, pre-RNA processing, and ribosome subunit assembly. Cells with high protein synthesis, like cancer cells and liver cells, tend to have more nucleoli.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Formation of the basal body: Centrioles form the basal body.
C. Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: Catalase in peroxisomes does this.
D. Degradation of ubiquitin-tagged proteins: That's the job of proteasomes.
E. Beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids: That happens in peroxisomes.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fever, cough, and green sputum for 4 days. She takes an oral contraceptive and works as a daycare teacher. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), respiratory rate is 22/min, and she has crackles over the right lower lobe. Chest x-ray shows consolidation. She is started on an antibiotic that binds the small subunit of bacterial ribosomes but doesn't affect her own. Which pairing correctly describes the two ribosome types?
A. Bacterial 80S (40S and 60S); human 70S (30S and 50S)
B. Bacterial 70S (30S and 50S); human 80S (40S and 60S)
C. Both 70S
D. Both 80S
E. Bacterial 70S (40S and 30S); human 80S (50S and 60S)
Answer: B. Bacterial 70S (30S and 50S); human 80S (40S and 60S)
Why this is correct: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of a 30S small and 50S large subunit. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, made of a 40S small and 60S large subunit.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bacterial 80S (40S and 60S); human 70S (30S and 50S): These are reversed.
C. Both 70S: Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S.
D. Both 80S: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S.
E. Bacterial 70S (40S and 30S); human 80S (50S and 60S): The subunit pairings are wrong.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 3
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental regression and an enlarged liver. He was born at term and met early milestones. His parents are first cousins. His liver is palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Studies show that his cells can't break down material delivered to one organelle, which is highly acidic and whose enzymes are made in the rough ER and passed to the Golgi. His weight is at the 10th percentile, and he has coarse facial features. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and his CBC is normal. Where does this organelle originate?
A. From free ribosomes in the cytosol
B. From centrioles
C. From the Golgi body
D. From the plasma membrane by scramblase activity
E. From the nucleolus
Answer: C. From the Golgi body
Why this is correct: Lysosomes originate from the Golgi, are highly acidic, and get their enzymes from the rough ER by way of the Golgi. Peroxisomes don't come from the Golgi; their enzymes are made on free ribosomes, like mitochondrial proteins.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. From free ribosomes in the cytosol: That's how peroxisomal enzymes are made.
B. From centrioles: Centrioles form basal bodies.
D. From the plasma membrane by scramblase activity: Scramblases move phospholipids between leaflets.
E. From the nucleolus: The nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 4
A 6-month-old girl is evaluated for poor feeding, low muscle tone, and an enlarged liver. She was born at term. Her parents are healthy. She has a large anterior fontanelle, and her liver is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Studies show a defect in an organelle that doesn't come from the Golgi, whose enzymes are made on free ribosomes, and that handles beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids and alpha oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids. Which organelle is defective?
A. Proteasome
B. Lysosome
C. Microsome
D. Peroxisome
E. Nucleolus
Answer: D. Peroxisome
Why this is correct: Peroxisomes don't originate from the Golgi, and their enzymes are made by free ribosomes, like mitochondria. They carry out beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids and alpha oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids, and their catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proteasome: Proteasomes degrade ubiquitin-tagged proteins.
B. Lysosome: Lysosomes come from the Golgi and get enzymes from the rough ER.
C. Microsome: Microsomes are ER and membrane vesicles formed during centrifugation.
E. Nucleolus: The nucleolus makes ribosomes.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 5
A 45-year-old man is exposed to radiation during a workplace accident and has damage from free radicals. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. His vital signs are stable. Hydrogen peroxide forms in his cells as they neutralize reactive oxygen species. An enzyme in one organelle breaks this hydrogen peroxide down into water. He has redness and peeling of the skin on his forearms and mild nausea. Pulse is 88/min, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg, and his CBC shows a mildly low lymphocyte count. Which enzyme and organelle are these?
A. Proteases in proteasomes
B. Glycosylases in the nucleolus
C. Catalase in peroxisomes
D. Acid hydrolases in lysosomes
E. Catalase in lysosomes
Answer: C. Catalase in peroxisomes
Why this is correct: Catalase in peroxisomes decomposes hydrogen peroxide, which is used to neutralize free radicals, into water.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proteases in proteasomes: Proteasomes degrade tagged proteins.
B. Glycosylases in the nucleolus: The nucleolus makes rRNA.
D. Acid hydrolases in lysosomes: Lysosomal enzymes break down macromolecules, not peroxide.
E. Catalase in lysosomes: Catalase is a peroxisomal enzyme.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 6
A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive vision loss, extra fingers, and kidney cysts. He's in sixth grade and plays the trumpet. His physician explains that in most of his cells, a centriole attaches to the inner side of the plasma membrane and forms a structure that grows a single antenna-like projection. His blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg, and his BMI is above the 97th percentile. His creatinine is mildly elevated. What does this structure form in most non-dividing cells?
A. A beating motile cilium in every cell
B. The nucleolus
C. A microvillus
D. A nonmotile primary cilium
E. A lysosome
Answer: D. A nonmotile primary cilium
Why this is correct: In non-dividing cells, centrioles attach to the inner plasma membrane to form a basal body. It can form the base of a flagellum or beating cilium, but in most cells it forms a nonmotile primary cilium.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A beating motile cilium in every cell: Motile cilia are limited to cells like airway epithelium and sperm.
B. The nucleolus: The nucleolus is inside the nucleus.
C. A microvillus: Microvilli are actin structures.
E. A lysosome: Lysosomes come from the Golgi.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 7
A 30-year-old woman donates blood for the first time. She is healthy, runs marathons, and takes no medications. Her hemoglobin is 13.6 g/dL. A student studying her red cells finds they have no nucleus, mitochondria, or ribosomes but still degrade damaged proteins tagged with ubiquitin. Pulse is 58/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Her ferritin is normal. Which structure do mature red blood cells still have?
A. Rough ER
B. Proteasomes
C. Mitochondria
D. Lysosomes
E. Peroxisomes
Answer: B. Proteasomes
Why this is correct: Red blood cells have only proteasomes and no other organelles. Proteasomes have regulatory proteins that bind ubiquitin and core proteins that do the degrading.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Rough ER: Mature RBCs lack ER.
C. Mitochondria: Mature RBCs lack mitochondria.
D. Lysosomes: Mature RBCs lack lysosomes.
E. Peroxisomes: Mature RBCs lack peroxisomes.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 8
A 65-year-old man receives chemotherapy for lymphoma. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Two days later, his tumor cells begin to die. As they die, calcium floods into the cells and one phospholipid that normally sits on the inner leaflet appears on the outer surface, signaling macrophages to engulf the cells. He had a large abdominal mass and an LDH of 1,400 U/L at diagnosis. His vital signs are stable, and his potassium and uric acid are being monitored. Which phospholipid is exposed, and which enzyme exposes it?
A. Phosphatidylserine, exposed by scramblases
B. Phosphatidylcholine, exposed by flippases
C. Sphingomyelin, exposed by floppases
D. Glycolipids, exposed by flippases
E. Phosphatidylserine, hidden by floppases
Answer: A. Phosphatidylserine, exposed by scramblases
Why this is correct: Negatively charged phospholipids (PS, PE, PI) sit on the inner leaflet, while PC, SM, and glycolipids sit on the outer leaflet. An influx of calcium activates scramblases that display PS, signaling apoptosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Phosphatidylcholine, exposed by flippases: PC is normally on the outer leaflet.
C. Sphingomyelin, exposed by floppases: SM is already on the outer leaflet.
D. Glycolipids, exposed by flippases: Glycolipids are normally on the outer leaflet.
E. Phosphatidylserine, hidden by floppases: The signal is PS appearing on the outside through scramblases.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 9
A 34-year-old woman with a mitochondrial disorder has two children. She has mild hearing loss and diabetes and takes insulin. Her son has seizures, muscle weakness, and lactic acidosis, while her daughter has only mild exercise intolerance, even though both inherited the same mitochondrial mutation from her. She takes insulin and wears hearing aids. Her son's lactate is 6.2 mmol/L, and his MRI shows lesions in both basal ganglia, while her daughter's lactate is normal. What explains the difference in severity between her children?
A. Lyonization
B. Anticipation
C. Heteroplasmy
D. Imprinting
E. Codominance
Answer: C. Heteroplasmy
Why this is correct: Heteroplasmy is when the severity of mitochondrial mutations changes from one child to another, because each child inherits a different mix of mutant and normal mitochondria.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lyonization: Lyonization is random X inactivation.
B. Anticipation: Anticipation is earlier onset in each generation from repeat expansion.
D. Imprinting: Imprinting silences genes by parent of origin.
E. Codominance: Codominance is expression of both alleles, not mitochondrial variation.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Question 10
A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is enrolled in a study of liver drug metabolism. He drinks a pint of vodka daily and takes no medications. A sample of his liver is homogenized and centrifuged, and the researchers collect a fraction of small vesicles derived from the smooth and rough ER, Golgi, and plasma membrane to measure drug-metabolizing enzymes. His liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and his AST is higher than his ALT. His ultrasound shows a fatty liver. What is this fraction called?
A. The nuclear fraction
B. The mitochondrial fraction
C. The microsomal fraction
D. The peroxisomal fraction
E. The proteasomal fraction
Answer: C. The microsomal fraction
Why this is correct: The microsomal fraction is made of vesicles derived from the smooth and rough ER, Golgi, and plasma membrane during centrifugation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The nuclear fraction: The nuclear fraction contains nuclei.
B. The mitochondrial fraction: Mitochondria aren't the ER-derived vesicles described.
D. The peroxisomal fraction: Peroxisomes don't come from the ER and Golgi.
E. The proteasomal fraction: Proteasomes are protein complexes, not membrane vesicles.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 11
A 60-year-old woman with myeloma starts bortezomib, which blocks the structure that degrades damaged or unneeded proteins. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine. Her oncologist explains that this structure has one part that recognizes and binds ubiquitin and another part that does the degrading. She has back pain, anemia, and an IgG M-spike. Her calcium is 11.2 mg/dL. Which part binds ubiquitin?
A. The 30S subunit
B. The regulatory proteins (RP)
C. The core proteins (CP)
D. Catalase
E. Lysosomal hydrolases
Answer: B. The regulatory proteins (RP)
Why this is correct: Proteasomes have regulatory proteins (RP) that bind ubiquitin and core proteins (CP) that do the degrading.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The 30S subunit: That's part of a bacterial ribosome.
C. The core proteins (CP): The core proteins do the degrading.
D. Catalase: Catalase is a peroxisomal enzyme.
E. Lysosomal hydrolases: Lysosomes aren't proteasomes.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Week 2: Cell Biology & Pharmacology / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes

Question 12
A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of episodes of flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing. She has lost 4 kg and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, and she has a murmur over the right heart. Urine 5-HIAA is elevated, and CT shows liver masses from a neuroendocrine tumor making large amounts of serotonin. Her tumor is diverting an amino acid away from its other products, and she develops a scaly, sun-exposed rash from niacin deficiency. Which amino acid is being diverted?
A. Beta-alanine
B. Tryptophan
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Leucine
Answer: B. Tryptophan
Why this is correct: Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin, niacin, and melatonin. Heavy serotonin production uses up tryptophan, leaving less for niacin.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Beta-alanine: Beta-alanine is used to make coenzyme A.
C. Tyrosine: Tyrosine makes dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, and melanin.
D. Histidine: Histidine makes histamine.
E. Leucine: Leucine is purely ketogenic and isn't a serotonin precursor.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 13
A 3-week-old girl is brought to the physician for a follow-up of an abnormal newborn screen. She was born at term and is feeding well. She has fair skin compared with her parents. Her physician explains that her condition affects the amino acid used to make dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, and melanin. Her parents are both of Northern European descent and have brown hair and eyes. Her weight is at the 50th percentile, and her exam is otherwise normal. Which amino acid is this?
A. Tryptophan
B. Beta-alanine
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Lysine
Answer: C. Tyrosine
Why this is correct: Tyrosine is the precursor of dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, and melanin.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Tryptophan: Tryptophan makes serotonin, niacin, and melatonin.
B. Beta-alanine: Beta-alanine makes coenzyme A.
D. Histidine: Histidine makes histamine.
E. Lysine: Lysine isn't the precursor of catecholamines.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 14

Pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. She has diffuse raised wheals and mild wheezing. Her symptoms are driven by a mediator released from mast cells that is made from an amino acid by decarboxylation. She has no history of anaphylaxis and has eaten shrimp before without problems. Which amino acid is the precursor?
A. Beta-alanine
B. Leucine
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Tryptophan
Answer: D. Histidine
Why this is correct: Histidine is the precursor of histamine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Beta-alanine: Beta-alanine makes coenzyme A.
B. Leucine: Leucine is a ketogenic amino acid.
C. Tyrosine: Tyrosine makes catecholamines, thyroxine, and melanin.
E. Tryptophan: Tryptophan makes serotonin, niacin, and melatonin.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 15
A 55-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue. He follows a restrictive diet and takes several supplements. His physician is reviewing how his cells make coenzyme A, which is needed to carry acyl groups in energy metabolism. He has a BMI of 20 and has lost 3 kg over a year. His hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL, and his albumin is 3.4 g/dL. Which amino acid derivative is used to make coenzyme A?
A. Lysine
B. Beta-alanine
C. Tryptophan
D. Tyrosine
E. Histidine
Answer: B. Beta-alanine
Why this is correct: Beta-alanine is used to make coenzyme A.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lysine: Lysine isn't the listed CoA precursor.
C. Tryptophan: Tryptophan makes serotonin, niacin, and melatonin.
D. Tyrosine: Tyrosine makes catecholamines, thyroxine, and melanin.
E. Histidine: Histidine makes histamine.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 16
A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of fatigue and hair thinning after starting a very restrictive vegan diet 6 months ago. She runs cross-country and eats mostly fruit and rice. Her BMI is 17.8, and her albumin is low. Her physician explains that her diet may be missing amino acids her body can't make. Pulse is 54/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Her hair is thin and brittle, and she has mild ankle swelling. Which group lists only essential amino acids?
A. Proline, arginine, methionine, and threonine
B. Tyrosine, cysteine, glutamine, and leucine
C. Phenylalanine, valine, threonine, and lysine
D. Aspartate, glutamate, valine, and histidine
E. Alanine, glycine, serine, and lysine
Answer: C. Phenylalanine, valine, threonine, and lysine
Why this is correct: The essential amino acids are phenylalanine, valine, tryptophan, threonine, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, and lysine (PVT TIM HaLL).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proline, arginine, methionine, and threonine: Proline and arginine aren't on the essential list.
B. Tyrosine, cysteine, glutamine, and leucine: Tyrosine, cysteine, and glutamine aren't on the essential list.
D. Aspartate, glutamate, valine, and histidine: Aspartate and glutamate aren't essential.
E. Alanine, glycine, serine, and lysine: Alanine, glycine, and serine aren't essential.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 17
A 5-year-old boy with a rare metabolic disorder is placed on a ketogenic diet by his neurologist to control seizures. He takes levetiracetam. His dietitian explains that some amino acids can only be converted to ketone bodies and never to glucose. He has had up to 10 seizures a day despite two medications. His growth is at the 25th percentile, and his exam is otherwise normal. Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?
A. Leucine and lysine
B. Tryptophan and threonine
C. Histidine and valine
D. Isoleucine and phenylalanine
E. Alanine and glycine
Answer: A. Leucine and lysine
Why this is correct: Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids (two L's, and L follows K).
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Tryptophan and threonine: These are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
C. Histidine and valine: These aren't purely ketogenic.
D. Isoleucine and phenylalanine: These are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
E. Alanine and glycine: These aren't purely ketogenic.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 18
A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is enrolled in a nutrition study. She takes metformin and walks daily. The study tracks amino acids whose carbon skeletons can be used to make both glucose and ketone bodies. Her BMI is 31, and her HbA1c is 7.4%. She follows a high-protein diet. Which group contains only amino acids that are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
A. Histidine, valine, and methionine
B. Leucine, lysine, isoleucine, and threonine
C. Leucine and lysine
D. Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine
E. Tyrosine, histidine, and lysine
Answer: D. Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine
Why this is correct: Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine (TTIP) are both glucogenic and ketogenic. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Histidine, valine, and methionine: These aren't on the glucogenic-and-ketogenic list.
B. Leucine, lysine, isoleucine, and threonine: Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
C. Leucine and lysine: These are purely ketogenic.
E. Tyrosine, histidine, and lysine: Lysine is purely ketogenic, and the others aren't on the list.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 19
A 45-year-old man has a peptide hormone measured as part of an endocrine workup. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. The lab report lists the sequence of a short peptide fragment. His physician reminds the resident that peptide sequences are written in a standard direction. He has had fatigue and a 3-kg weight loss. Blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg, and his electrolytes are normal. In which direction are protein sequences written?
A. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus
B. From the 3' end to the 5' end
C. From the C-terminus to the N-terminus
D. Alphabetically by amino acid
E. From the 5' end to the 3' end
Answer: A. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus
Why this is correct: Proteins are listed from the N-terminus to the C-terminus.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. From the 3' end to the 5' end: That describes nucleic acids, and in reverse.
C. From the C-terminus to the N-terminus: Sequences start at the N-terminus.
D. Alphabetically by amino acid: Order follows the chain, not the alphabet.
E. From the 5' end to the 3' end: 5' to 3' describes nucleic acids.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 20
A 46-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is started on a medication to help him stop drinking. He has had two DUIs and wants to stay sober. His liver enzymes are mildly elevated. Two weeks later he drinks at a party and within minutes has flushing, pounding headache, nausea, and palpitations. Pulse is 118/min. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. He is flushed and diaphoretic but alert. How does his medication cause these symptoms?
A. It competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
B. It inhibits cytochrome oxidase
C. It noncompetitively inhibits catalase
D. It increases acetic acid production
E. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up
Answer: E. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up
Why this is correct: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, which normally converts acetaldehyde to acetic acid. Acetaldehyde builds up and causes severe hangover-like symptoms.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase: That's fomepizole.
B. It inhibits cytochrome oxidase: That's the target of cyanide.
C. It noncompetitively inhibits catalase: Catalase isn't the target.
D. It increases acetic acid production: Blocking ALDH decreases acetic acid.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 21
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after drinking antifreeze in a suicide attempt 2 hours ago. He is drowsy but arousable. Pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. His anion gap and osmolar gap are elevated. He is given an antidote that competes with the toxin for the enzyme that starts its breakdown, so toxic downstream products aren't made. His glucose is normal, and serum ethanol is undetectable. Urine shows calcium oxalate crystals. Which antidote and enzyme are these?
A. Disulfiram, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
B. Disulfiram, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase
C. Fomepizole, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase
D. Hydroxocobalamin, for cyanide targets
E. Fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
Answer: E. Fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
Why this is correct: Fomepizole competes for alcohol dehydrogenase and is used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning to stop toxic downstream products from being made.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Disulfiram, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase.
B. Disulfiram, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase: Disulfiram is used for alcohol use disorder, not poisoning.
C. Fomepizole, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase: Fomepizole competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase.
D. Hydroxocobalamin, for cyanide targets: Hydroxocobalamin is used for cyanide poisoning.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 22
A 40-year-old firefighter is brought to the emergency department after being trapped in a burning house with plastic furniture. He is confused and has a headache. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97%. His lactate is 11 mmol/L, and his venous blood is unusually bright red. He is given an antidote for a toxin that targets enzymes in the electron transport chain. His carboxyhemoglobin is only mildly elevated. He has soot around his nose and mouth. Which antidote is this?
A. Fomepizole
B. Beta-carotene
C. Hydroxocobalamin
D. Catalase
E. Disulfiram
Answer: C. Hydroxocobalamin
Why this is correct: Cyanide targets enzymes in the electron transport chain, and hydroxocobalamin is used against it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fomepizole: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.
B. Beta-carotene: Beta-carotene isn't a cyanide antidote.
D. Catalase: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide and isn't an antidote.
E. Disulfiram: Disulfiram is used for alcohol use disorder.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 23
A 21-year-old college student of East Asian descent comes to the physician because her face and neck turn bright red with palpitations and nausea after just a few sips of alcohol. She has no other medical problems and takes no medications. Her vital signs and exam are normal. Genetic testing shows a variant in the enzyme that processes acetaldehyde. Pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg. Her liver enzymes are normal. How does this variant change the enzyme's kinetics?
A. It decreases Km and increases Vmax
B. It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
C. It increases Km and reduces Vmax
D. It increases acetic acid production
E. It has no effect on Km or Vmax
Answer: C. It increases Km and reduces Vmax
Why this is correct: ALDH2 deficiency is a mutation in the enzyme that processes acetaldehyde. It increases Km and reduces Vmax, so acetaldehyde builds up and causes flushing.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It decreases Km and increases Vmax: That would make the enzyme work better.
B. It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase: The variant is in aldehyde dehydrogenase.
D. It increases acetic acid production: Acetaldehyde builds up because less is converted to acetic acid.
E. It has no effect on Km or Vmax: The variant changes both.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 26
A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of chronic diarrhea and weight loss. She has celiac disease and has struggled with her gluten-free diet. Her BMI is 18.9, and her iron is low. Duodenal biopsy shows blunted villi and damaged microvilli. The pathologist explains that normal microvilli are stable, uniform structures built on linear actin filaments that are capped at the plus end. Her tissue transglutaminase antibodies are elevated. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with an MCV of 76. Which proteins create these linear filaments?
A. Dynein
B. The Arp2/3 complex
C. Gamma tubulin
D. Formins
E. Spectrin
Answer: D. Formins
Why this is correct: Formins create linear actin filaments. In microvilli, bundling proteins cross-link the parallel filaments, a stable cap at the plus end stops growth, and the minus end attaches to the terminal web.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Dynein: Dynein is a microtubule motor.
B. The Arp2/3 complex: Arp2/3 makes branched filaments at 70 degrees.
C. Gamma tubulin: Gamma tubulin starts microtubules at the MTOC.
E. Spectrin: Spectrin forms the red cell membrane skeleton.

Question 36
A 50-year-old woman with breast cancer starts paclitaxel. She has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine. Her oncologist explains that the drug acts on microtubules, which are built from a repeating basic unit and grow mainly from one end. Her tumor is 3 cm with two involved axillary nodes. Her vital signs and CBC are normal before the first dose. Which statement correctly describes microtubule structure?
A. Microtubules have 9 protofilaments
B. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with beta tubulin at the plus end

D. Gamma-delta dimers form the basic unit
E. Actin monomers form 13 protofilaments
Answer: B. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with beta tubulin at the plus end
Why this is correct: The basic unit is a dimer of alpha and beta tubulin. Beta is the plus end and alpha the minus end, and 13 protofilaments form each microtubule.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Microtubules have 9 protofilaments: Microtubules have 13 protofilaments.
C. Alpha tubulin is at the plus end: Beta tubulin is at the plus end.
D. Gamma-delta dimers form the basic unit: The basic unit is alpha-beta tubulin.
E. Actin monomers form 13 protofilaments: Actin forms microfilaments, not microtubules.

Question 38
A 60-year-old man with lymphoma receives vincristine and later develops numbness in his feet. He has diabetes and takes metformin. His oncologist explains that microtubules normally switch between growing and shrinking at their plus end depending on whether a cap is present. He has decreased vibration sense and absent ankle reflexes. His B12 and HbA1c are normal. What determines whether a microtubule grows or shrinks?
A. GTP-bound tubulin at the plus end allows growth, and GTP hydrolysis leads to shrinkage
B. Tau phosphorylation alone
C. ATP binding at the minus end
D. GDP-bound tubulin at the plus end allows growth
E. Kinesin binding at the minus end
Answer: A. GTP-bound tubulin at the plus end allows growth, and GTP hydrolysis leads to shrinkage
Why this is correct: Tubulin bound to GTP supports growth (rescue), and GTP hydrolysis leads to shrinkage (catastrophe). The GTP cap sits at the plus (beta) end.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Tau phosphorylation alone: Tau is a MAP, not the growth switch described.
C. ATP binding at the minus end: The GTP cap is at the plus end.
D. GDP-bound tubulin at the plus end allows growth: GTP, not GDP, supports growth.
E. Kinesin binding at the minus end: Kinesin is a motor, not the growth switch.

Question 43
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a daily wet cough, chronic sinus congestion, and recurrent ear infections since infancy. She has had pneumonia three times. Question 46
A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of slowness, stiffness, and a shuffling gait for a year. He has also had depression and weight loss. His father had similar symptoms in his 50s. He has a masked face and cogwheel rigidity. A trial of levodopa gives no benefit. Genetic testing shows a mutation in dynactin 1. His handwriting has become small, and he has lost 8 kg. B. It's a microtubule-associated protein that aggregates
C. It's a cargo adaptor that makes dynein hyperactive
D. It starts microtubules at the MTOC
E. It carries cargo on its own using ATP
Answer: A. It activates and regulates dynein
Why this is correct: Perry syndrome comes from mutations in dynactin 1, an activator and regulator of dynein. It causes Parkinson-type symptoms that can't be treated with medication.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It's a microtubule-associated protein that aggregates: That's tau.
C. It's a cargo adaptor that makes dynein hyperactive: That's Bicaudal-D.
D. It starts microtubules at the MTOC: That's gamma tubulin.
E. It carries cargo on its own using ATP: That describes kinesin.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 47
A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of weakness in his legs that has worsened over 2 years. He has muscle wasting and cramps, and his reflexes are reduced in his legs. He works as a carpenter. Genetic testing shows a mutation in Bicaudal-D, a cargo adaptor for a microtubule motor. His sensation is normal. Serum CK is mildly elevated, and nerve conduction studies show motor neuron loss. What effect does this mutation have?
A. It blocks dynactin
B. It makes kinesin inactive
C. It causes tau to aggregate
D. It shortens actin filaments
E. It makes dynein hyperactive
Answer: E. It makes dynein hyperactive
Why this is correct: Bicaudal-D is a cargo adaptor for dynein. Mutations linked to spinal muscular atrophy and ALS cause dynein to be hyperactive.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It blocks dynactin: Dynactin is a separate dynein activator; Bicaudal-D is a cargo adaptor.
B. It makes kinesin inactive: Bicaudal-D is a dynein adaptor.
C. It causes tau to aggregate: Tau aggregation is Alzheimer disease.
D. It shortens actin filaments: That's cytochalasin D.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Question 48
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her daughter because of worsening memory over 3 years. She gets lost driving and repeats questions. She has hypertension and takes lisinopril. Her exam is otherwise normal, and her B12 and TSH are normal. MRI shows temporal lobe atrophy. At autopsy years later, her neurons contain tangles made of a protein that normally binds microtubules. She scores 18/30 on a cognitive screening test. Her vital signs are normal. Which statement about this protein is correct?
A. Tau no longer binds microtubules and forms neurofibrillary tangles
B. Spectrin forms the tangles
C. Dynactin is mutated
D. Tau binds microtubules too tightly
E. Gamma tubulin aggregates
Answer: A. Tau no longer binds microtubules and forms neurofibrillary tangles
Why this is correct: In Alzheimer disease, neurofibrillary tangles are aggregates of tau, a microtubule-associated protein. Tau no longer binds microtubules, and it's debated whether disease comes from loss of normal tau function or from toxic aggregates.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Spectrin forms the tangles: Spectrin is a red cell protein.
C. Dynactin is mutated: Dynactin mutations cause Perry syndrome.
D. Tau binds microtubules too tightly: In Alzheimer disease, tau no longer binds microtubules.
E. Gamma tubulin aggregates: Gamma tubulin isn't the tangle protein.

Question 49
A 34-year-old man with celiac disease has a biopsy that shows damaged intestinal microvilli. He takes no medications and follows a gluten-free diet. The pathologist explains that normal microvilli are stable because their parallel actin filaments are bundled, capped at the plus end, and anchored at the minus end. His tissue transglutaminase antibodies are elevated. His hemoglobin is 11.6 g/dL. What anchors the minus end?
A. A basal body
B. Gamma tubulin at the MTOC
C. Dystrophin at the ECM
D. The terminal web attached to the cortical actin cytoskeleton
E. Fascin at the tip
Answer: D. The terminal web attached to the cortical actin cytoskeleton
Why this is correct: Microvilli are stable, uniform structures. Bundling proteins cross-link their parallel actin filaments, a stable cap at the plus end stops growth, and the minus end attaches to the terminal web, which is attached to the cortical actin cytoskeleton.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A basal body: Basal bodies anchor cilia.
B. Gamma tubulin at the MTOC: That anchors microtubules.
C. Dystrophin at the ECM: Dystrophin anchors muscle actin.
E. Fascin at the tip: Fascin cross-links filopodia.

Question 50
A 30-year-old woman has a small bowel biopsy during a workup for diarrhea. She has irritable bowel syndrome and takes fiber supplements. The pathologist reviews how intestinal cells move nutrients. Transport across the surface facing the gut lumen and transport across the surface facing the blood use different mechanisms. Her stool studies and celiac testing are negative. Her biopsy shows normal villi. Which pairing is correct?
A. Active transport on the apical side and passive transport on the basolateral side
B. Only endocytosis on the apical side
C. Passive transport on both sides
D. Passive transport on the apical side and active on the basolateral side
E. Active transport on both sides
Answer: A. Active transport on the apical side and passive transport on the basolateral side
Why this is correct: The apical side faces the external milieu and uses active transport. The basolateral side faces the internal milieu and uses passive transport.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Only endocytosis on the apical side: The apical side uses active transport.
C. Passive transport on both sides: The apical side uses active transport.
D. Passive transport on the apical side and active on the basolateral side: These are reversed.
E. Active transport on both sides: The basolateral side uses passive transport.

Question 51
A 26-year-old woman with gastroenteritis is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium. She has had watery diarrhea for 2 days after a work lunch. Pulse is 104/min, and her mucous membranes are dry. Her physician explains that glucose in the solution pulls sodium, and water with it, into her intestinal cells through a transporter that also carries galactose. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), and blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg. Her serum sodium is 136 mEq/L. Which transporter is this?
A. GLUT5
B. SGLT2
C. SGLT1
D. GLUT2
E. GLUT4
Answer: C. SGLT1
Why this is correct: SGLT1 in the intestine transports D-glucose and D-galactose with sodium. Sodium is pumped out on the basolateral side, and the symporter moves sugar in along with sodium down its gradient. SGLT1 has higher affinity than SGLT2.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GLUT5: GLUT5 carries fructose.
B. SGLT2: SGLT2 is in the kidney and carries glucose only.
D. GLUT2: GLUT2 is a low-affinity facilitative transporter.
E. GLUT4: GLUT4 is insulin-responsive in muscle and fat.

Question 52
A 2-week-old girl is brought to the physician because of severe watery diarrhea since her first feedings. She was born at term and has lost 10% of her birth weight. Her parents are first cousins. She is afebrile with sunken fontanelles. Her stool is acidic. When her formula is switched to one that uses fructose as the only sugar, the diarrhea stops. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), and she is alert. Her stool contains reducing sugars. Which transporter is defective?
A. GLUT1
B. GLUT4
C. SGLT2
D. SGLT1
E. GLUT5
Answer: D. SGLT1
Why this is correct: Glucose-galactose malabsorption comes from genetic defects in SGLT1. Children can't absorb glucose and galactose and have diarrhea, while fructose uses a different transporter (GLUT5).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GLUT1: GLUT1 defects cause neurologic disease.
B. GLUT4: GLUT4 is insulin-responsive in muscle and fat.
C. SGLT2: SGLT2 is a kidney transporter.
E. GLUT5: GLUT5 carries fructose, which she absorbs normally.

Question 53
A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is started on a drug that makes her kidneys stop reabsorbing glucose. She takes metformin and lisinopril. Her HbA1c is 8.4%. Three weeks later she comes to the physician because of vaginal itching and discharge and feels thirsty. Her glucose is lower, and her urine glucose is very high. Her creatinine is normal, and her BMI is 34. Blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Which transporter does her new drug inhibit, and why did these side effects occur?
A. GLUT2; insulin release is blocked
B. GLUT5; fructose is lost in the urine
C. SGLT1; glucose isn't absorbed from the gut
D. GLUT4; insulin can't move glucose into muscle
E. SGLT2; glucose left in the urine pulls water with it and feeds yeast
Answer: E. SGLT2; glucose left in the urine pulls water with it and feeds yeast
Why this is correct: SGLT2 inhibitors (phlorizin analogs such as Jardiance, Farxiga, Invokana) block glucose reabsorption in the kidney. Glucose stays in the urine, taking water with it and causing dehydration, and it raises the chance of yeast infections.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GLUT2; insulin release is blocked: That wouldn't cause glucosuria this way.
B. GLUT5; fructose is lost in the urine: GLUT5 carries fructose.
C. SGLT1; glucose isn't absorbed from the gut: SGLT1 inhibition would affect the intestine.
D. GLUT4; insulin can't move glucose into muscle: The drug acts in the kidney.

Question 54
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for seizures that started in infancy, developmental delay, and clumsy movements. He was born at term. His blood glucose is normal, but his CSF glucose is low. His symptoms improve on a ketogenic diet. His parents are healthy. His head circumference is at the 10th percentile, and he walks with a wide-based gait. Which transporter is deficient?
A. GLUT2
B. SGLT2
C. GLUT4
D. SGLT1
E. GLUT1
Answer: E. GLUT1
Why this is correct: GLUT1 is ubiquitous, handles basal glucose uptake, and is critical for transporting glucose across the blood-brain barrier. GLUT1 deficiency syndromes cause seizures, developmental delay, and neurobehavioral problems.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GLUT2: GLUT2 is in the liver, pancreas, kidney, and gut.
B. SGLT2: SGLT2 is in the kidney.
C. GLUT4: GLUT4 is in muscle, heart, and fat.
D. SGLT1: SGLT1 defects cause diarrhea.

Question 55
A 62-year-old man with lung cancer is scheduled for a PET scan to look for spread. He smoked for 40 years and has COPD. He asks why the radioactive glucose tracer has to be injected instead of taken by mouth. His biopsy showed adenocarcinoma of the right upper lobe. His glucose is normal, and he has been fasting for 6 hours. What is the reason?
A. FDG is a substrate of SGLT2 only
B. The GI tract absorbs glucose through SGLTs, and FDG is a substrate of GLUTs
C. FDG blocks insulin release
D. FDG only enters tumor cells
E. FDG is destroyed by stomach acid
Answer: B. The GI tract absorbs glucose through SGLTs, and FDG is a substrate of GLUTs
Why this is correct: GLUT-based imaging uses 18FDG, which enters all cells because it's a substrate of all GLUTs. It must be injected because the GI tract absorbs glucose using SGLTs.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. FDG is a substrate of SGLT2 only: FDG is a GLUT substrate.
C. FDG blocks insulin release: FDG isn't used to change insulin.
D. FDG only enters tumor cells: FDG enters all cells.
E. FDG is destroyed by stomach acid: The reason given is that intestinal uptake uses SGLTs.

Question 56
A 25-year-old man eats a large pasta dinner. He is healthy and plays soccer. After the meal, his blood glucose rises, and his pancreatic beta cells sense the rise through a low-affinity transporter that is only fully active after eating. This transporter triggers insulin secretion. His fasting glucose is 88 mg/dL, and his BMI is 23. He takes no medications. Which transporter is it?
A. GLUT2
B. GLUT5
C. GLUT1
D. GLUT4
E. SGLT1
Answer: A. GLUT2
Why this is correct: GLUT2 is a low-affinity transporter in the liver, pancreatic beta cells, kidney, and small intestine. Its low affinity means it's mainly active after eating, and it acts as the glucose sensor for insulin secretion in beta cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. GLUT5: GLUT5 carries fructose.
C. GLUT1: GLUT1 handles basal glucose uptake with average affinity.
D. GLUT4: GLUT4 responds to insulin; it doesn't trigger insulin release.
E. SGLT1: SGLT1 absorbs glucose in the gut.

Question 57
A 30-year-old woman has had high blood sugar since her teens. She has a normal BMI and no autoantibodies. Her insulin levels are low for her glucose level. Genetic testing shows an inactivating mutation in the transporter that lets her beta cells sense glucose. Her mother and grandmother also developed diabetes in their teens. Her fasting glucose is 138 mg/dL, and her C-peptide is low. What is the expected consequence?
A. Hypoinsulinemia and diabetes
B. Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia
C. Diarrhea after fructose

Answer: A. Hypoinsulinemia and diabetes

Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Diarrhea after fructose: That's fructose malabsorption.
D. Seizures from low CSF glucose: That's GLUT1 deficiency.
E. Glucose-galactose malabsorption: That's an SGLT1 defect.

Question 58

Question 60
A 2-day-old boy has repeated low blood sugars despite frequent feeds and needs IV dextrose. He was born at 4.5 kg to a mother without diabetes. Blood glucose is 32 mg/dL with an inappropriately high insulin level. Genetic testing shows a mutation that restricts potassium exit from his pancreatic beta cells. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F). His ketones are low. Why does he release too much insulin?
A. The membrane stays more positive, so the beta cells keep releasing insulin
B. GLUT4 is stuck on the surface
C. Increased K+ exit hyperpolarizes the cell
D. GLUT2 is absent
E. SGLT2 is overactive
Answer: A. The membrane stays more positive, so the beta cells keep releasing insulin
Why this is correct: In familial persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy, restricted K+ exit keeps the beta cell membrane more positive, and too much insulin is released. Mutations that increase K+ release lower insulin.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. GLUT4 is stuck on the surface: GLUT4 isn't the cause of insulin overproduction.
C. Increased K+ exit hyperpolarizes the cell: Increased K+ exit would lower insulin.
D. GLUT2 is absent: GLUT2 inactivation causes low insulin.
E. SGLT2 is overactive: SGLT2 is a kidney transporter.

Question 61
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is started on glipizide. He takes metformin and has hypertension. His physician explains that the drug works on his beta cells in the same way as the mutation that causes persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy. His HbA1c is 8.2%, and his creatinine is normal. His BMI is 32. How does this drug raise insulin?
A. It blocks K+ from leaving beta cells, so calcium channels open and insulin is released
B. It increases K+ exit from beta cells
C. It inhibits SGLT2
D. It moves GLUT4 to the muscle surface
E. It blocks GLUT2
Answer: A. It blocks K+ from leaving beta cells, so calcium channels open and insulin is released
Why this is correct: Sulfonylureas are hypoglycemic drugs that work like FPHHI. They block K+ from leaving, which keeps the positive charge in the cell, so voltage-gated calcium channels open and insulin is released.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It increases K+ exit from beta cells: More K+ exit would lower insulin.
C. It inhibits SGLT2: That's the mechanism of drugs like Jardiance.
D. It moves GLUT4 to the muscle surface: That's the effect of insulin and exercise.
E. It blocks GLUT2: Blocking GLUT2 would reduce insulin.

Question 62
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a scaly, red rash on his face and arms that worsens in sunlight and episodes of unsteady walking. He eats a normal diet. His urine shows increased neutral amino acids. His physician explains that a defect in neutral amino acid transporters is leaving him short of a vitamin made from one of those amino acids. He is at the 25th percentile for height and weight. His parents are healthy. What is the diagnosis?
A. Glucose-galactose malabsorption
B. Fructose malabsorption
C. Cystinosis
D. Hartnup disease
E. Cystinuria
Answer: D. Hartnup disease
Why this is correct: Hartnup disease is a genetic defect in neutral amino acid transporters. Neutral amino acids are excreted, which leads to tryptophan deficiency and, from that, niacin deficiency.

B. Fructose malabsorption: That's a GLUT5 problem.
C. Cystinosis: Cystinosis is defective cystine transport out of lysosomes.
E. Cystinuria: Cystinuria involves cationic amino acids and cystine stones.

Question 63
A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department with severe flank pain radiating to his groin. This is his fourth kidney stone. He drinks little water and takes no medications. Pulse is 104/min, and he has left costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows hexagonal crystals, and a urine sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. His stone is yellow and waxy. His urine pH is 5.5. CT shows a radiopaque stone in the left ureter. Which amino acids are poorly absorbed in this condition?
A. Glucose and galactose
B. Leucine and lysine only
C. Cysteine and the cationic amino acids arginine, lysine, and histidine
D. Fructose
E. Neutral amino acids like tryptophan
Answer: C. Cysteine and the cationic amino acids arginine, lysine, and histidine
Why this is correct: In cystinuria, cationic amino acids (arginine, lysine, histidine) and cysteine aren't absorbed. The sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive, and yellow, waxy kidney stones form. It can be confused with cystinosis, which is defective cystine transport out of lysosomes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glucose and galactose: That's SGLT1 deficiency.
B. Leucine and lysine only: Leucine isn't involved in cystinuria.
D. Fructose: That's fructose malabsorption.
E. Neutral amino acids like tryptophan: That's Hartnup disease.

Question 64

Question 65
A 24-year-old man has cholera-like watery diarrhea after a trip abroad. He has no other medical problems. Pulse is 110/min, and his mucous membranes are dry. He's given an oral rehydration solution. His physician explains that sodium-glucose transport into his intestinal cells works because another step keeps sodium low inside the cell. His sodium is 134 mEq/L, and his creatinine is mildly elevated. He is alert and able to drink. Where does that step happen?

Answer: E. Sodium is pumped out across the basolateral membrane

Question 66
A 60-year-old man with heart failure and atrial fibrillation takes metoprolol, which blocks a G protein-coupled receptor, and diltiazem, which blocks a voltage-gated calcium channel. He asks his pharmacist whether most drugs work this way. He also has hypertension. His heart rate is 72/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Which statement about small-molecule drug targets is correct?
A. Most drugs bind their targets irreversibly
B. Most drugs target proteins such as GPCRs, enzymes, ion channels, nuclear receptors, and transporters
C. Most drugs target DNA directly
D. Most drugs are monoclonal antibodies
E. Only GPCRs are drug targets
Answer: B. Most drugs target proteins such as GPCRs, enzymes, ion channels, nuclear receptors, and transporters
Why this is correct: Small-molecule drug targets include GPCRs, enzymes, ligand- and voltage-gated ion channels, transcription factors, nuclear receptors, transport and structural proteins, and RNA. Most drugs are these; GPCRs are about 12% and ion channels about 19%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Most drugs bind their targets irreversibly: Binding is usually reversible.
C. Most drugs target DNA directly: DNA isn't listed as the main target.
D. Most drugs are monoclonal antibodies: Monoclonal antibodies are biologics, not small molecules.
E. Only GPCRs are drug targets: Many other target classes exist.

Question 67
A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is started on adalimumab, a monoclonal antibody given by injection. She takes methotrexate and folic acid. She asks how this drug differs from her small-molecule tablets. She has morning stiffness and swelling of her MCP joints. Her ESR is 46 mm/h, and her rheumatoid factor is positive. Which category of drug does adalimumab belong to?
A. A cytochrome P450 enzyme

C. An inverse agonist
D. A biologic
E. A small-molecule GPCR agonist
Answer: D. A biologic
Why this is correct: Biologics include monoclonal antibodies, growth factors, and allergens.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A cytochrome P450 enzyme: CYP enzymes metabolize drugs.
B. An allosteric modulator: That describes a binding site, not a drug category.
C. An inverse agonist: That describes how a drug shifts receptor states.
E. A small-molecule GPCR agonist: Adalimumab is an antibody, not a small molecule.

Question 68
A 34-year-old woman with seasonal allergies is enrolled in a trial of a new antihistamine. She uses a nasal steroid spray. The investigators report the drug concentration at which half of her histamine receptors are occupied. She has sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose every spring. Her vital signs are normal. What is this value called?
A. Bioavailability
B. ED50
C. TD50
D. Vmax
E. KD
Answer: E. KD
Why this is correct: Drugs work by reversibly occupying their target. KD is the concentration of drug needed to bind half of the targets, and it reflects potency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bioavailability: Bioavailability is the fraction of a drug reaching circulation.
B. ED50: ED50 is the effective dose in half of people.
C. TD50: TD50 is the toxic dose in half of people.
D. Vmax: Vmax is the maximal rate of an enzyme reaction.

Question 69
A 20-year-old woman with asthma comes to the emergency department with wheezing and shortness of breath after running in cold air. She uses an inhaled steroid. How is albuterol classified in the two-state model?
A. An inverse agonist
B. A partial agonist
C. A competitive antagonist
D. A negative allosteric modulator
E. A full agonist
Answer: E. A full agonist
Why this is correct: In the two-state model, GPCRs and ion channels exist in inactive and active forms. Full agonists shift the equilibrium toward the active conformation, partial agonists shift it partway, and inverse agonists shift it toward the inactive form.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An inverse agonist: An inverse agonist shifts the receptor toward its inactive state.
B. A partial agonist: A partial agonist only partly shifts the receptor to the active state.
C. A competitive antagonist: A competitive antagonist blocks the agonist without activating the receptor.
D. A negative allosteric modulator: That binds a separate site to reduce the response.

Question 73
A 58-year-old man with hypertension is choosing between two blood pressure drugs. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Drug A binds half of its target receptors at 1 nM, and Drug B needs 100 nM to do the same. At full doses, both lower blood pressure by the same maximum amount. His blood pressure averages 156/94 mm Hg. His creatinine and potassium are normal. Which statement is correct?
A. Potency and efficacy are the same thing
B. Drug B has greater efficacy
C. Drug A is more potent, and the two drugs have equal efficacy
D. Drug B is more potent
E. Drug A has greater efficacy
Answer: C. Drug A is more potent, and the two drugs have equal efficacy
Why this is correct: Potency refers to the concentration needed to bind the target (KD). Efficacy refers to the maximal physiologic effect. Drug A needs less drug, so it's more potent, and both reach the same maximum, so efficacy is equal.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Potency and efficacy are the same thing: They're separate properties.
B. Drug B has greater efficacy: Both reach the same maximum effect.
D. Drug B is more potent: Drug B needs more drug, so it's less potent.
E. Drug A has greater efficacy: Both reach the same maximum effect.

Question 74

Question 76
A 36-year-old woman with generalized anxiety is prescribed a drug that binds her GABA receptor at a site separate from where GABA itself binds. Question 77
A pharmacist compares two anticonvulsants for a 30-year-old woman with epilepsy. She has no other medical problems. Drug A has a TD50 of 200 mg and an ED50 of 20 mg. Drug B has a TD50 of 60 mg and an ED50 of 30 mg. She has had two seizures in the past year and wants to become pregnant soon. Her liver and kidney function are normal. Which drug is safer, and why?
A. Drug A, because its ED50 is higher
B. Drug B, because its therapeutic index is larger
C. Drug A, because its therapeutic index of 10 is larger than Drug B's index of 2
D. Drug B, because its TD50 is lower
E. They're equally safe
Answer: C. Drug A, because its therapeutic index of 10 is larger than Drug B's index of 2
Why this is correct: The therapeutic index is TD50 divided by ED50. A larger number is better because the toxic and effective doses are farther apart. Drug A's index is 200/20 = 10, and Drug B's is 60/30 = 2.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Drug A, because its ED50 is higher: Drug A's ED50 is lower, and safety depends on the ratio.
B. Drug B, because its therapeutic index is larger: Drug B's index is 2, which is smaller.
D. Drug B, because its TD50 is lower: A lower TD50 means toxicity at lower doses.
E. They're equally safe: Their therapeutic indexes differ.

Question 78
A 55-year-old woman has high blood pressure and an elevated heart rate. A hormone binds a receptor on her vascular smooth muscle that couples to a G protein activating phospholipase C. PIP2 is split into DAG and IP3, and IP3 releases calcium. Her pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. Her potassium and TSH are normal. Which G protein alpha subunit is involved?
A. Gαi
B. Gαs
C. Gαq
D. Gα12/13
E. Gαt
Answer: C. Gαq
Why this is correct: Gαq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP2 into DAG and IP3. IP3 opens calcium channels, and calcium activates calmodulin. In smooth muscle, calcium activates myosin light chain kinase for contraction.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Gαi: Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
B. Gαs: Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase.
D. Gα12/13: Gα12/13 activates RhoA.
E. Gαt: Gαt activates PDE6 in rhodopsin signaling.

C. Gαi → adenylyl cyclase activation: Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
E. NO → soluble guanylate cyclase → cGMP: That's the cGMP pathway.

Question 89
A 34-year-old woman is choosing between two oral drugs for migraine prevention. She takes an oral contraceptive and works as a teacher. Her pharmacist explains that for a drug to be absorbed, it has to cross the lipid bilayer of intestinal cells. She has four migraines a month. Her vital signs and neurologic exam are normal. Which properties determine how well a drug permeates a lipid bilayer?
A. Its therapeutic index
B. Its CYP metabolism alone
C. Size, hydrophobicity, and the lipid-water partition coefficient
D. Its clearance
E. Its KD and efficacy
Answer: C. Size, hydrophobicity, and the lipid-water partition coefficient
Why this is correct: Absorption is getting a drug into circulation. Permeation through the lipid bilayer depends on size, hydrophobicity, and the lipid-water coefficient.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Its therapeutic index: That compares toxic and effective doses.
B. Its CYP metabolism alone: Metabolism doesn't determine membrane permeation.
D. Its clearance: Clearance describes removal from plasma.
E. Its KD and efficacy: Those are pharmacodynamic properties.

Question 91
A 55-year-old man is enrolled in a study of a new antibiotic. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. He receives the drug intravenously one week and orally the next. The area under the plasma concentration-time curve is 60 mg·h/L after the IV dose and 30 mg·h/L after the oral dose. His kidney and liver function are normal. He weighs 80 kg. What is the oral bioavailability?
A. 30%
B. 25%
C. 200%
D. 100%
E. 50%
Answer: E. 50%
Why this is correct: Bioavailability (F) is how much of the drug reaches systemic circulation, calculated as AUC oral divided by AUC IV. Here it's 30/60 = 0.5, or 50%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 30%: The oral AUC value isn't itself the bioavailability.
B. 25%: That would need an oral AUC of 15.
C. 200%: That's IV divided by oral.
D. 100%: That would need equal AUCs.

A 70-kg man with a bacterial infection is given 500 mg of an antibiotic intravenously. He has diabetes and takes metformin. After distribution, his plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. B. 5 L
C. 0.02 L
D. 5,000 L
E. 50 L
Answer: E. 50 L
Why this is correct: Volume of distribution is the apparent volume in which a drug is distributed, calculated as amount divided by concentration. Here it's 500 mg / 10 mg/L = 50 L.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 70 L: His body weight doesn't equal the Vd.
B. 5 L: That's plasma volume, not this drug's calculated Vd.
C. 0.02 L: That divides concentration by amount.
D. 5,000 L: That multiplies instead of divides.

Week 2: Cell Biology & Pharmacology / Patterns of Inheritance

Question 97
A 28-year-old woman and her husband come for preconception counseling. An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 2,500 people in their population. Neither has a family history of it. They ask how common carriers are. Both are healthy and take no medications. Their families come from the same region. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the approximate carrier frequency?
A. About 1 in 50
B. About 1 in 25
C. About 1 in 100
D. About 1 in 2,500
E. About 1 in 5
Answer: B. About 1 in 25
Why this is correct: In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, q² is the frequency of affected (aa) people. If q² = 1/2,500, then q = 1/50 and p is about 1. Carriers are 2pq, about 2 × 1/50 = 1/25.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. About 1 in 50: That's q, the allele frequency.
C. About 1 in 100: That halves the carrier frequency.
D. About 1 in 2,500: That's the disease frequency, q².
E. About 1 in 5: That's far too high.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Question 98
A 30-year-old man is found to carry a recessive allele for a genetic disorder. He has no symptoms. In his population, the frequency of the recessive allele is 0.1. His physician explains the Hardy-Weinberg equation. His vital signs and exam are normal. He and his partner are planning a pregnancy. What fraction of the population is expected to be affected homozygotes?
A. 1%
B. 18%
C. 20%
D. 10%
E. 81%
Answer: A. 1%
Why this is correct: Under Hardy-Weinberg, p² is AA, 2pq is Aa, and q² is aa. With q = 0.1, q² = 0.01, or 1%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 18%: That's 2pq, the carrier frequency.
C. 20%: That doubles q.
D. 10%: That's q, the allele frequency.
E. 81%: That's p², the unaffected homozygotes.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Question 99
A 26-year-old woman is referred for genetic counseling after her sister was diagnosed with an autosomal recessive condition. In their population, the recessive allele has a frequency of 0.2. The counselor explains the Hardy-Weinberg equation. She is healthy and takes an oral contraceptive. Her vital signs and exam are normal. What fraction of the population is expected to be heterozygous carriers?
A. 20%
B. 16%
C. 64%
D. 32%
E. 4%
Answer: D. 32%
Why this is correct: Under Hardy-Weinberg, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes. With q = 0.2 and p = 0.8, 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 20%: That's q, the allele frequency.
B. 16%: That's pq without doubling.
C. 64%: That's p², the unaffected homozygotes.
E. 4%: That's q², the affected frequency.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Question 100
A 35-year-old woman asks about her risk of being a carrier for a recessive condition in her population. In her population, 36% of people are homozygous for the normal allele. She is healthy and 16 weeks pregnant. Her vital signs and exam are normal. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of the recessive allele?
A. 0.4
B. 0.48
C. 0.64
D. 0.6
E. 0.16
Answer: A. 0.4
Why this is correct: p² is the frequency of AA homozygotes. If p² = 0.36, then p = 0.6, and q = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 0.48: That's 2pq.
C. 0.64: That's 1 − 0.36.
D. 0.6: That's p, the normal allele frequency.
E. 0.16: That's q², not q.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Week 3: Metabolism / Cellular Energetics

Question 1
A 24-year-old man is enrolled in a study of muscle energy metabolism. He is healthy, runs 20 miles a week, and takes no medications. His vital signs are normal, and his BMI is 22. A biopsy of his thigh muscle taken at rest shows ATP 8 mM, ADP 2 mM, and AMP 0 mM. The investigators calculate the adenylate energy charge, which a cell normally keeps near 0.9. He eats a balanced diet and had breakfast 3 hours before the biopsy. What is his muscle's energy charge?
A. 0.9
B. 0.8
C. 0.5
D. 1.0
E. 0.2
Answer: A. 0.9
Why this is correct: Energy charge is ([ATP] + ½[ADP]) / ([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]). Here it's (8 + 1) / 10 = 0.9, the level cells aim to maintain.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 0.8: That's ATP divided by the total without adding half the ADP.
C. 0.5: That would mean far more ADP and AMP.
D. 1.0: That would require all adenine nucleotides to be ATP.
E. 0.2: That's ADP divided by the total.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 30-year-old woman runs a marathon. She is healthy and takes no medications. Near mile 22 her muscle ATP falls and AMP rises as an enzyme interconverts adenine nucleotides. Her pulse is 172/min and her lactate is 6 mmol/L. She drinks sports drinks during the race and ate a pasta dinner the night before. Her glucose is 82 mg/dL, and she is sweating heavily but alert. Her muscles are working at a high rate, and their ATP is being used faster than it's replaced. As her adenylate energy charge drops, how do her muscle cells respond?
A. Glycogen synthesis increases
B. Catabolic pathways turn on and anabolic pathways shut down to make ATP
C. Fatty acid synthesis increases
D. Anabolic pathways turn on to store energy
E. Both anabolic and catabolic pathways shut down
Answer: B. Catabolic pathways turn on and anabolic pathways shut down to make ATP
Why this is correct: Adenylate kinase interconverts AMP, ADP, and ATP and acts as a metabolic monitor. When the energy charge is low, anabolic pathways shut down and catabolic pathways turn on to make ATP; when it's high, catabolic pathways slow.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glycogen synthesis increases: Synthesis is anabolic and is shut down.
C. Fatty acid synthesis increases: That's anabolic and is shut down.
D. Anabolic pathways turn on to store energy: A low charge shuts anabolic pathways down.
E. Both anabolic and catabolic pathways shut down: Catabolic pathways are turned on.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 3
A 19-year-old sprinter comes to the physician for a sports physical. He is healthy, takes a creatine supplement, and runs the 100-meter dash. His vital signs are normal. He asks where his muscles get energy in the first few seconds of a sprint before glycolysis ramps up. His physician explains that a high-energy phosphate compound in muscle quickly regenerates ATP. Pulse is 58/min, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and his BMI is 23. His CK and creatinine are normal. Which enzyme catalyzes this reaction?
A. Creatine kinase
B. Hexokinase
C. ATP synthase
D. Adenylate kinase
E. Pyruvate kinase
Answer: A. Creatine kinase
Why this is correct: Phosphocreatine is a ready source of energy for ATP synthesis in muscle through transphosphorylation, and creatine kinase catalyzes the reaction.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Hexokinase: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose.
C. ATP synthase: ATP synthase (complex V) makes most ATP in mitochondria, not this rapid reaction.
D. Adenylate kinase: Adenylate kinase interconverts AMP, ADP, and ATP.
E. Pyruvate kinase: Pyruvate kinase acts in glycolysis.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 4
A 45-year-old man is studied in a metabolic chamber after an overnight fast. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. His BMI is 29. He eats a mixed diet and hasn't exercised today. Pulse is 72/min, blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg, and his resting glucose is 96 mg/dL. His oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. What is his respiratory quotient?
A. 450
B. 0.2
C. 1.25
D. 0.8
E. 50
Answer: D. 0.8
Why this is correct: The respiratory quotient is CO2 produced divided by O2 consumed: 200 / 250 = 0.8. It estimates the mix of fuels being oxidized.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 450: That adds the two values.
B. 0.2: That subtracts rather than divides.
C. 1.25: That's O2 divided by CO2.
E. 50: That's the difference between the values.

Question 5
A 35-year-old woman on a very low-carbohydrate diet comes to the physician because she feels short of breath on long runs. She takes no medications. Her vital signs and exam are normal. Her physician explains that the fuel she is mostly burning releases 9 kcal/g but requires more oxygen per unit of energy than carbohydrates do. She has lost 6 kg over 3 months and feels well otherwise. Her urine ketones are positive, and her glucose is 84 mg/dL. Why does fat require more oxygen to oxidize than carbohydrate?
A. Fat is burned only by glycolysis
B. Fatty acids are more reduced, while carbohydrates are already more oxidized
C. Fatty acids are more oxidized than carbohydrates
D. Carbohydrates give 9 kcal/g
E. Fat requires no oxygen
Answer: B. Fatty acids are more reduced, while carbohydrates are already more oxidized
Why this is correct: Carbohydrates give 4 kcal/g and are more oxidized, so they need less oxygen to release energy. Fatty acids give 9 kcal/g and are more reduced, so they need more oxygen.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fat is burned only by glycolysis: Fat is oxidized in mitochondria.
C. Fatty acids are more oxidized than carbohydrates: It's the reverse.
D. Carbohydrates give 9 kcal/g: Carbohydrates give 4 kcal/g.
E. Fat requires no oxygen: Fat oxidation needs a lot of oxygen.

Question 6
A 50-year-old man with a mitochondrial disorder is evaluated for muscle fatigue. He takes coenzyme Q10. His lactate is 3.8 mmol/L at rest. His physician explains that in healthy cells, ADP and NAD+ stimulate a key regulated TCA cycle enzyme, while ATP and NADH inhibit it, matching the cycle's rate to the cell's energy needs. B. Isocitrate dehydrogenase
C. Citrate synthase
D. Pyruvate kinase
E. HMG-CoA reductase
Answer: B. Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Why this is correct: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by ATP and NADH and stimulated by ADP and NAD+. Citrate synthase is inhibited by ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA, and citrate, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase by ATP, NADH, and succinyl-CoA.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase: It's inhibited by ATP, NADH, and succinyl-CoA.
C. Citrate synthase: Citrate synthase is inhibited by downstream products, not described as stimulated by ADP.
D. Pyruvate kinase: That's a glycolytic enzyme.
E. HMG-CoA reductase: That's the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.

Question 7
A 40-year-old woman with obesity is enrolled in a trial of a drug that lowers fatty acid synthesis in the liver. She has prediabetes and takes metformin. Her BMI is 36. The drug blocks the mitochondrial transporter that exchanges citrate for malate, so citrate can't reach the cytoplasm. Her triglycerides are 240 mg/dL, and ultrasound shows a fatty liver. D. Citrate in the cytoplasm is the source of acetyl-CoA via citrate lyase
E. Malate is converted to fatty acids
Answer: D. Citrate in the cytoplasm is the source of acetyl-CoA via citrate lyase
Why this is correct: The mitochondrial tricarboxylate transporter exchanges citrate for malate. In the cytoplasm, citrate lyase converts citrate to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, so inhibitors of the transporter reduce fatty acid synthesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Citrate directly inhibits fatty acid synthase: Citrate is the carbon source, not an inhibitor here.
B. It blocks HMG-CoA reductase: That's cholesterol synthesis.
C. The transporter moves carnitine: The carnitine shuttle moves fatty acids into mitochondria.
E. Malate is converted to fatty acids: Malate is exchanged for citrate.

Question 8

What does amphibolic mean?
A. The pathway takes part in both catabolism and anabolism
B. The pathway only breaks molecules down
C. The pathway runs without oxygen
D. The pathway only builds molecules
E. The pathway only occurs in the cytoplasm
Answer: A. The pathway takes part in both catabolism and anabolism
Why this is correct: An amphibolic process involves both anabolism and catabolism. The TCA cycle oxidizes carbohydrates, lipids, and amino acids and provides intermediates for biosynthesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The pathway only breaks molecules down: That's catabolic only.
C. The pathway runs without oxygen: That describes anaerobic glycolysis.
D. The pathway only builds molecules: That's anabolic only.
E. The pathway only occurs in the cytoplasm: The TCA cycle is mitochondrial.

Question 9
A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for exercise intolerance and muscle cramps. Her parents are healthy. Her vital signs are normal, and her CK rises after exercise. Studies show her muscle cells can't trap glucose after it enters because the first enzyme of glycolysis isn't working. She was born at term and has normal development. Her glucose is 90 mg/dL, and her lactate after exercise is lower than expected. Her exam at rest is normal. What does this enzyme normally do?
A. Converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell
B. Converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose
C. Converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
D. Converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate
E. Converts pyruvate to lactate
Answer: A. Converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell
Why this is correct: Hexokinase performs the first step of glycolysis, converting intracellular glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which traps glucose in the cell.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose: That's glucose-6-phosphatase.
C. Converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate: That's PFK.
D. Converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate: That's pyruvate kinase.
E. Converts pyruvate to lactate: That's lactate dehydrogenase.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 10
A 55-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and has studies of his muscle metabolism. He has hypertension and takes amlodipine. Which pair of molecules activates this enzyme?

Why this is correct: Phosphofructokinase is activated by high AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by high ATP and citrate.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. ATP and acetyl-CoA: These inhibit pyruvate kinase.
