D. NADH and succinyl-CoA: These inhibit TCA cycle enzymes.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 11
A 60-year-old woman has high rates of fat oxidation during a prolonged fast before surgery. She has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin, which was held. Her glucose is 88 mg/dL. In her liver, high ATP and high acetyl-CoA slow the last step of glycolysis. She hasn't eaten for 16 hours before her procedure. Pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. A. Citrate synthase, activated by NADH
B. PFK, activated by citrate
C. Pyruvate kinase, which is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
D. Pyruvate kinase, activated by acetyl-CoA
E. Hexokinase, activated by ATP
Answer: C. Pyruvate kinase, which is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Why this is correct: Pyruvate kinase converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate. It's activated by high fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by high ATP and acetyl-CoA.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. PFK, activated by citrate: Citrate inhibits PFK.

E. Hexokinase, activated by ATP: ATP doesn't activate hexokinase this way.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 12
A 68-year-old man with COPD comes to the emergency department with worsening shortness of breath for 3 days. He smoked for 45 years and uses home oxygen. Respiratory rate is 30/min, oxygen saturation is 82% on his usual oxygen, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Arterial blood gas shows a low pH, and lactate is 5.1 mmol/L. He has used two extra albuterol treatments at home. His hemoglobin is 15.8 g/dL, and his kidney and liver function are normal. He isn't taking metformin. Which process explains his elevated lactate?
A. Glycogen synthesis in muscle
B. Hypoxia pushes pyruvate to lactate through lactate dehydrogenase
C. Increased urea production
D. Overactive pyruvate dehydrogenase
E. Excess 2,3-BPG production
Answer: B. Hypoxia pushes pyruvate to lactate through lactate dehydrogenase
Why this is correct: Anaerobic glycolysis occurs in hypoxic conditions like COPD, exercise, and anemia, converting pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. Lactic acidosis can also come from impaired pyruvate clearance, like PDH deficiency, or from renal or hepatic dysfunction.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glycogen synthesis in muscle: Glycogen synthesis doesn't make lactate.
C. Increased urea production: Urea is unrelated to lactate.
D. Overactive pyruvate dehydrogenase: PDH activity reduces lactate.
E. Excess 2,3-BPG production: 2,3-BPG affects oxygen release, not lactate.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 13
A 25-year-old man travels from sea level to a ski resort at 9,000 feet. He is healthy and takes no medications. On day 3 his headache has improved. His hemoglobin is 15.2 g/dL, and oxygen saturation is 91%. His red cells have increased a glycolytic byproduct made from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate that helps them unload oxygen to tissues. How does this molecule affect hemoglobin?
A. It stabilizes the low-affinity state, shifting the curve to the right
B. It binds fetal hemoglobin tightly
C. It stabilizes the high-affinity state, shifting the curve to the left
D. It blocks glycolysis
E. It oxidizes iron to the ferric state
Answer: A. It stabilizes the low-affinity state, shifting the curve to the right
Why this is correct: 2,3-BPG is made from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and stabilizes hemoglobin's low-affinity state. More BPG shifts the oxygen curve to the right, so oxygen is released more easily to tissues.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It binds fetal hemoglobin tightly: Fetal hemoglobin doesn't bind BPG.
C. It stabilizes the high-affinity state, shifting the curve to the left: That would make oxygen harder to deliver.
D. It blocks glycolysis: BPG comes from glycolysis.
E. It oxidizes iron to the ferric state: That describes methemoglobin.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Question 14
A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit. She is healthy and takes a prenatal vitamin. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg, and fetal heart rate is 144/min. She asks how her baby can pull oxygen from her blood across the placenta. Her hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, and her glucose tolerance test was normal. The fetus is growing at the 50th percentile. What explains the fetus's higher oxygen affinity?
A. The placenta converts BPG to lactate
B. Fetal blood has more AMP
C. Fetal hemoglobin binds more 2,3-BPG
D. Fetal red cells have mitochondria
E. Fetal hemoglobin doesn't bind 2,3-BPG
Answer: E. Fetal hemoglobin doesn't bind 2,3-BPG
Why this is correct: Fetal hemoglobin doesn't bind 2,3-BPG, so it has a higher affinity for oxygen and can take oxygen from maternal blood.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The placenta converts BPG to lactate: That isn't the mechanism.
B. Fetal blood has more AMP: AMP isn't the explanation.
C. Fetal hemoglobin binds more 2,3-BPG: More BPG would lower affinity.
D. Fetal red cells have mitochondria: Red cells lack mitochondria.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Question 15
A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for lifelong jaundice, anemia, and an enlarged spleen. His parents are healthy cousins. His hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, and reticulocytes are 14%. His direct Coombs test is negative, G6PD activity is normal, and his smear shows red cells with thorny projections. Enzyme testing shows a chronic, autosomal recessive defect in the last step of glycolysis. He has had two blood transfusions. His bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated. Why do his red cells take this shape?
A. Excess 2,3-BPG polymerizes hemoglobin
B. Low ATP means the Na+/K+ pumps fail
C. Antibodies coat the cells
D. Oxidized hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies
E. Spectrin is defective
Answer: B. Low ATP means the Na+/K+ pumps fail
Why this is correct: Red cells lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP. In glycolytic enzyme deficiencies like pyruvate kinase deficiency, ATP isn't made fast enough, Na+/K+ pumps fail, and echinocytes form, causing hemolytic anemia. PK deficiency is chronic and autosomal recessive.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Excess 2,3-BPG polymerizes hemoglobin: BPG doesn't polymerize hemoglobin.
C. Antibodies coat the cells: His Coombs test is negative.
D. Oxidized hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies: That's G6PD deficiency.
E. Spectrin is defective: That's a membrane skeleton disorder.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 16
A 22-year-old woman eats a large pasta dinner. She is healthy. After the meal, her liver begins storing glucose as glycogen. A protein acts as the primer on which new glycogen chains are built, and the synthesizing enzyme is activated by rising glucose-6-phosphate. Her glucose rises to 148 mg/dL after the meal, and her insulin rises. She has a normal BMI and doesn't have diabetes. Her physician uses the meal to explain how the liver stores glucose. Which pairing is correct?
A. Glycogenin is activated by glucagon
B. Glycogen phosphorylase is the primer
C. Debranching enzyme is the primer
D. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
E. Glycogen synthase is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Answer: D. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
Why this is correct: Glycogenin is the primer for glycogen production. Glycogen synthase builds glycogen, needs a branching enzyme, and is allosterically activated by glucose-6-phosphate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glycogenin is activated by glucagon: Glycogenin is a primer; glucagon activates phosphorylase.
B. Glycogen phosphorylase is the primer: Phosphorylase breaks glycogen down.
C. Debranching enzyme is the primer: The debrancher helps break glycogen down.
E. Glycogen synthase is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate: G6P activates the synthase.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 17
A 34-year-old woman has an episode of low blood sugar after skipping lunch. She takes no medications and works as a nurse. Her glucose is 62 mg/dL. Glucagon rises and her liver begins breaking down glycogen. She works as a nurse and has been on her feet all morning. She is sweaty and shaky, and her pulse is 104/min. Her liver responds within minutes to raise her glucose. Which statement about the glycogen-degrading enzyme is correct?
A. It's inhibited by glucagon
B. It's activated by glucagon and epinephrine and inhibited by glucose and glucose-6-phosphate
C. It's activated by glucose-6-phosphate
D. It's activated by insulin
E. It needs a branching enzyme
Answer: B. It's activated by glucagon and epinephrine and inhibited by glucose and glucose-6-phosphate
Why this is correct: Glycogen phosphorylase breaks down glycogen and needs a debranching enzyme. Glucagon and epinephrine activate it, and glucose and glucose-6-phosphate allosterically inhibit it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It's inhibited by glucagon: Glucagon activates it.
C. It's activated by glucose-6-phosphate: G6P inhibits phosphorylase and activates the synthase.
D. It's activated by insulin: Insulin isn't listed as activating it.
E. It needs a branching enzyme: It needs a debranching enzyme.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 18
A 20-year-old man is sprinting in a track meet. He is healthy and takes no medications. His muscles need to break down glycogen quickly. Muscle contraction releases calcium, and rising AMP signals low energy. He's running the 400-meter dash. His pulse is 188/min, and his muscles are contracting forcefully. His blood glucose is 92 mg/dL. How do these signals affect glycogen breakdown in his muscle?
A. They activate glycogen synthase
B. High AMP and calcium activate glycogen phosphorylase
C. They activate glucose-6-phosphatase in muscle
D. They trigger gluconeogenesis in muscle
E. They inhibit glycogen phosphorylase
Answer: B. High AMP and calcium activate glycogen phosphorylase
Why this is correct: Skeletal muscle needs to make ATP rapidly by breaking down glycogen. Glycogen phosphorylase in muscle is activated by high AMP and calcium, and glycolysis is also activated by AMP.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. They activate glycogen synthase: Synthase builds glycogen.
C. They activate glucose-6-phosphatase in muscle: That enzyme releases glucose from the liver.
D. They trigger gluconeogenesis in muscle: Gluconeogenesis happens in the liver.
E. They inhibit glycogen phosphorylase: They activate it.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 19
A 35-year-old woman runs a half marathon. She is healthy and takes a daily multivitamin. Afterward her lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. Her muscles send lactate and alanine to her liver, which converts them to glucose and sends the glucose back to her muscles. Her glucose is 78 mg/dL after the race. She drank water but no sports drinks. Her pulse is 150/min at the finish line. What is this cycle called?
A. The TCA cycle
B. The pentose phosphate pathway
C. The Cori cycle
D. The polyol pathway
E. The urea cycle
Answer: C. The Cori cycle
Why this is correct: In the Cori cycle, pyruvate from skeletal muscle becomes lactate and alanine, which travel to the liver. The liver makes glucose through gluconeogenesis and returns it to the muscle.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The TCA cycle: The TCA cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA.
B. The pentose phosphate pathway: That makes NADPH and ribose.
D. The polyol pathway: That makes sorbitol.
E. The urea cycle: The urea cycle disposes of ammonia.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 20
A 5-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she becomes sweaty, shaky, and irritable 2 to 3 hours after feeds. She was born at term. Her parents are healthy. She has a doll-like face, a protuberant abdomen, and her liver is palpable 7 cm below the costal margin. Glucose during an episode is 36 mg/dL, and lactate, uric acid, and triglycerides are elevated. Glucagon doesn't raise her glucose. Her kidneys are enlarged on ultrasound. Why can't gluconeogenesis compensate?
A. Phosphorylase is deficient, but gluconeogenesis compensates
B. A lysosomal enzyme is deficient
C. Muscle phosphorylase is deficient
D. The brancher enzyme is deficient
E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, so glucose can't be released even when made by gluconeogenesis
Answer: E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, so glucose can't be released even when made by gluconeogenesis
Why this is correct: Von Gierke disease (type I) is a glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Glucose stays trapped in liver cells, causing hepatomegaly. Gluconeogenesis can't compensate because its final step also needs glucose-6-phosphatase to release glucose.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Phosphorylase is deficient, but gluconeogenesis compensates: That's Hers disease, which is milder.
B. A lysosomal enzyme is deficient: That's Pompe disease.
C. Muscle phosphorylase is deficient: That's McArdle disease.
D. The brancher enzyme is deficient: That's Andersen disease.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 21
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for a protuberant abdomen noticed by his grandmother. He was born at term, is growing at the 20th percentile, and takes no medications. His liver is palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Fasting glucose is 62 mg/dL, mildly low, and lactate and uric acid are normal. Liver biopsy shows increased glycogen from a defective phosphorylase. His lactate and uric acid are normal. His development is on track. Why are his symptoms milder than in von Gierke disease?
A. Gluconeogenesis can still compensate to maintain blood glucose
B. The immune system attacks unbranched glycogen
C. His muscle phosphorylase is defective
D. Lysosomal glycogen can't be broken down
E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is missing
Answer: A. Gluconeogenesis can still compensate to maintain blood glucose
Why this is correct: Hers disease (type VI) is a defective liver phosphorylase. Glycogen builds up and causes hepatomegaly and milder von Gierke-like symptoms, but blood glucose can be compensated by gluconeogenesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The immune system attacks unbranched glycogen: That's Andersen disease.
C. His muscle phosphorylase is defective: That's McArdle disease, which affects muscle.
D. Lysosomal glycogen can't be broken down: That's Pompe disease.
E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is missing: That's von Gierke disease.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 22

He takes no medications and works as a lifeguard. His exam is normal at rest. CK is 18,000 U/L after exercise, and his urine is positive for heme without red cells. Question 23

Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Muscle phosphorylase: That's McArdle disease.

Question 25
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he is floppy and feeds poorly, tiring after a few minutes. He was born at term. His tongue is large, and he has poor head control. Question 26

Week 3: Metabolism / Energy Balance & Nutrition

Question 27
A 40-year-old man wants to lose weight and meets with a dietitian. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. His BMI is 31, and he works at a desk job. The dietitian explains the components of his total daily energy expenditure. He walks about 4,000 steps a day and eats about 2,800 kcal. His blood pressure is 136/86 mm Hg, and his fasting glucose is 104 mg/dL. Which component accounts for about half of his daily energy use?
A. Non-exercise activity thermogenesis
B. Brown fat thermogenesis
C. Thermic effect of food
D. Basal metabolic rate
E. Exercise-associated thermogenesis
Answer: D. Basal metabolic rate
Why this is correct: Basal metabolic rate makes up about 50% of total daily energy expenditure. Exercise-associated thermogenesis is about 25%, non-exercise activity thermogenesis about 15%, and the thermic effect of food is the increase in metabolic rate after eating.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Non-exercise activity thermogenesis: That's about 15%.
B. Brown fat thermogenesis: That isn't one of the components listed.
C. Thermic effect of food: That's the smallest component described.
E. Exercise-associated thermogenesis: That's about 25%.

Question 28
A 28-year-old woman on a high-protein diet asks her physician why she feels warm after meals. She lifts weights 4 days a week and takes a protein supplement. Her vital signs and BMI are normal. Her physician explains that eating raises her metabolic rate, and this increase is greatest for one macronutrient. She eats about 160 g of protein a day. Her kidney function is normal, and her BMI is 22. Which one?
A. All are equal
B. Lipid
C. Alcohol
D. Protein
E. Carbohydrate
Answer: D. Protein
Why this is correct: The thermic effect of food is the increase in metabolic rate after eating. It's greatest for protein and least for lipids, because protein takes more energy to break down.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. All are equal: The effect differs by macronutrient.
B. Lipid: Lipids have the smallest thermic effect.
C. Alcohol: Alcohol isn't discussed as having the largest effect.
E. Carbohydrate: Carbohydrate is intermediate.

Question 29
A 52-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine visit. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. He weighs 110 kg and is 2.0 m tall. His blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg, and his waist circumference is 106 cm. He walks his dog daily and eats out often. His fasting glucose is 138 mg/dL, and his LDL is 142 mg/dL. What is his BMI?
A. 55 kg/m²
B. 27.5 kg/m²
C. 22 kg/m²
D. 220 kg/m²
E. 36.7 kg/m²
Answer: B. 27.5 kg/m²
Why this is correct: BMI is weight in kg divided by height in meters squared: 110 / (2.0)² = 110 / 4 = 27.5.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 55 kg/m²: That divides by height without squaring it.
C. 22 kg/m²: That miscalculates the ratio.
D. 220 kg/m²: That multiplies by height.
E. 36.7 kg/m²: That divides by 3 instead of 4.

Question 31

Question 32
A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for severe obesity that started in infancy. She is always hungry and cries for food. Her parents are first cousins. Her weight is far above the 99th percentile. Her serum leptin is undetectable. Genetic testing confirms loss of the leptin gene. Her BMI is far above the 99th percentile. Her insulin is elevated, and her thyroid function is normal. C. No treatment is effective
D. Insulin
E. Statins

Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 33
A 38-year-old woman with obesity comes to the physician for weight management. She has tried many diets. She has hypertension and prediabetes. Her BMI is 41. Her serum leptin level is very high. She takes lisinopril and metformin. Her fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL, and her waist circumference is 112 cm. She eats large portions and says she never feels full. Why isn't her high leptin reducing her appetite?
A. Her fat cells don't make leptin
B. She has leptin resistance
C. Her insulin is too low to release leptin
D. Leptin increases appetite
E. She has a genetic loss of leptin
Answer: B. She has leptin resistance

Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Her fat cells don't make leptin: Her high levels show they do.
C. Her insulin is too low to release leptin: Her leptin is already high.
D. Leptin increases appetite: Leptin lowers the desire to eat.
E. She has a genetic loss of leptin: Her leptin is high, not absent.

Question 34
A 50-year-old man is brought to a clinic after months of severe famine in his region. He has lost over 30% of his body weight. His fat stores are gone, and he has muscle wasting. He has a cough and fever, and he isn't able to fight off infections. His albumin is very low. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and he has crackles at the right lung base. His glucose is 58 mg/dL, and his lymphocyte count is low. What is the most common cause of death at this stage?
A. Gallstones
B. Ketoacidosis from excess insulin
C. Infection from loss of immune function
D. Hyperglycemia
E. Obesity-related heart disease
Answer: C. Infection from loss of immune function
Why this is correct: In starvation, fat reserves are depleted and protein is the only source left. Proteins essential to cells are degraded, and loss of immune function leads to infection, the most common cause of death.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Gallstones: Gallstones aren't the leading cause of death here.
B. Ketoacidosis from excess insulin: Insulin is low in starvation.
D. Hyperglycemia: Glucose is low in starvation.
E. Obesity-related heart disease: He has lost most of his weight.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Week 3: Metabolism / Minor Pathways of Hexose Metabolism

Question 35
A 2-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting, poor feeding, and yellow skin for several days. She is breastfed. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). She is jaundiced with an enlarged liver, and both lenses are cloudy. Blood cultures grow E. coli. Urine is positive for reducing substances. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her weight has fallen below her birth weight, and her ALT and bilirubin are elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
A. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase
B. Fructokinase
C. Aldolase B
D. Glucose-6-phosphatase
E. Aldose reductase
Answer: A. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase
Why this is correct: Classic galactosemia is an autosomal recessive GALT deficiency. It presents in the first weeks of life because infants get galactose from milk, with vomiting, diarrhea, hepatomegaly, jaundice, and cataracts from the polyol pathway.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Fructokinase: Fructokinase deficiency isn't this presentation.
C. Aldolase B: That's hereditary fructose intolerance, which starts when fructose is introduced.
D. Glucose-6-phosphatase: That's von Gierke disease.
E. Aldose reductase: Aldose reductase makes sorbitol; it isn't deficient here.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 36
A 7-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of vomiting, sweating, and lethargy that began after his parents started him on pureed fruit. B. Hereditary fructose intolerance; fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol

E. Hereditary fructose intolerance; lactose only

Why this is correct: Hereditary fructose intolerance is an aldolase B defect that appears when fructose-containing foods are introduced. It resembles galactosemia, and timing of onset tells them apart. Patients must avoid fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol, since sorbitol can also be turned into fructose.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Von Gierke disease; long fasting: His symptoms started with fruit.
C. Classic galactosemia; lactose: Galactosemia starts in the first weeks with milk.
D. Glucose-galactose malabsorption; glucose: That causes diarrhea from the first feeds.
E. Hereditary fructose intolerance; lactose only: Fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol must be avoided.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 37
A 7-month-old boy with hereditary fructose intolerance comes to the emergency department after eating fruit at daycare. He is lethargic and vomiting. His glucose is 42 mg/dL, and his lactate is 6.2 mmol/L. His physician explains why lactate builds up in both HFI and galactosemia. Pulse is 168/min, and he is mildly dehydrated. His liver is enlarged, and his phosphate is low. His ALT is 180 U/L. What is the mechanism?
A. Fructose directly inhibits lactate dehydrogenase
B. Excess 2,3-BPG blocks oxygen delivery
C. Sorbitol builds up in the muscle
D. Phosphate is trapped in the sugar intermediate, shutting down the ETC and forcing pyruvate to lactate
E. The urea cycle backs up
Answer: D. Phosphate is trapped in the sugar intermediate, shutting down the ETC and forcing pyruvate to lactate
Why this is correct: In both diseases, phosphate is trapped in the accumulated intermediate. Without inorganic phosphate, ATP can't be made, the ETC and TCA cycle shut down, and fatty acids can't be used. Glycolysis becomes the only energy source, and pyruvate is converted to lactate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fructose directly inhibits lactate dehydrogenase: That would reduce lactate.
B. Excess 2,3-BPG blocks oxygen delivery: BPG isn't the cause.
C. Sorbitol builds up in the muscle: The mechanism is phosphate trapping.
E. The urea cycle backs up: That causes hyperammonemia.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 38
A 25-year-old man drinks large amounts of sweetened soda every day. He has a BMI of 32 and fatty liver on ultrasound. His triglycerides are 280 mg/dL. His physician explains that the first enzyme that processes fructose in the liver isn't regulated by hormones, so fructose floods into glycolysis. He doesn't drink alcohol and has no hepatitis. His ALT is mildly elevated. Which enzyme is this?
A. Phosphofructokinase
B. Fructokinase
C. Hexokinase
D. Aldolase B
E. GALT
Answer: B. Fructokinase
Why this is correct: Fructose metabolism happens in the liver. Fructokinase isn't a regulated enzyme, so it bypasses hormonal control and feeds metabolites into glycolysis unregulated (the 'fat gene'). It's also much faster than aldolase B, so fructose-1-phosphate can build up and lower free phosphate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Phosphofructokinase: PFK is highly regulated.
C. Hexokinase: Hexokinase isn't the fructose-specific enzyme.
D. Aldolase B: Aldolase B is slower than fructokinase.
E. GALT: GALT processes galactose.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 39
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years comes to the physician because of blurry vision and burning pain in her feet. Her HbA1c has been above 9% for years. She takes metformin and insulin. She has decreased sensation to vibration in both feet and early cataracts on eye exam. Her blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg, and she has microalbuminuria. Fundoscopy shows dot-blot hemorrhages. What mechanism contributes to her lens and nerve damage?
A. Fructokinase is deficient
B. Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which gets trapped in cells
C. Galactose builds up from GALT deficiency
D. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency traps glucose
E. Lipoprotein lipase is deficient
Answer: B. Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which gets trapped in cells
Why this is correct: In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts aldose sugars to sugar alcohols. Sorbitol is very hydrophilic and can't leave the cell, and it builds up in the lens and nerves because those tissues process it poorly. Chronic hyperglycemia drives this, causing cataracts, neuropathy, retinopathy, and nephropathy.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fructokinase is deficient: That isn't the cause of diabetic complications.
C. Galactose builds up from GALT deficiency: She has diabetes, not galactosemia.
D. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency traps glucose: That's von Gierke disease.
E. Lipoprotein lipase is deficient: That causes hypertriglyceridemia.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 40
A 16-year-old girl is being treated for leukemia, and her rapidly dividing cancer cells are using a glucose pathway heavily. She takes no other medications. Her physician explains that this pathway makes a reduced cofactor that keeps cells in a reducing environment and a sugar needed to build nucleotides. Her WBC is 48,000/mm³ with many blasts. She is receiving chemotherapy and is being monitored for tumor lysis. Which two products are these?
A. ATP and pyruvate
B. Lactate and alanine
C. NADH and acetyl-CoA
D. Sorbitol and fructose
E. NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate
Answer: E. NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate
Why this is correct: The pentose phosphate shunt is active in dividing tissues, tissues under oxidative stress like red cells, and tissues with high biosynthetic activity. NADPH maintains a reducing environment and helps eliminate oxidative radicals, and ribose-5-phosphate is used to make purines and pyrimidines.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ATP and pyruvate: Those come from glycolysis.
B. Lactate and alanine: Those are Cori cycle products.
C. NADH and acetyl-CoA: Those come from other pathways.
D. Sorbitol and fructose: Those come from the polyol pathway.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 41
A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with confusion and an unsteady gait. He drinks a fifth of vodka daily and eats poorly. His eye movements are abnormal. His physician wants to estimate his thiamine stores by measuring the activity of a cytosolic enzyme in his red cells that needs thiamine pyrophosphate. He has horizontal nystagmus and a wide-based gait. His glucose is 92 mg/dL. His hemoglobin is 11.6 g/dL with an MCV of 104. Which enzyme is measured?
A. Aldose reductase
B. Lactate dehydrogenase
C. Transketolase
D. Glutathione peroxidase
E. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Answer: C. Transketolase
Why this is correct: Transketolase is a cytosolic pentose phosphate pathway enzyme that requires thiamine pyrophosphate; most other thiamine-dependent enzymes are mitochondrial. Transketolase activity in red cells estimates the body's thiamine reserves.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Aldose reductase: That's part of the polyol pathway.
B. Lactate dehydrogenase: LDH doesn't require thiamine.
D. Glutathione peroxidase: That uses selenium.
E. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase: G6PD doesn't use thiamine.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 42
A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department with dark urine and back pain 2 days after starting a sulfa antibiotic for a urinary infection. He has no prior illness. He is pale and jaundiced. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, and a supravital stain shows clumps of denatured hemoglobin attached to the red cell membranes. His brother had a similar episode. His hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, reticulocytes are 9%, and LDH is high. His direct Coombs test is negative. Why are his red cells vulnerable?
A. ATP falls and Na+/K+ pumps fail
B. Without NADPH, glutathione can't be reduced to fight oxidative stress
C. Antibodies coat the red cells
D. Sorbitol builds up in red cells
E. Transketolase can't work without thiamine
Answer: B. Without NADPH, glutathione can't be reduced to fight oxidative stress
Why this is correct: In G6PD deficiency, NADPH can't be made, so glutathione can't be reduced back to its active form, and red cells are exposed to oxidative stress. This causes episodic hemolytic anemia during infections or with oxidant drugs, and Heinz bodies and bite cells appear. The gene is on the X chromosome.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ATP falls and Na+/K+ pumps fail: That's pyruvate kinase deficiency, which is chronic.
C. Antibodies coat the red cells: That's autoimmune hemolysis.
D. Sorbitol builds up in red cells: That's the polyol pathway.
E. Transketolase can't work without thiamine: That's thiamine deficiency.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 43
A 26-year-old woman is evaluated for a slow-growing thyroid nodule. She follows a diet very low in seafood and grains grown in selenium-poor soil. Her physician mentions that an enzyme containing four selenium atoms is needed to break down hydrogen peroxide as part of her cells' antioxidant defense. She has a goiter on exam, and her TSH is mildly elevated. Her diet is otherwise adequate in calories. Which enzyme is this?
A. Glutathione reductase
B. NADPH oxidase
C. Transketolase
D. Myeloperoxidase
E. Glutathione peroxidase
Answer: E. Glutathione peroxidase
Why this is correct: Glutathione peroxidase contains four selenium ions and catalyzes the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glutathione reductase: That uses NADPH to reduce glutathione, not selenium.
B. NADPH oxidase: That makes superoxide.
C. Transketolase: That needs thiamine.
D. Myeloperoxidase: That makes hypochlorous acid.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 44
A 30-year-old woman has a bacterial skin abscess drained. She takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). In her neutrophils, oxygen consumption rises sharply as a sequence of enzymes produces a potent bactericidal compound. The abscess is on her thigh and drained 8 mL of pus. Her WBC is 13,400/mm³ with neutrophilia. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which sequence produces hypochlorous acid?
A. Myeloperoxidase → catalase → NADPH oxidase
B. G6PD → transketolase → myeloperoxidase
C. Superoxide dismutase → NADPH oxidase → catalase
D. NADPH oxidase → superoxide dismutase → myeloperoxidase
E. Glutathione peroxidase → catalase → myeloperoxidase
Answer: D. NADPH oxidase → superoxide dismutase → myeloperoxidase
Why this is correct: In the respiratory burst, NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, superoxide dismutase converts it to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase makes hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Myeloperoxidase → catalase → NADPH oxidase: The order is wrong.
B. G6PD → transketolase → myeloperoxidase: Those are pentose phosphate enzymes.
C. Superoxide dismutase → NADPH oxidase → catalase: NADPH oxidase comes first.
E. Glutathione peroxidase → catalase → myeloperoxidase: Glutathione peroxidase breaks peroxide down.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 45
A 5-year-old boy is admitted with a liver abscess growing Staphylococcus aureus. He has had several skin abscesses and a Serratia pneumonia. His maternal uncle had similar infections. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). His neutrophil count is normal. He is at the 25th percentile for weight. His immunoglobulins are elevated, and a flow cytometry test of his neutrophils is abnormal. What defect explains why he gets infections with catalase-positive organisms?
A. Deficient glutathione peroxidase
B. Deficient NADPH oxidase, so his cells can't make superoxide, peroxide, or HOCl
C. Deficient myeloperoxidase
D. Deficient transketolase
E. Deficient G6PD in red cells
Answer: B. Deficient NADPH oxidase, so his cells can't make superoxide, peroxide, or HOCl
Why this is correct: Chronic granulomatous disease is an immunodeficiency from deficient NADPH oxidase; about 75% of cases are X-linked. Without superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and HOCl, catalase-expressing bacteria escape destruction.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Deficient glutathione peroxidase: That's an antioxidant enzyme.
C. Deficient myeloperoxidase: NADPH oxidase is the defect in CGD.
D. Deficient transketolase: That's a pentose phosphate enzyme.
E. Deficient G6PD in red cells: That causes hemolysis, not these infections.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 46
A 60-year-old man with diabetes is enrolled in a study of oxidative damage to cell membranes. He takes metformin and smokes. The investigators measure a three-carbon lipid breakdown product in his blood to estimate how much lipid peroxidation and membrane damage has occurred. His HbA1c is 8.6%, and he has a 30-pack-year smoking history. His blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Which molecule are they measuring?

B. Lactate
C. Sorbitol
D. Acetoacetate
E. Propionyl-CoA
Answer: A. Malondialdehyde
Why this is correct: Malondialdehyde is a three-carbon lipid breakdown product. Measuring it estimates the extent of lipid peroxidation and membrane damage.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Sorbitol: That's a polyol pathway product.
D. Acetoacetate: That's a ketone body.

Question 47
A 30-year-old woman skips breakfast and lunch on a busy day. She takes no medications. By afternoon her glucagon is high and insulin is low. In her adipose tissue, an enzyme begins breaking triglycerides down to diglycerides and monoglycerides. She drinks only coffee. Her glucose is 76 mg/dL. Her physician explains how fat is released from her adipose tissue when she hasn't eaten. How is this enzyme regulated?
A. Glucagon activates it by phosphorylation, and insulin turns it off
B. It's located on endothelial cells
C. Insulin activates it
D. It's activated by ApoCII
E. It's active when dephosphorylated
Answer: A. Glucagon activates it by phosphorylation, and insulin turns it off
Why this is correct: Adipose triglyceride lipase is turned on by glucagon and off by insulin, and it's active when phosphorylated. It converts triglyceride to diglyceride and monoglyceride.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It's located on endothelial cells: That's lipoprotein lipase.
C. Insulin activates it: Insulin turns ATGL off.
D. It's activated by ApoCII: That's lipoprotein lipase.
E. It's active when dephosphorylated: ATGL is active when phosphorylated.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 48
A 22-year-old man is evaluated for muscle cramps and weakness during long bike rides, especially when he skips meals. He takes no medications. After a long ride, his CK is 9,000 U/L and his urine is dark. His glucose is normal. Studies show that long-chain fatty acids can't enter his muscle mitochondria. His glucose and ketones are normal after exercise. His CK is normal at rest, and he has no family history of muscle disease. Which system is defective?
A. The peroxisome
B. The carnitine shuttle
C. Lipoprotein lipase
D. MCAD
E. The tricarboxylate transporter
Answer: B. The carnitine shuttle
Why this is correct: Short and medium fatty acids enter mitochondria directly, while long-chain fatty acids need the carnitine shuttle (CAT-I and CAT-II). Deficiency of carnitine or these enzymes causes muscle weakness and cramps with exercise.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The peroxisome: Peroxisomes shorten very long-chain fatty acids.
C. Lipoprotein lipase: LPL acts on lipoproteins in the blood.
D. MCAD: MCAD is inside the mitochondria and causes fasting hypoglycemia.
E. The tricarboxylate transporter: That moves citrate out of mitochondria.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 49
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of new behavior problems, declining school performance, and trouble with coordination. His skin has become darker, and his blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. MRI shows white matter damage. His maternal uncle died of a similar illness. Studies show a deficiency in peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase, and very long-chain fatty acids are elevated. His ACTH is elevated, and his cortisol is low. His vision is starting to fail. What is the diagnosis?
A. MCAD deficiency
B. Carnitine deficiency
C. Refsum disease
D. Adrenoleukodystrophy
E. Zellweger syndrome
Answer: D. Adrenoleukodystrophy
Why this is correct: Very long-chain fatty acids must be shortened in peroxisomes before entering mitochondria. Adrenoleukodystrophy is a deficiency of peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. MCAD deficiency: MCAD causes fasting hypoglycemia.
B. Carnitine deficiency: That affects long-chain fatty acid entry into mitochondria.
C. Refsum disease: Refsum is a defect in alpha oxidation.
E. Zellweger syndrome: Zellweger is the absence of functional peroxisomes, usually in infants.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 50
A 2-month-old girl is evaluated for severe floppiness, seizures, and poor feeding since birth. She has a high forehead, flat face, and enlarged liver. Her parents are healthy. Her very long-chain fatty acids are elevated, and studies show her cells lack functional peroxisomes. She has hepatomegaly and poor muscle tone. Her liver enzymes are elevated, and MRI shows abnormal brain development. What is the diagnosis?
A. MCAD deficiency
B. Pompe disease
C. Zellweger syndrome
D. Adrenoleukodystrophy
E. Refsum disease
Answer: C. Zellweger syndrome
Why this is correct: Zellweger syndrome is the absence of functional peroxisomes, so very long-chain fatty acids can't be processed, and diet must be altered.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. MCAD deficiency: MCAD is a mitochondrial beta-oxidation defect.
B. Pompe disease: Pompe is a lysosomal glycogen storage disease.
D. Adrenoleukodystrophy: ALD is a deficiency of one peroxisomal enzyme, not absent peroxisomes.
E. Refsum disease: Refsum is an alpha-oxidation defect.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 51
A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening night vision and unsteady walking. He has dry, scaly skin and a shortened fourth toe. His parents are first cousins. His serum phytanic acid is elevated. He is told to avoid foods with branched-chain fatty acids. He had several fractures of his feet as a teenager. His ECG shows a mild conduction delay. Which process is defective?
A. Ketone breakdown by thiophorase
B. Beta oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids
C. Omega oxidation in the ER
D. Alpha oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids in the peroxisome
E. Carnitine transport of long-chain fatty acids
Answer: D. Alpha oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids in the peroxisome
Why this is correct: Alpha oxidation handles long, branched-chain fatty acids in peroxisomes, starting at the alpha carbon with alpha-hydroxylase. Refsum disease is a mutated alpha-hydroxylase, and diets avoid branched fatty acids like phytanic acid.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ketone breakdown by thiophorase: That's how tissues use ketones.
B. Beta oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids: That's MCAD deficiency.
C. Omega oxidation in the ER: Omega oxidation is a backup pathway.
E. Carnitine transport of long-chain fatty acids: That's the carnitine shuttle.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 52
A 14-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because he couldn't be woken this morning after a day of vomiting from a stomach virus. He didn't eat dinner. He was previously healthy. His glucose is 30 mg/dL, and urine ketones are low. His liver is mildly enlarged. Urine shows dicarboxylic acids. He is lethargic but responds to pain. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), and pulse is 150/min. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
A. HMG-CoA reductase
B. Glucose-6-phosphatase
C. Alpha-hydroxylase
D. Peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase
E. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Answer: E. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Why this is correct: MCAD deficiency causes fasting intolerance, impaired ketogenesis, hypoglycemia, vomiting, coma, and death. When beta oxidation is blocked, omega oxidation in the ER increases, and its products are a marker of MCAD deficiency. MCAD deficiency is also thought to contribute to SIDS.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. HMG-CoA reductase: That's the cholesterol synthesis enzyme.
B. Glucose-6-phosphatase: That causes hypoglycemia with high lactate and a large liver from early infancy.
C. Alpha-hydroxylase: That's Refsum disease.
D. Peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase: That's ALD.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 53
A 5-year-old boy in Jamaica develops vomiting, lethargy, and hypoglycemia several hours after eating unripe fruit from a tree near his home. He was previously healthy. His glucose is 32 mg/dL, and his urine ketones are low. He was previously healthy and eats a normal diet. He is lethargic, and his liver is mildly enlarged. His ammonia is mildly elevated. What mechanism explains his illness?
A. A toxin in the fruit inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, mimicking MCAD deficiency
B. The fruit contains fructose that he can't process
C. The toxin blocks HMG-CoA reductase
D. The toxin blocks the urea cycle
E. The toxin blocks glucose-6-phosphatase
Answer: A. A toxin in the fruit inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, mimicking MCAD deficiency
Why this is correct: Ackee fruit contains a substance that inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, causing an acute MCAD-like picture with hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The fruit contains fructose that he can't process: That's hereditary fructose intolerance.
C. The toxin blocks HMG-CoA reductase: That's the statin target.
D. The toxin blocks the urea cycle: That would cause hyperammonemia.
E. The toxin blocks glucose-6-phosphatase: That's von Gierke disease.

Question 54
A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has an enlarged liver on exam. He drinks a pint of whiskey daily. His AST is higher than his ALT, and ultrasound shows a fatty liver. His physician explains that metabolizing alcohol uses up a cofactor that the third step of beta oxidation needs. He has no history of hepatitis, and his albumin is 3.5 g/dL. His triglycerides are 260 mg/dL. Which cofactor is depleted?
A. NADPH
B. NAD+
C. Thiamine
D. FAD alone
E. Biotin
Answer: B. NAD+
Why this is correct: Ethanol metabolism uses up NAD+. The third step of beta oxidation needs NAD+, so beta oxidation can't proceed and fat builds up in the liver.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. NADPH: NADPH is made by the pentose phosphate pathway.
C. Thiamine: Thiamine is a cofactor for other enzymes.
D. FAD alone: The step described needs NAD+.
E. Biotin: Biotin is a carboxylase cofactor.

Question 55
A 4-month-old girl is evaluated for poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. She was born at term. Her parents are first cousins. Her blood gas shows metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap. Her physician explains that odd-chain fatty acids and some amino acids produce a three-carbon product that must be converted by a biotin-dependent carboxylase and a B12-dependent mutase. Her ammonia is mildly elevated, and her glucose is 64 mg/dL. Her physician suspects an organic acidemia. What is this three-carbon product?
A. Acetoacetate
B. Malonyl-CoA
C. Propionyl-CoA
D. Acetyl-CoA
E. Malondialdehyde
Answer: C. Propionyl-CoA
Why this is correct: Oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids ends with a three-carbon product, propionyl-CoA, which can be converted to glucose. Dysfunction of the carboxylase or mutase causes propionic or methylmalonic aciduria.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Acetoacetate: That's a ketone body.
B. Malonyl-CoA: Malonyl-CoA is used in fatty acid synthesis.
D. Acetyl-CoA: Acetyl-CoA is a two-carbon product.
E. Malondialdehyde: That marks lipid peroxidation.

Question 56
A 30-year-old woman has fasted for 3 days. She is healthy and takes no medications. Her urine ketones are strongly positive, and her beta-hydroxybutyrate is elevated. Her liver is making ketones for the rest of her body. She drinks water and black coffee only. Her glucose is 66 mg/dL, and her insulin is low. Her muscles and heart are using the ketones her liver releases. Why can't her liver use the ketones it makes?
A. Ketones can't enter liver cells
B. The liver has no mitochondria
C. The liver lacks carnitine
D. The liver lacks thiophorase, which peripheral tissues need to use ketones
E. The liver lacks HMG-CoA reductase
Answer: D. The liver lacks thiophorase, which peripheral tissues need to use ketones
Why this is correct: Ketones are made in liver mitochondria during prolonged fasting. Thiophorase breaks acetoacetate down to acetyl-CoA for use in the TCA cycle of peripheral tissues. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it makes ketones but can't use them.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ketones can't enter liver cells: The problem is the missing enzyme.
B. The liver has no mitochondria: Ketones are made in liver mitochondria.
C. The liver lacks carnitine: Carnitine moves fatty acids into mitochondria.
E. The liver lacks HMG-CoA reductase: That's the cholesterol enzyme.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 57
A 35-year-old man eats a large, carbohydrate-rich meal. He is healthy and takes no medications. His insulin is high, and his liver is making fatty acids. Acetyl-CoA leaves the mitochondria as citrate. His meal included rice, bread, and dessert. His glucose rises to 162 mg/dL. His physician explains that excess carbohydrate can be converted to fat for storage. Which enzyme then makes malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA?
A. HMG-CoA reductase
B. Thiophorase
C. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
D. Acyl-CoA synthetase
E. Fatty acid synthase
Answer: C. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Why this is correct: In fatty acid synthesis, acetyl-CoA leaves the mitochondria as citrate, acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA, and fatty acid synthase extends the chain by adding malonyl-CoA.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. HMG-CoA reductase: That's cholesterol synthesis.
B. Thiophorase: That breaks down ketones.
D. Acyl-CoA synthetase: That activates fatty acids for oxidation.
E. Fatty acid synthase: That extends the chain using malonyl-CoA.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 58

Question 59
A 55-year-old man has an LDL of 190 mg/dL at a routine visit. He smokes and has hypertension. His father had a heart attack at 52. He is started on atorvastatin. He is overweight and walks twice a week. His HDL is 38 mg/dL, and his triglycerides are 180 mg/dL. His blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. How does this drug lower cholesterol?
A. It blocks MTP
B. It inhibits 7-alpha-hydroxylase
C. It inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase
D. It activates lipoprotein lipase
E. It inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis
Answer: E. It inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis
Why this is correct: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis and is active when not phosphorylated. Statins inhibit it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It blocks MTP: That would block chylomicron and VLDL assembly.
B. It inhibits 7-alpha-hydroxylase: That enzyme breaks cholesterol down to bile acids.
C. It inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase: That's the fatty acid synthesis enzyme.
D. It activates lipoprotein lipase: LPL breaks down triglycerides.

Question 60
A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is enrolled in a study of cholesterol synthesis. He takes insulin and has an LDL of 160 mg/dL. After meals his insulin is high, and his hepatic cholesterol synthesis rises. His BMI is 32. His HbA1c is 8.9%, and his triglycerides are 210 mg/dL. How does high insulin affect HMG-CoA reductase?
A. It degrades the reductase
B. It has no effect on the reductase
C. It promotes phosphorylation, which activates the reductase
D. It promotes kinase activity, inactivating the reductase
E. It promotes phosphatase activity, dephosphorylating and activating the reductase
Answer: E. It promotes phosphatase activity, dephosphorylating and activating the reductase
Why this is correct: HMG-CoA reductase is active when not phosphorylated. High insulin promotes phosphatase activity, activating the reductase, while high glucagon promotes kinase activity, inactivating it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It degrades the reductase: The effect is through phosphorylation state.
B. It has no effect on the reductase: Insulin activates it.
C. It promotes phosphorylation, which activates the reductase: Phosphorylation inactivates it.
D. It promotes kinase activity, inactivating the reductase: That's the effect of glucagon.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 61
A 50-year-old woman starts a statin, and her cells' cholesterol content falls. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Her physician explains that when cellular cholesterol is low, a regulatory complex that normally stays in the ER moves to the Golgi, and a signal reaches the nucleus. She takes atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Her LDL has fallen from 170 to 90 mg/dL, and her liver enzymes are normal. What is the effect of this signal?
A. It degrades LDL receptors
B. It blocks ApoB100 synthesis
C. It activates transcription of the HMG-CoA reductase gene
D. It activates 7-alpha-hydroxylase
E. It shuts off HMG-CoA reductase transcription
Answer: C. It activates transcription of the HMG-CoA reductase gene
Why this is correct: The HMG-CoA reductase gene is regulated by cellular cholesterol. High cholesterol keeps the regulatory complex in the ER. Low cholesterol moves it to the Golgi, and a signal goes to the nucleus to activate the gene.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It degrades LDL receptors: That isn't the effect described.
B. It blocks ApoB100 synthesis: That isn't the effect described.
D. It activates 7-alpha-hydroxylase: That's bile acid synthesis.
E. It shuts off HMG-CoA reductase transcription: Low cholesterol turns the gene on.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 62
A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. She has had four children and is overweight. Her BMI is 32, and Murphy sign is positive. Ultrasound shows gallstones, which are made of cholesterol. Studies show reduced conversion of cholesterol to bile acids. Her ALT and bilirubin are normal. She has no fever, and she recently lost weight on a strict diet. Which enzyme is deficient?
A. LCAT
B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
C. HMG-CoA reductase
D. Lipoprotein lipase
E. 7-alpha-hydroxylase
Answer: E. 7-alpha-hydroxylase
Why this is correct: Cholesterol is eliminated by conversion to bile acids. 7-alpha-hydroxylase converts cholesterol to primary bile acids, and its deficiency prevents cholesterol breakdown. When bile cholesterol is above 15%, it can aggregate into gallstones.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. LCAT: LCAT forms cholesterol esters in HDL.
B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: That's fatty acid synthesis.
C. HMG-CoA reductase: That's the synthesis enzyme.
D. Lipoprotein lipase: LPL breaks down triglycerides.

Question 63
A 30-year-old man fasts overnight before a lipid panel. He is healthy and takes no medications. His glucagon is high, and his fat cells are releasing free fatty acids into his blood. His triglycerides and cholesterol are carried in lipoproteins. His glucose is 88 mg/dL, and his triglycerides are 110 mg/dL. His albumin is normal. How are the free fatty acids transported in his blood?
A. Bound to ApoB100
B. Bound to albumin
C. In chylomicrons
D. In HDL
E. Free in plasma with no carrier
Answer: B. Bound to albumin
Why this is correct: Free fatty acids are transported with albumin, while triglycerides, cholesterol, and cholesterol esters must travel in lipoproteins.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bound to ApoB100: ApoB100 is a lipoprotein apoprotein.
C. In chylomicrons: Chylomicrons carry dietary lipids.
D. In HDL: HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver.
E. Free in plasma with no carrier: Fatty acids need albumin to travel.

Question 64
A 34-year-old woman eats a fatty meal. She is healthy and takes no medications. In her intestinal cells, dietary lipids are assembled in the smooth ER into large particles and secreted into the lymph. These particles carry an apoprotein made in the rough ER that can't bind the LDL receptor. Her glucose rises modestly after the meal. Her physician uses the meal to explain how dietary fat is absorbed. Which particle and apoprotein are these?
A. LDL with ApoB100
B. HDL with ApoA1
C. Chylomicrons with ApoB100
D. VLDL with ApoB100
E. Chylomicrons with ApoB48
Answer: E. Chylomicrons with ApoB48
Why this is correct: Chylomicrons are assembled in intestinal mucosal cells, are mostly triglyceride, and are secreted into the lymph. The rough ER makes ApoB48 in the intestine and ApoB100 in the liver, from the same gene. ApoB48 lacks the LDL receptor-binding region.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. LDL with ApoB100: LDL comes from IDL, not the intestine.
B. HDL with ApoA1: HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver.
C. Chylomicrons with ApoB100: Intestinal chylomicrons carry ApoB48.
D. VLDL with ApoB100: VLDL is made in the liver with ApoB100.

Question 65
A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for chronic greasy, foul-smelling stools, poor weight gain, and an unsteady gait. His parents are first cousins. He is below the 3rd percentile for weight and has decreased reflexes. His smear shows red cells with spiky projections, and his cholesterol and triglycerides are very low. Answer: C. Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein
Why this is correct: Abetalipoproteinemia is an MTP defect, so chylomicrons and VLDL can't be assembled. It causes retinal degeneration, ataxic neuropathy, acanthocytes, and fat malabsorption with steatorrhea, largely from fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Diet is shifted to shorter fatty acids.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 66
A 9-year-old boy is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. It's his third episode of pancreatitis. He doesn't drink alcohol and has no gallstones. Question 67
A 50-year-old man comes to the physician for chest pain on exertion. He has diabetes and takes metformin. He has yellow deposits in his palm creases. Question 68
A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with chest pain and is diagnosed with a heart attack. He doesn't smoke or have diabetes. His father died of a heart attack at 38. He has yellow nodules on his Achilles tendons. His LDL is 320 mg/dL with normal triglycerides. His blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. His troponin is elevated, and his HDL is 44 mg/dL. Why do macrophages in his arteries fill with cholesterol?
A. LPL deposits triglycerides in macrophages
B. HDL is oxidized
C. Macrophage LDL receptors are overexpressed
D. Chylomicrons are deposited in the arteries
E. Oxidized LDL is taken up by scavenger receptors that aren't down-regulated by cellular cholesterol
Answer: E. Oxidized LDL is taken up by scavenger receptors that aren't down-regulated by cellular cholesterol
Why this is correct: LDL receptor deficiency (type II) raises plasma LDL and cholesterol. The longer LDL stays in plasma, the more it's oxidized. Macrophages take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors that aren't down-regulated by cholesterol status, forming foam cells in plaques.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. LPL deposits triglycerides in macrophages: That's not the mechanism.
B. HDL is oxidized: The oxidized particle is LDL.
C. Macrophage LDL receptors are overexpressed: Uptake is through scavenger receptors.
D. Chylomicrons are deposited in the arteries: The problem is LDL.

Question 69
A 14-year-old boy is evaluated for enlarged, orange-yellow tonsils. He also has numbness in his hands and an enlarged spleen. His HDL is nearly undetectable. His physician explains that cholesterol and phospholipids from his peripheral cells can't be loaded onto new HDL particles, and he has a higher risk of heart disease. His parents are healthy cousins. C. ABCA1

Answer: C. ABCA1

Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 70
A 40-year-old woman is evaluated for cloudy corneas and protein in her urine. Her HDL is low, and her HDL particles are small and disc-shaped rather than spherical. Studies show her plasma can't convert free cholesterol to cholesterol ester on HDL. Her blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. Her parents are first cousins, and her hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. D. Lipoprotein lipase

A. CETP: CETP exchanges triglyceride for cholesterol ester.
B. Hepatic lipase: Hepatic lipase hydrolyzes lipids in HDL and IDL.

Question 71
A 55-year-old man is enrolled in a trial of a drug that raises HDL by blocking a plasma protein. He has hyperlipidemia and takes a statin. Question 72
A 46-year-old man has a lipid panel showing an LDL of 178 mg/dL at a workplace screening. He hadn't fasted and had eaten breakfast. He has no symptoms and takes no medications. His physician wants to confirm whether he has a dyslipidemia. His HDL is 46 mg/dL, and his triglycerides are 170 mg/dL. His blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. His father had a heart attack at 60. What is required to confirm the diagnosis?

B. A fasting lipid profile showing abnormal values on two separate occasions
C. A random glucose
D. A liver biopsy
E. Genetic testing in every case
Answer: B. A fasting lipid profile showing abnormal values on two separate occasions
Why this is correct: There's no natural cutoff between normal and abnormal lipid levels. To confirm a dyslipidemia, a fasting lipid profile must show pathologic values on two different occasions.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. A random glucose: That tests for diabetes.

Question 73
A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. She drinks two glasses of wine a night and takes acetaminophen often for headaches. Her liver is mildly tender. Her ALT is 240 U/L and AST is 190 U/L. Her bilirubin and albumin are normal. Her hepatitis serologies are negative. What do elevated ALT and AST indicate?
A. Muscle breakdown only
B. A urea cycle defect
C. Kidney failure
D. Liver damage releasing these enzymes into the blood
E. Hemolysis
Answer: D. Liver damage releasing these enzymes into the blood
Why this is correct: ALT and AST are found in the liver, and damage releases them into the blood, so elevated levels signal liver injury. ALT converts alanine to pyruvate, and AST converts aspartate to oxaloacetate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Muscle breakdown only: The pattern here points to the liver.
B. A urea cycle defect: That causes hyperammonemia.
C. Kidney failure: Kidney failure raises BUN.
E. Hemolysis: Hemolysis raises LDH and bilirubin.

Question 74
A 45-year-old man on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis develops numbness in his feet. He drinks daily and eats poorly. His physician explains that isoniazid depletes a vitamin whose active form is the cofactor for transaminases that move amino groups between amino acids. He has decreased sensation in both feet. His B12 and folate are normal. Which cofactor is this?
A. Vitamin B12
B. Thiamine pyrophosphate
C. Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)
D. Tetrahydrobiopterin
E. Biotin
Answer: C. Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)
Why this is correct: Transaminases (aminotransferases) move an amino acid's amine group onto alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate. PLP, the active form of vitamin B6, is their cofactor.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Vitamin B12: B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
B. Thiamine pyrophosphate: That's the cofactor for transketolase.
D. Tetrahydrobiopterin: That's the cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase.
E. Biotin: Biotin is the cofactor for propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

Question 75
A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis from hepatitis C is admitted with confusion. He takes spironolactone and furosemide. He has asterixis and ascites. Ammonia is 142 μmol/L, BUN is low at 5 mg/dL, and AST and ALT are elevated. He is started on a treatment that binds ammonia in the gut to keep it from entering the circulation. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and he is disoriented to date and place. Which treatment is this?

E. Allopurinol
Answer: B. Lactulose
Why this is correct: Hepatic encephalopathy results from reduced liver function and ammonia buildup in the brain, with low BUN, high ammonia, and high AST/ALT. Lactulose binds ammonia and prevents continued diffusion into circulation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Statins: Statins lower cholesterol.
C. Sodium benzoate alone: Benzoate is used in urea cycle disorders.

Question 76
A 60-year-old woman with liver disease is evaluated for why ammonia is so toxic to her brain. She has cirrhosis from fatty liver disease and takes lactulose. Her ammonia is 110 μmol/L. Her physician explains that at high ammonia, glutamate dehydrogenase runs in reverse in her brain to trap ammonia as glutamate. She is drowsy but arousable. Her BUN is low, and her albumin is 2.9 g/dL. Why does this harm her neurons?

C. It raises BUN
D. It increases NADPH production
E. It produces excess urea in the brain
Answer: A. It depletes alpha-ketoglutarate, which can shut down the TCA cycle
Why this is correct: When ammonia is high, glutamate dehydrogenase works in reverse to make glutamate from ammonia. This uses up alpha-ketoglutarate, which can shut down the Krebs cycle.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It blocks glycogen phosphorylase: That isn't the mechanism.
C. It raises BUN: Liver disease lowers BUN.
D. It increases NADPH production: That isn't the mechanism described.
E. It produces excess urea in the brain: The urea cycle is in the liver.

Question 77
A 7-year-old boy is recovering from a head injury, and his physician reviews how the brain disposes of ammonia. He has no liver disease. His ammonia is normal. In the brain, ammonia is combined with glutamate before it travels to the liver to reduce damage along the way. His CT shows a small contusion. He is recovering well and has no confusion. Which enzyme does this?
A. ALT
B. Glutamate dehydrogenase
C. Glutaminase
D. Glutamine synthetase
E. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Answer: D. Glutamine synthetase
Why this is correct: In the brain, ammonia is captured by glutamine synthetase, making glutamine. In the liver, glutaminase turns glutamine back into glutamate, and glutamate dehydrogenase releases free ammonia for the urea cycle.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 78
A 30-year-old woman with diabetic ketoacidosis is admitted to the ICU. Her pH is 7.12, bicarbonate is 8 mEq/L, and glucose is 480 mg/dL. Her kidneys increase ammonia production to buffer the extra acid in the tubules. Her urine ketones are large, and she is breathing deeply and rapidly. D. Glutamine synthetase

Answer: B. Glutaminase
Why this is correct: The kidneys take up glutamine and deaminate it with glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase. The ammonia produced neutralizes protons in the tubule, and metabolic acidosis increases glutaminase levels.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Lactate dehydrogenase: That makes lactate.
D. Glutamine synthetase: That makes glutamine, trapping ammonia in the brain.

Question 79
A 2-year-old girl in a refugee camp has been fed mainly starchy gruel since weaning. She has swollen legs, a large belly, peeling skin, and thin reddish hair. Her liver is enlarged. Albumin is 1.8 g/dL, AST and ALT are elevated, and BUN is low. She is lethargic and irritable. Her weight is below the 3rd percentile for her age. What is the diagnosis?
A. Hepatic encephalopathy
B. Chronic kidney disease
C. Kwashiorkor
D. Maple syrup urine disease

Answer: C. Kwashiorkor
Why this is correct: Kwashiorkor is a diet deficient in protein only. It causes low albumin, edema, fatty liver, raised ALT and AST, and low BUN. Marasmus is a deficiency of protein, carbohydrate, and fat, causing muscle wasting and gluconeogenesis without the edema.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hepatic encephalopathy: She has no confusion from liver failure.
B. Chronic kidney disease: CKD raises BUN.
D. Maple syrup urine disease: MSUD is an inborn error.
E. Marasmus: Marasmus causes wasting without edema.

Question 80

Question 81
A 68-year-old woman with long-standing chronic kidney disease is evaluated for confusion. She has diabetes and hypertension and isn't yet on dialysis. Her creatinine is 5.8 mg/dL, BUN is 98 mg/dL, and ammonia is elevated. Her blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg, and she has swelling in her legs. Her liver enzymes are normal. How does her kidney disease lead to both findings?

B. Ammonia is converted to lactate

Answer: D. Urea can't be excreted, so BUN rises and the whole ammonia disposal process backs up
Why this is correct: Chronic kidney disease causes high BUN because urea can't be excreted, which backs up the process and causes hyperammonemia. Both kidney and liver disease can cause hyperammonemia, but BUN is low in liver disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The liver stops making urea, so BUN falls: That's liver disease, with low BUN.

Question 82

Question 83
A 2-day-old boy becomes lethargic and stops feeding. He was born at term, and his mother's brother died in infancy of an unknown illness. Question 84

Besides stopping protein intake, which treatment captures excess nitrogen so it can be excreted?

C. Statins
D. Sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate, or phenylbutyrate
E. A high-protein diet
Answer: D. Sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate, or phenylbutyrate
Why this is correct: Urea cycle disorders are treated with a low-protein diet to make less ammonia. Excess nitrogen can be captured with sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate, or phenylbutyrate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Allopurinol: Allopurinol is used in the carrier challenge test.
B. Nitisinone: Nitisinone treats tyrosinemia type I.
C. Statins: Statins lower cholesterol.
E. A high-protein diet: More protein makes more ammonia.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 85
A 19-year-old man has followed a strict plant-based diet for 2 years. He runs cross-country and takes no supplements. His BMI is 19.5, and his albumin is 3.6 g/dL. His dietitian warns him that some plant diets are low in certain essential amino acids. He eats beans, rice, and vegetables but avoids soy. His hemoglobin is 13.0 g/dL. Which amino acids are plant diets typically insufficient in?
A. Alanine, glycine, and serine
B. Leucine, isoleucine, and valine only
C. Glutamine and aspartate
D. Tyrosine and cysteine only
E. Lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan
Answer: E. Lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan
Why this is correct: Plant diets are insufficient in lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Alanine, glycine, and serine: These aren't essential.
B. Leucine, isoleucine, and valine only: These are the branched-chain amino acids.
C. Glutamine and aspartate: These aren't essential.
D. Tyrosine and cysteine only: Tyrosine is conditional and depends on phenylalanine.

Question 86
A 25-year-old woman lifts weights and takes a branched-chain amino acid supplement. She has no medical problems. She eats a high-protein diet and wants to understand how her supplement is used. Which vitamin is required?

B. Vitamin B6
C. Tetrahydrobiopterin
D. Selenium
E. Biotin
Answer: B. Vitamin B6
Why this is correct: Branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) are all essential. BCAA aminotransferase removes the amino group and needs vitamin B6, producing alpha-keto acids that BCKD breaks down further.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Vitamin B12: B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

Question 87
A 5-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she has stopped feeding and alternates between being stiff and floppy. She was born at term to parents from a closed Mennonite community. Her urine and earwax smell like burnt sugar. Her feet look bluish. Plasma leucine is markedly elevated. She is lethargic and has a high-pitched cry. Her glucose is 60 mg/dL, and blood gas shows metabolic acidosis. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
A. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase
B. Ornithine transcarbamylase
C. Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
D. Phenylalanine hydroxylase
E. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase
Answer: C. Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
Why this is correct: Maple syrup urine disease is a deficiency of BCKD, so alpha-keto acids of the branched-chain amino acids build up, with very high leucine. It causes a sweet, burnt-sugar odor in urine, sweat, and earwax, cyanotic episodes, and a metabolic crisis with seizures, coma, and death if BCAAs aren't restricted.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase: That causes a cabbage odor.
B. Ornithine transcarbamylase: That causes hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria.
D. Phenylalanine hydroxylase: That causes PKU with a mousy odor.
E. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase: That causes a sweaty feet odor.

Question 88
A 7-day-old boy is admitted with vomiting, lethargy, and poor feeding. He was born at term. His parents are healthy. The nurses notice a smell like sweaty feet in his urine and on his skin. His blood gas shows metabolic acidosis. A defect after BCKD in the breakdown of one branched-chain amino acid is suspected. His ammonia is mildly elevated. His glucose is normal. Which enzyme is deficient, and what diet is needed?
A. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase; restrict leucine
B. BCKD; restrict all BCAAs
C. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase; restrict valine and isoleucine
D. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; restrict valine and isoleucine
E. Phenylalanine hydroxylase; restrict phenylalanine
Answer: A. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase; restrict leucine
Why this is correct: Isovaleric acidemia occurs after BCKD. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase is defective, so isovaleryl-CoA builds up, causing symptoms like MSUD with a sweaty feet odor. Treatment is a leucine-free diet.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. BCKD; restrict all BCAAs: That's MSUD with a burnt-sugar odor.
C. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase; restrict valine and isoleucine: That's propionic acidemia.
D. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; restrict valine and isoleucine: That's methylmalonic acidemia.
E. Phenylalanine hydroxylase; restrict phenylalanine: That's PKU.

Question 89
A 1-week-old girl is admitted with vomiting, lethargy, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Her parents are first cousins. Her ammonia is mildly elevated. Plasma propionic acid is high, and methylmalonic acid is normal. She is lethargic, and her glucose is 58 mg/dL. Her urine ketones are positive. Which enzyme is defective, and which cofactor does it use?
A. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which uses B12
B. BCKD, which uses thiamine
C. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase, which uses biotin
D. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase

Answer: C. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase, which uses biotin
Why this is correct: Propionic acidemia comes from defective propionyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent enzyme, raising propionic acid. Methylmalonic acidemia is a defect in B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Both need restriction of isoleucine and valine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which uses B12: That raises methylmalonic acid.
B. BCKD, which uses thiamine: That's MSUD.
D. Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase: That's isovaleric acidemia.
E. Phenylalanine hydroxylase, which uses BH4: That's PKU.

Question 90
A 3-month-old boy is evaluated for vomiting, poor weight gain, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. He was born at term. His parents are healthy. Question 91
A 1-year-old boy is evaluated for poor muscle tone, developmental delay, and episodes of rapid breathing. He was born at term. His lactate is 7.2 mmol/L, and his pyruvate is high, with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. Studies show pyruvate can't be converted to acetyl-CoA. His parents are healthy. His glucose is normal, and his ammonia is normal. Which diet is used to treat him?
A. A ketogenic diet
B. A fructose-free diet
C. A phenylalanine-restricted diet
D. A low-protein diet
E. A high-carbohydrate diet
Answer: A. A ketogenic diet
Why this is correct: In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, pyruvate can't become acetyl-CoA, so it's forced into lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. Treatment is a ketogenic diet, which doesn't feed into that pathway.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A fructose-free diet: That's hereditary fructose intolerance.
C. A phenylalanine-restricted diet: That's PKU.
D. A low-protein diet: That's for urea cycle disorders.
E. A high-carbohydrate diet: Carbohydrates would make more pyruvate and lactate.

Question 92
A 9-month-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay and eczema. He was born in a country without newborn screening. He has fair skin, blond hair, and blue eyes, unlike his parents, and a musty odor. His plasma phenylalanine is markedly elevated. His tetrahydrobiopterin levels are normal. His head circumference is at the 5th percentile. What is the treatment?
A. Give a ketogenic diet
B. Restrict branched-chain amino acids
C. Restrict phenylalanine and supplement tyrosine
D. Restrict tyrosine and supplement phenylalanine
E. Give nitisinone
Answer: C. Restrict phenylalanine and supplement tyrosine
Why this is correct: Typical PKU is a phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Excess phenylalanine becomes phenylpyruvate, a phenyl ketone, causing a mousy or musty odor. Treatment is restricting phenylalanine and supplementing tyrosine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Give a ketogenic diet: That's for PDH deficiency.
B. Restrict branched-chain amino acids: That's MSUD.
D. Restrict tyrosine and supplement phenylalanine: This is reversed.
E. Give nitisinone: That's for tyrosinemia type I.

Question 93

Question 94
A 26-year-old woman with PKU comes for preconception counseling. She stopped her special diet as a teenager and feels well. Her phenylalanine level is 1,100 μmol/L. She has no other medical problems. Question 95
A 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of back and knee pain that has worsened over 10 years. He works as a mechanic and takes ibuprofen. Answer: C. Homogentisic acid oxidase

Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 96
