Question 91
A 64-year-old man with metastatic kidney cancer comes to the physician for follow-up. He responded to an anti-angiogenic drug for a year, but his latest CT shows his lung metastases are growing again. He has hypertension, which worsened on the drug, and takes amlodipine. His vital signs are otherwise normal, and his creatinine is stable. His oncologist plans to switch to another anti-angiogenic drug. What must be true of the new drug for it to have a chance of working?
A. It must be cytotoxic rather than cytostatic
B. It must block telomerase
C. It must target VEGF again at a higher dose
D. It must act on a different target
E. It must be given with trastuzumab
Answer: D. It must act on a different target
Why this is correct: Tumors often get around anti-angiogenic drugs because many pathways can compensate for vessel formation. If one drug fails, it can be switched, but the new drug must have a different target.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It must be cytotoxic rather than cytostatic: Switching targets, not the drug type, is the key.
B. It must block telomerase: Telomerase isn't an angiogenesis target.
C. It must target VEGF again at a higher dose: The tumor has already escaped that target through other pathways.
E. It must be given with trastuzumab: Trastuzumab targets HER2, which isn't related to his kidney cancer.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Week 5: Cancer / Cancer Survival Mechanisms

Question 92
A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of painless blood in his urine for 2 weeks. He smoked a pack a day for 35 years and worked in a dye factory. He takes tamsulosin for an enlarged prostate. Vital signs are normal, and his abdominal exam is unremarkable. Urinalysis shows many red cells without casts. Cystoscopy shows a papillary mass in the bladder, and biopsy shows urothelial carcinoma. Tumor testing shows amplification of CCND1. How does this change drive tumor growth?
A. Cyclin D ubiquitinates p53
B. Cyclin D activates CDK4/6, which inactivates Rb so cells pass from G1 to S unchecked
C. Cyclin D activates Rb
D. Cyclin D activates BCR-ABL
E. Cyclin D inhibits telomerase
Answer: B. Cyclin D activates CDK4/6, which inactivates Rb so cells pass from G1 to S unchecked
Why this is correct: Cyclin D binds CDK4/6 and keeps it active, which inactivates Rb. Without Rb holding back E2F, the G1-to-S transition goes unchecked. Drugs have been developed to inhibit CDK/cyclin D.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Cyclin D ubiquitinates p53: MDM2, not cyclin D, tags p53 for degradation.
C. Cyclin D activates Rb: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 inactivates Rb.
D. Cyclin D activates BCR-ABL: BCR-ABL comes from t(9;22) and is independent of cyclin D.
E. Cyclin D inhibits telomerase: Cyclin D doesn't act on telomerase.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Question 93
A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a first-time seizure and 6 months of mild headaches. He has no other medical problems and works as an engineer. Vital signs are normal, and his neurologic exam is normal after the seizure. MRI shows a non-enhancing mass in the left frontal lobe. The tumor is removed and shows a slowly growing brain tumor. Tumor testing shows a mutation in isocitrate dehydrogenase. What does the mutant enzyme produce, and what is its effect?
A. Citrate, which increases fatty acid synthesis
B. 2-HG, which increases methylation of tumor suppressor genes
C. Glutamine, which fuels the TCA cycle
D. Lactate, which inhibits apoptosis
E. VEGF, which stimulates new vessels
Answer: B. 2-HG, which increases methylation of tumor suppressor genes
Why this is correct: Mutated isocitrate dehydrogenase converts alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-HG, which increases methylation of tumor suppressors.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Citrate, which increases fatty acid synthesis: Citrate comes from the retrograde TCA cycle, but that isn't the product of the mutant enzyme.
C. Glutamine, which fuels the TCA cycle: Cancer cells consume glutamine; the mutant enzyme doesn't make it.
D. Lactate, which inhibits apoptosis: Lactate comes from glycolysis in the Warburg effect.
E. VEGF, which stimulates new vessels: VEGF is a protein growth factor, not a product of IDH.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Question 94
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and blood in his stool. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, and colonoscopy shows a mass in the transverse colon. It is removed, and pathology shows adenocarcinoma. As part of a research study, his tumor cells are grown in culture. They keep dividing well past the number of divisions normal cells can make, and their chromosome ends aren't shortening. Which enzyme is most likely overexpressed?
A. Caspase-3
B. Isocitrate dehydrogenase
C. PARP
D. Telomerase
E. Ribonucleotide reductase
Answer: D. Telomerase
Why this is correct: Telomeres protect chromosome ends, and their loss usually makes cells stop growing or die. Most cancer cells overexpress telomerase, which makes them immortal and can serve as a molecular marker for cancer.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Caspase-3: Caspase-3 cleaves PARP and causes cell death.
B. Isocitrate dehydrogenase: IDH mutations produce 2-HG and don't maintain telomeres.
C. PARP: PARP helps repair DNA damage and doesn't maintain telomeres.
E. Ribonucleotide reductase: Ribonucleotide reductase makes deoxyribonucleotides.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Question 95
A 60-year-old woman with non-small cell lung cancer starts radiation therapy. She smoked for 35 years and has COPD. Sequencing shows her tumor has a normal TP53 gene. In a research study, her tumor cells are exposed to radiation in the lab, and in these cells the cell cycle stops before DNA replication so the damage can be repaired. Which protein does p53 turn on to cause this arrest?
A. MDM2
B. Cyclin D
C. BCL2
D. E2F
E. p21
Answer: E. p21
Why this is correct: p53 is the master regulator of the cell cycle and survival. As a transcription factor, it turns on p21, which inhibits progression through G1.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. MDM2: MDM2 tags p53 for destruction; it doesn't carry out the arrest.
B. Cyclin D: Cyclin D drives the cell cycle forward with CDK4/6.
C. BCL2: BCL2 is anti-apoptotic and doesn't stop the cell cycle.
D. E2F: E2F promotes cell cycle progression and is held in check by Rb.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Question 96
A 58-year-old man with acute leukemia is enrolled in a trial of a new drug. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. His WBC is 34,000/mm³ with many blasts. Studies of his leukemia cells show that the drug triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, and cytochrome c is released from the mitochondria within hours. Which caspase is activated first in this pathway?
A. Caspase-8
B. Caspase-1
C. Caspase-9
D. PARP
E. Caspase-3
Answer: C. Caspase-9
Why this is correct: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, cytochrome c release activates caspase-9, then caspase-3. Caspase-3 cleaves PARP, which leads to cell death. The extrinsic pathway uses caspase-8 instead.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Caspase-8: Caspase-8 is activated in the extrinsic pathway by death receptors.
B. Caspase-1: Caspase-1 isn't part of these apoptosis pathways in this material.
D. PARP: PARP is cleaved by caspase-3; it isn't a caspase.
E. Caspase-3: Caspase-3 comes after caspase-9 and cleaves PARP.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Question 97
A 70-year-old woman comes to the physician because of new lumps under her arm and a 5-kg weight loss. She had a small melanoma removed from her back 10 years ago with clear margins and has had normal skin checks since. She takes a statin. There are firm, enlarged nodes in her left axilla, and biopsy shows metastatic melanoma. Her physician explains that tumor cells likely remained after surgery, and her immune system kept them in check for a decade while selecting for variants that could better survive immune attack. The tumor has now begun to grow uncontrolled. Which phase of cancer immunoediting has she entered?
A. Escape
B. Equilibrium
C. Extravasation
D. Elimination
E. Anergy
Answer: A. Escape
Why this is correct: Immunoediting has three phases. In elimination, immune surveillance destroys tumor cells. In equilibrium, the immune system selects for variants that better survive attack. In escape, the immunologically sculpted tumor grows uncontrolled despite a working immune system.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Equilibrium: Equilibrium describes the decade of control and selection, which has now ended.
C. Extravasation: Extravasation is a step in metastasis, not immunoediting.
D. Elimination: Elimination is the phase where immune surveillance destroys tumor cells.
E. Anergy: Anergy isn't one of the immunoediting phases.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Week 5: Cancer / Personalized Medicine

Question 98
A 24-year-old man has relapsed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia after two rounds of chemotherapy. He has no other medical problems. His own T cells are collected, engineered to express a receptor that recognizes his cancer cells, and infused back. Four days later he has a temperature of 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse of 128/min, and blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. Blood cultures are negative, and his CRP and ferritin are very high. His blasts are falling rapidly. Which statement about this therapy is correct?
A. It uses T cells from a matched donor
B. It is mainly used for solid tumors like melanoma
C. It doesn't cause graft-versus-host disease, but rapid T-cell expansion can cause severe inflammation
D. His fever is caused by graft-versus-host disease
E. It uses lymphocytes isolated from his resected tumor
Answer: C. It doesn't cause graft-versus-host disease, but rapid T-cell expansion can cause severe inflammation
Why this is correct: CAR-T therapy uses the patient's own re-engineered T cells, so there's no graft-versus-host disease. The cells expand so quickly that they can cause inflammation needing anti-inflammatory treatment, and the therapy is used for liquid cancers.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It uses T cells from a matched donor: CAR-T uses the patient's own T cells.
B. It is mainly used for solid tumors like melanoma: CAR-T is used for liquid cancers; TIL therapy is used for melanoma and lung cancer.
D. His fever is caused by graft-versus-host disease: His own cells can't cause graft-versus-host disease.
E. It uses lymphocytes isolated from his resected tumor: Isolating lymphocytes from a resected tumor describes TIL therapy.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 99
A 49-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up after a lumpectomy for a 1.8-cm hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Her lymph nodes were negative. She has no family history of cancer and takes no medications. Her vital signs and exam are normal. She is starting endocrine therapy. Her oncologist sends the tumor for a genomic test to estimate her risk of relapse before deciding on other treatment. How will the result guide her treatment?
A. A high-risk result means she gets chemotherapy, and a low-risk result means she can skip it
B. A low-risk result means she needs radiation instead
C. The test determines her germline BRCA status
D. The test measures PD-L1 to select immunotherapy
E. The test decides whether she needs surgery
Answer: A. A high-risk result means she gets chemotherapy, and a low-risk result means she can skip it
Why this is correct: After surgery, breast cancers can be tested genetically for risk of relapse. Patients at high risk receive chemotherapy, and those at low risk don't need it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A low-risk result means she needs radiation instead: The test is used to decide on chemotherapy.
C. The test determines her germline BRCA status: Germline testing looks at inherited mutations, not relapse risk in the tumor.
D. The test measures PD-L1 to select immunotherapy: PD-L1 is used to stratify immunotherapy response.
E. The test decides whether she needs surgery: She has already had surgery.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 100
A 45-year-old man with metastatic melanoma comes for treatment after his disease progressed on immune checkpoint inhibitors. He has no other medical problems, and his performance status is good. One of his metastases is surgically removed. Lymphocytes found within the tumor are isolated, grown in large numbers in the lab, and infused back into him. His oncologist explains why these particular cells were chosen. What is the rationale for this approach?
A. The cells are engineered with a chimeric antigen receptor
B. The cells block VEGF
C. These lymphocytes have already shown they can recognize and survive the tumor
D. The cells come from a matched donor to cause graft-versus-tumor
E. It works only for liquid cancers
Answer: C. These lymphocytes have already shown they can recognize and survive the tumor
Why this is correct: In TIL therapy, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are isolated, expanded, and reinfused. Because they've already proven they can evade destruction by the tumor, they should be effective against it. It's used in melanoma and lung cancer.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The cells are engineered with a chimeric antigen receptor: Engineering a chimeric receptor describes CAR-T therapy.
B. The cells block VEGF: Blocking VEGF is anti-angiogenic therapy.
D. The cells come from a matched donor to cause graft-versus-tumor: TIL therapy uses the patient's own lymphocytes.
E. It works only for liquid cancers: TIL therapy is used for solid tumors like melanoma; CAR-T is for liquid cancers.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Week 6: Immunology / Basics of Innate Immunity

Question 1
A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up after a cold 2 weeks ago. She works as a kindergarten teacher, takes a daily multivitamin, and runs three times a week. Her physician explains that the cells that controlled her viral infection in the first few days don't have antigen receptors but can recognize and kill infected cells that have stopped displaying a certain surface molecule. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg. Her lungs are clear, and she has no lymphadenopathy. Which molecule's loss triggers these cells?
A. CD40
B. MHC class II
C. Sialyl-Lewis X
D. CD18
E. MHC class I
Answer: E. MHC class I
Why this is correct: Natural killer cells are innate lymphoid cells that lack antigen receptors. They're activated by type I interferons and IL-12 and kill cells that have lost MHC class I, which often happens with viral infection.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD40: CD40 on B cells and macrophages binds CD40L on T cells.
B. MHC class II: MHC class II is expressed on professional APCs; NK cells respond to loss of class I.
C. Sialyl-Lewis X: Sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes binds selectins during rolling.
D. CD18: CD18 is a neutrophil integrin subunit missing in LAD-1.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of many warts on her hands and feet that haven't responded to over-the-counter treatments. She has had pneumonia three times and several sinus infections. She plays the clarinet and is in the sixth grade. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Her CBC shows a very low neutrophil count, but a bone marrow biopsy shows plenty of neutrophils that aren't leaving the marrow. Her immunoglobulin levels are low. A variant in which gene is most likely?
A. BTK
B. NADPH oxidase
C. CXCR4
D. CD18
E. NLRP3
Answer: C. CXCR4
Why this is correct: WHIM syndrome (warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections, myelokathexis) is caused by a variant in CXCR4, a chemokine receptor. Neutrophils are retained in the marrow, causing neutropenia, and patients are susceptible to HPV warts.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA with absent B cells, not marrow retention of neutrophils.
B. NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD, where neutrophil counts are normal but they can't make an oxidative burst.
D. CD18: CD18 defects cause LAD-1 with high blood neutrophil counts.
E. NLRP3: NLRP3 gain of function causes FCAS1.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 3
A 45-year-old man with hepatitis C is started on an injected cytokine therapy. He also has hypertension treated with amlodipine and smokes a pack a day. His physician explains that the drug works inside infected cells to interfere with viral replication and also activates natural killer cells. He contracted the virus from a blood transfusion in the 1980s. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. His liver edge is palpable, and his ALT is 88 U/L. Which class of cytokine is this most likely?
A. Type I interferon (IFN-α or IFN-β)
B. IL-8
C. IL-10
D. Type II interferon (IFN-γ)
E. TGF-β
Answer: A. Type I interferon (IFN-α or IFN-β)
Why this is correct: Type I interferons respond to viral infections from inside cells and interfere with viral replication. They also interact with NK cells. Type II interferon (IFN-γ) mainly activates macrophages.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. IL-8: IL-8 is a neutrophil chemotactic factor.
C. IL-10: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits immune activation.
D. Type II interferon (IFN-γ): IFN-γ mainly activates macrophages.
E. TGF-β: TGF-β is anti-inflammatory and activates Treg cells.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 4
A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with fever, chills, and burning with urination for 2 days. She takes an oral contraceptive and drinks alcohol socially. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. She has right costovertebral angle tenderness. Her fever is driven by cytokines released by immune cells that act on the hypothalamus. Urinalysis shows many white cells and nitrites. Her WBC is 16,200/mm³. Which set of cytokines are the endogenous pyrogens?
A. IFN-α and IFN-β
B. IL-2 and IL-7
C. IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α
D. IL-10 and TGF-β
E. IL-4 and IL-5
Answer: C. IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α
Why this is correct: IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α are endogenous pyrogens that raise body temperature. Fever helps because most pathogens can't grow well at higher temperatures.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IFN-α and IFN-β: Type I interferons are antiviral, not the listed pyrogens.
B. IL-2 and IL-7: These use the common gamma chain receptors and aren't the listed pyrogens.
D. IL-10 and TGF-β: These are anti-inflammatory cytokines.
E. IL-4 and IL-5: IL-4 comes from Th2 cells and IL-5 recruits eosinophils; neither is a listed pyrogen.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 5
A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had worsening morning stiffness and swelling of her hands despite methotrexate. She works as an accountant and has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her rheumatologist adds an injected drug that acts as a decoy receptor, binding TNF-α so it can't engage its normal receptor. Her symptoms have kept her from typing for more than an hour at a time. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Her MCP and wrist joints are warm and swollen, and her ESR is 58 mm/h. Which drug is this?
A. Eculizumab
B. Omalizumab
C. Etanercept
D. Mepolizumab
E. Tacrolimus
Answer: C. Etanercept
Why this is correct: Etanercept is a fusion protein of human IgG with a TNF receptor. It acts as a decoy that binds TNF so it can't bind its receptor, reducing inflammation in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Eculizumab: Eculizumab binds C5 and treats PNH.
B. Omalizumab: Omalizumab binds IgE.
D. Mepolizumab: Mepolizumab binds IL-5.
E. Tacrolimus: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 6
A 30-year-old man is recovering from a skin infection on his forearm that was drained a week ago. He has no other medical problems and works as a line cook. As the infection resolves, macrophages and dendritic cells in the tissue release a cytokine that shuts down inflammatory cytokines and blocks further activation of innate cells by PAMPs. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and pulse is 76/min. The drained area has a clean granulating base with minimal surrounding redness. Which cytokine is this?
A. IL-10
B. IL-12
C. IL-1β
D. IL-8
E. TNF-α
Answer: A. IL-10
Why this is correct: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine made by macrophages and dendritic cells. It inhibits inflammatory cytokines, blocks innate cell activation by PAMPs, and dampens some adaptive responses.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. IL-12: IL-12 activates NK and T cells to make IFN-γ.
C. IL-1β: IL-1β is pro-inflammatory and causes fever.
D. IL-8: IL-8 recruits neutrophils.
E. TNF-α: TNF-α is pro-inflammatory.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 7
A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and dark urine that is worst in the morning. Three months ago she had a clot in her hepatic vein. She takes no medications and works as a veterinarian. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL, LDH is high, and haptoglobin is undetectable. Flow cytometry shows her red cells lack CD59 and DAF. She has no jaundice history and no family history of anemia. Pulse is 102/min, and her spleen isn't palpable. What is the underlying defect, and which drug treats it?
A. NADPH oxidase deficiency; eculizumab
B. C1 inhibitor deficiency; etanercept
C. A PIGA defect; omalizumab
D. TLR4 deficiency; eculizumab
E. A PIGA defect preventing the lipid anchor for complement regulators; eculizumab
Answer: E. A PIGA defect preventing the lipid anchor for complement regulators; eculizumab
Why this is correct: In PNH, a PIGA defect prevents synthesis of the lipid tail shared by HRF, protectin (CD59), and DAF, which regulate complement lysis. Fragile red cells are lysed. Eculizumab binds C5 and prevents its cleavage, improving anemia and thrombosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. NADPH oxidase deficiency; eculizumab: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD.
B. C1 inhibitor deficiency; etanercept: C1INH deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, and etanercept blocks TNF.
C. A PIGA defect; omalizumab: Omalizumab binds IgE and doesn't affect complement.
D. TLR4 deficiency; eculizumab: TLR4 variants affect LPS responses, not red cell complement protection.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Question 8
A 3-year-old girl is admitted with pneumonia. She was born at term, attends daycare, and has had several ear infections this year. As bacteria enter her lungs, a liver-made acute phase protein that recognizes mannose-containing sugars on the bacterial surface binds them and starts the complement cascade. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), respiratory rate is 42/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. She has crackles over the right lower lobe, and chest X-ray shows consolidation. Which pathway is this?
A. The STING pathway
B. The alternative pathway
C. The classical pathway
D. The lectin pathway
E. The inflammasome pathway
Answer: D. The lectin pathway
Why this is correct: In the lectin pathway, IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α shift liver protein secretion toward acute phase reactants like mannose-binding lectin. MBL recognizes mannose-containing carbohydrates on organisms and starts the complement cascade.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The STING pathway: STING detects cytosolic dsDNA and makes type I interferons.
B. The alternative pathway: The alternative pathway starts when C3b lands directly on a pathogen.
C. The classical pathway: The classical pathway starts when antibodies or CRP activate C1.
E. The inflammasome pathway: The inflammasome activates caspase-1 to make IL-1β.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 9
A 45-year-old man is admitted with pneumococcal pneumonia. He has COPD and uses an albuterol inhaler. Two days after admission, his antibodies against the organism and C-reactive protein coat the bacterial surface and activate the first component of a complement pathway. He smoked for 30 years and quit last year. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 89%. Sputum shows gram-positive diplococci. Which pathway is this, and which component is activated?
A. The classical pathway, starting with C5b
B. The lectin pathway, starting with MBL
C. The alternative pathway, starting with C3b landing directly
D. The alternative pathway, starting with C1
E. The classical pathway, starting with C1
Answer: E. The classical pathway, starting with C1
Why this is correct: In the classical pathway, IgM, IgG, or C-reactive protein deposit on the pathogen and activate C1. C1 inhibitor keeps C1 activation in check.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The classical pathway, starting with C5b: C5b begins formation of the membrane attack complex at the end of the cascade.
B. The lectin pathway, starting with MBL: The lectin pathway starts with mannose-binding lectin, not antibody or CRP.
C. The alternative pathway, starting with C3b landing directly: The alternative pathway doesn't need antibody.
D. The alternative pathway, starting with C1: C1 belongs to the classical pathway.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 10
A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with painless swelling of her lips and tongue that began after a dental cleaning. She has had similar episodes of swelling in her hands and abdomen since age 12. She has no hives, and antihistamines haven't helped. Her mother has the same problem. Her C1 inhibitor level is low. Her lips and tongue are markedly swollen, but her airway is patent and there's no wheezing. She takes no medications and has no rash. Which statement best describes her condition?
A. IgE-mediated angioedema from mast cell histamine
B. Chronic urticaria from an antibody to FcεRI
C. Type 2 hereditary angioedema from a quantitative deficiency
D. Type 1 hereditary angioedema from a quantitative C1 inhibitor deficiency, with bradykinin causing the swelling
E. Acquired angioedema from an antibody to C1INH
Answer: D. Type 1 hereditary angioedema from a quantitative C1 inhibitor deficiency, with bradykinin causing the swelling
Why this is correct: Hereditary angioedema comes from not enough C1 inhibitor, which leads to excess bradykinin and painless swelling. Type 1 is a quantitative deficiency in heterozygotes, type 2 is a functional deficiency with a normal level, and acquired forms can come from antibodies to C1INH.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgE-mediated angioedema from mast cell histamine: Her swelling doesn't respond to antihistamines and is bradykinin mediated.
B. Chronic urticaria from an antibody to FcεRI: She has no hives, and this is a complement regulation problem.
C. Type 2 hereditary angioedema from a quantitative deficiency: Type 2 is a functional deficiency, usually with normal levels.
E. Acquired angioedema from an antibody to C1INH: Her family history and early onset point to the inherited form.
Objective: Describe the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and management of specific diseases covered in the CBL component of the module (e.g., sickle cell disease, fragile X syndrome, breast cancer, hereditary angioedema, acute myelogenous leukemia, HIV/AIDS etc.) (CBO 1.2)

Question 11
A 60-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with septic shock from E. coli pyelonephritis. He has diabetes and takes insulin. His family asks why he got so sick when his brother recovered quickly from a similar infection. Genetic testing shows he carries a variant in a receptor on the cell membrane that normally recognizes bacterial lipopolysaccharide. His blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg despite fluids, and he's started on norepinephrine. His lactate is 5.8 mmol/L. Which receptor is it?
A. TLR9
B. TLR4
C. NLRP3
D. TLR3
E. TLR7
Answer: B. TLR4
Why this is correct: TLR4 (with TLR2) is an external TLR that recognizes bacterial LPS. People with a TLR4 variant are less responsive to LPS and more susceptible to septic shock.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. TLR9: TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA inside endosomes.
C. NLRP3: NLRP3 is an intracellular NOD-like receptor that forms the inflammasome.
D. TLR3: TLR3 is internal and recognizes dsRNA.
E. TLR7: TLR7 recognizes ssRNA.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 12
A 7-year-old boy is admitted with fever, confusion, and seizures. MRI shows temporal lobe lesions, and CSF PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus 1. This is his second episode of HSV encephalitis. Question 13
A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of several flat, skin-colored genital warts. She has been with the same partner for 3 years and takes no medications.
