Question 14
A 28-year-old man comes to the physician because of a sore throat, fever, and body aches for 3 days. He works in construction, smokes marijuana occasionally, and has no chronic conditions. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and he has tender anterior cervical nodes. His physician explains that his dendritic cells detected the bacteria partly through an endosomal receptor that responds to DNA containing a feature common in bacterial genomes but rare in human DNA. Which receptor and feature are involved?
A. TLR3, which recognizes dsRNA
B. STING, which recognizes methylated CpG
C. TLR7, which recognizes ssRNA
D. TLR9, which recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA
E. TLR4, which recognizes methylated CpG
Answer: D. TLR9, which recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA
Why this is correct: TLR9 is an internal TLR that recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA found in many bacterial and viral genomes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. TLR3, which recognizes dsRNA: TLR3 recognizes RNA, not DNA.
B. STING, which recognizes methylated CpG: STING detects cytosolic dsDNA and makes interferons; the question describes an endosomal TLR.
C. TLR7, which recognizes ssRNA: TLR7 recognizes RNA.
E. TLR4, which recognizes methylated CpG: TLR4 recognizes LPS.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 15
A 3-year-old boy has had pneumococcal meningitis and two episodes of staphylococcal sepsis. He has never had a serious viral infection. He was born at term and his development is normal. Temperature during his current admission is 38.1°C (100.6°F), even though his blood cultures are positive, and his CRP is barely elevated. Genetic testing shows a defect in the adaptor that binds activated TLR4 and starts the kinase cascade through IRAK4. Which protein is defective?
A. MyD88
B. NEMO
C. BTK
D. NADPH oxidase
E. UNC93B
Answer: A. MyD88
Why this is correct: MyD88 binds activated TLR4. IRAK4 then binds MyD88 and starts a kinase cascade through TRAF6 and IKK. Deficiency of either MyD88 or IRAK4 causes an immunodeficiency with a predisposition to bacterial infections.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. NEMO: NEMO is the gamma subunit of IKK, downstream of IRAK4, and causes ectodermal dysplasia.
C. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA.
D. NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD.
E. UNC93B: UNC93B defects cause HSV susceptibility.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 16
A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent bacterial pneumonia and sinusitis. He has sparse hair with unusual whirls, pegged and gapped teeth, and he can't sweat, so he overheats in the summer. His mother had a swirling pattern of skin pigmentation as a child. His IgM is normal, but IgG and IgA are low from impaired class switching. He was born at term and walked at 13 months. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and he has crackles over the left lung. Which protein is defective?
A. CD40 ligand
B. MyD88
C. STAT3
D. NEMO (the gamma subunit of IKK)
E. BTK
Answer: D. NEMO (the gamma subunit of IKK)
Why this is correct: IKK phosphorylates IκB so NF-κB is released to activate cytokine and adhesion genes. A variant in its gamma subunit, NEMO, causes bacterial infections, anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, pegged teeth, abnormal hair whirls, incontinentia pigmenti, and impaired class switching.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD40 ligand: CD40L defects cause hyper-IgM without ectodermal dysplasia.
B. MyD88: MyD88 deficiency causes bacterial infections without ectodermal findings.
C. STAT3: STAT3 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome.
E. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA with absent B cells.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 17
A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a red, hot, swollen area on his forearm 2 days after a scrape at the gym. He has no chronic illnesses and takes no medications. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 104/min, and there is a 6-cm area of warm erythema. In his tissue macrophages, bacterial PAMPs activate an intracellular receptor that assembles a complex, binds pro-caspase-1, and produces active caspase-1, which cleaves a precursor into a potent cytokine. Which cytokine is produced?
A. IL-1β
B. IL-5
C. IL-10
D. TNF-α
E. IFN-α
Answer: A. IL-1β
Why this is correct: Activated NLRP3 (cryopyrin) forms the inflammasome and binds pro-caspase-1. Proteolysis makes caspase-1, which cleaves pro-IL-1β into IL-1β, a very strong pro-inflammatory cytokine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. IL-5: IL-5 recruits eosinophils.
C. IL-10: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory.
D. TNF-α: TNF-α isn't made by caspase-1 cleavage.
E. IFN-α: Type I interferons come from STING and RIG-I pathways.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 18
A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she gets an itchy rash, fever, and joint aches every time she is exposed to cold weather, even an air-conditioned classroom. Her father and grandmother have the same problem. She takes no medications and is doing well in school. Her exam today is normal. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), and her joints are not swollen today. Her CBC and ESR drawn during a recent episode showed leukocytosis and inflammation. What is the most likely cause?
A. Type III hypersensitivity to cold
B. An NLRP3 loss-of-function mutation
C. An autoantibody to FcεRI
D. An autosomal dominant NLRP3 gain-of-function mutation causing an overactive inflammasome
E. C1 inhibitor deficiency
Answer: D. An autosomal dominant NLRP3 gain-of-function mutation causing an overactive inflammasome
Why this is correct: Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS1) is an autosomal dominant NLRP3 gain-of-function disorder. Hyperactivity of the inflammasome causes a rash after cold exposure. Autoinflammatory diseases are driven by the innate immune system.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type III hypersensitivity to cold: This is an innate autoinflammatory disorder, not immune complex disease.
B. An NLRP3 loss-of-function mutation: FCAS1 is a gain-of-function disorder.
C. An autoantibody to FcεRI: That causes chronic autoimmune urticaria, not a dominantly inherited cold-triggered syndrome.
E. C1 inhibitor deficiency: C1INH deficiency causes painless swelling, not a cold-triggered rash with fever.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 19
A 58-year-old woman with COVID-19 is admitted with fever and hypoxia. She has hypertension and obesity. Her physician explains that one normal part of her early defense involves cytoplasmic receptors that detect viral RNA and release type I interferons, while another pathway detects cytosolic double-stranded DNA. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Which receptor family detects cytoplasmic viral RNA?
A. RIG-I-like receptors
B. NLRP3
C. STING
D. C-type lectin receptors
E. TLR4
Answer: A. RIG-I-like receptors
Why this is correct: RIG-I-like receptors detect cytoplasmic viral RNA and release type I interferons and cytokines, a normal part of the response to COVID-19. STING detects cytosolic dsDNA and also leads to type I interferon production.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. NLRP3: NLRP3 forms the inflammasome.
C. STING: STING detects cytosolic dsDNA, not RNA.
D. C-type lectin receptors: C-type lectins recognize carbohydrates.
E. TLR4: TLR4 is on the cell surface and recognizes LPS.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 20
A 16-year-old girl has had oral thrush and thick, discolored fingernails from yeast infections since early childhood despite repeated antifungal courses. She has never had a bloodstream infection. She's on her school's swim team and takes no daily medications. Her CBC and immunoglobulin levels are normal, and HIV testing is negative. Defects in a C-type lectin receptor pathway that recognizes fungal carbohydrates are found. Temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F). She has white plaques on her tongue and buccal mucosa, and several fingernails are thickened and yellow. Which pathway is most likely affected?
A. TLR3
B. NADPH oxidase
C. NLRP3
D. Dectin-1
E. CD18
Answer: D. Dectin-1
Why this is correct: C-type lectin receptors recognize carbohydrates found in fungi, mycobacteria, hepatitis C, and HIV-1. Defects in the dectin-1 pathway cause familial chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. TLR3: TLR3 defects predispose to HSV.
B. NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD with deep bacterial and fungal abscesses.
C. NLRP3: NLRP3 gain of function causes FCAS1.
E. CD18: CD18 defects cause LAD-1 with bacterial infections.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 21
A 40-year-old man is stung by a bee on his forearm while gardening. Within minutes, the area is red and swollen. He takes lisinopril for hypertension and has no known allergies. Endothelial cells near the sting quickly release a selectin stored in Weibel-Palade bodies in response to histamine, and later make another selectin in response to TNF and IL-1. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. There's a 4-cm raised, red, warm area around the sting with no hives elsewhere. Which selectin is released from Weibel-Palade bodies?
A. ICAM-1
B. PECAM-1
C. CD18
D. P-selectin
E. E-selectin
Answer: D. P-selectin
Why this is correct: Selectins on endothelial cells bind sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes to start rolling. P-selectin is released from Weibel-Palade bodies in response to histamine, while E-selectin is induced by TNF and IL-1.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ICAM-1: ICAM-1 is the endothelial integrin ligand for firm adhesion.
B. PECAM-1: PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis between endothelial cells.
C. CD18: CD18 is a neutrophil integrin subunit.
E. E-selectin: E-selectin is induced by TNF and IL-1, not stored in Weibel-Palade bodies.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 22
A 3-year-old girl has had recurrent bacterial pneumonia and skin infections since infancy. She also has short stature and developmental delay. Her parents are first cousins. Her WBC count is 30,000/mm³ with mostly neutrophils, but neutrophils fail to roll along the endothelium because selectins can't bind a sugar on their surface. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). She has a skin infection on her leg that has no pus despite marked redness. Which condition does she have?
A. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2
B. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1
C. WHIM syndrome
D. Chronic granulomatous disease
E. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Answer: A. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2
Why this is correct: In LAD-2, selectins can't bind sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes, so rolling fails and neutrophils can't reach infections. LAD-1 is a CD18 defect, and LAD-3 affects CD11/CD18.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1: LAD-1 is a defect in the CD18 integrin, which affects firm adhesion, not selectin binding.
C. WHIM syndrome: WHIM involves neutrophils retained in the marrow, so blood counts are low.
D. Chronic granulomatous disease: CGD involves failure of the oxidative burst.
E. Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Chediak-Higashi involves giant granules and silvery hair.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 23
A 6-month-old boy is admitted with a deep skin infection on his buttock that has no pus. He has had several similar infections and a lingering infection around his umbilical stump as a newborn. He was born at term and is breastfed. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). His WBC is 45,000/mm³ with mostly neutrophils. Flow cytometry shows his neutrophils lack a subunit of the integrin that binds ICAM-1. Which subunit is missing?
A. CXCR4
B. Sialyl-Lewis X
C. NADPH oxidase
D. CD18
E. PECAM-1
Answer: D. CD18
Why this is correct: In LAD-1, neutrophils lack CD18, part of the CD11/CD18 integrin that binds ICAM-1 on endothelium for firm adhesion. Neutrophils can't leave the blood, so blood neutrophil counts are high.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CXCR4: CXCR4 variants cause WHIM with low blood neutrophils.
B. Sialyl-Lewis X: Loss of selectin binding to sialyl-Lewis X is LAD-2.
C. NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD.
E. PECAM-1: PECAM-1 is an endothelial molecule used in diapedesis.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 24
A 22-year-old woman develops a painful abscess at the site of an old ear piercing. She has asthma and uses an albuterol inhaler. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Neutrophils that have stopped and adhered to the nearby endothelium squeeze between endothelial cells to leave the blood, guided by a chemokine gradient. She works as a hairstylist and takes no other medications. The earlobe is red, warm, and fluctuant. Which molecule mediates this step?
A. PECAM-1
B. E-selectin
C. ICAM-1
D. Sialyl-Lewis X
E. CD59
Answer: A. PECAM-1
Why this is correct: Diapedesis is mediated by PECAM-1, an adhesion molecule between endothelial cells, and guided by a chemokine gradient (CXCL8). Neutrophils can use collagenase to get through the basement membrane.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. E-selectin: Selectins mediate rolling, which comes before diapedesis.
C. ICAM-1: ICAM-1 mediates firm adhesion before diapedesis.
D. Sialyl-Lewis X: Sialyl-Lewis X binds selectins during rolling.
E. CD59: CD59 (protectin) regulates complement lysis.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 25
A 5-year-old boy is brought in for his third pneumonia this year and several severe skin infections. He has silvery-blond hair and pale skin, unlike his siblings, and he sunburns easily. He is in kindergarten and his vaccines are up to date. A blood smear shows neutrophils with very large cytoplasmic granules. His parents have dark hair and brown eyes. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and he has crackles over the right lung base. What is the diagnosis?
A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
B. Chronic granulomatous disease
C. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1
D. Hyper-IgE syndrome
E. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Answer: A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Why this is correct: Chediak-Higashi syndrome comes from lysosomal trafficking problems that create large granules in neutrophils, which interfere with diapedesis. Patients have silvery-blond hair and severe childhood infections, and HSCT has helped some patients.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Chronic granulomatous disease: CGD neutrophils can't make an oxidative burst but don't have giant granules or silvery hair.
C. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1: LAD-1 causes high neutrophil counts without giant granules.
D. Hyper-IgE syndrome: Hyper-IgE syndrome causes eczema, staph abscesses, and high IgE.
E. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: WAS causes eczema, small platelets, and infections.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 26
A 7-year-old boy is admitted with a liver abscess. He has had Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and osteomyelitis in the past, and he takes daily antibiotics prescribed by another physician. His maternal uncle had similar infections. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). A flow cytometry test shows his neutrophils don't change fluorescence when stimulated. He was born at term and developed normally. There is a tender, enlarged liver on exam. Which enzyme is defective, and what else is expected?
A. BTK; B cells are absent
B. NADPH oxidase; immunoglobulin levels are often very elevated
C. CD18; neutrophil count is very high
D. Myeloperoxidase; immunoglobulins are very low
E. NADPH oxidase; immunoglobulins are absent
Answer: B. NADPH oxidase; immunoglobulin levels are often very elevated
Why this is correct: CGD comes from a defective NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes can't make an oxidative burst. The DHR flow cytometry assay shows no response. It can be X-linked or autosomal recessive, and immunoglobulins are often very elevated. It needs lifelong antibiotics and antifungals, and stem cell transplant is the only cure.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. BTK; B cells are absent: That describes XLA.
C. CD18; neutrophil count is very high: That describes LAD-1.
D. Myeloperoxidase; immunoglobulins are very low: The defect in CGD is NADPH oxidase, and immunoglobulins are elevated.
E. NADPH oxidase; immunoglobulins are absent: Immunoglobulins are elevated, not absent, in CGD.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 27
A 2-year-old girl who received the BCG vaccine at birth in her home country is admitted with fever, weight loss, and enlarged lymph nodes that grow a weakly virulent mycobacterium. She has also had Salmonella bacteremia. Her parents are first cousins. Her T, B, and NK cell counts are normal. She has had poor weight gain for 6 months. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), and she has hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged cervical and axillary nodes. A defect in which pathway is most likely?
A. The IL-12/IFN-γ pathway
B. The complement membrane attack complex
C. The BTK pathway
D. The NLRP3 inflammasome
E. The CD40/CD40L pathway
Answer: A. The IL-12/IFN-γ pathway
Why this is correct: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease comes from defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ pathway, including TLR2, IL-12, and IFN-γ. Patients get infections with BCG (BCGosis), TB, non-TB mycobacteria, and Salmonella.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The complement membrane attack complex: MAC defects predispose to other infections, not mycobacteria.
C. The BTK pathway: BTK defects cause XLA.
D. The NLRP3 inflammasome: NLRP3 gain of function causes FCAS1.
E. The CD40/CD40L pathway: CD40L defects cause hyper-IgM.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Week 6: Immunology / Inflammation

Question 28
A 35-year-old carpenter comes to the physician 2 days after getting a large splinter in his palm. He removed most of it himself. He smokes and has no other medical problems. The area is red, warm, swollen, and painful, and he can't grip his hammer. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). There's a small fragment of wood still visible under the skin, and the surrounding area is 3 cm across. Which mediator is a major contributor to the swelling?
A. Nitric oxide, which increases vascular permeability
B. IL-10, which increases vascular permeability
C. Hepcidin, which increases blood flow
D. TGF-β, which dilates vessels
E. Histamine, which increases vascular permeability
Answer: E. Histamine, which increases vascular permeability
Why this is correct: Increased vascular permeability lets protein-rich fluid escape into tissue, causing swelling (tumor) and sometimes loss of function. Histamine is a major contributor. Vasodilation, partly through nitric oxide, causes redness.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Nitric oxide, which increases vascular permeability: Nitric oxide is a mediator of vasodilation.
B. IL-10, which increases vascular permeability: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory.
C. Hepcidin, which increases blood flow: Hepcidin lowers iron availability.
D. TGF-β, which dilates vessels: TGF-β is anti-inflammatory.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 29
A 60-year-old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has type 2 diabetes and hypothyroidism. On day 1, sputum contains mostly neutrophils. On day 3, a repeat sample shows a growing number of mononuclear cells that ingest bacteria, act as antigen-presenting cells, and make IL-8 to recruit more neutrophils. She is on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Temperature has fallen from 39.0°C (102.2°F) to 37.8°C (100°F), and her oxygen saturation has improved to 94%. Which cells are these?
A. Mast cells
B. Eosinophils
C. NK cells
D. Plasma cells
E. Macrophages
Answer: E. Macrophages
Why this is correct: Macrophages arrive 2 to 3 days after neutrophils. They ingest and destroy injurious agents, manage continued acute and chronic inflammation, produce IL-8 to recruit more neutrophils, and act as antigen-presenting cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Mast cells: Mast cells release histamine in immediate reactions.
B. Eosinophils: Eosinophils drive late-phase allergic reactions and fight parasites.
C. NK cells: NK cells kill cells missing MHC class I.
D. Plasma cells: Plasma cells make antibodies.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 30
A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a painful, swollen area on his thigh that started as a small bump a week ago. He works in a warehouse and has no chronic illnesses. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). There is a 3-cm fluctuant, tender mass. Incision releases thick yellow fluid. His blood glucose is 102 mg/dL, and he has no history of injection drug use. The surrounding skin is red and warm. What best explains the formation of this lesion?
A. Wound dehiscence
B. A granuloma formed by clustered macrophages
C. A keloid from excess collagen
D. A type IV hypersensitivity reaction
E. Neutrophils and macrophages released microbicidal products that damaged normal tissue, forming a localized collection of pus
Answer: E. Neutrophils and macrophages released microbicidal products that damaged normal tissue, forming a localized collection of pus
Why this is correct: Neutrophils and macrophages can't tell offender from host, so microbicidal products are released into tissue and damage normal cells. This collateral damage forms an abscess, a localized collection of purulent inflammatory and necrotic tissue.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Wound dehiscence: Dehiscence is rupture of a closed wound.
B. A granuloma formed by clustered macrophages: Granulomas are tightly clustered macrophages and don't contain pus.
C. A keloid from excess collagen: A keloid is a raised scar.
D. A type IV hypersensitivity reaction: Type IV reactions are T cell mediated and don't form pus.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 31
A 45-year-old man who emigrated from Peru 5 years ago has a chronic cough and weight loss. He works as a cook and doesn't smoke. Chest CT shows upper lobe nodules, and biopsy shows tightly clustered immune cells around the organisms. He has had night sweats for 3 months and lost 6 kg. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). His tuberculin skin test is positive. Which cell defines this lesion?
A. Eosinophils
B. Mast cells
C. Macrophages
D. Neutrophils
E. Platelets
Answer: C. Macrophages
Why this is correct: Granulomas are areas of tightly clustered immune cells that form around infections or foreign objects, most commonly in the lungs. They're defined by the presence of macrophages, and chronic inflammation is dominated by mononuclear cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Eosinophils: Eosinophils dominate allergic and parasitic inflammation.
B. Mast cells: Mast cells drive immediate hypersensitivity.
D. Neutrophils: Neutrophils dominate acute inflammation and abscesses.
E. Platelets: Platelets aren't the defining cell of a granuloma.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 32
A 70-year-old woman comes to the physician because of new headaches, jaw pain when chewing, and shoulder stiffness. She takes a statin and a baby aspirin. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is markedly elevated. She has a tender, thickened right temporal artery. Her hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, and CRP is elevated. Which liver-made protein explains the elevated ESR?
A. Fibrinogen, which makes red cells stack into rouleaux and settle faster
B. Mannose-binding lectin, which starts complement
C. Hepcidin, which lowers iron
D. IL-10, which suppresses inflammation
E. C1 inhibitor, which blocks bradykinin
Answer: A. Fibrinogen, which makes red cells stack into rouleaux and settle faster
Why this is correct: Acute phase proteins are made in the liver after IL-6, IL-1, and TNF stimulation. Fibrinogen binds red cells and makes them stack into rouleaux, which sediment faster; this is the basis of the ESR.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Mannose-binding lectin, which starts complement: MBL starts the lectin pathway but doesn't cause rouleaux.
C. Hepcidin, which lowers iron: Hepcidin causes anemia of chronic disease, not a high ESR.
D. IL-10, which suppresses inflammation: IL-10 is a cytokine, not an acute phase protein.
E. C1 inhibitor, which blocks bradykinin: C1INH regulates C1.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 33
A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years comes to the physician because of fatigue. He takes methotrexate and folic acid and has no bleeding. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with a normal MCV, and ferritin is high while serum iron is low. He tires easily climbing stairs. His hands show swelling of the MCP joints, and his ESR is 45 mm/h. Which protein made by the liver in response to inflammation explains his anemia?
A. TNF-α
B. C-reactive protein
C. Mannose-binding lectin
D. Hepcidin
E. Fibrinogen
Answer: D. Hepcidin
Why this is correct: Hepcidin is an acute phase protein that reduces iron availability and absorption, causing anemia of chronic disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. TNF-α: TNF-α stimulates acute phase proteins but isn't the one that blocks iron.
B. C-reactive protein: CRP activates the classical complement pathway but doesn't block iron.
C. Mannose-binding lectin: MBL starts the lectin pathway.
E. Fibrinogen: Fibrinogen raises the ESR by forming rouleaux.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 34
A 19-year-old college student comes to the emergency department with right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and fever for 12 hours. She takes an oral contraceptive and drinks alcohol on weekends. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and she has rebound tenderness. Her WBC is 17,500/mm³ with many immature neutrophils (bands). She had an uncomplicated appendectomy 2 hours after arrival. What explains this blood finding?
A. An eosinophilic late-phase reaction
B. Chronic inflammation causing lymphocytosis
C. Neutrophils trapped in the marrow
D. Acute inflammation causing neutrophilia with a left shift
E. Loss of CD18 on neutrophils
Answer: D. Acute inflammation causing neutrophilia with a left shift
Why this is correct: Leukocytosis from inflammation is caused by cytokines like TNF and IL-1. Acute inflammation causes neutrophilia with accelerated release of immature cells (a left shift), while chronic inflammation raises the lymphocyte count.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An eosinophilic late-phase reaction: Eosinophilia isn't described.
B. Chronic inflammation causing lymphocytosis: Chronic inflammation increases lymphocytes, not immature neutrophils.
C. Neutrophils trapped in the marrow: Marrow retention (myelokathexis) causes neutropenia.
E. Loss of CD18 on neutrophils: LAD-1 causes a high count from failed extravasation, not a left shift from acute illness.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 35
A 64-year-old man has a heart attack affecting the anterior wall of his left ventricle. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and smoked for 40 years. Six weeks later, echocardiography shows a thin, non-contracting region. He had a stent placed in the left anterior descending artery but arrived at the hospital 8 hours after symptoms began. He now takes aspirin, clopidogrel, a statin, and metoprolol. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and he has mild shortness of breath climbing stairs. Why did the heart heal this way?
A. A keloid replaced the muscle
B. Cardiac muscle is permanent tissue, so it's repaired with a fibrous scar
C. Cardiac muscle is stable tissue that regenerated
D. Cardiac muscle is labile tissue that regenerated
E. The scar formed by primary intention
Answer: B. Cardiac muscle is permanent tissue, so it's repaired with a fibrous scar
Why this is correct: Permanent tissues lack reparative potential, so damage is repaired with a fibrous scar. Labile tissues continuously regenerate from stem cells, and stable tissues have quiescent cells that can re-enter the cycle.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A keloid replaced the muscle: A keloid is an overgrown skin scar.
C. Cardiac muscle is stable tissue that regenerated: Stable tissue could regenerate, which didn't happen.
D. Cardiac muscle is labile tissue that regenerated: Labile tissue would regenerate native tissue.
E. The scar formed by primary intention: Primary intention refers to closing skin wounds with sutures.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 36
A 38-year-old woman has a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones. She has a BMI of 31 and takes no medications. Her small incisions are closed with sutures and heal with thin, barely visible scars. A week later her son falls off his bike and gets a deep scrape on his knee that is left open and fills in gradually from the bottom with red, bumpy tissue, leaving a larger scar. Which statement best describes these two healing processes?
A. Both healed by regeneration without scarring
B. Her incisions healed by secondary intention and her son's by primary intention
C. Both healed by primary intention
D. Her son's wound formed a keloid
E. Her incisions healed by primary intention and her son's wound by secondary intention
Answer: E. Her incisions healed by primary intention and her son's wound by secondary intention
Why this is correct: Primary intention is achieved by closing the wound edges with sutures or staples, as with surgical incisions. Secondary intention lays down new tissue from the base of the wound upward, often with visible granulation tissue, larger scars, and a higher infection risk.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Both healed by regeneration without scarring: Both left scars, so repair occurred.
B. Her incisions healed by secondary intention and her son's by primary intention: These are reversed.
C. Both healed by primary intention: The open scrape healed from the base up, which is secondary intention.
D. Her son's wound formed a keloid: A keloid grows beyond the wound's borders; this is normal granulation tissue.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 37
A 45-year-old man has an appendectomy through a small open incision. He has hypertension and drinks two beers a night. On postoperative day 5, the wound edges look pink and firm. His preoperative labs were normal, and he received one dose of cefazolin. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and there's no drainage from the wound. He's eating and walking without difficulty. Which process is dominant at this point in healing?
A. The wound is at full tensile strength
B. Fibroblasts replace type III collagen with type I collagen
C. Neutrophils release proteolytic enzymes and a clot forms a scab
D. Eosinophils clear debris
E. Macrophages replace neutrophils, fibroblasts lay down type III collagen, and granulation tissue fills the incision
Answer: E. Macrophages replace neutrophils, fibroblasts lay down type III collagen, and granulation tissue fills the incision
Why this is correct: The proliferative phase (days 3 to 7) is when macrophages replace neutrophils, fibroblasts deposit loose type III collagen, angiogenesis forms new vessels, epithelial cells proliferate, granulation tissue fills the incision, and myofibroblasts contract the wound.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The wound is at full tensile strength: Strength increases later during remodeling.
B. Fibroblasts replace type III collagen with type I collagen: That's remodeling, which runs from 1 week to 6 months.
C. Neutrophils release proteolytic enzymes and a clot forms a scab: That's the inflammatory phase in the first 24 to 48 hours.
D. Eosinophils clear debris: Neutrophils and macrophages clear debris; eosinophils aren't part of this.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 38
A 29-year-old woman had a C-section 4 months ago. She is breastfeeding and taking a prenatal vitamin. Her scar has gradually become flatter and stronger. The C-section was uncomplicated, and she had no wound infection. Her baby is growing well. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg, and the 12-cm scar is pale and flat without tenderness. Which change in the wound explains its increasing tensile strength?
A. Fibroblasts replacing type III collagen with type I collagen
B. Neutrophils releasing proteolytic enzymes
C. Myofibroblasts contracting the wound
D. Replacing type I collagen with type III collagen
E. Formation of a scab from dehydration
Answer: A. Fibroblasts replacing type III collagen with type I collagen
Why this is correct: In the remodeling phase (1 week to 6 months), fibroblasts replace type III collagen with type I collagen, which increases the wound's tensile strength.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Neutrophils releasing proteolytic enzymes: That's part of the early inflammatory phase.
C. Myofibroblasts contracting the wound: Contraction happens in the proliferative phase and doesn't add strength.
D. Replacing type I collagen with type III collagen: It's type III that's replaced by type I.
E. Formation of a scab from dehydration: A scab forms early in the inflammatory phase.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 39
A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because the scar from an ear piercing has grown into a large, firm, raised nodule. It now extends well beyond the site of the original hole. He's otherwise healthy and works as a barista. He got the piercing a year ago, and it healed without infection. He has no other skin lesions, and his older brother has a similar scar on his chest. The nodule is shiny, firm, and non-tender. What is the lesion?
A. Keloid
B. Granuloma
C. Wound dehiscence
D. Ulceration
E. Contracture
Answer: A. Keloid
Why this is correct: A keloid is an accumulation of excess collagen that produces a raised scar growing beyond the boundaries of the original wound.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Granuloma: A granuloma is a cluster of macrophages around an infection or foreign body.
C. Wound dehiscence: Dehiscence is rupture of a closed wound.
D. Ulceration: An ulcer is a local defect where surface cells are lost.
E. Contracture: A contracture is an exaggerated wound contraction that deforms tissue.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Question 40
A 34-year-old man had severe burns to his right elbow in a house fire 6 months ago. The burns healed, but he can no longer fully straighten his arm, and the skin across the joint is tight and puckered. He's in physical therapy and takes ibuprofen for pain. He didn't have skin grafting at the time of the injury. He has no other medical problems. The scar across the front of his elbow is thick and pulls the joint into flexion. What is the most likely cause of his limited movement?
A. Healing by primary intention
B. Ulceration from atherosclerosis
C. Wound dehiscence
D. A contracture from exaggerated wound contraction
E. A keloid
Answer: D. A contracture from exaggerated wound contraction
Why this is correct: Wound contraction is normal in healing, but a contracture is an exaggeration of it that causes deformity of the wound and surrounding tissue. It's often seen in burns and can compromise joint movement.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Healing by primary intention: Primary intention is closure with sutures.
B. Ulceration from atherosclerosis: An ulcer is a surface tissue defect.
C. Wound dehiscence: Dehiscence is rupture of the wound from pressure.
E. A keloid: A keloid is excess collagen that grows beyond the wound, not a contraction.
Objective: Begin developing critical thinking, analytical, and reasoning skills and correlate physical exam, imaging, and lab findings to draw appropriate conclusions (CBO 2.5)

Week 6: Immunology / The Adaptive Immune System

Question 41
An 8-month-old boy is brought to the physician for his fourth ear infection and a recent pneumonia. He was healthy until about 6 months of age. His mother's brother died of pneumonia as a child. He has barely visible tonsils. His lymphocyte count is normal, but flow cytometry shows B cells are essentially absent, and all immunoglobulin classes are very low. He was born at term and received all his vaccines on schedule. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and his right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Which protein is defective, and how is he treated?
A. CD40 ligand; daily antibiotic prophylaxis
B. RAG1; antibody replacement
C. Common gamma chain; HSCT
D. Bruton tyrosine kinase; antibody replacement
E. AIRE; thymus transplant
Answer: D. Bruton tyrosine kinase; antibody replacement
Why this is correct: X-linked agammaglobulinemia comes from a defect in BTK, a signaling molecule needed at a B cell development checkpoint. B cells don't develop, so the child can't make antibodies. Total lymphocytes can look normal, which is why flow cytometry matters, and treatment is antibody replacement.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD40 ligand; daily antibiotic prophylaxis: CD40L defects cause hyper-IgM with normal or high IgM.
B. RAG1; antibody replacement: RAG defects cause SCID affecting both T and B cells.
C. Common gamma chain; HSCT: Common gamma chain deficiency causes T-B+NK- SCID.
E. AIRE; thymus transplant: AIRE defects cause APECED autoimmunity.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 42
A 15-year-old girl has had oral and nail candidiasis since childhood, and she developed low calcium from hypoparathyroidism at 9 and adrenal insufficiency at 13. She takes hydrocortisone, calcium, and calcitriol. Genetic testing shows a variant in the gene that controls the self-antigen library in the thymus. Her parents are first cousins. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), and she has white plaques on her tongue and thickened, discolored nails. Which gene is it?
A. CXCR4
B. BTK
C. STAT3
D. NLRP3
E. AIRE
Answer: E. AIRE
Why this is correct: AIRE oversees the thymic self-antigen library used to eliminate self-reactive T cells. Variants cause APECED (APS-1), with autoimmune endocrine disease and chronic candidiasis, and the IL-17 family is involved.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CXCR4: CXCR4 variants cause WHIM.
B. BTK: BTK variants cause XLA.
C. STAT3: STAT3 variants cause hyper-IgE syndrome.
D. NLRP3: NLRP3 variants cause FCAS1.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 43
A 3-year-old boy is being evaluated for recurrent infections. His immunologist explains how T cells mature in the thymus. Immature T cells express both CD4 and CD8, and a cell whose receptor recognizes self-peptide on MHC class I is selected to survive. He was born at term and is growing well. His parents are healthy, and his older sister has never had serious infections. What happens to that cell?
A. It keeps both CD4 and CD8
B. It loses CD4 and becomes a CD8 T cell
C. It becomes a B cell
D. It loses CD8 and becomes a CD4 T cell
E. It is eliminated by negative selection
Answer: B. It loses CD4 and becomes a CD8 T cell
Why this is correct: Pro-T cells are double negative, and immature T cells are double positive. In positive selection, cells that recognize MHC class I lose CD4 and become CD8 T cells, while those recognizing MHC class II lose CD8 and become CD4 T cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It keeps both CD4 and CD8: Mature T cells have only one.
C. It becomes a B cell: T cells don't become B cells.
D. It loses CD8 and becomes a CD4 T cell: That happens to cells recognizing MHC class II.
E. It is eliminated by negative selection: Negative selection removes cells that don't recognize self or recognize it too strongly.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 44
A 2-day-old boy has tetany and a seizure. He was born at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He has a cleft palate, low-set ears, and a loud murmur, and echocardiogram shows an interrupted aortic arch. His calcium is 6.1 mg/dL, and chest X-ray shows no thymic shadow. Flow cytometry shows no functional T cells. The mother is 29 years old and had routine prenatal care. Oxygen saturation is 94%, and heart rate is 162/min. Which treatment addresses his immune defect?
A. Thymus transplant
B. Eculizumab
C. Lifelong antifungals
D. Physical therapy
E. Antibody replacement
Answer: A. Thymus transplant
Why this is correct: DiGeorge anomaly comes from 22q11.2 deletions (CATCH-22: cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia). In complete DiGeorge, there's no thymus and no functional T cells, and treatment is thymus transplant.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Eculizumab: Eculizumab treats PNH.
C. Lifelong antifungals: That's part of CGD management.
D. Physical therapy: Physical therapy is used in ataxia-telangiectasia.
E. Antibody replacement: Antibody replacement treats XLA.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 45
A 3-week-old boy is called back after his state newborn screen. He was born at term, is breastfeeding well, and has no symptoms. His screen shows very low levels of the DNA circles cut out during T cell receptor gene rearrangement. His weight is at the 50th percentile, and his exam is normal. A repeat test confirms the result. What does this result suggest?
A. A problem with T cell development, such as SCID
B. Excess eosinophils
C. Normal immune development
D. A complement deficiency
E. A B cell development problem only
Answer: A. A problem with T cell development, such as SCID
Why this is correct: TRECs (T cell receptor excision circles) are unused DNA byproducts of receptor splicing. Newborn screens include TREC counts, and a low count signals a T cell development problem, with SCID as a serious cause.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Excess eosinophils: TRECs don't measure eosinophils.
C. Normal immune development: A very low TREC count is abnormal.
D. A complement deficiency: Complement is screened with CH50 and AH50.
E. A B cell development problem only: TRECs reflect T cell, not B cell, development; BRECs reflect B cells.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Week 6: Immunology / B Cell & T Cell Receptors and Their Antigens

Question 46
A 60-year-old man with myeloma has a serum electrophoresis showing a large amount of a single antibody. His physician explains the structure of antibodies. Each antibody has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains held together by disulfide bonds. He has back pain, anemia, and high calcium. He is a retired truck driver and takes no medications. Which part of the antibody binds antigen, and what determines its class?
A. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the heavy chain type determines class
B. The Fc region binds antigen, and kappa versus lambda determines class
C. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class
D. The hinge binds antigen, and the J chain determines class
E. The C-terminal constant region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class
Answer: A. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the heavy chain type determines class
Why this is correct: The antigen-binding site is the variable region at the N-terminus of the heavy and light chains. The constant region is at the C-terminus. Antibody class is determined by the heavy chain (gamma, alpha, mu, epsilon, delta).
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The Fc region binds antigen, and kappa versus lambda determines class: Fc is constant, and light chain type doesn't determine class.
C. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class: The heavy chain determines class.
D. The hinge binds antigen, and the J chain determines class: The J chain links IgM and dimeric IgA and doesn't determine class.
E. The C-terminal constant region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class: The variable region binds antigen, and the heavy chain determines class.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 47
A lab working on a treatment for a 45-year-old woman's snakebite digests IgG antibodies with the enzyme papain. The woman is stable in the ICU on IV fluids. The lab wants fragments that can bind the venom but don't have the Fc region. She was bitten on the ankle while hiking 6 hours earlier. Her ankle is swollen and bruised, and her blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. What does papain digestion produce?
A. Two heavy chains and two light chains
B. One Fab and two Fc fragments
C. One F(ab')2 fragment and a degraded Fc
D. Four identical Fab fragments
E. Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment
Answer: E. Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment
Why this is correct: Papain cuts at the flexible hinge above the disulfide link between heavy chains. Light chains stay attached, giving three pieces: two Fab fragments that still bind antigen and one Fc fragment. Pepsin cuts below the link, giving one F(ab')2 and degrading the stem.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Two heavy chains and two light chains: Papain doesn't separate heavy from light chains.
B. One Fab and two Fc fragments: There's only one Fc per IgG.
C. One F(ab')2 fragment and a degraded Fc: That's what pepsin produces.
D. Four identical Fab fragments: Each IgG has only two antigen-binding arms.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 48
A 55-year-old man receives a mouse-derived monoclonal antibody for a severe transplant rejection episode. He has diabetes and takes insulin. A week later he develops fever and a rash, and testing shows he has made antibodies against the drug. The drug company describes how the original antibody was made by fusing mouse B cells with cancer cells. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and he has hives on his trunk and aching joints. What is this fused cell called, and what is the patient's reaction?
A. A hybridoma; graft-versus-host disease
B. A memory B cell; a HAMA reaction
C. A hybridoma; hyperacute rejection
D. A hybridoma; a human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA) reaction
E. A plasma cell; serum sickness from polyclonal antibodies
Answer: D. A hybridoma; a human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA) reaction
Why this is correct: Monoclonal antibodies are made by fusing antibody-producing B cells with cancer cells to make an immortal hybridoma. Humans can react to mouse (-omab) antibodies as foreign proteins, a HAMA reaction. Chimeric (-ximab), humanized (-zumab), and human (-umab) antibodies reduce this problem.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A hybridoma; graft-versus-host disease: GVHD is donor T cells attacking the host.
B. A memory B cell; a HAMA reaction: The fused cell is a hybridoma, not a memory B cell.
C. A hybridoma; hyperacute rejection: Hyperacute rejection is antibody-mediated graft destruction.
E. A plasma cell; serum sickness from polyclonal antibodies: The fused cell is a hybridoma, and his response is directed at a mouse monoclonal antibody.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 49
A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes has studies of her T cells as part of a research project. The researcher explains that the T cell receptor resembles the antigen-binding arm of an antibody, with two chains that each have one variable and one constant region. She was diagnosed with diabetes at 11 and uses an insulin pump. Her HbA1c is 7.4%, and her exam is normal. Which T cell receptor chain corresponds to the antibody heavy chain?
A. The J chain
B. The alpha chain
C. The beta chain
D. The kappa chain
E. The CD3 chain
Answer: C. The beta chain
Why this is correct: T cell receptors are dimers of alpha and beta chains (or gamma and delta in a separate population). Each chain has one variable and one constant region with CDRs. The alpha chain is analogous to the light chain and the beta chain to the heavy chain.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The J chain: The J chain links IgM and dimeric IgA.
B. The alpha chain: The alpha chain is analogous to the light chain.
D. The kappa chain: Kappa is an antibody light chain.
E. The CD3 chain: CD3 is part of the TCR complex for signaling.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 50
A 4-month-old boy is evaluated after an abnormal newborn screen. He was born at term and has had thrush and diarrhea. His immunologist explains that his defect affects gene rearrangement. In developing B cells, the heavy chain variable region is built from three segment types, while the light chain uses only two. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), and he is below the 5th percentile for weight. His lymphocyte count is very low. Which segment is found only in the heavy chain (and TCR beta)?
A. J segments
B. D (diversity) segments
C. C segments
D. Switch segments
E. V segments
Answer: B. D (diversity) segments
Why this is correct: Light chain (and TCR alpha) variable regions are built from V and J segments. Heavy chain (and TCR beta) variable regions use V, D, and J: a J joins a D first, then DJ joins a V. Unused DNA is looped out.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. J segments: Both chain types use J segments.
C. C segments: Constant regions aren't rearranged in V(D)J recombination.
D. Switch segments: Switch regions are used in class switching, not V(D)J recombination.
E. V segments: Both chain types use V segments.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 51
A 5-month-old girl has recurrent thrush, chronic diarrhea, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. She was born at term, and her parents are healthy. Flow cytometry shows no T or B cells, but NK cells are present. Testing shows a defect in the enzyme that cleaves hairpin loops and helps add P and N nucleotides during V(D)J recombination. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), respiratory rate is 58/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Her weight is below the 3rd percentile. Which enzyme is defective?
A. Common gamma chain
B. CD40 ligand
C. ADA
D. RAG1/RAG2
E. BTK
Answer: D. RAG1/RAG2
Why this is correct: RAG-1 and RAG-2 cut DNA for V(D)J recombination and contribute to junctional diversity by opening hairpin loops and adding palindromic (P) and random (N) nucleotides. Complete RAG deficiency causes autosomal recessive SCID.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Common gamma chain: Common gamma chain deficiency causes T-B+NK- SCID.
B. CD40 ligand: CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM.
C. ADA: ADA deficiency causes SCID from toxic metabolites, not recombination failure.
E. BTK: BTK deficiency affects only B cells.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 52
A 3-month-old boy is admitted with a red, scaly rash covering his entire body, diarrhea, and poor weight gain. He has hair loss, enlarged lymph nodes, and hepatosplenomegaly. His CBC shows marked eosinophilia. He was born at term and his parents are first cousins. Testing shows partial function of RAG. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). His weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile. What is the diagnosis?
A. Atopic dermatitis
B. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
C. Omenn syndrome
D. Hyper-IgE syndrome
E. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Answer: C. Omenn syndrome
Why this is correct: Omenn syndrome is a leaky SCID caused by partial RAG function. Patients can't make the diversity needed to fight infection and have erythroderma, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, alopecia, and hepatosplenomegaly, resembling graft-versus-host disease. HSCT is the treatment.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Atopic dermatitis: Atopic dermatitis doesn't cause SCID with RAG defects.
B. Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Chediak-Higashi causes giant granules and silvery hair.
D. Hyper-IgE syndrome: Hyper-IgE syndrome causes eczema and staph abscesses, with a STAT3 variant.
E. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: WAS causes eczema with small platelets.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 53
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has become increasingly unsteady when walking over the past 2 years. She has had several sinus infections and two pneumonias. She has small dilated blood vessels on the whites of her eyes. Her alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. Her parents ask about imaging. She was born at term and walked at 13 months. Her gait is wide-based, and she falls often. Which statement about her condition is correct?
A. She has an X-linked disorder
B. She has DiGeorge anomaly and needs a thymus transplant
C. She has a DNA repair defect and is sensitive to ionizing radiation
D. She has a RAG defect and needs HSCT
E. The telangiectasias always appear before the ataxia
Answer: C. She has a DNA repair defect and is sensitive to ionizing radiation
Why this is correct: Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair defect. Because receptor formation depends on splicing and repair, patients are immunodeficient, prone to malignancy, sensitive to ionizing radiation, and have high AFP. Ataxia appears before the telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, and malignancy.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. She has an X-linked disorder: Ataxia-telangiectasia is autosomal recessive.
B. She has DiGeorge anomaly and needs a thymus transplant: DiGeorge involves heart defects and hypocalcemia.
D. She has a RAG defect and needs HSCT: RAG defects cause SCID, not progressive ataxia with high AFP.
E. The telangiectasias always appear before the ataxia: Ataxia comes first.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 54
A 9-year-old boy is admitted with a rapidly growing abdominal mass and right lower quadrant pain. He was born in the United States and has no history of immunodeficiency. His LDH is very high, and biopsy shows a high-grade B cell lymphoma. Cytogenetics show a gene moved next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain region on chromosome 14. He has lost 3 kg in the last month. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and a large, firm mass is palpable in the right lower quadrant. Which gene is it?
A. BCL2
B. BTK
C. RAG1
D. AIRE
E. MYC
Answer: E. MYC
Why this is correct: Errors in the cutting and pasting of receptor genes can move DNA to the wrong place. Translocation of MYC to the immunoglobulin heavy chain region on chromosome 14 causes unregulated MYC expression and Burkitt lymphoma.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. BCL2: BCL2 translocation occurs in a different lymphoma.
B. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA.
C. RAG1: RAG1 defects cause SCID, not a translocation lymphoma.
D. AIRE: AIRE defects cause APECED.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 55
A 14-year-old boy with seasonal allergies comes to the physician for his allergy shots. He plays baseball and takes cetirizine. His physician explains that his B cells started out making IgM and IgD, but under direction from cytokines they began making IgE with the same antigen specificity. His total IgE is elevated, and skin testing is positive for grass and tree pollen. His lungs are clear. How does this change happen?
A. The VDJ region is joined to a different heavy chain constant gene, and the DNA in between is looped out
B. Alternative splicing of the light chain
C. The light chain switches from kappa to lambda
D. A new V(D)J recombination creates a new variable region
E. The B cell becomes a T cell
Answer: A. The VDJ region is joined to a different heavy chain constant gene, and the DNA in between is looped out
Why this is correct: In class switching, cytokines direct the B cell to join its VDJ to a different heavy chain gene. The same VDJ that made mu and delta chains can make other heavy chains after intervening DNA is looped out, so specificity stays the same.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Alternative splicing of the light chain: Light chains don't determine class.
C. The light chain switches from kappa to lambda: Class is determined by the heavy chain.
D. A new V(D)J recombination creates a new variable region: Class switching keeps the same VDJ, so specificity doesn't change.
E. The B cell becomes a T cell: B cells don't become T cells.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 56
A 10-year-old girl comes to the physician because of joint pain that moves from her knees to her wrists and a new heart murmur. She had a sore throat with fever about 3 weeks ago that went away without treatment. She's in the fourth grade and has no allergies. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Her knees and wrists are warm and tender, and she has a new blowing murmur at the apex. Her ASO titer is elevated. Which mechanism explains her heart findings?
A. Immune complexes deposit in heart valves in a type III reaction
B. T cells directly attack the heart in a type IV reaction
C. Antibodies against Streptococcus pyogenes cross-react with heart antigens in a type II reaction
D. IgE activates mast cells in the heart
E. The bacteria directly infect the heart valve
Answer: C. Antibodies against Streptococcus pyogenes cross-react with heart antigens in a type II reaction
Why this is correct: In rheumatic fever, antibodies made against Strep pyogenes cross-react with self antigens in the heart and joints (molecular mimicry). This type II hypersensitivity can destroy heart valves.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Immune complexes deposit in heart valves in a type III reaction: Rheumatic fever is described as a type II cross-reactive reaction.
B. T cells directly attack the heart in a type IV reaction: The mechanism described is antibody cross-reactivity.
D. IgE activates mast cells in the heart: That's a type I mechanism.
E. The bacteria directly infect the heart valve: The damage comes from cross-reactive antibodies, not direct infection.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Week 6: Immunology / Antibody Function

Question 57
A 6-month-old girl is brought for a well visit. She was born at term, is breastfed, and is meeting milestones. Her mother asks how breast milk protects her from gut infections. The physician explains that an antibody in breast milk coats the gut lining and keeps bacteria and viruses from attaching to their receptors on intestinal cells. She has never had a diarrheal illness, and her immunizations are up to date. Her weight is at the 60th percentile. Which antibody does this?
A. IgD
B. IgG
C. Dimeric IgA
D. IgE
E. Pentameric IgM
Answer: C. Dimeric IgA
Why this is correct: Blocking entry by preventing pathogens from attaching to their receptors is a function only IgA performs. Dimeric IgA, joined by the J chain, protects mucosal surfaces and is the antibody transported across epithelium.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgD: IgD mainly acts as a B cell co-receptor.
B. IgG: IgG neutralizes toxins in tissues and crosses the placenta but isn't the antibody that blocks entry at mucosa.
D. IgE: IgE defends against parasites and causes allergy.
E. Pentameric IgM: IgM is the first antibody made and activates complement.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 58
A 58-year-old farmer comes to the emergency department after stepping on a rusty nail in his barn. He doesn't remember his last tetanus shot. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. The wound is cleaned and he receives a tetanus vaccine. The wound on the sole of his foot is 1 cm deep. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and he has no jaw stiffness. How does this vaccine prevent disease?
A. It activates cytotoxic T cells to kill the bacteria
B. It produces IgG that neutralizes the tetanus toxin
C. It produces IgA that blocks the bacteria from entering the wound
D. It kills the bacteria through complement
E. It produces IgE that activates mast cells
Answer: B. It produces IgG that neutralizes the tetanus toxin
Why this is correct: Clostridium tetani causes tetanus through its toxin tetanospasmin. The tetanus shot creates neutralizing IgG against the neurotoxin, which prevents disease. IgG neutralizes toxins in tissues, and IgA does so at mucosal surfaces.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It activates cytotoxic T cells to kill the bacteria: The protection comes from neutralizing antibody.
C. It produces IgA that blocks the bacteria from entering the wound: IgA protects mucosal surfaces; the vaccine makes IgG against the toxin.
D. It kills the bacteria through complement: The vaccine targets the toxin, not the bacteria.
E. It produces IgE that activates mast cells: IgE is involved in allergy and parasite defense.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 59
A 3-day-old boy has an IgG level higher than his mother's. He was born at 39 weeks and is feeding well. His mother, a 31-year-old nurse, asks how her son can have more IgG than she does. His mother had routine prenatal care and a vaginal delivery. His exam is normal, and his weight is 3.4 kg. Which receptor explains this?
A. FcRn, which actively transports maternal IgG across the placenta
B. CR1 on red cells
C. FcεRI, which transports IgE
D. The J chain, which transports IgA
E. CD40 on B cells
Answer: A. FcRn, which actively transports maternal IgG across the placenta
Why this is correct: FcRn (the Brambell receptor) protects IgG from endosomal degradation, extending its time in circulation. It also actively transports maternal IgG across the placenta, so a baby should have higher IgG levels than the mother.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. CR1 on red cells: CR1 helps clear immune complexes.
C. FcεRI, which transports IgE: FcεRI is a high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells.
D. The J chain, which transports IgA: The J chain links IgM and dimeric IgA.
E. CD40 on B cells: CD40 is involved in T cell help and class switching.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 60
A 60-year-old woman with lymphoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody that binds a protein on her tumor cells. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine. Her oncologist explains that NK cells recognize the bound antibody through their Fc receptors, and crosslinking of these receptors kills the tumor cells by apoptosis. She was diagnosed 6 months ago after noticing enlarged lymph nodes in her neck. Her CBC shows a lymphocytosis. What is this mechanism called, and which antibody subclasses best support it?
A. Opsonization, supported by IgE
B. Neutralization, supported by IgA
C. ADCC, supported by IgM
D. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, supported by IgG1 and IgG3
E. Complement lysis, supported by IgD
Answer: D. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, supported by IgG1 and IgG3
Why this is correct: In ADCC, NK cells recognize antibody bound to targets through their Fc receptors. Crosslinking activates the NK cell and the target dies by apoptosis rather than phagocytosis. IgG1 and IgG3 support ADCC.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Opsonization, supported by IgE: Opsonization leads to phagocytosis and uses IgG; IgE sensitizes mast cells.
B. Neutralization, supported by IgA: Neutralization blocks binding, not killing by NK cells.
C. ADCC, supported by IgM: IgG1 and IgG3 support ADCC.
E. Complement lysis, supported by IgD: IgM and IgG activate complement; IgD doesn't.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 61
A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of joint pain, a facial rash, and foamy urine. She works as a graphic designer and takes no medications. Urinalysis shows protein and red cell casts. Her physician explains that circulating antigen-antibody complexes normally get tagged with complement, bind a receptor on red blood cells, and are cleared in the spleen and liver. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg. Her ANA is positive, and C3 and C4 are low. Which receptor is this, and what happens when clearance fails?
A. FcεRI; mast cells release histamine
B. FcRn; IgG is degraded faster
C. CD59; red cells lyse
D. CD18; neutrophils can't leave the blood
E. Complement receptor 1 (CR1); immune complexes deposit in small vessels and kidneys
Answer: E. Complement receptor 1 (CR1); immune complexes deposit in small vessels and kidneys
Why this is correct: Immune complexes tagged with C4b and C3b bind CR1 on red cells and are cleaned off in the spleen and liver. Without clearance, they aggregate at small vessel basement membranes. In SLE, widespread immune complex deposition can damage glomeruli, and some people get lupus-like disease because they can't tag complexes with C4b or C3b.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. FcεRI; mast cells release histamine: FcεRI is involved in allergy.
B. FcRn; IgG is degraded faster: FcRn protects IgG from degradation.
C. CD59; red cells lyse: CD59 regulates complement lysis of red cells in PNH.
D. CD18; neutrophils can't leave the blood: CD18 is a neutrophil integrin.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 62
A 22-year-old man develops fever and swollen lymph nodes 5 days after being exposed to a new infection. He works as a lifeguard and has no medical problems. His physician orders an antibody test that looks for the first antibody class made in a new immune response, secreted as a pentamer and a potent activator of complement. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). He has tender cervical nodes and a mild sore throat. Which antibody is this?
A. IgA
B. IgM
C. IgD
D. IgG
E. IgE
Answer: B. IgM
Why this is correct: IgM is secreted by plasma cells as a pentamer. It's the first antibody made in an immune response and a potent activator of the complement system.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgA: IgA protects mucosal surfaces and can be a dimer.
C. IgD: IgD mainly serves as a B cell co-receptor.
D. IgG: IgG is the most abundant serum antibody but comes later in the primary response.
E. IgE: IgE is involved in allergy and parasite defense.

Question 63
A 35-year-old woman collapses with hives, wheezing, and low blood pressure 10 minutes after eating shrimp at a restaurant. She has asthma and uses an inhaled steroid. She's treated with epinephrine and recovers. A blood test drawn an hour later helps confirm that her mast cells were activated. Her blood pressure dropped to 78/44 mm Hg before treatment, and she had diffuse wheezing. She has never had a food reaction before. Which marker is this?

E. Hepcidin

B. IL-10: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine.
