Week 6: Immunology / T Cell Receptors & the MHC

Question 64
A 26-year-old man develops a sore throat and fever from a viral infection. He works as a waiter and has no chronic illnesses. His infected pharyngeal cells break down viral proteins in the cytoplasm and display the fragments to cytotoxic T cells. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). His throat is red without exudates, and he has mild cervical lymphadenopathy. Which molecule presents these fragments, and which cells express it?
A. CD40, expressed on B cells
B. MHC class I, expressed only on dendritic cells
C. MHC class I, which is expressed on all nucleated cells
D. MHC class II, expressed on all nucleated cells
E. MHC class II, expressed only on professional APCs
Answer: C. MHC class I, which is expressed on all nucleated cells
Why this is correct: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells deal with antigens inside cells, such as viruses, and receive peptides on MHC class I. MHC class I has a single alpha chain with beta-2 microglobulin, and all nucleated cells express it because any of them can become infected.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD40, expressed on B cells: CD40 interacts with CD40L for T cell help.
B. MHC class I, expressed only on dendritic cells: All nucleated cells express MHC class I.
D. MHC class II, expressed on all nucleated cells: MHC class II is found on professional APCs.
E. MHC class II, expressed only on professional APCs: MHC class II presents to CD4 T cells.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 65
A 4-year-old girl has a bacterial skin infection. She attends preschool and has eczema treated with moisturizers. In her lymph node, a dendritic cell that took up the bacteria presents peptides from them to helper T cells. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). There is a honey-crusted lesion on her cheek and a tender node in front of her ear. Which molecule does it use, and which T cell co-receptor binds it?
A. MHC class II, bound by CD4
B. MHC class I, bound by CD8
C. MHC class I, bound by CD4
D. FcRn, bound by CD4
E. MHC class II, bound by CD8
Answer: A. MHC class II, bound by CD4
Why this is correct: Helper (CD4) T cells deal with antigens that started outside the cell and receive peptides on MHC class II, which has an alpha and a beta chain. Professional APCs (macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells) express MHC class II, and CD4 binds it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. MHC class I, bound by CD8: MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells.
C. MHC class I, bound by CD4: CD4 binds MHC class II.
D. FcRn, bound by CD4: FcRn transports IgG.
E. MHC class II, bound by CD8: CD8 binds MHC class I.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 66
A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV is about to start antiretroviral therapy that includes abacavir. He works as a teacher and has no other medical problems. Before prescribing, his physician orders a genetic test. His CD4 count is 420/mm³, and his viral load is 30,000 copies/mL. He has no rash or fever. What is the test looking for?
A. A CCR5 deletion, which predicts drug toxicity
B. A TAP deficiency, which predicts poor CD8 responses
C. HLA-B27, which predicts arthritis
D. A TLR4 variant, which predicts septic shock
E. HLA-B57, which raises the risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir
Answer: E. HLA-B57, which raises the risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir
Why this is correct: HLA typing can help predict drug reactions. Patients with HLA-B57 are at greater risk of severe hypersensitivity to abacavir, and the FDA recommends screening for this allele before starting therapy.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A CCR5 deletion, which predicts drug toxicity: The recommended pre-abacavir test is HLA-B57.
B. A TAP deficiency, which predicts poor CD8 responses: TAP deficiency isn't screened before abacavir.
C. HLA-B27, which predicts arthritis: HLA-B27 is associated with some forms of arthritis, not abacavir reactions.
D. A TLR4 variant, which predicts septic shock: TLR4 variants affect LPS responses.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 67
A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because of lower back pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning and improves with exercise. He works in IT and plays basketball on weekends. He has no history of trauma. His physician orders HLA typing. His father had similar back pain beginning in his 20s. He has reduced forward bending of the lower spine, and his ESR is 34 mm/h. Which HLA allele is associated with some forms of arthritis like this?
A. HLA-B57
B. HLA-DQ
C. HLA-B27
D. HLA-DR
E. HLA-A
Answer: C. HLA-B27
Why this is correct: HLA typing matters for transplant matching, paternity, forensics, and predicting drug reactions, and some forms of arthritis are associated with HLA-B27.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. HLA-B57: HLA-B57 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity.
B. HLA-DQ: HLA-DQ isn't the arthritis association described.
D. HLA-DR: HLA-DR is a class II gene but isn't the allele linked to this arthritis.
E. HLA-A: HLA-A is a class I gene but isn't the listed arthritis association.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 68
A 9-year-old boy has had recurrent viral, bacterial, and fungal infections since early childhood, including chronic sinus infections. His parents are first cousins. Flow cytometry shows low CD8 T cells, and his cells have very little MHC class I on their surface, though MHC class I genes are normal. Peptides from the cytoplasm can't get into the ER. He is at the 10th percentile for height and weight. Temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), and he has chronic nasal congestion. Which protein is deficient?
A. AIRE
B. BTK
C. RAG1
D. CD40 ligand
E. TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing)
Answer: E. TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing)
Why this is correct: In the endogenous pathway, proteasome-made peptides are delivered into the ER by TAP and loaded onto MHC class I. TAP1 or TAP2 deficiency is autosomal recessive, causes bare lymphocyte syndrome with poor CD8 responses, and is treated with HSCT.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. AIRE: AIRE defects cause APECED.
B. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA.
C. RAG1: RAG1 defects cause SCID with absent T and B cells.
D. CD40 ligand: CD40L defects cause hyper-IgM.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 69
A 2-year-old girl has had severe viral and bacterial infections and chronic diarrhea since infancy. Her parents are first cousins. Her lymphocyte counts are close to normal, but flow cytometry shows her cells have very low expression of HLA molecules. Despite the name of her disorder, both class I and class II molecules are reduced. Her weight is below the 3rd percentile. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). What is the diagnosis and treatment?
A. DiGeorge anomaly; thymus transplant
B. Common gamma chain deficiency; thymus transplant
C. MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome); HSCT
D. XLA; antibody replacement
E. TAP deficiency; antibody replacement
Answer: C. MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome); HSCT
Why this is correct: MHC class II deficiency comes from defective synthesis of HLA molecules and, despite its name, affects both class I and class II. It causes bare lymphocyte syndrome, is autosomal recessive, and is treated with HSCT.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. DiGeorge anomaly; thymus transplant: DiGeorge involves thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcemia, and heart defects.
B. Common gamma chain deficiency; thymus transplant: Common gamma chain deficiency causes T-B+NK- SCID.
D. XLA; antibody replacement: XLA involves absent B cells.
E. TAP deficiency; antibody replacement: TAP deficiency mainly lowers class I and is also treated with HSCT.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 70
A 48-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receives a deceased-donor kidney. He has diabetes and has been on dialysis for 3 years. Minutes after the vessels are connected, the kidney turns mottled and dark, and biopsy shows widespread thrombosis. A clerical error is found: the kidney was ABO incompatible. His blood pressure had been well controlled with amlodipine. He had no prior transplants. What type of rejection is this?
A. Chronic rejection
B. Hyperacute rejection
C. Graft-versus-host disease
D. Acute rejection
E. Type IV hypersensitivity
Answer: B. Hyperacute rejection
Why this is correct: Hyperacute rejection is antibody mediated, happens suddenly, and causes massive thrombosis that's hard to stop. It's caused by ABO mismatches or other pre-existing antibodies to donor antigens. ABO antigens are on red cells and on the vascular endothelium of solid organs.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chronic rejection: Chronic rejection develops over months to years with arteriosclerosis.
C. Graft-versus-host disease: GVHD is donor T cells attacking the host.
D. Acute rejection: Acute rejection takes days to months and is T cell or antibody mediated.
E. Type IV hypersensitivity: The immediate antibody-mediated thrombosis is hyperacute rejection.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 71
A 58-year-old woman received a kidney transplant 6 years ago and has taken tacrolimus and mycophenolate since. She has hypertension and gout. Her creatinine has slowly risen over the past 2 years, and biopsy shows thickened, narrowed arteries in the graft. She has no fever or pain over the graft. Blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Chronic rejection
B. Type I hypersensitivity
C. Graft-versus-host disease
D. Hyperacute rejection
E. Acute rejection
Answer: A. Chronic rejection
Why this is correct: Chronic rejection develops over months to years and is marked by arteriosclerosis in the graft. Hyperacute rejection happens immediately with thrombosis, and acute rejection develops over days to months.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Type I hypersensitivity: Type I reactions are IgE mediated.
C. Graft-versus-host disease: GVHD involves donor T cells attacking the host, usually after stem cell transplant.
D. Hyperacute rejection: Hyperacute rejection happens within minutes.
E. Acute rejection: Her gradual course over years with arteriosclerosis points to chronic rejection.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 72
A 22-year-old man received a hematopoietic stem cell transplant from his sister for leukemia 5 weeks ago. He now has a red rash on his palms and soles, diarrhea, and elevated liver enzymes. He takes acyclovir and fluconazole prophylaxis. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). His leukemia is in remission, and his donor cells have engrafted. His bilirubin is 2.8 mg/dL. What best explains his symptoms?
A. IgE is activating his mast cells
B. Preformed antibodies are causing thrombosis
C. His T cells are attacking the donor cells
D. Donor T cells are attacking his tissues
E. Immune complexes are depositing in his skin
Answer: D. Donor T cells are attacking his tissues
Why this is correct: In graft-versus-host disease, T cells in the graft attack host cells in the immunocompromised patient.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgE is activating his mast cells: That's a type I reaction.
B. Preformed antibodies are causing thrombosis: That's hyperacute rejection.
C. His T cells are attacking the donor cells: That describes rejection of the graft.
E. Immune complexes are depositing in his skin: That describes type III hypersensitivity.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 73
A 30-year-old woman with type A blood needs a transfusion after heavy bleeding during childbirth. She has had no prior transfusions or pregnancies. Her physician explains that she already has antibodies against type B red cells even though she's never been exposed to them. Her hemoglobin is 6.9 g/dL, and blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. She is given crossmatched type A blood. What class are these antibodies?
A. IgA
B. IgG
C. IgD
D. IgE
E. IgM
Answer: E. IgM
Why this is correct: People with type O, A, or B blood make IgM antibodies (isohemagglutinins) against the blood types they don't have. IgM/isohemagglutinin titers are also used as a functional antibody test.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgA: IgA protects mucosa.
B. IgG: Isohemagglutinins are described as IgM.
C. IgD: IgD is a B cell co-receptor.
D. IgE: IgE is involved in allergy.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 74
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a runny nose and sneezing every spring, and his mother is worried because he has started wheezing when he plays outside. He had severe eczema as an infant that has mostly cleared. His father has asthma. His lungs have scattered wheezes, and he has pale, boggy nasal mucosa. His IgE is elevated. Which term describes this progression of diseases?
A. Immunoediting
B. Anticipation
C. Serum sickness
D. Molecular mimicry
E. The atopic march
Answer: E. The atopic march
Why this is correct: Atopy refers to asthma, rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis. They tend to be inherited and to appear in sequence within a person (atopic dermatitis in infancy, then rhinitis, then asthma), which is called the atopic march.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Immunoediting: Immunoediting describes the immune response to tumors.
B. Anticipation: Anticipation is earlier onset in each generation from repeat expansion.
C. Serum sickness: Serum sickness is a systemic immune complex reaction.
D. Molecular mimicry: Molecular mimicry is antibody cross-reactivity with self antigens.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 75
A 32-year-old woman has severe allergic asthma that remains poorly controlled despite high-dose inhaled steroids and a long-acting bronchodilator. She has a dog allergy and a high serum IgE level. She works in a bakery. Her pulmonologist starts an injected monoclonal antibody that keeps IgE from binding the high-affinity receptor on mast cells. She has needed four courses of oral prednisone this year. Her FEV1 is 62% of predicted. Which drug is this?
A. Tezepelumab
B. Eculizumab
C. Mepolizumab
D. Etanercept

Answer: E. Omalizumab
Why this is correct: Omalizumab binds IgE and prevents it from interacting with FcεRI. It's approved for allergic asthma and chronic urticaria.

Question 76
A 45-year-old man has severe asthma with frequent flares and a blood eosinophil count of 900/μL. He also has chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. He works as a firefighter and has never smoked. His physician prescribes a monoclonal antibody that binds a cytokine needed for eosinophil differentiation, maturation, and activation. He has needed oral prednisone five times this year. His FEV1 is 58% of predicted, and his IgE is mildly elevated. Which drug is this, and what does it bind?
A. Mepolizumab, which binds IL-5
B. Tezepelumab, which binds IL-5
C. Omalizumab, which binds IgE
D. Infliximab, which binds IL-5
E. Benralizumab, which binds IL-5 itself
Answer: A. Mepolizumab, which binds IL-5
Why this is correct: Mepolizumab binds IL-5, interfering with eosinophil differentiation, maturation, and activation. It's used for eosinophilic asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and eosinophilic granulomatosis. Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Tezepelumab, which binds IL-5: Tezepelumab binds TSLP.
C. Omalizumab, which binds IgE: Omalizumab binds IgE, not IL-5.
D. Infliximab, which binds IL-5: Infliximab binds TNF-α.
E. Benralizumab, which binds IL-5 itself: Benralizumab binds the IL-5 receptor on eosinophils, not IL-5.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 77
A 28-year-old woman has severe asthma that flares even when her IgE and eosinophil counts are normal. She takes high-dose inhaled steroids and has had three courses of oral prednisone this year. She works as a daycare teacher. Her pulmonologist chooses an antibody against an epithelial alarmin made in the airway that activates innate lymphoid cells. Her FEV1 is 60% of predicted, and she has no nasal polyps. Which drug and target are these?
A. Etanercept, which binds TNF
B. Omalizumab, which binds IgE
C. Tezepelumab, which binds TSLP
D. Alefacept, which binds CD2
E. Mepolizumab, which binds IL-5
Answer: C. Tezepelumab, which binds TSLP
Why this is correct: Thymic stromal lymphopoietin is an alarmin made by airway epithelial cells that activates ILCs, which make Th2-type cytokines. It's important in asthma, and allergic symptoms can come through this pathway without IgE. Tezepelumab is a monoclonal antibody to TSLP for severe asthma.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Etanercept, which binds TNF: Etanercept is used for autoimmune disease like RA.
B. Omalizumab, which binds IgE: Her asthma isn't driven by IgE.
D. Alefacept, which binds CD2: Alefacept blocks T cell activation through CD2.
E. Mepolizumab, which binds IL-5: Mepolizumab targets IL-5 and eosinophils.

Question 78
A 24-year-old woman with cat allergy visits a friend who has two cats. Within minutes she has sneezing, itchy eyes, and wheezing that improve with her inhaler. About 6 hours later, her chest tightness and cough return and last into the next day. She's in graduate school and takes no daily medications. She has no fever. Which cells mainly drive the reaction that began 6 hours later?
A. Neutrophils forming pus
B. Cytotoxic T cells releasing perforin
C. Eosinophils releasing toxic mediators and pro-inflammatory cytokines
D. Plasma cells releasing IgM
E. Mast cells releasing histamine
Answer: C. Eosinophils releasing toxic mediators and pro-inflammatory cytokines
Why this is correct: Early phase reactions come mainly from mast cell and basophil release of histamine. Late phase reactions come mainly from eosinophilic inflammation with toxic eosinophil mediators and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Neutrophils forming pus: Neutrophils drive acute infections.
B. Cytotoxic T cells releasing perforin: That describes type IV and antiviral responses.
D. Plasma cells releasing IgM: IgM isn't the driver of the late-phase allergic reaction.
E. Mast cells releasing histamine: Mast cell histamine drives the early phase.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 79
A 12-year-old boy with mild persistent asthma and allergic rhinitis is started on a daily oral tablet that blocks inflammation, smooth muscle contraction, and mucus secretion caused by mediators synthesized when mast cells are activated. He plays trumpet in the school band and uses an albuterol inhaler as needed. His symptoms worsen in the spring. His lungs have faint expiratory wheezes, and his FEV1 improves after albuterol. Which receptor does this drug block?
A. IL-5 receptor
B. CysLT1
C. H1
D. FcεRI
E. TNF receptor
Answer: B. CysLT1
Why this is correct: Leukotrienes are synthesized by activated mast cells and cause inflammation, smooth muscle contraction, and mucus secretion by binding CysLT1. Antileukotrienes are CysLT1 antagonists. Antihistamines work at the H1 receptor as inverse agonists.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IL-5 receptor: The IL-5 receptor is targeted by benralizumab.
C. H1: H1 is the histamine receptor targeted by antihistamines.
D. FcεRI: FcεRI is the IgE receptor, blocked indirectly by omalizumab.
E. TNF receptor: TNF is blocked by etanercept and anti-TNF antibodies.

Question 80
A 42-year-old woman has had itchy hives on most days for the past 8 months. They come and go within 24 hours and aren't linked to any food or medication. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis and takes levothyroxine. Her total IgE is normal. She has no swelling of her lips or tongue and no fever. The hives are raised, red, and blanching on her trunk and arms. What is the most frequent cause of this condition in adults?
A. C1 inhibitor deficiency
B. An autoantibody to FcεRI that activates mast cells without IgE
C. Immune complex deposition in the skin
D. An NLRP3 gain-of-function mutation
E. An IgE response to a food allergen
Answer: B. An autoantibody to FcεRI that activates mast cells without IgE
Why this is correct: Urticaria and angioedema are rarely IgE mediated in adults. The most frequent cause is an autoantibody to the FcεRI receptor, a stimulatory type II reaction that activates mast cells without IgE. In children, IgE-dependent mechanisms are more common.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. C1 inhibitor deficiency: C1INH deficiency causes swelling without hives.
C. Immune complex deposition in the skin: That's a type III mechanism.
D. An NLRP3 gain-of-function mutation: That causes cold-triggered FCAS1.
E. An IgE response to a food allergen: IgE-mediated urticaria is rare in adults.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 81
A 60-year-old man is treated with high-dose IV penicillin for endocarditis. He has a mechanical aortic valve and takes warfarin. After 10 days, he becomes pale and jaundiced. His hemoglobin falls from 12.5 to 8.2 g/dL, and his direct Coombs test is positive for IgG. He has no history of anemia and has received no transfusions. His LDH is elevated, and haptoglobin is low. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
A. Type I
B. Type II (cytotoxic)
C. Type IV
D. Type III
E. Anaphylactoid
Answer: B. Type II (cytotoxic)
Why this is correct: Type II reactions are antibody mediated (IgG or IgM) against cellular or matrix antigens, causing cell destruction, and can activate complement. Cytotoxic reactions are often hemolytic and caused by drugs like penicillin or blood group antigens.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type I: Type I reactions are IgE mediated and immediate.
C. Type IV: Type IV reactions are T cell mediated and delayed.
D. Type III: Type III reactions come from immune complexes.
E. Anaphylactoid: Anaphylactoid refers to non-IgE reactions that mimic anaphylaxis.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 82
A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of weight loss, a racing heart, heat intolerance, and anxiety for 3 months. She works as a paralegal and drinks two cups of coffee a day. Pulse is 112/min. Her thyroid is diffusely enlarged, and her eyes appear prominent. Antibodies bind and activate a receptor on thyroid cells, causing unregulated thyroxine production. She has a fine tremor in her hands. Her TSH is suppressed, and free T4 is high. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
A. Type I
B. Type III
C. Type II, stimulatory
D. Type II, cytotoxic
E. Type IV
Answer: C. Type II, stimulatory
Why this is correct: Stimulatory or inhibitory type II reactions involve IgG binding to a cell surface receptor. Antibodies to the TSH receptor can stimulate unregulated thyroxine synthesis (hyperthyroidism) or block TSH (hypothyroidism).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type I: Type I reactions are IgE mediated.
B. Type III: Type III involves immune complexes.
D. Type II, cytotoxic: Cytotoxic reactions destroy cells, often causing hemolysis.
E. Type IV: Type IV is T cell mediated.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 83
A 35-year-old man develops fever, a rash, and aching joints 10 days after receiving an antitoxin made from horse serum for a snakebite. He has no other medical problems and works as a park ranger. His symptoms fade over the next week as the foreign protein is cleared. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). He has a hive-like rash on his trunk and swollen, tender knees and wrists. What type of reaction is this?
A. An Arthus reaction
B. Graft-versus-host disease
C. Contact dermatitis
D. Serum sickness, a systemic immune complex (type III) reaction
E. Anaphylaxis
Answer: D. Serum sickness, a systemic immune complex (type III) reaction
Why this is correct: Type III reactions come from immune complexes. Medium-sized complexes get trapped in small vessels, activate complement, and cause vasculitis. Serum sickness is a systemic reaction with rash, arthritis, and fever, and symptoms subside as antigen is cleared and antibody is in excess.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An Arthus reaction: An Arthus reaction is a localized skin or tissue reaction at the injection site.
B. Graft-versus-host disease: GVHD involves donor T cells.
C. Contact dermatitis: Contact dermatitis is a type IV reaction.
E. Anaphylaxis: Anaphylaxis is an immediate IgE reaction.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 84
A 52-year-old man who raises pigeons comes to the physician because of cough, shortness of breath, and fever that begin a few hours after he cleans the coops. Symptoms improve when he's away on vacation. He's never smoked and has no other medical problems. Chest CT shows diffuse small nodules. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. He has fine crackles at both lung bases. What is the mechanism of his illness?
A. Neutrophils can't leave the blood
B. IgE activates mast cells in the airway
C. Antibodies cross-react with lung antigens
D. Inhaled antigen triggers IgG, and immune complexes deposit in the alveoli
E. Cytotoxic T cells destroy alveolar cells
Answer: D. Inhaled antigen triggers IgG, and immune complexes deposit in the alveoli
Why this is correct: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a localized type III reaction caused by inhaling an antigen that provokes an IgG response, with immune complexes depositing in the alveoli.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Neutrophils can't leave the blood: That describes leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
B. IgE activates mast cells in the airway: That's allergic asthma, a type I reaction.
C. Antibodies cross-react with lung antigens: That describes molecular mimicry.
E. Cytotoxic T cells destroy alveolar cells: That describes type IV injury.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 85
A 16-year-old boy comes to the physician because of an itchy, blistering rash on his forearms and legs that started 2 days after he cleared brush in the woods. He has no fever and takes no medications. The rash is in streaks where plants touched his skin. The lesions are red, raised, and have small blisters. His friend who went with him has the same rash. What is the mechanism of this reaction?
A. Type III, mediated by immune complexes
B. Type II, mediated by IgG against skin cells
C. An autoinflammatory reaction from NLRP3
D. Type IV, a delayed T cell-mediated reaction
E. Type I, mediated by IgE
Answer: D. Type IV, a delayed T cell-mediated reaction
Why this is correct: Type IV hypersensitivity is cell mediated and delayed. Examples include contact dermatitis from poison ivy and tuberculin skin test reactions.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type III, mediated by immune complexes: Type III reactions involve immune complexes.
B. Type II, mediated by IgG against skin cells: Type II reactions are antibody mediated.
C. An autoinflammatory reaction from NLRP3: NLRP3 gain of function causes cold-triggered rashes.
E. Type I, mediated by IgE: Type I reactions are immediate.
Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Week 6: Immunology / B Cell & T Cell Activation

Question 86
A 2-year-old boy is admitted with Pneumocystis pneumonia. He has also had recurrent sinus infections and diarrhea. His maternal uncle died of infection in childhood. His IgM is high, while IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low. His B cell count is normal. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. His weight is at the 10th percentile. Which molecule is most likely defective?
A. STAT3
B. BTK
C. NADPH oxidase
D. Common gamma chain
E. CD40 ligand
Answer: E. CD40 ligand
Why this is correct: In hyper-IgM syndromes, IgM is normal or high but IgG, IgA, and IgE are low because class switching can't happen. CD40L on T cells binds CD40 on B cells and macrophages; CD40L deficiency is X-linked, and CD40 deficiency is autosomal recessive. Management includes daily antibiotic prophylaxis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. STAT3: STAT3 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome.
B. BTK: BTK defects cause XLA with absent B cells.
C. NADPH oxidase: That causes CGD.
D. Common gamma chain: That causes T-B+NK- SCID.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 87
A 2-month-old girl is brought for her well-child visit and receives a vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type b. She was born at term and is breastfeeding well. Her mother asks why the vaccine links the bacterial capsule sugar to a protein. She is at the 50th percentile for weight and has a normal exam. She is also getting her other scheduled vaccines. What is the reason?
A. Polysaccharides alone trigger only T-independent IgM responses, and the protein lets helper T cells assist
B. Infants can't make IgM
C. The protein activates complement directly
D. Polysaccharides are presented on MHC class I
E. The protein keeps the vaccine from being degraded
Answer: A. Polysaccharides alone trigger only T-independent IgM responses, and the protein lets helper T cells assist
Why this is correct: Polysaccharides can activate B cells without T cell help by cross-linking receptors, but this makes IgM only without class switching. MHC class II presents peptides, not sugars, so conjugate vaccines attach an immunogenic protein. The B cell takes up the conjugate and presents its peptides to Th cells, which help make antibody against the polysaccharide.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Infants can't make IgM: The problem is that polysaccharides alone give only IgM.
C. The protein activates complement directly: The benefit comes from T cell help.
D. Polysaccharides are presented on MHC class I: MHC class II presents peptides, and polysaccharides aren't presented this way.
E. The protein keeps the vaccine from being degraded: The protein is there to recruit T cell help.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 88
A 45-year-old woman receives a vaccine that contains an adjuvant. She has hypertension and works as a librarian. Her physician explains that the adjuvant helps macrophages express a molecule needed to fully activate T cells, so T cells aren't activated by accident. She is getting a newer protein vaccine before a trip abroad. Her exam is normal. Which interaction provides this second signal?
A. FcRn binding IgG
B. PECAM-1 binding CD18
C. B7 on the APC binding CD28 on the T cell
D. CD4 binding MHC class I
E. CD40 binding MHC class I
Answer: C. B7 on the APC binding CD28 on the T cell
Why this is correct: To prevent unwanted activation, B7 on the APC must bind CD28 on the T cell. B7 is naturally expressed on dendritic cells but must be induced on macrophages by adjuvants.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. FcRn binding IgG: FcRn protects and transports IgG.
B. PECAM-1 binding CD18: PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis.
D. CD4 binding MHC class I: CD4 binds MHC class II.
E. CD40 binding MHC class I: CD40 binds CD40L.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 89
A 20-year-old woman has a viral infection. She's a college student and takes an oral contraceptive. Activated cytotoxic T cells leave the lymph node and find her infected cells displaying viral peptide on MHC class I. She has a sore throat, fever of 38.3°C (100.9°F), and swollen cervical nodes. She has no chronic illnesses. Which molecules in the cytotoxic T cells' lytic granules kill the infected cells?
A. Major basic protein and ECP
B. C5b-C9
C. Tryptase and histamine
D. Granzyme B and perforin
E. Myeloperoxidase and NADPH oxidase
Answer: D. Granzyme B and perforin
Why this is correct: Activated cytotoxic T cells find and destroy virus-infected cells bearing the right peptide on MHC class I. Their lytic granules contain granzyme B and perforin, and they can also trigger apoptosis and release IFN-γ.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Major basic protein and ECP: These are toxic eosinophil enzymes.
B. C5b-C9: The membrane attack complex is part of complement.
C. Tryptase and histamine: These come from mast cells.
E. Myeloperoxidase and NADPH oxidase: These are neutrophil killing tools.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 90
An 18-month-old boy has had eczema since infancy, bloody stools, and four ear infections. His maternal uncle had similar problems and died of a bleeding complication. His platelet count is 30,000/mm³, and the platelets are unusually small. He was born at term. He has eczematous patches on his cheeks and in the creases of his elbows, and petechiae on his legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
B. XLA
C. Hyper-IgE syndrome
D. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
E. DiGeorge anomaly
Answer: D. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Why this is correct: WAS is X-linked recessive. The WAS protein regulates actin polymerization in platelets and lymphocytes, and its loss causes microthrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections from poor T cell function. HSCT is the treatment.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Chediak-Higashi causes giant granules and silvery hair.
B. XLA: XLA doesn't cause eczema or thrombocytopenia.
C. Hyper-IgE syndrome: Hyper-IgE causes eczema and staph abscesses but not small platelets.
E. DiGeorge anomaly: DiGeorge involves heart defects and hypocalcemia.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 91
A 5-month-old boy has had thrush, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. His mother's brother died as an infant from infections. His lymphocyte count is low, and flow cytometry shows no T cells or NK cells, but B cells are present. The receptors for IL-2, 4, 7, 9, and 15 don't work. He was born at term. His weight is below the 3rd percentile, and there's no thymic shadow on chest X-ray. What is the diagnosis?
A. Common gamma chain deficiency
B. CD3 deficiency
C. RAG deficiency
D. ADA deficiency
E. XLA
Answer: A. Common gamma chain deficiency
Why this is correct: The receptors for IL-2, 4, 7, 9, and 15 share a common gamma chain. Defects cause X-linked SCID with a T-B+NK- pattern, because T and NK cells need these receptors and B cells don't. HSCT is the treatment.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. CD3 deficiency: CD3 deficiency is T-B+NK+, with NK cells present.
C. RAG deficiency: RAG deficiency causes T-B- SCID.
D. ADA deficiency: ADA deficiency is autosomal recessive and affects lymphocytes through toxic metabolites.
E. XLA: XLA affects B cells.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Week 6: Immunology / Immunosuppressants

Question 92
A 52-year-old man received a liver transplant 3 months ago and takes tacrolimus and prednisone. He has a history of hepatitis C that was cured. His creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.9 mg/dL, and he has a new tremor in his hands. Blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. His tacrolimus level is above the target range. What is tacrolimus's mechanism, and which side effects are these?
A. It inhibits lymphocyte proliferation; GI upset
B. It binds CD3; cytokine release syndrome
C. It inhibits calcineurin; nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity
D. It blocks TNF; infections
E. It inhibits JAK; bone marrow suppression
Answer: C. It inhibits calcineurin; nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity
Why this is correct: Calcineurin is a phosphatase that regulates T cell activation. Calcineurin inhibitors like cyclosporine and tacrolimus are used in transplants, GVHD, and autoimmune disease, and their side effects include nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It inhibits lymphocyte proliferation; GI upset: That describes antiproliferative drugs.
B. It binds CD3; cytokine release syndrome: That's muromonab-CD3.
D. It blocks TNF; infections: TNF blockers include etanercept and infliximab.
E. It inhibits JAK; bone marrow suppression: JAK inhibitors are a different class.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 93
A 45-year-old woman with Crohn disease has taken high-dose prednisone for most of the past year. She now has groin pain when walking, a rounder face, and new high blood sugar. Her blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. MRI of the hip shows bone death in the femoral head. She has lost muscle bulk in her thighs and has trouble getting up from a chair. Her glucose is 212 mg/dL. Which drug class caused these effects?
A. Monoclonal anti-CD3
B. Calcineurin inhibitors
C. Antiproliferative drugs
D. TNF inhibitors
E. Glucocorticoids
Answer: E. Glucocorticoids
Why this is correct: Glucocorticoids are first-line immunosuppressants that interfere with activated lymphoid cells and inflammatory mediators. Side effects include protein breakdown, hyperglycemia, avascular necrosis of bone, iatrogenic Cushing syndrome with moon facies, myopathy, and hypertension.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Monoclonal anti-CD3: Its side effects are HAMA and cytokine release syndrome.
B. Calcineurin inhibitors: Their main side effects are nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
C. Antiproliferative drugs: Their main side effects are marrow suppression and GI upset.
D. TNF inhibitors: These aren't linked to moon facies and avascular necrosis in this material.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 94
A 50-year-old man has steroid-resistant rejection of a kidney transplant received 2 months ago. He is given a mouse monoclonal antibody that recognizes CD3 on T cells. Within an hour, he develops high fever, chills, and low blood pressure. He had been taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. Temperature rises to 39.6°C (103.3°F), and blood pressure falls to 84/50 mm Hg. What explains this reaction?
A. Hyperacute rejection of the kidney
B. Graft-versus-host disease
C. Nephrotoxicity from calcineurin inhibition
D. Cytokine release syndrome from T cells as the drug inactivates and deletes them
E. An IgE reaction to the antibody
Answer: D. Cytokine release syndrome from T cells as the drug inactivates and deletes them
Why this is correct: Muromonab-CD3 (OKT3) recognizes CD3, inactivates T cells, and rapidly deletes them. It's used for allograft rejection, including steroid-resistant rejection, and can cause cytokine release syndrome and HAMA reactions.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hyperacute rejection of the kidney: Hyperacute rejection happens within minutes of transplant.
B. Graft-versus-host disease: GVHD involves donor T cells attacking the host.
C. Nephrotoxicity from calcineurin inhibition: That's a calcineurin inhibitor effect.
E. An IgE reaction to the antibody: The reaction described is cytokine release.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Question 95
A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis still has swollen, painful hands despite methotrexate. She has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine, and she works as a hairdresser. Her rheumatologist prescribes an oral drug from a newer class of anti-inflammatory agents that block the tyrosine kinases activated when cytokines bind their receptors, preventing phosphorylation of the transcription factors that carry the signal to the nucleus. Her ESR is 52 mm/h, and her rheumatoid factor is positive. What pathway does this drug block?
A. Calcineurin
B. JAK-STAT
C. TNF-α binding its receptor
D. C5 cleavage
E. IgE binding FcεRI
Answer: B. JAK-STAT
Why this is correct: When cytokines bind their receptor subunits, the subunits aggregate and activate Janus kinases (JAKs), which phosphorylate STATs (signal transducers and activators of transcription). Jakinibs are a newer class of anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit this pathway.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Calcineurin: Calcineurin is a phosphatase blocked by tacrolimus and cyclosporine.
C. TNF-α binding its receptor: That's blocked by etanercept and anti-TNF antibodies.
D. C5 cleavage: That's blocked by eculizumab.
E. IgE binding FcεRI: That's blocked by omalizumab.
Objective: Recommend the most appropriate and efficient therapeutic management and prevention strategies for patients with the diseases covered in the module (CBO 2.7)

Week 6: Immunology / Inborn Errors of Immunity

Question 96
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, poor feeding, and a spreading skin infection on his thigh. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and had a normal newborn hearing screen. His parents are first cousins. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse is 176/min, and respirations are 52/min. His CBC shows almost no neutrophils and a very low lymphocyte count. Genetic testing shows mutations in both copies of AK2. What is the only curative treatment?
A. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant
B. Eculizumab
C. Lifelong antibiotics and antifungals
D. Thymus transplant
E. Antibody replacement alone
Answer: A. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant
Why this is correct: Reticular dysgenesis is the most severe form of SCID. Mutations in both copies of AK2 impair hematopoietic stem cell differentiation, affecting both innate and adaptive immunity and causing agranulocytosis with lymphopenia. It's autosomal recessive, and HSCT is the only treatment.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Eculizumab: Eculizumab blocks C5 in PNH.
C. Lifelong antibiotics and antifungals: That's the regimen for CGD; it wouldn't correct a stem cell defect.
D. Thymus transplant: Thymus transplant treats complete DiGeorge anomaly, where the defect is the thymus itself.
E. Antibody replacement alone: Antibody replacement treats XLA, but it wouldn't replace missing neutrophils and T cells.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 97
A 7-month-old girl has had thrush, chronic diarrhea, and repeated pneumonia. She was born at term and her parents are second cousins. Flow cytometry shows no T cells, while B cells and NK cells are present, though her B cells don't function normally. Testing shows a defect in part of the T cell receptor complex responsible for signal transduction. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and her weight is below the 5th percentile. She has white plaques on her tongue. What is the diagnosis?
A. Common gamma chain deficiency
B. XLA
C. CD3 deficiency
D. Reticular dysgenesis
E. RAG deficiency
Answer: C. CD3 deficiency
Why this is correct: CD3 is part of the T cell receptor complex and aids signal transduction. CD3 deficiency is autosomal recessive and causes SCID with a T-B+NK+ pattern, since B and NK cells don't use CD3.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Common gamma chain deficiency: Common gamma chain deficiency causes T-B+NK-, with NK cells absent.
B. XLA: XLA affects B cells only.
D. Reticular dysgenesis: Reticular dysgenesis also wipes out neutrophils.
E. RAG deficiency: RAG deficiency causes T-B- SCID.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 98
A 7-month-old girl has had three ear infections and a bout of bronchiolitis since she turned 4 months old. She was born at term, attends daycare, and is growing well. Her IgG level is low, while IgM and IgA are near normal for age, and her vaccine responses are adequate. Her B cell count is normal. She has no family history of immunodeficiency. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and her exam today is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Common variable immunodeficiency
B. X-linked agammaglobulinemia
C. SCID
D. Hyper-IgM syndrome
E. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
Answer: E. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
Why this is correct: In transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, the infant's own IgG production is delayed as maternal antibody declines, so IgG stays low for a few months. It resolves with time.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Common variable immunodeficiency: CVID needs two or more low immunoglobulin classes without another explanation, and it isn't a transient infant pattern.
B. X-linked agammaglobulinemia: XLA has essentially absent B cells and is X-linked, and she's a girl with normal B cells.
C. SCID: SCID causes severe infections and low lymphocytes.
D. Hyper-IgM syndrome: Hyper-IgM involves failed class switching, not a delay that resolves.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 99
A 12-year-old girl has had eczema, recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, and two pneumonias complicated by lung abscesses. She also has had candida infections of her nails and a fracture from a minor fall. Her IgE and eosinophils are very high. Genetic testing shows an autosomal dominant variant that keeps helper T cells from making IL-17. She has a broad nose and retained baby teeth. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Which gene is it?
A. CXCR4
B. STAT3
C. AIRE
D. NADPH oxidase
E. WAS
Answer: B. STAT3
Why this is correct: Type I hyper-IgE syndrome comes from an autosomal dominant STAT3 variant that keeps helper T cells from making IL-17, which is needed against bacteria and fungi. Patients get staph and candida infections, lung abscesses, eczema, eosinophilia, and skeletal abnormalities.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CXCR4: CXCR4 defects cause WHIM.
C. AIRE: AIRE defects cause APECED.
D. NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD.
E. WAS: WAS gene defects cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Question 100
A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of her fourth pneumonia in 3 years and chronic sinusitis. She was healthy as a child. She has had recurrent Giardia infections. She works as a pharmacist and doesn't smoke. Her IgG and IgA are both low, IgM is low-normal, and B cell counts are normal. HIV testing is negative. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and she has crackles at the right lung base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Chronic granulomatous disease
B. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
C. X-linked agammaglobulinemia
D. Common variable immunodeficiency
E. DiGeorge anomaly
Answer: D. Common variable immunodeficiency
Why this is correct: CVID is a heterogeneous group of disorders with an acquired humoral immunodeficiency phenotype. It's diagnosed when two or more immunoglobulin classes are low without another explanation, and defects in BAFF, TACI, and APRIL are common causes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chronic granulomatous disease: CGD causes high immunoglobulins with deep abscesses.
B. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy: THI occurs in infants and resolves.
C. X-linked agammaglobulinemia: XLA begins in infancy in boys with absent B cells.
E. DiGeorge anomaly: DiGeorge involves T cell defects from birth.
Objective: Recognize the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency in children and adults (CBO 1.2)

Week 7: Hematology / Hematopoiesis & the Lymphoid System

Question 1
A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She has had mild nausea that has improved, takes a prenatal vitamin, and works as a dental hygienist. Her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, and fundal height matches her dates. An ultrasound shows a normally growing fetus. She asks where her baby's blood cells are being made right now. At this stage of pregnancy, which organ is the dominant site of fetal hematopoiesis?
A. The AGM region
B. The lymph nodes
C. The thymus
D. The yolk sac
E. The liver
Answer: E. The liver
Why this is correct: Blood production moves from the yolk sac (3 to 8 weeks) to the liver (6 weeks to birth), spleen (10 to 28 weeks), and bone marrow (18 weeks onward). The liver is the dominant source through mid-gestation. The mnemonic is Young Liver Synthesizes Blood.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The AGM region: The AGM region gives rise to the first true HSCs at weeks 4 to 6 but isn't the dominant site at 20 weeks.
B. The lymph nodes: Lymph nodes aren't a site of fetal hematopoiesis.
C. The thymus: The thymus is where T cells mature, not the main site of fetal blood production.
D. The yolk sac: The yolk sac makes primitive cells only in the first 8 weeks.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 45-year-old man with relapsed lymphoma is preparing for an autologous stem cell transplant. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril and works as a mail carrier. His hematologist gives him daily injections of a growth factor for several days and then collects his stem cells from the peripheral blood by apheresis. His exam is normal, and his CBC shows a rising white count. Which surface marker is used to identify and count the stem cells in the collection?
A. CD5
B. CD20
C. CD138
D. CD34
E. TdT
Answer: D. CD34
Why this is correct: HSCs are CD34+ CD38- Lin-, and CD34 is the marker used clinically to select and quantify stem cell grafts. G-CSF mobilizes HSCs out of the marrow niche into blood so they can be collected by apheresis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD5: CD5 is a T cell marker aberrantly expressed in CLL and mantle cell lymphoma.
B. CD20: CD20 is a B cell marker targeted by rituximab.
C. CD138: CD138 marks plasma cells.
E. TdT: TdT marks lymphoblasts.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Question 3
A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department with fever and chills that began 6 hours ago. He had his spleen removed after a car crash 4 years ago and never received the recommended vaccines. He works as a bartender and smokes occasionally. Temperature is 39.7°C (103.5°F), pulse is 134/min, and blood pressure is 82/46 mm Hg. A blood smear shows small, round, dark purple inclusions in many red cells. What are these inclusions, and which organism is most likely causing his sepsis?
A. Heinz bodies; Staphylococcus aureus
B. Howell-Jolly bodies; Escherichia coli
C. Howell-Jolly bodies; Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Basophilic stippling; Pseudomonas aeruginosa
E. Auer rods; Streptococcus pneumoniae
Answer: C. Howell-Jolly bodies; Streptococcus pneumoniae
Why this is correct: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants the spleen normally removes, so seeing them means asplenia. Without a spleen, patients can't clear encapsulated organisms like S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitidis, so they should be vaccinated before splenectomy, and fever is an emergency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Heinz bodies; Staphylococcus aureus: Heinz bodies are precipitated hemoglobin seen in G6PD deficiency.
B. Howell-Jolly bodies; Escherichia coli: The classic threat after splenectomy is encapsulated organisms like S. pneumoniae.
D. Basophilic stippling; Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Basophilic stippling suggests lead poisoning.
E. Auer rods; Streptococcus pneumoniae: Auer rods are found in myeloid blasts.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 4
A 3-month-old boy with a known 22q11 deletion has a lymph node biopsy during evaluation for recurrent infections. He had surgery for a heart defect at 2 weeks of age and takes calcium supplements. His weight is at the 10th percentile, and he has thrush. The pathologist notes that the node's follicles look normal but one zone between the follicles and the medulla is nearly empty. Which zone is depleted, and why?
A. The paracortex, because T cells are absent
B. The cortex, because B cells are absent
C. The germinal centers, because B cells can't class switch
D. The subcapsular sinus, because lymph can't enter
E. The medulla, because plasma cells are absent
Answer: A. The paracortex, because T cells are absent
Why this is correct: The paracortex is the T cell zone, containing T cells and high endothelial venules. In DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia), T cells are absent, so the paracortex looks empty. The cortex contains B cell follicles, and the medulla contains plasma cells and macrophages.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The cortex, because B cells are absent: B cell follicles in the cortex are described as normal.
C. The germinal centers, because B cells can't class switch: Germinal centers are in the cortex and described as normal.
D. The subcapsular sinus, because lymph can't enter: Lymph flow isn't the issue in DiGeorge.
E. The medulla, because plasma cells are absent: Plasma cells in the medulla aren't the defect in DiGeorge.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Week 7: Hematology / Heme Synthesis & the Porphyrias

Question 5
A 42-year-old man is treated with isoniazid for latent tuberculosis found on a work screening. He drinks two beers a night and eats poorly. Four months later he has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with an MCV of 74, and serum iron and ferritin are high. A marrow iron stain shows iron-laden mitochondria forming rings around erythroblast nuclei. Which step of heme synthesis is impaired?
A. Formation of δ-ALA by ALA synthase, which needs vitamin B6
B. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity
C. Conversion of PBG by PBG deaminase
D. Formation of porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase
E. Globin chain synthesis
Answer: A. Formation of δ-ALA by ALA synthase, which needs vitamin B6
Why this is correct: δ-ALA synthase makes δ-ALA from succinyl CoA and glycine in the mitochondria. It's the rate-limiting step and requires vitamin B6. Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency, heme synthesis fails, iron builds up in mitochondria, and ringed sideroblasts appear.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity: UROD deficiency causes PCT.
C. Conversion of PBG by PBG deaminase: PBG deaminase deficiency causes AIP.
D. Formation of porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase: ALA dehydratase needs zinc and is inhibited by lead.
E. Globin chain synthesis: Globin chain defects cause thalassemia, not ringed sideroblasts.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 6
A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and anxiety that began 2 days after she started phenobarbital for seizures. She has also been dieting heavily. She has tingling in her hands and says she's seeing things. Pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft, and a urine sample turns dark red after sitting in the light. She has no rash. Which treatment most directly addresses the cause of her attack?
A. Iron supplementation
B. Phlebotomy
C. Low-dose chloroquine
D. IV hemin and glucose to suppress hepatic ALA synthase
E. Beta-carotene
Answer: D. IV hemin and glucose to suppress hepatic ALA synthase
Why this is correct: AIP is a PBG deaminase deficiency. P450-inducing drugs like barbiturates use up heme, which releases feedback inhibition of ALAS1, and ALA and PBG build up. IV hemin restores negative feedback on ALAS1, and glucose also inhibits ALAS. She should also stop the precipitating drug.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Iron supplementation: Iron doesn't correct the ALAS1 surge.
B. Phlebotomy: Phlebotomy treats PCT, not AIP.
C. Low-dose chloroquine: Chloroquine is used in PCT.
E. Beta-carotene: Beta-carotene treats EPP.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 7
A 52-year-old man with hepatitis C comes to the physician because of fragile skin and blisters on the backs of his hands that leave scars. He drinks a six-pack of beer most days and works outdoors as a roofer. He has hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed areas and excess hair on his cheeks. His urine is tea-colored. Which enzyme is deficient, and which treatment is appropriate?
A. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; phlebotomy and avoiding sun and alcohol
B. PBG deaminase; IV hemin
C. ALA dehydratase; chelation
D. Ferrochelatase; beta-carotene
E. ALA synthase; vitamin B6
Answer: A. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; phlebotomy and avoiding sun and alcohol
Why this is correct: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria. UROD deficiency causes uroporphyrin to build up in skin, producing blistering photosensitivity. Triggers include alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, estrogen, and iron overload. Treatment is avoiding sun and alcohol, phlebotomy to remove iron, and low-dose chloroquine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. PBG deaminase; IV hemin: That's AIP, which has no photosensitivity.
C. ALA dehydratase; chelation: ALAD inhibition is part of lead poisoning.
D. Ferrochelatase; beta-carotene: That's EPP, which causes painful non-blistering photosensitivity.
E. ALA synthase; vitamin B6: B6-responsive ALAS problems cause sideroblastic anemia.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 8
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he cries in pain within minutes of going outside in the sun, even on cloudy days. His hands and face become red and swollen, but he never gets blisters. His father had the same problem as a child. He's in third grade and takes no medications. His exam today is normal. RBC protoporphyrin is elevated. Which treatment is recommended?
A. Phlebotomy
B. Oral iron
C. Chelation
D. Beta-carotene and sun avoidance
E. IV hemin
Answer: D. Beta-carotene and sun avoidance
Why this is correct: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is an autosomal dominant ferrochelatase deficiency. Protoporphyrin IX builds up and causes immediate burning pain and swelling with sun exposure but no blisters. It's treated with beta-carotene, which scavenges free radicals, and sun avoidance.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Phlebotomy: Phlebotomy treats PCT.
B. Oral iron: Iron doesn't treat EPP.
C. Chelation: Chelation treats lead poisoning.
E. IV hemin: Hemin treats acute attacks of AIP.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 9
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of irritability, abdominal pain, and loss of words she used to say. Her family lives in a house built in 1925 that is being renovated. She is pale, and x-rays show dense lines at the metaphyses of her long bones. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with an MCV of 71, and her smear shows small blue dots in red cells. Which enzymes are inhibited, and what explains the blue dots?
A. ALA synthase; iron trapped in mitochondria
B. UROD; uroporphyrin in red cells
C. G6PD; Heinz bodies
D. PBG deaminase; porphobilinogen deposits
E. ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; ribosomal aggregates from impaired rRNA degradation
Answer: E. ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; ribosomal aggregates from impaired rRNA degradation
Why this is correct: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, raising δ-ALA and protoporphyrin. It causes a microcytic, sideroblastic anemia, encephalopathy, abdominal colic, and lead lines. Basophilic stippling represents ribosomal aggregates because lead inhibits rRNA degradation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ALA synthase; iron trapped in mitochondria: ALAS isn't the lead target, though ringed sideroblasts can occur.
B. UROD; uroporphyrin in red cells: UROD deficiency is PCT.
C. G6PD; Heinz bodies: Heinz bodies come from oxidized hemoglobin in G6PD deficiency.
D. PBG deaminase; porphobilinogen deposits: PBG deaminase deficiency is AIP.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 10
A biochemistry student studies heme regulation in a 30-year-old man who has lived at high altitude for 6 months and has an elevated hemoglobin. His marrow is making more heme, while his liver's heme production is unchanged. He has no symptoms and runs daily. His oxygen saturation is 93% at rest, and his exam is normal. His EPO level is elevated, and he takes no medications. Which statement explains the difference in how heme synthesis is regulated in the two tissues?
A. Marrow ALAS2 is driven by erythropoietin and controlled by iron through an iron response element, while liver ALAS1 is inhibited by heme
B. Both are inhibited by heme
C. Marrow ALAS2 is induced by barbiturates
D. Both are controlled only by vitamin B6 levels
E. Liver ALAS1 is driven by EPO
Answer: A. Marrow ALAS2 is driven by erythropoietin and controlled by iron through an iron response element, while liver ALAS1 is inhibited by heme
Why this is correct: Hepatic ALAS1 is regulated by heme negative feedback, so it can respond to drug demands on P450. Erythroid ALAS2 isn't regulated by heme feedback; EPO stimulates it, and iron controls its translation through an IRE, blocking it when iron is low.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Both are inhibited by heme: Marrow ALAS2 isn't regulated by heme feedback.
C. Marrow ALAS2 is induced by barbiturates: Drug induction affects hepatic heme use through P450.
D. Both are controlled only by vitamin B6 levels: B6 is a cofactor, not the tissue-specific regulator.
E. Liver ALAS1 is driven by EPO: EPO acts on the marrow.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Week 7: Hematology / Anemia

Question 11
A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs for 3 months. Her periods have become very heavy since she had a copper IUD placed. She craves ice and chews it constantly. She is a vegetarian and takes no supplements. She is pale, and her nails are spoon shaped. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL and MCV is 70 fL. Which pattern of iron studies is expected?
A. Low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
B. Normal ferritin, normal TIBC, normal saturation
C. High ferritin, low TIBC, low saturation
D. Low ferritin, low TIBC, high saturation
E. High ferritin, high iron, high saturation
Answer: A. Low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Why this is correct: In iron deficiency, ferritin is low (the most sensitive early marker), serum iron and saturation are low, and TIBC is high because the liver makes more transferrin to catch available iron. Pica and koilonychia are specific signs.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Normal ferritin, normal TIBC, normal saturation: That's typical of thalassemia trait.
C. High ferritin, low TIBC, low saturation: That's anemia of chronic disease.
D. Low ferritin, low TIBC, high saturation: In iron deficiency TIBC rises and saturation falls.
E. High ferritin, high iron, high saturation: That's sideroblastic anemia.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 12
A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 12 years comes to the physician because of fatigue. She takes methotrexate and folic acid, and her joints have been flaring. She has no bleeding. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL with an MCV of 79. Ferritin is high, TIBC is low, and serum iron is low. Oral iron hasn't helped. What explains why her iron isn't reaching her red cell precursors?
A. Lead blocks ferrochelatase
B. High hepcidin closes ferroportin and traps iron in cells
C. She lacks intrinsic factor
D. She has a globin chain deletion
E. Low hepcidin increases iron absorption
Answer: B. High hepcidin closes ferroportin and traps iron in cells
Why this is correct: In anemia of chronic disease, inflammation (IL-6) raises hepcidin, which closes ferroportin, locks iron in macrophages, and blocks gut absorption. Iron is present but hidden from red cell precursors, so supplementation is largely ineffective while hepcidin is high. Treatment targets the underlying disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lead blocks ferrochelatase: She has no lead exposure.
C. She lacks intrinsic factor: Intrinsic factor affects B12, not iron.
D. She has a globin chain deletion: Thalassemia doesn't cause high ferritin with low TIBC from inflammation.
E. Low hepcidin increases iron absorption: High hepcidin, not low, blocks iron.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 13
A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent comes for a pre-employment physical. He feels well, runs 5 miles a day, and takes no medications. His CBC shows hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, and red cell count 6.2 million/μL. His ferritin is normal. His vital signs are normal, and he has no pallor or splenomegaly. His father was told he had a mild anemia that never responded to iron. Which finding best supports thalassemia trait over iron deficiency, and which test confirms it?
A. Ringed sideroblasts; high serum iron
B. A positive Coombs test
C. A Mentzer index above 13; a low ferritin
D. Hypersegmented neutrophils; high MMA
E. A Mentzer index below 13; hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing elevated HbA2
Answer: E. A Mentzer index below 13; hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing elevated HbA2
Why this is correct: Thalassemias cause microcytosis out of proportion to the anemia. The Mentzer index (MCV divided by RBC count) is under 13 in thalassemia and over 13 in iron deficiency; his is 10. Elevated HbA2 on HPLC is the classic marker of β-thalassemia trait.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ringed sideroblasts; high serum iron: Those point to sideroblastic anemia.
B. A positive Coombs test: Coombs testing is for immune hemolysis.
C. A Mentzer index above 13; a low ferritin: That pattern points to iron deficiency.
D. Hypersegmented neutrophils; high MMA: Those point to B12 deficiency.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 14
A 62-year-old man with heavy alcohol use comes to the physician because of fatigue. He drinks a pint of vodka daily and eats poorly. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL with an MCV of 76. Serum iron and ferritin are high, and a Prussian blue stain of the marrow shows ringed sideroblasts. He has spider angiomas and a palpable liver edge. His B12 and folate are normal, and his reticulocyte count is low. What is the mechanism of his anemia?
A. Alcohol acts as a mitochondrial poison that impairs protoporphyrin synthesis, trapping iron in mitochondria
B. Chronic blood loss depletes iron
C. Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis
D. Hepcidin blocks iron absorption
E. A β-globin point mutation
Answer: A. Alcohol acts as a mitochondrial poison that impairs protoporphyrin synthesis, trapping iron in mitochondria
Why this is correct: Sideroblastic anemia is a defect in protoporphyrin synthesis with iron accumulating in mitochondria of erythroid precursors. Causes include alcohol (a mitochondrial poison), lead, and isoniazid (B6 deficiency). Iron and ferritin are high.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Chronic blood loss depletes iron: Iron deficiency has low iron and ferritin.
C. Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis: That causes macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils.
D. Hepcidin blocks iron absorption: That's anemia of chronic disease, with low serum iron.
E. A β-globin point mutation: Thalassemia doesn't cause ringed sideroblasts.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 15
A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and numbness and tingling in both feet for 4 months. She has trouble with balance in the dark. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis and takes levothyroxine. She is pale, and her tongue is smooth and beefy red. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, MCV is 114, and the smear shows neutrophils with 6 lobes. Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are both elevated. Why must folate alone never be used to treat her?
A. Folate would correct the anemia while her neurologic damage continues and can become irreversible
B. Folate raises methylmalonic acid
C. Folate would worsen the anemia
D. Folate causes hypersegmented neutrophils
E. Folate blocks intrinsic factor
Answer: A. Folate would correct the anemia while her neurologic damage continues and can become irreversible
Why this is correct: Elevated MMA is specific to B12 deficiency. Folate enters DNA synthesis downstream of B12, so it corrects the anemia but masks the deficiency while neurologic damage progresses. Pernicious anemia (antibodies to parietal cells or intrinsic factor) needs IM or very high-dose oral B12 and carries a higher gastric cancer risk.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Folate raises methylmalonic acid: MMA rises because of B12 deficiency.
C. Folate would worsen the anemia: Folate would improve the blood count, which is the danger.
D. Folate causes hypersegmented neutrophils: Hypersegmentation comes from the deficiency itself.
E. Folate blocks intrinsic factor: Folate doesn't affect intrinsic factor.
Objective: Demonstrate comprehension of clinical interventions to manage selected hematological, disorders (CBO 1.4)

Question 16
A 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation drinks several glasses of wine a day. She eats mostly fast food. She is tired but has no numbness or balance problems. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, MCV is 108, and the smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Homocysteine is elevated. This is her second pregnancy, and she hasn't been taking her prenatal vitamin. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and fundal height matches her dates. Which additional result would confirm folate deficiency rather than B12 deficiency?
A. An elevated methylmalonic acid level
B. A normal methylmalonic acid level
C. An elevated homocysteine level
D. Hypersegmented neutrophils
E. An elevated ferritin
Answer: B. A normal methylmalonic acid level
Why this is correct: Both B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and high homocysteine. Only B12 is needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, so a high MMA is specific for B12 deficiency, and a normal MMA fits folate deficiency. Folate deficiency also lacks neurologic symptoms.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An elevated methylmalonic acid level: High MMA points to B12 deficiency.
C. An elevated homocysteine level: Homocysteine rises in both.
D. Hypersegmented neutrophils: Both deficiencies cause them.
E. An elevated ferritin: Ferritin doesn't separate these deficiencies.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 17
A 36-year-old woman has iron deficiency anemia from heavy periods and is started on ferrous sulfate. She has GERD and takes an over-the-counter calcium carbonate antacid several times a day, and she likes to take her pills with a glass of milk at breakfast. Six weeks later her hemoglobin hasn't changed. She has no other medical problems and doesn't take any other medications. Her stool is dark, which is expected on iron, and her ferritin is still low. What advice would most likely improve her response?
A. Stop iron because it won't work with inflammation
B. Switch to folic acid
C. Take the iron with vitamin C and not with milk or antacids
D. Take the iron with milk to reduce stomach upset
E. Start IM B12 injections
Answer: C. Take the iron with vitamin C and not with milk or antacids
Why this is correct: Oral iron absorbs best in an acidic environment, so vitamin C helps. Calcium in milk and antacids blocks absorption.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stop iron because it won't work with inflammation: She has iron deficiency, not anemia of chronic disease.
B. Switch to folic acid: Folate doesn't treat iron deficiency.
D. Take the iron with milk to reduce stomach upset: Calcium in milk blocks iron absorption.
E. Start IM B12 injections: B12 treats B12 deficiency.
Objective: Demonstrate comprehension of clinical interventions to manage selected hematological, disorders (CBO 1.4)

Question 18
A 70-year-old man on hemodialysis for diabetic kidney disease comes to the physician because of fatigue. He takes insulin, amlodipine, and a phosphate binder. He has no bleeding. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with a normal MCV, reticulocytes are low, and iron studies are normal. His blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg, and he has pale conjunctivae. His B12, folate, and stool guaiac are normal. What is the cause of his anemia?
A. Hemolysis from a mechanical valve
B. Iron deficiency
C. Low erythropoietin production by the kidneys
D. B12 deficiency
E. Aplastic anemia with pancytopenia
Answer: C. Low erythropoietin production by the kidneys
Why this is correct: In chronic kidney disease, the kidneys make too little EPO, causing a normocytic, non-hemolytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hemolysis from a mechanical valve: He has low reticulocytes, which argues against hemolysis.
B. Iron deficiency: His iron studies are normal.
D. B12 deficiency: His MCV is normal.
E. Aplastic anemia with pancytopenia: His problem is limited to red cells and explained by kidney disease.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Week 7: Hematology / Hemolytic Anemias

Question 19
A 16-year-old girl comes to the emergency department with dark red urine and back pain. She had a sore throat and fever 3 days ago. She takes no medications. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and she is pale and mildly jaundiced. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, LDH is very high, and haptoglobin is undetectable. Her urine contains free hemoglobin, and a week later tubular cells in her urine stain for iron. What does this pattern indicate?
A. Iron deficiency
B. A production failure
C. Intravascular hemolysis
D. Anemia of chronic disease
E. Extravascular hemolysis
Answer: C. Intravascular hemolysis
Why this is correct: In intravascular hemolysis, red cells burst in vessels, causing hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and later hemosiderinuria. Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and drops to near zero, making it the most specific sign. Extravascular hemolysis causes spherocytes and splenomegaly with haptoglobin only mildly low.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Iron deficiency: Iron deficiency doesn't cause hemoglobinuria.
B. A production failure: Hemolysis labs are positive, so this isn't a production problem.
D. Anemia of chronic disease: ACD isn't hemolytic.
E. Extravascular hemolysis: Extravascular hemolysis doesn't cause hemoglobinuria or near-zero haptoglobin.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 20
A 12-year-old boy comes to the physician because of intermittent yellowing of his eyes and right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. His father had his spleen removed as a teenager. He plays soccer and takes no medications. His spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL, MCHC is elevated, and the smear shows small round red cells without central pallor. His direct Coombs test is negative. Which test confirms the diagnosis, and what is the definitive treatment?
A. G6PD assay; avoid fava beans
B. Hemoglobin electrophoresis; hydroxyurea
C. Direct Coombs test; steroids
D. Osmotic fragility test; splenectomy
E. Iron studies; oral iron
Answer: D. Osmotic fragility test; splenectomy
Why this is correct: Hereditary spherocytosis comes from defects in spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Cells lose membrane, become spheres, and are trapped in the spleen. MCHC is high, osmotic fragility is positive, and Coombs is negative. Splenectomy stops the hemolysis, and excess unconjugated bilirubin raises the risk of pigmented gallstones.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. G6PD assay; avoid fava beans: G6PD deficiency causes bite cells, not spherocytes.
B. Hemoglobin electrophoresis; hydroxyurea: Those are for sickle cell disease.
C. Direct Coombs test; steroids: Coombs is negative, and steroids treat warm AIHA.
E. Iron studies; oral iron: This isn't iron deficiency.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)
