Question 75
A 60-year-old woman has had painless lymph nodes in her neck and groin that have grown and shrunk for 3 years. She has no fever or weight loss and works as an accountant. Node biopsy shows a nodular pattern that effaces the node, without tingible-body macrophages or a preserved mantle zone. The cells are CD10+ and BCL2+. Which translocation is expected, and why do the cells survive?
A. t(8;14), which activates MYC
B. t(11;14), which activates cyclin D1
C. t(11;18), which activates MALT signaling
D. t(14;18), which places BCL2 next to IgH and blocks apoptosis
E. t(9;22), which activates ABL
Answer: D. t(14;18), which places BCL2 next to IgH and blocks apoptosis
Why this is correct: Follicular lymphoma is a germinal center B cell neoplasm. t(14;18) puts BCL2 under the IgH promoter, and BCL2 stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane to prevent cytochrome c release, so cells that should die survive. Unlike reactive follicles, FL is BCL2 positive, lacks tingible-body macrophages, and disrupts node architecture.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. t(8;14), which activates MYC: That's Burkitt lymphoma.
B. t(11;14), which activates cyclin D1: That's mantle cell lymphoma.
C. t(11;18), which activates MALT signaling: That's marginal zone MALT lymphoma.
E. t(9;22), which activates ABL: That's CML and Ph+ ALL.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 76
A 58-year-old man has had epigastric pain for years and never took medications for it. He smokes and drinks socially. Endoscopy shows a thickened gastric fold, and biopsy shows a low-grade B cell lymphoma with t(11;18), along with organisms that are urease positive. He has lost 3 kg over 6 months. He has no lymphadenopathy, and his CBC is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
A. Antibiotics to eradicate H. pylori
B. Gastrectomy
C. R-CHOP
D. Cladribine
E. Imatinib
Answer: A. Antibiotics to eradicate H. pylori
Why this is correct: Marginal zone lymphoma of MALT arises in chronic inflammation: the stomach with H. pylori, the thyroid with Hashimoto's, and salivary glands with Sjögren syndrome. It's associated with t(11;18), and gastric MALT lymphoma can be cured by treating H. pylori with antibiotics alone.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Gastrectomy: Antibiotics alone can cure it.
C. R-CHOP: Aggressive chemotherapy isn't the first step for early gastric MALT lymphoma.
D. Cladribine: Cladribine treats hairy cell leukemia.
E. Imatinib: Imatinib treats CML.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of pharmacological, surgical, genetic, complementary, and alternative therapies in management of patients with inherited diseases (e.g., sickle cell disease), cancer (e.g., breast cancer), inherited and immunological disorders (e.g., hereditary angioedema) and infectious diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS) covered in the CBL component of the module (CBO 1.4)

Question 77
A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, diffuse lymph node enlargement, and black stools. He has hypertension and takes amlodipine. Colonoscopy shows many polyps, and his tonsils are enlarged. Flow cytometry shows B cells that are CD5 positive but CD23 negative, and a nuclear stain for cyclin D1 is positive. He has lost 6 kg in 3 months. His spleen is enlarged, and his CBC shows a lymphocytosis of 18,000/μL. Which translocation is present?
A. t(8;14)
B. t(11;14)
C. t(11;18)
D. t(14;18)
E. t(12;21)
Answer: B. t(11;14)
Why this is correct: Mantle cell lymphoma expands the mantle zone around follicles and often involves the GI tract and Waldeyer's ring. t(11;14) moves cyclin D1 next to IgH, driving the G1-to-S transition. It's CD5+ like CLL but CD23 negative, which is the key difference, and it's aggressive.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. t(8;14): t(8;14) is Burkitt lymphoma.
C. t(11;18): t(11;18) is MALT lymphoma.
D. t(14;18): t(14;18) is follicular lymphoma.
E. t(12;21): t(12;21) is a childhood B-ALL finding.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 78
A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rapidly enlarging mass in her neck over 4 weeks, fevers, and night sweats. She has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Biopsy shows diffuse sheets of large B cells with nuclei more than twice the size of a normal lymphocyte, destroying the node's architecture. Her LDH is elevated. PET scan shows disease limited to lymph nodes above the diaphragm. Which statement about this lymphoma is correct?
A. It's mainly a childhood lymphoma
B. It's the most common lymphoma in adults and is potentially curable with R-CHOP
C. It's cured by treating H. pylori
D. It's defined by t(8;14)
E. It's indolent and usually incurable
Answer: B. It's the most common lymphoma in adults and is potentially curable with R-CHOP
Why this is correct: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common NHL and lymphoma overall in adults. It's aggressive but potentially curable with R-CHOP. It can arise de novo or from a low-grade lymphoma, and the germinal center subtype has a better prognosis than the activated B-cell subtype.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It's mainly a childhood lymphoma: Only about 15% of childhood lymphomas are DLBCL.
C. It's cured by treating H. pylori: That's gastric MALT lymphoma.
D. It's defined by t(8;14): That defines Burkitt lymphoma.
E. It's indolent and usually incurable: That describes follicular lymphoma.

Question 79
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain and a mass in his right lower abdomen that has grown quickly over 2 weeks. He was born in the United States and has no history of immunodeficiency. His LDH and uric acid are very high. Biopsy of a mass at the ileocecal valve shows sheets of intermediate-sized cells with scattered pale macrophages, and Ki-67 is nearly 100%. Which translocation is expected?
A. t(14;18), activating BCL2
B. t(15;17), forming PML-RARA
C. t(8;14), moving c-MYC next to IgH
D. t(11;14), activating cyclin D1
E. t(12;21), with a good prognosis
Answer: C. t(8;14), moving c-MYC next to IgH
Why this is correct: Burkitt lymphoma is highly aggressive. t(8;14) moves c-MYC to IgH, driving massive growth. It has a starry-sky pattern (tingible-body macrophages among tumor cells) and a Ki-67 near 100%. The sporadic form involves the abdomen, often the ileocecal valve, while the endemic African form involves the jaw and is linked to EBV.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. t(14;18), activating BCL2: That's follicular lymphoma.
B. t(15;17), forming PML-RARA: That's APL.
D. t(11;14), activating cyclin D1: That's mantle cell lymphoma.
E. t(12;21), with a good prognosis: That's childhood B-ALL.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 80
A 64-year-old man comes to the physician because of itchy, scaly patches on his buttocks and trunk that have been present for years and are now thickening into plaques. Creams for eczema and psoriasis haven't helped. He works as an office manager. Biopsy shows atypical CD4+ T cells clustered within the epidermis. Two years later he develops red skin over his whole body, and his blood contains T cells with brain-like nuclei. What happened?
A. CLL underwent Richter transformation
B. Contact dermatitis spread systemically
C. Hairy cell leukemia developed
D. Mycosis fungoides progressed to Sézary syndrome
E. Psoriasis progressed to erythroderma
Answer: D. Mycosis fungoides progressed to Sézary syndrome
Why this is correct: Mycosis fungoides is the most common T cell lymphoma, mimicking common dermatoses and progressing from patch to plaque to tumor. Pautrier microabscesses of CD4+ T cells form in the epidermis. When it spreads to the blood, it's Sézary syndrome, with cerebriform nuclei and erythroderma.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CLL underwent Richter transformation: This is a T cell disorder.
B. Contact dermatitis spread systemically: The findings are neoplastic.
C. Hairy cell leukemia developed: Hairy cell leukemia is a B cell disorder.
E. Psoriasis progressed to erythroderma: The biopsy shows neoplastic T cells.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 81
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of bruising, pallor, and leg pain for 3 weeks. She attends kindergarten and has no other medical problems. WBC is 8,000/mm³ with blasts, hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, and platelets are 34,000/mm³. Marrow blasts are TdT+, CD19+, and CD10+. She is pale, with petechiae on her legs and mild hepatosplenomegaly. She has no testicular or CNS involvement on exam. Which cytogenetic finding would predict a good prognosis?
A. t(9;22)
B. 11q23 rearrangement
C. t(15;17)
D. t(8;14)
E. t(12;21)
Answer: E. t(12;21)
Why this is correct: B-ALL is the most common childhood malignancy (peak age 3 to 7) and is TdT positive. t(12;21) predicts a good prognosis and is common in children. Age 2 to 10, a low WBC at diagnosis, and a rapid response to therapy are also favorable.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. t(9;22): The Philadelphia chromosome is a poor prognostic marker in ALL.
B. 11q23 rearrangement: KMT2A rearrangement is a poor-prognosis finding in AML.
C. t(15;17): t(15;17) defines APL.
D. t(8;14): t(8;14) defines Burkitt lymphoma.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 82
A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, bruising, and bone pain for a month. He has diabetes and takes metformin. His marrow is replaced by lymphoblasts that are TdT+, CD19+, and CD10+, and cytogenetics show t(9;22). He is pale, with bruises on his arms. WBC is 26,000/mm³ with many blasts, and platelets are 31,000/mm³. How does this translocation affect his disease compared with how it affects CML?
A. In ALL it predicts a good prognosis
B. It means he actually has CML
C. It's only found in children
D. In ALL it marks a poor prognosis, while in CML it's the defining lesion and drug target
E. It predicts response to ATRA
Answer: D. In ALL it marks a poor prognosis, while in CML it's the defining lesion and drug target
Why this is correct: The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), is far more common in adult ALL than childhood ALL and confers a poor prognosis. In CML it's the defining lesion and the target of imatinib. Same translocation, different disease by lineage.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. In ALL it predicts a good prognosis: In ALL it's a poor-prognosis marker.
B. It means he actually has CML: TdT+ CD19+ CD10+ lymphoblasts indicate B-ALL.
C. It's only found in children: It's far more common in adults.
E. It predicts response to ATRA: ATRA targets PML-RARA.
Objective: Apply principles of cytogenetics to identify chromosomal aberrations in various diseases (CBO 1.2)

Question 83
A 6-year-old boy with newly diagnosed B-ALL is starting treatment. He has no other medical problems. His oncologist explains that in addition to systemic chemotherapy, he will receive chemotherapy injected into the spinal fluid even though his first lumbar puncture was normal. His WBC at diagnosis was 12,000/mm³, and his cytogenetics show t(12;21). He has no testicular enlargement. Why is this done?
A. Because he has the Philadelphia chromosome
B. To prevent tumor lysis syndrome
C. Because B-ALL starts in the brain
D. To treat an existing brain mass
E. ALL can hide in sanctuary sites like the CNS and testes
Answer: E. ALL can hide in sanctuary sites like the CNS and testes
Why this is correct: ALL hides in sanctuary sites, the CNS and testes, where systemic chemotherapy reaches poorly. Prophylactic intrathecal chemotherapy is mandatory. Meningeal or testicular involvement at presentation is an unfavorable feature.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Because he has the Philadelphia chromosome: Intrathecal prophylaxis is given in ALL regardless.
B. To prevent tumor lysis syndrome: Intrathecal therapy doesn't prevent tumor lysis.
C. Because B-ALL starts in the brain: B-ALL starts in the marrow.
D. To treat an existing brain mass: His lumbar puncture was normal; this is prophylaxis.

Question 84
A 16-year-old boy comes to the emergency department because of a cough, shortness of breath when lying flat, and swelling of his face and neck for a week. He plays football and has no other medical history. The veins on his chest are distended. Chest x-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows cells that are TdT+, CD2+, CD3+, and CD7+. What is the diagnosis?

B. Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma

D. B-cell ALL
E. Mycosis fungoides
Answer: C. T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
Why this is correct: T-ALL classically presents in adolescent males as a thymic mass in a teenager: an anterior mediastinal mass that can cause SVC syndrome or airway compression. Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Burkitt lymphoma: Burkitt is a mature B cell lymphoma, TdT negative.

E. Mycosis fungoides: MF is a skin T cell lymphoma in older adults.

Question 85
A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump above her collarbone, night sweats, and itching. She has lost 4 kg. Chest imaging shows a mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows large binucleate cells with prominent nucleoli within a background of eosinophils, plasma cells, and histiocytes. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). She has a firm, painless 3-cm supraclavicular node and no hepatosplenomegaly. What immunophenotype do the large cells have?
A. CD138+, CD38+
B. CD15+, CD30+, CD45-negative
C. TdT+, CD3+, CD7+
D. CD5+, CD23+, CD19+
E. CD20+, CD45+, CD15-negative, CD30-negative
Answer: B. CD15+, CD30+, CD45-negative
Why this is correct: Reed-Sternberg cells are large binucleate cells with owl's-eye nucleoli. They're CD15+ and CD30+, CD45 negative, with variable B cell markers. They're a minority of the mass, which is mostly reactive inflammatory cells drawn in by their cytokines.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD138+, CD38+: That's plasma cells in myeloma.
C. TdT+, CD3+, CD7+: That's T-ALL.
D. CD5+, CD23+, CD19+: That's CLL/SLL.
E. CD20+, CD45+, CD15-negative, CD30-negative: That's the popcorn cell of NLPHL.

Question 86
A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a cough and a feeling of fullness in her chest. She's a graduate student and takes an oral contraceptive. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules and Reed-Sternberg variants sitting in clear spaces. She has had night sweats for 2 months. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), and she has a painless supraclavicular node. Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is this?
A. Lymphocyte depleted
B. Mixed cellularity
C. Nodular lymphocyte predominant
D. Lymphocyte rich
E. Nodular sclerosis
Answer: E. Nodular sclerosis
Why this is correct: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, favors young women, and often presents with a mediastinal mass. It shows collagen bands and lacunar cells (RS cells in empty spaces).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lymphocyte depleted: Lymphocyte-depleted has the worst prognosis and occurs in HIV and the elderly.
B. Mixed cellularity: Mixed cellularity is associated with EBV and many eosinophils.
C. Nodular lymphocyte predominant: NLPHL has popcorn cells and doesn't usually involve the mediastinum.
D. Lymphocyte rich: Lymphocyte-rich has the best prognosis but doesn't show collagen bands and lacunar cells.

Question 87

Question 88
A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of a slowly growing lump in his neck over a year. He has no fever or weight loss and works as an electrician. Biopsy shows large cells with folded, lobulated nuclei resembling popcorn. They are CD20+ and CD45+, and CD15 and CD30 are negative. The node is 2 cm, rubbery, and nontender. His CBC and LDH are normal, and CT shows no mediastinal involvement. Which statement about this condition is correct?
A. It is very indolent and can recur late, unlike classical Hodgkin lymphoma
B. It's Burkitt lymphoma
C. It's classical Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis
D. It's CLL
E. It usually presents with a mediastinal mass
Answer: A. It is very indolent and can recur late, unlike classical Hodgkin lymphoma
Why this is correct: Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma has popcorn (L&H) cells that are CD20+, CD45+, CD15 negative, and CD30 negative, the opposite of classical HL. It's very indolent, can recur late, and doesn't usually involve the mediastinum.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It's Burkitt lymphoma: Burkitt has a starry-sky pattern and t(8;14).
C. It's classical Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis: The immunophenotype is the opposite of classical HL.
D. It's CLL: CLL cells are small and CD5+ CD23+.
E. It usually presents with a mediastinal mass: NLPHL doesn't typically involve the mediastinum.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 89
A 67-year-old woman has a serum protein electrophoresis during a workup for neuropathy. She feels well and takes a statin. It shows an IgG M-spike of 1.8 g/dL. Her marrow has 6% plasma cells, and her calcium, creatinine, hemoglobin, and bone x-rays are all normal. She has no bone pain, fatigue, or infections. Her urine protein electrophoresis is normal. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
A. MGUS; monitor over time
B. CLL; watchful waiting
C. Multiple myeloma; start chemotherapy
D. Smoldering myeloma; start chemotherapy
E. Waldenström macroglobulinemia; plasmapheresis
Answer: A. MGUS; monitor over time
Why this is correct: MGUS has fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, an M-protein under 3 g/dL, and no CRAB features. About 1% progress to myeloma per year, so it's monitored rather than treated. CRAB features are what convert a precursor state into treated myeloma.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. CLL; watchful waiting: CLL involves B lymphocytes, not a plasma cell M-spike.
C. Multiple myeloma; start chemotherapy: She has no CRAB features.
D. Smoldering myeloma; start chemotherapy: Her plasma cells are under 10% and M-spike under 3 g/dL.
E. Waldenström macroglobulinemia; plasmapheresis: Her spike is IgG, not IgM.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 90
A 70-year-old African American man comes to the emergency department because of back pain, constipation, confusion, and increased urination. He has had two pneumonias this year. He is pale and tender over his spine. Calcium is 13.4 mg/dL, creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL, and hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL. The smear shows red cells stacked like poker chips, and x-rays show punched-out lesions in his skull. Why are his red cells stacked?
A. HbC crystals
B. Cold agglutinins bind the red cells
C. High serum protein reduces the charge repulsion that normally keeps red cells apart
D. Spherocytes from warm AIHA
E. Fibrinogen from DIC
Answer: C. High serum protein reduces the charge repulsion that normally keeps red cells apart
Why this is correct: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell neoplasm defined by CRAB features: hypercalcemia, renal failure from light chains, anemia, and lytic bone lesions. Rouleaux form because the high serum protein reduces the charge repulsion between red cells. The marrow has more than 10% plasma cells that are CD138+ and CD38+.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. HbC crystals: HbC crystals form inside red cells.
B. Cold agglutinins bind the red cells: Cold agglutinins cause clumping, not rouleaux from high protein.
D. Spherocytes from warm AIHA: Spherocytes don't stack into rouleaux.
E. Fibrinogen from DIC: He has no DIC.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 91
A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of blurred vision, headaches, and frequent nosebleeds. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. Retinal exam shows dilated, tortuous veins. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgM spike. Bone x-rays are normal. He has lost 4 kg and has fatigue. He has lymphadenopathy and an enlarged spleen, and his hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Cold AIHA
B. Polycythemia vera
C. Waldenström macroglobulinemia
D. Multiple myeloma
E. MGUS
Answer: C. Waldenström macroglobulinemia
Why this is correct: Waldenström macroglobulinemia involves an IgM spike and presents with hyperviscosity symptoms rather than lytic bone lesions, which distinguishes it from multiple myeloma.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Cold AIHA: Cold AIHA involves IgM against red cells, not a monoclonal spike with hyperviscosity.
B. Polycythemia vera: PV causes high hemoglobin, not an IgM spike.
D. Multiple myeloma: Myeloma usually has an IgG or IgA spike with lytic bone lesions.
E. MGUS: MGUS doesn't cause hyperviscosity symptoms.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Week 7: Hematology / Protozoan Parasites of the Blood

Question 92
A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever and chills 9 months after returning from a year of volunteer work in Papua New Guinea. He was treated for malaria there and felt well afterward. He takes no medications and hasn't traveled since. Temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), and his spleen is palpable. The smear shows enlarged red cells with Schüffner dots. What caused this episode, and what should be added to his treatment?
A. Drug-resistant P. falciparum; artesunate
B. Babesia infection; atovaquone and azithromycin
C. Dormant hypnozoites in his liver; primaquine or tafenoquine after checking G6PD
D. Reinfection; chloroquine alone
E. Sequestered schizonts; quinine
Answer: C. Dormant hypnozoites in his liver; primaquine or tafenoquine after checking G6PD
Why this is correct: P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites in the liver that cause relapse months to years later. They need chloroquine for the blood stage plus primaquine or tafenoquine to eradicate hypnozoites. G6PD status must be checked first because these drugs can cause severe hemolysis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Drug-resistant P. falciparum; artesunate: P. falciparum doesn't form hypnozoites or relapse.
B. Babesia infection; atovaquone and azithromycin: Babesia causes Maltese crosses and has no liver stage.
D. Reinfection; chloroquine alone: He hasn't traveled, so this is relapse.
E. Sequestered schizonts; quinine: Relapse comes from hepatic hypnozoites.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of action of major classes of antimicrobial drugs and recommend appropriate antibiotic treatments for infectious diseases based on patient factors, pathogens involved, and pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs (CBO 1.4)

Question 93
A 6-year-old girl in Malawi has had fever for 3 days and then has seizures and becomes unresponsive. Her family uses a torn bed net. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F), and glucose is 40 mg/dL. Retinal exam shows whitening and hemorrhages. The smear shows ring forms and crescent-shaped gametocytes but no schizonts. She has been vomiting and hasn't eaten for a day. Her hemoglobin is 6.2 g/dL, and 9% of her red cells are parasitized. What explains her brain involvement?
A. Trypomastigotes destroy neurons
B. Parasites only infect old red cells
C. Merozoites form a Maltese cross in brain vessels
D. Infected red cells express PfEMP1 and stick to cerebral capillaries
E. Hypnozoites reactivated in her brain
Answer: D. Infected red cells express PfEMP1 and stick to cerebral capillaries
Why this is correct: Only P. falciparum exports PfEMP1, producing sticky knobs that cause cytoadherence and rosetting. Parasitized cells sequester in cerebral capillaries, causing occlusion, edema, and anoxia. Schizonts are rarely seen on the smear because heavily infected cells are sequestered.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Trypomastigotes destroy neurons: That describes Chagas disease.
B. Parasites only infect old red cells: That's P. malariae, which has low parasitemia.
C. Merozoites form a Maltese cross in brain vessels: Maltese crosses are Babesia.
E. Hypnozoites reactivated in her brain: Hypnozoites are in the liver of vivax and ovale.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 94
A 45-year-old man who immigrated from Nigeria 10 years ago comes to the physician because of fevers that come every third day. He has had mild anemia for years and takes no medications. His spleen is slightly enlarged. The smear shows band-shaped trophozoites stretched across red cells and schizonts arranged like a rosette. The infected red cells are older cells. Which species is this?
A. Babesia microti
B. Plasmodium knowlesi
C. Plasmodium falciparum
D. Plasmodium malariae
E. Plasmodium vivax
Answer: D. Plasmodium malariae
Why this is correct: P. malariae infects only senescent red cells, causing the lowest parasite burden. It has a 72-hour (quartan) fever cycle, doesn't relapse, and shows band-form trophozoites and rosette schizonts.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Babesia microti: Babesia forms Maltese crosses.
B. Plasmodium knowlesi: Knowlesi resembles malariae on smear but causes daily fevers.
C. Plasmodium falciparum: Falciparum causes 48-hour or irregular fevers with crescent gametocytes.
E. Plasmodium vivax: Vivax has a 48-hour cycle and enlarged red cells with Schüffner dots.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 95
A 30-year-old woman from Ghana moves to Indonesia for work and lives in an area where P. vivax is common. She doesn't take prophylaxis and is never infected over 3 years, while several coworkers get vivax malaria. She has no chronic illnesses. She works as an engineer and lives in a rural town. Her coworkers are mostly from Southeast Asia and Europe. Which red cell feature most likely protects her?
A. She has high fetal hemoglobin
B. She lacks the Duffy antigen
C. She has G6PD deficiency
D. She has sickle cell trait
E. She has hereditary spherocytosis
Answer: B. She lacks the Duffy antigen
Why this is correct: P. vivax uses the Duffy antigen as its red cell receptor. Duffy negativity, common in West and Central Africans, gives nearly complete protection from P. vivax.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. She has high fetal hemoglobin: HbF isn't the vivax protection described.
C. She has G6PD deficiency: G6PD deficiency partially protects against falciparum.
D. She has sickle cell trait: Sickle trait protects against severe falciparum malaria.
E. She has hereditary spherocytosis: HS isn't listed as protective.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 96
A 7-year-old boy in Kenya has had several episodes of mild malaria but never a severe one, while two of his siblings had cerebral malaria. His hemoglobin electrophoresis shows about 60% HbA and 38% HbS. He has no pain crises. He lives in a rural village and sleeps under a bed net most nights. His hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL, and he has normal growth. Which statement is correct?
A. His HbS prevents all malaria infection
B. He is fully protected from P. vivax
C. His sickle cell trait gives him about 80 to 90% protection from severe or fatal falciparum malaria
D. He has sickle cell disease
E. His HbS makes malaria more severe
Answer: C. His sickle cell trait gives him about 80 to 90% protection from severe or fatal falciparum malaria
Why this is correct: Several red cell abnormalities common in endemic regions blunt P. falciparum. HbAS (sickle trait) gives 80 to 90% protection from severe or fatal malaria, a classic example of balancing selection.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. His HbS prevents all malaria infection: He still gets mild infections.
B. He is fully protected from P. vivax: Duffy negativity, not sickle trait, protects against vivax.
D. He has sickle cell disease: He has trait (HbAS) with plenty of HbA.
E. His HbS makes malaria more severe: Sickle trait protects against severe falciparum malaria.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 97
A 35-year-old woman returning from Haiti has uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. She takes an oral contraceptive and has no other illnesses. Because chloroquine sensitivity persists in the Caribbean, she is treated with chloroquine. She visited family there for 3 weeks and didn't take prophylaxis. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and 1% of red cells are parasitized. She is alert and able to take oral medications. How does this drug kill the parasite?
A. It binds free heme and blocks heme polymerase so toxic heme accumulates
B. It inhibits parasite dihydrofolate reductase
C. It kills hepatic hypnozoites
D. It generates reactive oxygen species through an endoperoxide bridge
E. It collapses the parasite's mitochondrial electron transport
Answer: A. It binds free heme and blocks heme polymerase so toxic heme accumulates
Why this is correct: The parasite digests hemoglobin into toxic heme, which its heme polymerase converts to inert hemozoin. Chloroquine, quinine, mefloquine, and amodiaquine bind free heme and block the polymerase, so heme builds up and kills the parasite. The shared mechanism explains cross-resistance.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It inhibits parasite dihydrofolate reductase: That's proguanil.
C. It kills hepatic hypnozoites: That's primaquine and tafenoquine.
D. It generates reactive oxygen species through an endoperoxide bridge: That's the artemisinin mechanism.
E. It collapses the parasite's mitochondrial electron transport: That's atovaquone.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of action of major classes of antimicrobial drugs and recommend appropriate antibiotic treatments for infectious diseases based on patient factors, pathogens involved, and pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs (CBO 1.4)

Question 98
A 28-year-old man returns from Ghana, where he didn't take prophylaxis, and is admitted with confusion, jaundice, and dark urine. Temperature is 40.0°C (104°F), and 12% of his red cells are parasitized with P. falciparum. His creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. He is a 28-year-old graduate student who spent 2 months on a research trip. His platelets are 45,000/mm³, and his glucose is 58 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate treatment?
A. Primaquine alone
B. Benznidazole
C. IV artesunate plus supportive care
D. Oral chloroquine
E. Atovaquone and azithromycin
Answer: C. IV artesunate plus supportive care
Why this is correct: Severe malaria is treated with IV artesunate plus supportive care. Artemisinins generate reactive oxygen species through an endoperoxide bridge.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Primaquine alone: Primaquine targets hypnozoites, which falciparum doesn't form.
B. Benznidazole: Benznidazole treats Chagas disease.
D. Oral chloroquine: Chloroquine is for uncomplicated Caribbean falciparum or non-falciparum species.
E. Atovaquone and azithromycin: That combination treats mild babesiosis.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of action of major classes of antimicrobial drugs and recommend appropriate antibiotic treatments for infectious diseases based on patient factors, pathogens involved, and pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs (CBO 1.4)

Question 99
A 68-year-old man from Connecticut comes to the emergency department with fever, fatigue, and dark urine in July. He had his spleen removed after a car crash years ago. He gardens and hikes often but doesn't recall a tick bite. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, platelets are low, and LDH and bilirubin are elevated. The smear shows red cell inclusions arranged as a tetrad. Which statement about this infection is correct?
A. It relapses from hypnozoites
B. It has no liver stage, and his asplenia raises his risk of severe disease
C. It is carried by Anopheles mosquitoes
D. It is treated with chloroquine and primaquine
E. It multiplies by schizogony in hepatocytes
Answer: B. It has no liver stage, and his asplenia raises his risk of severe disease
Why this is correct: Babesia is carried by Ixodes ticks, the same vector as Lyme disease. Sporozoites invade red cells directly without a liver stage and multiply by merogony. The Maltese cross tetrad is pathognomonic. Asplenia, age over 50, and immunocompromise raise the risk of severe disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It relapses from hypnozoites: Hypnozoites are a feature of P. vivax and ovale.
C. It is carried by Anopheles mosquitoes: Babesia is carried by Ixodes ticks.
D. It is treated with chloroquine and primaquine: Babesiosis is treated with atovaquone plus azithromycin or clindamycin plus quinine.
E. It multiplies by schizogony in hepatocytes: That's Plasmodium.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 100
A 52-year-old woman who emigrated from rural Bolivia 20 years ago comes to the physician because of progressive trouble swallowing and constipation. She grew up in a mud-brick house with a thatched roof. She has had palpitations and ankle swelling, and echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an apical aneurysm. Serology for anti-T. cruzi IgG is positive. Which statement about her management is correct?
A. Antiparasitic drugs won't reverse her established organ damage, so she needs standard management of her heart and GI disease
B. She was infected by the bite of an Anopheles mosquito
C. Primaquine will clear the dormant liver stage
D. She needs atovaquone and azithromycin
E. Benznidazole will reverse her megaesophagus
Answer: A. Antiparasitic drugs won't reverse her established organ damage, so she needs standard management of her heart and GI disease
Why this is correct: Chagas disease is spread when triatomine bug feces are rubbed into a bite wound. Chronic infection destroys myenteric neurons and cardiac tissue, causing megaesophagus, megacolon, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Benznidazole or nifurtimox work best early, and no antitrypanosomal drug reverses established organ damage.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. She was infected by the bite of an Anopheles mosquito: Chagas is spread by triatomine bug feces.
C. Primaquine will clear the dormant liver stage: T. cruzi has no hypnozoite stage.
D. She needs atovaquone and azithromycin: That treats babesiosis.
E. Benznidazole will reverse her megaesophagus: Established organ damage isn't reversed.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Week 7: Hematology / Hematopoiesis & the Lymphoid System

Question 1
A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department with fever and chills that began 8 hours ago. He had his spleen removed after a motorcycle crash 3 years ago and never received the recommended vaccines. He works as a welder and smokes occasionally. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 136/min, and blood pressure is 80/44 mm Hg. He is confused. His WBC is 24,000/mm³. His peripheral smear is shown. What do the red cell inclusions indicate, and which organism most likely caused his sepsis? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Howell-Jolly_body.png)
A. Howell-Jolly bodies from absent splenic function; Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Malaria rings; Plasmodium falciparum
C. Basophilic stippling from lead; Staphylococcus aureus
D. Ringed sideroblasts from B6 deficiency; Salmonella
E. Heinz bodies from G6PD deficiency; Escherichia coli
Answer: A. Howell-Jolly bodies from absent splenic function; Streptococcus pneumoniae
Why this is correct: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants that the spleen normally removes, so seeing them means the patient has no spleen or a non-functioning one. Asplenic patients can't clear encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis), should be vaccinated before splenectomy, and fever is a medical emergency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Malaria rings; Plasmodium falciparum: He has no travel history, and these are nuclear remnants.
C. Basophilic stippling from lead; Staphylococcus aureus: Basophilic stippling is ribosomal aggregates in lead poisoning.
D. Ringed sideroblasts from B6 deficiency; Salmonella: Ringed sideroblasts are seen in marrow with an iron stain.
E. Heinz bodies from G6PD deficiency; Escherichia coli: Heinz bodies are precipitated hemoglobin removed by the spleen.
Image credit: Paulo Henrique Orlandi Mourao and Mikael Häggström, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 70-year-old man dies of a heart attack, and an autopsy is performed. He had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and took lisinopril and atorvastatin. A pathology student reviews tissue from the anterior mediastinum and finds that most of it has been replaced by fat, with a small remaining area of lymphoid tissue. Within the pale central zone of that tissue, she sees the pink, onion-skin structures shown. Which organ is this, and which process happens in the zone that contains these structures? ![Histology section](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/Thymic_corpuscle.jpg)
A. A Peyer's patch; M-cell antigen sampling
B. The thymus; positive selection of T cells
C. The thymus; negative selection of T cells
D. The spleen; red cell filtration in the cords
E. A lymph node; germinal center B cell proliferation
Answer: C. The thymus; negative selection of T cells
Why this is correct: Hassall's corpuscles are onion-skin layers of epithelial reticular cells found only in the thymic medulla. The medulla is where negative selection happens, with AIRE displaying tissue self-antigens. The thymus is largest in childhood and replaced by fat after puberty.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A Peyer's patch; M-cell antigen sampling: Peyer's patches are in the ileum.
B. The thymus; positive selection of T cells: Positive selection happens in the cortex.
D. The spleen; red cell filtration in the cords: The spleen doesn't have Hassall's corpuscles.
E. A lymph node; germinal center B cell proliferation: Germinal centers are pale but lack onion-skin layering.
Image credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 3
A 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease comes for a routine visit. She has had several pain crises this year and takes hydroxyurea and folic acid. She is afebrile, and her vital signs are normal. Her spleen isn't palpable, and ultrasound shows a small, shrunken spleen. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, and reticulocytes are 10%. Her smear shows sickle cells and the red cell inclusions in the image. Her bilirubin is 3.0 mg/dL, and her WBC is 11,200/mm³. What explains the inclusions? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Howell-Jolly_body.png)
A. Lead poisoning
B. Malaria
C. B6 deficiency
D. G6PD deficiency
E. Functional autosplenectomy from repeated splenic infarction
Answer: E. Functional autosplenectomy from repeated splenic infarction
Why this is correct: Howell-Jolly bodies mean the spleen isn't clearing nuclear remnants. In sickle cell disease, repeated infarction causes functional autosplenectomy, which produces the same infection risk as surgical asplenia.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lead poisoning: Lead causes basophilic stippling.
B. Malaria: The inclusions are nuclear remnants, not parasites.
C. B6 deficiency: B6 deficiency causes ringed sideroblasts in the marrow.
D. G6PD deficiency: G6PD causes Heinz bodies and bite cells.

Question 4
A 35-year-old man is scheduled for elective splenectomy in 3 weeks for refractory immune thrombocytopenia. He takes prednisone and has no other medical problems. His platelets are 18,000/mm³. His physician explains that after surgery his smear will show inclusions like the ones in the image, and that he'll be at higher risk for certain infections. His vital signs are normal, and his hemoglobin is 13.8 g/dL. He works as an accountant and has never had a serious infection. What should be done before surgery? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Howell-Jolly_body.png)
A. Nothing is needed
B. Give primaquine
C. Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms
D. Start iron supplementation
E. Transfuse red cells
Answer: C. Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms
Why this is correct: After splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies appear because the spleen no longer removes nuclear remnants. Patients should be vaccinated against encapsulated organisms before surgery, and post-splenectomy fever is treated as an emergency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Nothing is needed: Vaccination is required first.
B. Give primaquine: Primaquine treats malaria hypnozoites.
D. Start iron supplementation: Iron isn't needed for splenectomy.
E. Transfuse red cells: That isn't a pre-splenectomy requirement.

Question 5
A newborn boy has seizures on day 2 of life. He was born at term. His calcium is 6.4 mg/dL, and echocardiogram shows a conotruncal heart defect. Chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. A pathology slide from a normal infant's anterior mediastinum is reviewed for comparison, showing the structures in the image. He has a small jaw and low-set ears. His lymphocyte count is low, and a lymph node sample shows an empty paracortex. From which embryologic structure does this organ develop? ![Histology section](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/Thymic_corpuscle.jpg)
A. The third pharyngeal pouch
B. The yolk sac
C. The first pharyngeal arch
D. The AGM region
E. The fetal liver
Answer: A. The third pharyngeal pouch
Why this is correct: This is DiGeorge syndrome: thymic aplasia, hypoparathyroidism, and conotruncal defects. The thymus, which contains Hassall's corpuscles, develops from the third pharyngeal pouch (Thymus = Third pharyngeal pouch).
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The yolk sac: The yolk sac is an early hematopoietic site.
C. The first pharyngeal arch: That isn't the thymus's origin.
D. The AGM region: That's where the first true HSCs arise.
E. The fetal liver: The liver is a fetal hematopoietic site.

Question 6
A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for multiple autoimmune conditions, including hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, along with chronic candidal nail infections. Her brother has similar problems. She takes hydrocortisone and calcitriol. Her vital signs are normal, and her calcium is 7.8 mg/dL on treatment. Her antibody testing shows many autoantibodies. Genetic testing shows a mutation in a transcription factor expressed in the organ shown in the image, in the region containing these onion-skin structures. What is this protein's normal role? ![Histology section](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/Thymic_corpuscle.jpg)
A. It displays tissue self-antigens in the thymic medulla for negative selection
B. It mobilizes stem cells into the blood
C. It produces thymic hormones for red cells
D. It drives positive selection in the cortex
E. It promotes B-cell class switching
Answer: A. It displays tissue self-antigens in the thymic medulla for negative selection
Why this is correct: AIRE enforces central T-cell tolerance in the thymic medulla by displaying tissue-specific self-antigens so self-reactive T cells are deleted. About 98% of thymocytes don't survive selection.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It mobilizes stem cells into the blood: That's G-CSF.
C. It produces thymic hormones for red cells: That isn't AIRE's role.
D. It drives positive selection in the cortex: Positive selection is in the cortex and doesn't depend on AIRE.
E. It promotes B-cell class switching: That happens in germinal centers.

Question 7
A 20-year-old man has a tender, enlarged lymph node after a skin infection. He has no weight loss and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), and he has a healing cellulitis on his forearm. His WBC is 11,800/mm³. His node is tender and mobile. A biopsy is done, and the pale areas in the follicles shown in the image are examined. What happens in these pale areas? ![Lymph node biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bd/Intrapulmonary_lymph_node_%287493541864%29.jpg)
A. T cells enter through HEVs in the follicle
B. Red cells are filtered
C. HSCs self-renew
D. T cells undergo negative selection
E. B cells proliferate, switch isotypes, and undergo affinity maturation
Answer: E. B cells proliferate, switch isotypes, and undergo affinity maturation
Why this is correct: Secondary follicles have pale germinal centers, showing active stimulation. B cells there proliferate, isotype switch, and undergo affinity maturation. Germinal centers are an exam look-alike for Hassall's corpuscles, but only Hassall's show onion-skin layering.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. T cells enter through HEVs in the follicle: HEVs are in the paracortex.
B. Red cells are filtered: That's the splenic red pulp.
C. HSCs self-renew: That's the bone marrow.
D. T cells undergo negative selection: That's the thymic medulla.

Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Week 7: Hematology / Heme Synthesis & the Porphyrias

Question 8
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of irritability, abdominal pain, and losing words she used to say. Her family lives in a house built in 1925 that is being renovated, and she has been seen chewing on windowsills. She is pale. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL with an MCV of 72 fL. X-rays show dense lines at the ends of her long bones. Her peripheral smear is shown. Which enzymes are inhibited? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/77/Basophilic_stippling_2.jpg)
A. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
B. ALA synthase
C. PBG deaminase
D. ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
E. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Answer: D. ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
Why this is correct: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, raising δ-ALA and protoporphyrin. It causes a microcytic, sideroblastic anemia with basophilic stippling (ribosomal aggregates, because lead inhibits rRNA degradation), encephalopathy, colic, and lead lines.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase: That's porphyria cutanea tarda.
B. ALA synthase: ALAS deficiency from low B6 causes sideroblastic anemia, but lead targets ALAD and ferrochelatase.
C. PBG deaminase: That's acute intermittent porphyria.
E. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase: That's G6PD deficiency with bite cells.
Image credit: Prof. Erhabor Osaro, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 9
A 44-year-old man is being treated with isoniazid for latent tuberculosis found on a work screening. He drinks two beers a night and eats poorly. After 4 months he has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with an MCV of 74 fL, and serum iron and ferritin are high. His B12 and folate are normal. He has no history of lead exposure. A marrow aspirate stained with Prussian blue is shown. Which step of heme synthesis is impaired? ![Bone marrow aspirate, iron stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/82/Ring_Sideroblast_smear_2010-01-13.JPG)
A. Iron absorption through ferroportin
B. Formation of δ-ALA by ALA synthase, which requires vitamin B6
C. Heme breakdown to bilirubin
D. Globin chain synthesis
E. DNA synthesis from B12 deficiency
Answer: B. Formation of δ-ALA by ALA synthase, which requires vitamin B6
Why this is correct: Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency, and B6 is the cofactor for ALA synthase, the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis. Heme synthesis fails, iron builds up in mitochondria, and ringed sideroblasts appear on Prussian blue stain.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Iron absorption through ferroportin: That's blocked by hepcidin in anemia of chronic disease.
C. Heme breakdown to bilirubin: That's part of red cell destruction.
D. Globin chain synthesis: That's thalassemia.
E. DNA synthesis from B12 deficiency: That causes megaloblastic anemia.
Image credit: Paulo Henrique Orlandi Mourao, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 10
A 42-year-old man who works at a battery recycling plant comes to the physician because of cramping abdominal pain and weakness in his right hand. He can't extend his wrist. He takes no medications. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL with an MCV of 74 fL. His urinary ALA is elevated. His blood lead level is high. His gums show a dark line, and his reticulocyte count is low. His smear is shown. Which additional marrow finding would be expected? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/77/Basophilic_stippling_2.jpg)
A. Megaloblasts from B12 deficiency
B. Ringed sideroblasts
C. Marrow fibrosis
D. Clonal plasma cells
E. Hassall's corpuscles
Answer: B. Ringed sideroblasts
Why this is correct: Lead inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase, causing abdominal pain, wrist drop, and mental status changes, with basophilic stippling, elevated ALA, and ringed sideroblasts. Treatment is removing the exposure and chelation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Megaloblasts from B12 deficiency: Lead causes a microcytic anemia.
C. Marrow fibrosis: That's primary myelofibrosis.
D. Clonal plasma cells: That's myeloma.
E. Hassall's corpuscles: Those are in the thymus.
Image credit: Prof. Erhabor Osaro, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 11
A 4-year-old boy with pica is found to have a blood lead level well above normal. He lives in an older apartment with peeling paint. He is irritable, and his hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL. His hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with an MCV of 71 fL. X-rays of his knees show dense metaphyseal lines. His development has slowed. His smear is shown, with fine blue dots throughout some red cells. What causes these dots? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/77/Basophilic_stippling_2.jpg)
A. Malaria parasites
B. Nuclear remnants left by an absent spleen
C. Precipitated oxidized hemoglobin
D. Iron-laden mitochondria
E. Aggregated ribosomes, because lead inhibits rRNA degradation
Answer: E. Aggregated ribosomes, because lead inhibits rRNA degradation
Why this is correct: Basophilic stippling in lead poisoning comes from ribosomal aggregates, because lead inhibits rRNA degradation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Malaria parasites: The dots are ribosomes.
B. Nuclear remnants left by an absent spleen: Those are Howell-Jolly bodies.
C. Precipitated oxidized hemoglobin: Those are Heinz bodies.
D. Iron-laden mitochondria: Those are ringed sideroblasts, seen on marrow iron stain.

Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 12
A 50-year-old man with sideroblastic anemia from isoniazid therapy returns for follow-up. He is still taking isoniazid for latent tuberculosis. He drinks two beers a night. His ALT is normal, and he has no neuropathy. His B12 and folate are normal. His marrow iron stain from last month is shown. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL, MCV is 73 fL, and ferritin and transferrin saturation are high. What should be added to his treatment? ![Bone marrow aspirate, iron stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/82/Ring_Sideroblast_smear_2010-01-13.JPG)
A. Oral iron
B. Vitamin B12
C. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
D. Folic acid alone
E. Hydroxyurea
Answer: C. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
Why this is correct: Isoniazid depletes B6, the cofactor for ALA synthase. Without it, heme synthesis fails and iron builds up in mitochondria, forming ringed sideroblasts. Replacing B6 restores ALA synthase activity.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Oral iron: His iron is already high.
B. Vitamin B12: B12 deficiency is macrocytic.
D. Folic acid alone: Folate isn't the missing cofactor.
E. Hydroxyurea: That's for sickle cell disease.
Image credit: Paulo Henrique Orlandi Mourao, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 13
A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of blisters and fragile skin on the backs of his hands that appear after sun exposure. He has chronic hepatitis C and drinks daily. His urine is tea-colored. He has darkening of the skin on his face. His ALT is mildly elevated, and his hemoglobin is normal. The lesions are shown. Urinary uroporphyrin is elevated. Which enzyme is deficient, and what is the treatment? ![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Blister_in_porphyria_cutanea_tarda.jpg)
A. ALA dehydratase; chelation
B. PBG deaminase; IV glucose and hemin
C. Ferrochelatase; beta-carotene
D. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; avoid sun and alcohol, phlebotomy, and low-dose chloroquine
E. ALA synthase; vitamin B6
Answer: D. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; avoid sun and alcohol, phlebotomy, and low-dose chloroquine
Why this is correct: PCT is a UROD deficiency causing blistering photosensitivity and hyperpigmentation, associated with hepatitis C and alcohol. Urinary uroporphyrin is high. Treatment is avoiding sun and alcohol, phlebotomy, and low-dose chloroquine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ALA dehydratase; chelation: That's lead poisoning.
B. PBG deaminase; IV glucose and hemin: That's AIP, with no photosensitivity.
C. Ferrochelatase; beta-carotene: That's EPP, with no blisters.
E. ALA synthase; vitamin B6: That's sideroblastic anemia.

Week 7: Hematology / Anemia

Question 14
A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs for 3 months. Her periods have become very heavy and last 8 days. She is a vegetarian and takes no supplements. She craves ice. Pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Her conjunctivae are pale. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL, MCV is 69 fL, and reticulocytes are low. Her peripheral smear is shown, with small red cells whose central pallor is more than a third of the cell. Which set of iron studies is expected? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Iron-deficiency_Anemia%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%284422704616%29.jpg)
A. High ferritin, low TIBC, low saturation
B. Normal ferritin and TIBC with a high HbA2
C. High ferritin, high iron, high saturation
D. Low ferritin, low TIBC, high saturation
E. Low ferritin, high TIBC, low saturation
Answer: E. Low ferritin, high TIBC, low saturation
Why this is correct: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with central pallor greater than one-third of the cell. Ferritin is low (the most sensitive early marker), TIBC is high because the liver makes more transferrin, and saturation is low.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. High ferritin, low TIBC, low saturation: That's anemia of chronic disease.
B. Normal ferritin and TIBC with a high HbA2: That's β-thalassemia trait.
C. High ferritin, high iron, high saturation: That's sideroblastic anemia.
D. Low ferritin, low TIBC, high saturation: In iron deficiency TIBC is high.
Image credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 15
A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, hair thinning, and brittle nails for 6 months. She has uterine fibroids with heavy bleeding and hasn't followed up with her gynecologist. She craves ice and chews it throughout the day. Her pulse is 102/min. Her platelets are normal, and her stool is negative for blood. Her fingernails are shown. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 71 fL. Which finding in this photo is most specific for her diagnosis? ![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Koilonychia_iron_deficiency_anemia.jpg)
A. Splinter hemorrhages from endocarditis
B. Koilonychia (spoon nails) from iron deficiency
C. Clubbing from lung disease
D. Jaundice from hemolysis
E. Glossitis from B12 deficiency
Answer: B. Koilonychia (spoon nails) from iron deficiency
Why this is correct: Koilonychia, or spoon-shaped nails, is a sign specific for iron deficiency. Pica, especially craving ice, also points to iron deficiency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Splinter hemorrhages from endocarditis: The photo shows spoon-shaped nails.
C. Clubbing from lung disease: The nails are concave, not clubbed.
D. Jaundice from hemolysis: Jaundice points to hemolysis, not these nail changes.
E. Glossitis from B12 deficiency: Glossitis is a tongue finding.

Question 16
A 60-year-old man who has followed a strict vegan diet for 15 years comes to the physician because of numbness in his feet and trouble with balance in the dark. He takes no supplements. His Romberg sign is positive, and vibration sense is reduced in both feet. His tongue is smooth and beefy red. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with an MCV of 116 fL. His smear is shown. Which lab finding separates his deficiency from folate deficiency? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Hypersegmented_Neutrophils_%2836831145373%29.jpg)
A. Low ferritin
B. Hypersegmented neutrophils
C. Elevated homocysteine
D. A high MCV
E. Elevated methylmalonic acid
Answer: E. Elevated methylmalonic acid
Why this is correct: Megaloblastic anemia shows hypersegmented neutrophils (more than 5 lobes). Both B12 and folate deficiency raise homocysteine, but only B12 is needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, so a high MMA is specific for B12 deficiency. B12 deficiency also causes neurologic symptoms.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Low ferritin: Ferritin reflects iron stores.
B. Hypersegmented neutrophils: Both deficiencies cause them.
C. Elevated homocysteine: Homocysteine rises in both deficiencies.
D. A high MCV: Both are macrocytic.

Question 17
A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue for 4 months. She had twins 8 months ago and is breastfeeding. She takes no supplements. Her conjunctivae are pale. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL, MCV is 70 fL, red cell count is 3.8 million/μL, and ferritin is 6 ng/mL. Her pulse is 98/min, and she craves ice. Her platelets are 420,000/mm³, and her TIBC is high. Her smear is shown. What is her Mentzer index, and what does it suggest? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Iron-deficiency_Anemia%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%284422704616%29.jpg)
A. About 266; anemia of chronic disease
B. About 18; thalassemia
C. About 18; iron deficiency
D. About 5; iron deficiency
E. About 9; thalassemia
Answer: C. About 18; iron deficiency
Why this is correct: The Mentzer index is MCV divided by the RBC count. 70 / 3.8 ≈ 18. Above 13 suggests iron deficiency, and below 13 suggests thalassemia.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. About 266; anemia of chronic disease: That multiplies the values.
B. About 18; thalassemia: Below 13 suggests thalassemia.
D. About 5; iron deficiency: That's the wrong calculation.
E. About 9; thalassemia: 70 / 3.8 is about 18.

Question 18
A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with iron deficiency from heavy periods. She eats a mostly plant-based diet. Her pulse is 96/min, and her conjunctivae are pale. Her TIBC is 460 μg/dL. Her smear is shown. She has no GI symptoms and takes an oral contraceptive now to control bleeding. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, and ferritin is 8 ng/mL. She asks how iron gets from her gut into her blood. Which protein moves iron out of the intestinal cell into the blood? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Iron-deficiency_Anemia%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%284422704616%29.jpg)
A. Transferrin
B. Intrinsic factor
C. DMT1
D. Ferritin
E. Ferroportin, which is regulated by hepcidin
Answer: E. Ferroportin, which is regulated by hepcidin
Why this is correct: Non-heme iron is reduced to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome B and enters the enterocyte through DMT1. It leaves into the blood through ferroportin, which hepcidin guards. High hepcidin in inflammation closes ferroportin and causes anemia of chronic disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Transferrin: Transferrin carries iron in the blood.
B. Intrinsic factor: That's needed for B12 absorption.
C. DMT1: DMT1 brings iron into the enterocyte.
D. Ferritin: Ferritin stores iron.

Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 19
A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and nail changes. He has had epigastric pain treated with over-the-counter antacids for a year and takes ibuprofen daily for back pain. He has no weight loss. His pulse is 104/min, and his conjunctivae are pale. His platelets are 450,000/mm³. His nails are shown. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL and MCV is 68 fL. Stool is positive for blood. A. High MCV and high MMA: That's B12 deficiency.
C. Normal ferritin and TIBC: That fits thalassemia.

Question 20
A 58-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism comes to the physician because of fatigue and tingling in her feet. She takes levothyroxine. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL with an MCV of 118 fL. She has decreased vibration sense in both feet and a positive Romberg sign. Her tongue is smooth and red. Her smear is shown. Her methylmalonic acid is elevated, and antibodies are found in her serum. Against what are these antibodies directed? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Hypersegmented_Neutrophils_%2836831145373%29.jpg)
A. Parietal cells or intrinsic factor
B. ADAMTS13
C. The TSH receptor
D. GpIb
E. Red cell membranes
Answer: A. Parietal cells or intrinsic factor
Why this is correct: Pernicious anemia is autoimmune, with antibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor, B12 can't be absorbed in the terminal ileum, causing megaloblastic anemia with neurologic symptoms.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. ADAMTS13: That's TTP.
C. The TSH receptor: That's Graves disease.
D. GpIb: GpIb is missing in Bernard-Soulier.
E. Red cell membranes: That's AIHA.

Question 21
A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder comes to the physician because of fatigue. He eats very little and drinks a fifth of vodka daily. He has no numbness or balance problems. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. His platelets are 110,000/mm³, and his ALT and AST are elevated. His B12 level is normal. His smear is shown. B. Vitamin B12: B12 deficiency raises MMA and causes neurologic symptoms.
D. Vitamin B6: B6 deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia.
E. Iron: Iron deficiency is microcytic.

Question 22
A 67-year-old man with Crohn disease had his terminal ileum removed 10 years ago. He now has fatigue and trouble feeling his feet. He takes mesalamine. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with an MCV of 114 fL. His vibration sense is reduced in both feet, and his Romberg sign is positive. His methylmalonic acid is elevated. His smear is shown. Why does he have this anemia? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Hypersegmented_Neutrophils_%2836831145373%29.jpg)
A. Iron can't be absorbed in the duodenum
B. Folate is lost in the stool
C. Mesalamine suppresses the marrow
D. Hepcidin blocks ferroportin
E. B12 can't be absorbed without the terminal ileum
Answer: E. B12 can't be absorbed without the terminal ileum
Why this is correct: B12 needs intrinsic factor for absorption in the terminal ileum. Crohn disease and ileal resection cause B12 deficiency, which impairs DNA synthesis and causes megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and neurologic symptoms.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Iron can't be absorbed in the duodenum: Iron deficiency is microcytic.
B. Folate is lost in the stool: Folate deficiency lacks neurologic symptoms.
C. Mesalamine suppresses the marrow: That isn't the cause described.
D. Hepcidin blocks ferroportin: That's anemia of chronic disease.

Week 7: Hematology / Hemolytic Anemias

Question 23
A 12-year-old boy comes to the physician because of intermittent yellow eyes and right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. His father had his spleen removed as a teenager. He plays soccer and takes no medications. His spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and ultrasound shows gallstones. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCHC is elevated, and reticulocytes are 9%. His smear is shown. His direct Coombs test is negative. What is the definitive treatment? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Peripheral_blood_smear_stained_with_MGG_from_a_patient_with_hereditary_spherocytosis.png)
A. Hydroxyurea
B. Avoiding oxidant drugs
C. Splenectomy
D. Steroids
E. Plasma exchange
Answer: C. Splenectomy
Why this is correct: Hereditary spherocytosis comes from defects in spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Cells lose membrane and become spheres that are trapped in the spleen. MCHC is high, osmotic fragility is positive, and Coombs is negative. Splenectomy stops the hemolysis, although spherocytes persist.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hydroxyurea: That treats sickle cell disease.
B. Avoiding oxidant drugs: That's for G6PD deficiency.
D. Steroids: Steroids treat warm AIHA, which is Coombs positive.
E. Plasma exchange: That treats TTP.
Image credit: Joan-Lluis Vives-Corrons, Elena Krishnevskaya, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 24
A 70-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia comes to the physician because of fatigue and yellow eyes for 2 weeks. He has been monitored without treatment for 5 years and takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Hemoglobin has fallen from 12.6 to 7.9 g/dL, reticulocytes are 11%, and LDH is high. His bilirubin is 3.4 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated. His spleen is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. His smear is shown. What result would distinguish his condition from hereditary spherocytosis? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/Warm_autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia_blood_smear.jpg)
A. A positive direct Coombs test for IgG
B. Heinz bodies
C. An elevated MCHC
D. A positive osmotic fragility test
E. A positive Coombs test for C3 only
Answer: A. A positive direct Coombs test for IgG
Why this is correct: Spherocytes appear in both hereditary spherocytosis and warm AIHA; the Coombs test separates them. Warm AIHA is IgG that binds red cells at body temperature, and it's associated with SLE, CLL, and drugs like penicillin. It's treated with steroids, splenectomy, or rituximab.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Heinz bodies: Heinz bodies are G6PD deficiency.
C. An elevated MCHC: Spherocytes of any cause can raise MCHC.
D. A positive osmotic fragility test: Both conditions can show osmotic fragility.
E. A positive Coombs test for C3 only: C3 on the Coombs test points to cold AIHA.

Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 25
A 21-year-old college student is recovering from walking pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma and is finishing azithromycin. When he walks to class in the cold, his fingertips and ears turn blue. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL. His bilirubin is mildly elevated. He has no enlarged lymph nodes. When his blood smear is made at room temperature, it looks like the slide on the right in the image shown, while the slide warmed to body temperature looks normal. Why are steroids a poor choice for him? ![Blood smear on slide](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Cold_agglutinin_disease_-_macroscopic_agglutination_on_blood_smear.jpg)
A. This is IgM-mediated cold AIHA, which responds poorly to steroids
B. He has G6PD deficiency
C. He has hereditary spherocytosis
D. This is warm AIHA, which worsens with steroids
E. He has TTP
Answer: A. This is IgM-mediated cold AIHA, which responds poorly to steroids
Why this is correct: Cold AIHA is caused by IgM that binds red cells in the cold, fixes complement, and causes agglutination. It's linked to Mycoplasma and mononucleosis. The direct Coombs detects C3. Treatment is avoiding cold and rituximab, and steroids work poorly.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. He has G6PD deficiency: G6PD deficiency causes bite cells.
C. He has hereditary spherocytosis: HS doesn't cause cold-induced agglutination.
D. This is warm AIHA, which worsens with steroids: Warm AIHA responds to steroids.
E. He has TTP: TTP causes schistocytes and low platelets.

Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 26
A 16-year-old girl with lifelong mild anemia and gallstones is evaluated. Her mother had her spleen removed. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL, MCHC is 37 g/dL, and reticulocytes are 8%. Her direct Coombs test is negative. Her spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Her bilirubin is 2.6 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated. Her osmotic fragility test is positive. Her smear is shown, with small round cells lacking central pallor. Which protein defect is most likely? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Peripheral_blood_smear_stained_with_MGG_from_a_patient_with_hereditary_spherocytosis.png)
A. ADAMTS13
B. Spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3
C. G6PD
D. Pyruvate kinase
E. β-globin
Answer: B. Spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3
Why this is correct: Hereditary spherocytosis is a defect in the membrane cytoskeleton (spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3). Cells lose membrane, become spheres with no central pallor, and are trapped in the spleen. MCHC is high, and Coombs is negative.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ADAMTS13: That's TTP.
C. G6PD: G6PD deficiency causes bite cells.
D. Pyruvate kinase: That's an enzyme defect, not a membrane defect.
E. β-globin: That's a hemoglobinopathy.
Image credit: Joan-Lluis Vives-Corrons, Elena Krishnevskaya, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 27
A 9-year-old boy with hereditary spherocytosis develops fatigue and pallor 5 days after a fever and rash. His hemoglobin, usually 10 g/dL, is now 5.8 g/dL. His reticulocyte count, usually 9%, is now 0.3%. He is pale but not jaundiced. His spleen is palpable, as it has been for years. His WBC and platelets are normal. His sister had a similar episode last year. His smear is shown. What best explains his reticulocyte count? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Peripheral_blood_smear_stained_with_MGG_from_a_patient_with_hereditary_spherocytosis.png)
A. His spleen has been removed
B. His Coombs test turned positive
C. He has developed iron overload
D. His marrow isn't responding, so red cell production has stopped
E. His hemolysis has stopped
Answer: D. His marrow isn't responding, so red cell production has stopped
Why this is correct: The reticulocyte count is the best indicator that the marrow is responding; above 2–3% corrected means a good response. A near-zero count during a drop in hemoglobin means production has stopped, so the problem isn't more hemolysis alone.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. His spleen has been removed: He still has hereditary spherocytosis with a spleen.
B. His Coombs test turned positive: The low count reflects marrow production.
C. He has developed iron overload: That doesn't stop reticulocyte production.
E. His hemolysis has stopped: Hemoglobin is falling, and reticulocytes reflect production.
Image credit: Joan-Lluis Vives-Corrons, Elena Krishnevskaya, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 28
A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus comes to the physician because of fatigue and yellow eyes for 10 days. She takes hydroxychloroquine. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, reticulocytes are 12%, LDH is high, and haptoglobin is low. Her direct Coombs test is positive for IgG. She also has a malar rash and joint pain. Her bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated. Her spleen is mildly enlarged. Her smear is shown. What is the first-line treatment? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/Warm_autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia_blood_smear.jpg)
A. Avoiding cold
B. Plasma exchange
C. Splenectomy first
D. Steroids
E. Hydroxyurea
Answer: D. Steroids
Why this is correct: Warm AIHA is IgG that binds red cells at body temperature and is associated with SLE, CLL, and drugs. The spleen bites off membrane, forming spherocytes. First-line treatment is steroids, followed by splenectomy or rituximab.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Avoiding cold: That's for cold AIHA.
B. Plasma exchange: That's for TTP.
C. Splenectomy first: Steroids come first.
E. Hydroxyurea: That's for sickle cell disease.

Question 29
A 60-year-old man is being treated with IV penicillin for endocarditis. On day 10 he develops fatigue and dark urine. Hemoglobin has fallen from 12.4 to 8.6 g/dL, and his LDH is high. His bilirubin is 3.4 mg/dL, and haptoglobin is low. His platelets are normal, and his PT and PTT are normal. His smear is shown. What test is needed to confirm the cause? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/Warm_autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia_blood_smear.jpg)
A. ADAMTS13 level
B. A direct Coombs test
C. G6PD level
D. Osmotic fragility
E. An indirect Coombs test
Answer: B. A direct Coombs test
Why this is correct: Spherocytes appear in hereditary spherocytosis and warm AIHA. Penicillin can cause warm AIHA. The direct Coombs test asks whether antibodies are attached to the red cell and confirms AIHA; the indirect Coombs checks serum and is used for pre-transfusion screening.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ADAMTS13 level: That's for TTP.
C. G6PD level: That's for G6PD deficiency.
D. Osmotic fragility: That doesn't separate HS from AIHA.
E. An indirect Coombs test: That checks for antibodies floating in serum.

Question 30
A 19-year-old college student has had sore throat, fever, and swollen neck nodes for 2 weeks. His spleen is palpable. His heterophile test is positive. He now has fatigue and dark urine. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL. His ALT is mildly elevated, and he has atypical lymphocytes. His bilirubin is 2.8 mg/dL, and haptoglobin is low. His blood clumps on the slide at room temperature as shown. Which antibody class is responsible? ![Blood smear on slide](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Cold_agglutinin_disease_-_macroscopic_agglutination_on_blood_smear.jpg)
A. IgG
B. IgA
C. No antibody is involved
D. IgE
E. IgM
Answer: E. IgM
Why this is correct: Cold AIHA is IgM that binds red cells in cold extremities, fixes complement, and causes agglutination. It's associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and mononucleosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgG: IgG causes warm AIHA.
B. IgA: IgA isn't the cause described.
C. No antibody is involved: Agglutination here is antibody-mediated.
D. IgE: IgE isn't involved.

Question 31
A 70-year-old woman comes to the physician because her fingers turn blue and numb in the winter. She has fatigue, and hemoglobin is 9.9 g/dL. Her ears also turn blue outdoors. Her bilirubin is mildly elevated, and haptoglobin is low. She has no enlarged lymph nodes. Her blood clumps when the smear is made at room temperature, as shown. Her direct Coombs test is positive. What does the Coombs test detect on her red cells? ![Blood smear on slide](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Cold_agglutinin_disease_-_macroscopic_agglutination_on_blood_smear.jpg)
A. IgE
B. Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody
C. Complement (C3)
D. Heinz bodies
E. IgG
Answer: C. Complement (C3)
Why this is correct: In cold AIHA, IgM binds red cells in the cold and fixes complement, so the direct Coombs detects C3 on the red cell. In warm AIHA it detects IgG.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgE: IgE isn't involved.
B. Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody: That's in TTP.
D. Heinz bodies: Those need a supravital stain.
E. IgG: IgG is detected in warm AIHA.

Week 7: Hematology / Hemoglobinopathies

Question 32
A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent comes for a pre-employment physical. He feels well, runs 5 miles a day, and takes no medications. His exam is normal, and his spleen isn't palpable. Hemoglobin is 12.0 g/dL, MCV is 63 fL, and red cell count is 6.1 million/μL. Ferritin is normal. His father has a similar blood count and was once given iron that didn't help. His reticulocyte count is normal. His peripheral smear is shown. Which test confirms the most likely diagnosis? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Target_Cells%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%2839144139915%29.jpg)
A. Osmotic fragility test
B. Prussian blue stain of marrow
C. Direct Coombs test
D. Hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing elevated HbA2
E. Serum ferritin
Answer: D. Hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing elevated HbA2
Why this is correct: Thalassemias show target cells with normal or high iron and ferritin, and microcytosis out of proportion to the anemia (Mentzer index MCV/RBC under 13). HPLC quantifies the fractions, and elevated HbA2 is the classic marker of β-thalassemia trait.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Osmotic fragility test: That's for hereditary spherocytosis.
B. Prussian blue stain of marrow: That finds ringed sideroblasts.
C. Direct Coombs test: That diagnoses autoimmune hemolysis.
E. Serum ferritin: His ferritin is already normal.
