Question 33
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician because his hands and feet have been swollen and painful for 2 days. His family recently moved from Ghana, and he didn't have a newborn screen. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), and he is pale. Hemoglobin is 7.3 g/dL, and reticulocytes are 12%. His spleen is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. His bilirubin is 2.8 mg/dL, and his parents both have sickle cell trait. His smear is shown. Which molecular change explains these cells? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Sickle_Cell_Anemia_%285610746554%29.jpg)
A. A spectrin mutation
B. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 6
C. Deletion of three α-globin genes
D. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 26
E. Glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of β-globin
Answer: E. Glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of β-globin
Why this is correct: Sickle cell disease comes from a GAG to GTG mutation that replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of β-globin. Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and distorts the cells. Symptoms appear around 6 months as HbF declines, and dactylitis is a common first sign.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A spectrin mutation: That causes spherocytes or elliptocytes.
B. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 6: That's HbC.
C. Deletion of three α-globin genes: That's HbH disease.
D. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 26: That's HbE.

Question 34
A 26-year-old woman of Southeast Asian descent is found to have mild microcytic anemia during prenatal screening. She feels well and takes a prenatal vitamin. Hemoglobin is 11.1 g/dL, MCV is 66 fL, ferritin is normal, and HbA2 is normal. Her ferritin is 90 ng/mL, and her iron studies are otherwise normal. Her pulse is 78/min, and her spleen isn't palpable. Her smear is shown. Her partner has a similar blood count. The pair is counseled that their fetus could inherit a severe form. What is the genetic basis of her condition? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Target_Cells%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%2839144139915%29.jpg)
A. A spectrin mutation
B. A point mutation in β-globin with high HbA2
C. Glutamic acid to valine at β6
D. Deletion of two α-globin genes on the same chromosome (cis)
E. Deletion of α-globin genes in trans
Answer: D. Deletion of two α-globin genes on the same chromosome (cis)
Why this is correct: α-thalassemia is caused by gene deletions, and target cells with normal iron studies suggest thalassemia. Cis deletions (both on one chromosome) are common in Asian populations and can produce a fetus missing all four genes; trans deletions are common in African populations. A normal HbA2 argues against β-thal trait.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A spectrin mutation: That causes spherocytosis.
B. A point mutation in β-globin with high HbA2: Her HbA2 is normal.
C. Glutamic acid to valine at β6: That's HbS.
E. Deletion of α-globin genes in trans: Trans deletions are typical in African populations.

Question 35
A 30-year-old man is found to have a low MCV on routine labs and was prescribed iron by another clinic. He took it for 3 months without improvement. He is of Greek descent and feels well. Hemoglobin is 12.3 g/dL, MCV is 64 fL, red cell count is 6.0 million/μL, and ferritin is 180 ng/mL. His spleen isn't palpable, and his reticulocyte count is normal. His brother has similar labs. His smear is shown. Which finding would confirm β-thalassemia trait? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Target_Cells%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%2839144139915%29.jpg)
A. Hypersegmented neutrophils
B. A Mentzer index above 13
C. A positive Coombs test
D. HbA2 above 3.5%
E. Low ferritin
Answer: D. HbA2 above 3.5%
Why this is correct: Target cells, normal or high ferritin, and a Mentzer index under 13 (64/6.0 ≈ 11) point to thalassemia. Increased HbA2 (above 3.5%) is diagnostic for β-thalassemia trait.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hypersegmented neutrophils: That's megaloblastic anemia.
B. A Mentzer index above 13: His is about 11.
C. A positive Coombs test: That's AIHA.
E. Low ferritin: His ferritin is high.

Question 36
A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has had three hospital admissions for pain crises this year and one episode of acute chest syndrome. He takes folic acid. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL. His reticulocyte count is 11%, and his bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL. His parents both have sickle cell trait. His smear is shown. His hematologist recommends a daily oral drug. How does it help? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Sickle_Cell_Anemia_%285610746554%29.jpg)
A. It raises 2,3-BPG
B. It lowers HbA2
C. It raises HbF, which inhibits HbS polymerization
D. It chelates iron
E. It inhibits JAK2
Answer: C. It raises HbF, which inhibits HbS polymerization
Why this is correct: HbF inhibits polymerization of HbS, which is why symptoms are delayed until about 6 months. Hydroxyurea increases HbF, and BCL11A gene editing uses the same lever.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It raises 2,3-BPG: That would promote sickling.
B. It lowers HbA2: That isn't the mechanism.
D. It chelates iron: That's for iron overload.
E. It inhibits JAK2: That's used for myelofibrosis.

Question 37
A 22-year-old man with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department with a painful erection that has lasted 5 hours. He takes hydroxyurea. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL, LDH is high, and haptoglobin is undetectable. He is in severe pain. His reticulocyte count is 12%, and his bilirubin is 3.6 mg/dL. His echocardiogram last year showed early pulmonary hypertension. His smear is shown. Which mechanism links his hemolysis to this complication? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Sickle_Cell_Anemia_%285610746554%29.jpg)
A. Antibodies attack the corpora
B. Iron deposition in the penis
C. HbF polymerizes
D. Low platelets cause bleeding
E. Free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing endothelial dysfunction
Answer: E. Free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing endothelial dysfunction
Why this is correct: In intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing endothelial dysfunction that leads to pulmonary hypertension and priapism.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Antibodies attack the corpora: That isn't the mechanism.
B. Iron deposition in the penis: That isn't the mechanism.
C. HbF polymerizes: HbF inhibits polymerization.
D. Low platelets cause bleeding: Priapism isn't bleeding.

Question 38
A 4-year-old girl with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department with a fever of 39.5°C (103.1°F). She has had several pain crises. She takes penicillin prophylaxis but missed doses this week. Pulse is 150/min, and blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg. Her WBC is 26,000/mm³. Her spleen isn't palpable. Her smear is shown, including small nuclear remnants in some red cells. Why is her fever an emergency? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Sickle_Cell_Anemia_%285610746554%29.jpg)
A. Fever causes lead release
B. Functional asplenia puts her at risk for overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms
C. Fever is never an emergency in children
D. She's at risk of malaria
E. Fever triggers TTP
Answer: B. Functional asplenia puts her at risk for overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms
Why this is correct: Repeated splenic infarction in sickle cell disease causes functional autosplenectomy, with Howell-Jolly bodies and the same infection risk as surgical asplenia. Fever in an asplenic patient is treated as an emergency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fever causes lead release: That isn't related.
C. Fever is never an emergency in children: Asplenia makes fever an emergency.
D. She's at risk of malaria: Her risk is from encapsulated bacteria.
E. Fever triggers TTP: That isn't the concern.

Week 7: Hematology / Hemostasis, Thrombosis & Bleeding Disorders

Question 39
A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, confusion, and abdominal pain. She takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and she has petechiae on her legs. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelets are 22,000/mm³, reticulocytes are 4.2%, creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL, and haptoglobin is undetectable. PT and PTT are normal. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL, and LDH is high. Her smear is shown. What is the most appropriate next step? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Micrograph_of_schistocytes.jpg)
A. Transfuse platelets
B. Give FFP and cryoprecipitate for DIC
C. Start plasma exchange immediately
D. Wait for ADAMTS13 results
E. Start steroids alone for warm AIHA
Answer: C. Start plasma exchange immediately
Why this is correct: Schistocytes (helmet cells) mean a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. With low platelets, confusion, mild renal failure, and normal PT/PTT, this is TTP from ADAMTS13 deficiency. Plasma exchange should start without waiting for ADAMTS13 results, and platelets shouldn't be transfused.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Transfuse platelets: Platelets add fuel to the fire in TTP.
B. Give FFP and cryoprecipitate for DIC: Her PT and PTT are normal.
D. Wait for ADAMTS13 results: Treatment shouldn't be delayed.
E. Start steroids alone for warm AIHA: Schistocytes and normal PT/PTT point to TTP.

Question 40
A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with TTP after presenting with fever, confusion, and low platelets. She works as a paralegal and doesn't smoke. Her pulse is 112/min. She has no medical history. She takes an oral contraceptive. Her platelets are 16,000/mm³, and her creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. Her PT and PTT are normal. Her smear is shown. Her ADAMTS13 activity comes back very low. How does this deficiency cause her disease? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Micrograph_of_schistocytes.jpg)
A. Large vWF multimers aren't cleaved, forming platelet microthrombi that shear red cells
B. Clotting factors are consumed
C. Red cell membranes lack spectrin
D. Antibodies coat red cells, and the spleen removes them
E. The platelet GpIb receptor is missing
Answer: A. Large vWF multimers aren't cleaved, forming platelet microthrombi that shear red cells
Why this is correct: TTP comes from ADAMTS13 deficiency. Without it, large vWF multimers aren't cleaved, platelets clump into microthrombi in small vessels, and passing red cells are sheared into schistocytes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Clotting factors are consumed: That's DIC, with a long PT and PTT.
C. Red cell membranes lack spectrin: That's spherocytosis.
D. Antibodies coat red cells, and the spleen removes them: That's AIHA.
E. The platelet GpIb receptor is missing: That's Bernard-Soulier.

Question 41
A 62-year-old man is admitted with sepsis from pneumonia. He has COPD and diabetes and takes metformin. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). On day 2 he oozes from his IV sites. He is on norepinephrine for low blood pressure. His hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, and his creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL. His smear is shown. Platelets are 40,000/mm³, PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and D-dimer is very high. What separates his condition from TTP? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Micrograph_of_schistocytes.jpg)
A. Elevated PT, PTT, and D-dimer
B. A positive Coombs test
C. Low platelets
D. Normal haptoglobin
E. The presence of schistocytes
Answer: A. Elevated PT, PTT, and D-dimer
Why this is correct: Schistocytes appear in TTP, HUS, and DIC. TTP has a normal PT and PTT, while DIC has elevated PT, PTT, and D-dimer because clotting factors are consumed.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A positive Coombs test: Neither is antibody-mediated hemolysis.
C. Low platelets: Both have low platelets.
D. Normal haptoglobin: Haptoglobin falls in both.
E. The presence of schistocytes: Schistocytes occur in both.

Question 42
A 14-year-old girl has had frequent nosebleeds and heavy periods since menarche. Her parents are first cousins. She has petechiae on her legs. Her PT and PTT are normal. Her mother's platelet count is also low. Platelets are 88,000/mm³, and her smear is shown with a platelet nearly the size of a red cell. Ristocetin-induced agglutination is abnormal and doesn't correct when normal plasma is added. Which protein is deficient? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/26/Giant_Platelet%2C_Peripheral_Blood_Smear_%286032662354%29.jpg)
A. GpIIb/IIIa
B. GpIb
C. ADAMTS13
D. von Willebrand factor
E. Factor VIII
Answer: B. GpIb
Why this is correct: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a deficiency of GpIb, the platelet receptor for vWF. It causes big platelets and thrombocytopenia. Ristocetin fails to correct with plasma because plasma supplies vWF but the receptor is still missing.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GpIIb/IIIa: Glanzmann has normal platelet size and normal ristocetin.
C. ADAMTS13: That's TTP.
D. von Willebrand factor: vWD corrects when normal plasma is added.
E. Factor VIII: That's hemophilia A, a secondary hemostasis defect.

Week 7: Hematology / Myeloid Neoplasms

Question 43
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue and a low blood count. She takes no medications and doesn't drink. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL with an MCV of 102 fL, WBC is 3,100/mm³, and platelets are 96,000/mm³. Her marrow is hypercellular with 4% blasts and dysplastic neutrophils. Her B12 and folate are normal, and she has no lead exposure. Her reticulocyte count is low. Her iron stain is shown. Which diagnosis best fits? ![Bone marrow aspirate, iron stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/82/Ring_Sideroblast_smear_2010-01-13.JPG)
A. Myelodysplastic syndrome
B. Lead poisoning
C. AML
D. Aplastic anemia
E. Iron deficiency
Answer: A. Myelodysplastic syndrome
Why this is correct: MDS shows dysplastic morphology such as ring sideroblasts and pseudo-Pelger-Huët cells, a hypercellular marrow with fewer than 20% blasts, and peripheral cytopenias from ineffective hematopoiesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Lead poisoning: She has no exposure, and her cytopenias involve all lines.
C. AML: AML requires at least 20% blasts.
D. Aplastic anemia: Aplastic anemia has a hypocellular marrow.
E. Iron deficiency: Iron deficiency doesn't cause ring sideroblasts.

Question 44
A 64-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, easy bruising, and two infections in the past month. He worked for 30 years in a factory that used benzene. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), and he has petechiae on his legs. WBC is 42,000/mm³ with 60% blasts, hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, and platelets are 18,000/mm³. His LDH and uric acid are elevated. His smear is shown. What does the needle-shaped inclusion in the blast tell you? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/Myeloblast_with_Auer_Rod_smear_2009-11-23_cropped.jpg)
A. This is a Howell-Jolly body
B. The cells are hairy B cells
C. The blasts are lymphoid
D. The cells are mature neutrophils
E. The blasts are myeloid, because Auer rods are never seen in lymphoid blasts
Answer: E. The blasts are myeloid, because Auer rods are never seen in lymphoid blasts
Why this is correct: The Auer rod is a needle-like crystalline aggregate of fused primary (azurophilic) granules and is the only truly definitive morphologic feature of myeloid blasts. It is never seen in lymphoid blasts. AML requires at least 20% blasts in blood or marrow.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This is a Howell-Jolly body: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants in red cells.
B. The cells are hairy B cells: Hairy cells have cytoplasmic projections, not Auer rods.
C. The blasts are lymphoid: Auer rods are never lymphoid.
D. The cells are mature neutrophils: Auer rods mark blasts.

Objective: Explain the principles by which the immune system maintains cellular homeostasis and tolerance to self and how its dysregulation contributes to disease process (CBO 1.2)

Question 45
A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department with blood in his urine and gum bleeding for 2 days. He has anxiety and takes sertraline. He has bruises on his arms. WBC is 4,000/mm³, hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, and platelets are 46,000/mm³. PT, PTT, and LDH are elevated, and fibrinogen and haptoglobin are low. His smear is shown, with abnormal promyelocytes containing bundles of Auer rods. What should be started right away, before genetic confirmation? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Faggot_cell_in_AML-M3.jpg)
A. Cladribine
B. Platelet transfusion alone while waiting for FISH
C. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)
D. Imatinib
E. Plasma exchange
Answer: C. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)
Why this is correct: This is APL, t(15;17) PML-RARA, with DIC on top of marrow failure. It's an emergency, and ATRA should be started empirically. ATRA binds the RARα part of the fusion protein, causing its degradation and letting the promyelocytes mature (differentiation therapy).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Cladribine: Cladribine treats hairy cell leukemia.
B. Platelet transfusion alone while waiting for FISH: Treatment shouldn't wait for FISH.
D. Imatinib: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML.
E. Plasma exchange: That treats TTP.

Question 46
A 74-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and a low blood count found at a routine visit. He was treated with chemotherapy for lymphoma 6 years ago. He has no fever or weight loss. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 104 fL, WBC is 2,800/mm³, and platelets are 88,000/mm³. B12 and folate are normal. His marrow is hypercellular with 6% blasts, and his smear is shown with bilobed, hypogranular neutrophils. What is the diagnosis? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/02/Hypogranular_neutrophil_with_a_pseudo-Pelger-Huet_nucleus_in_MDS.jpg)
A. Myelodysplastic syndrome
B. Aplastic anemia
C. B12 deficiency
D. Acute myeloid leukemia
E. Chronic myeloid leukemia
Answer: A. Myelodysplastic syndrome
Why this is correct: MDS shows dysplastic morphology such as pseudo-Pelger-Huët cells (hypogranular neutrophils with an abnormal bilobed nucleus) and ring sideroblasts, a hypercellular marrow with fewer than 20% blasts, and peripheral cytopenias. This reflects ineffective hematopoiesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Aplastic anemia: Aplastic anemia has a hypocellular marrow.
C. B12 deficiency: His B12 is normal, and B12 deficiency causes hypersegmented neutrophils.
D. Acute myeloid leukemia: AML requires at least 20% blasts.
E. Chronic myeloid leukemia: CML shows a high WBC with basophilia.

Question 47
A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, night sweats, and fullness in her left upper abdomen for 3 months. She takes no medications. Her spleen is palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. WBC is 148,000/mm³ with neutrophils at all stages of maturation and many basophils. Her platelets are 480,000/mm³, and uric acid is elevated. She has no enlarged lymph nodes. Her smear is shown. Her LAP score is low. How does the first-line drug for this condition work? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/Chronic_Myeloid_Leukemia_smear_2009-04-09.JPG)
A. It occupies the ATP-binding site of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase
B. It kills all rapidly dividing cells
C. It inhibits JAK2
D. It induces degradation of PML-RARA
E. It inhibits adenosine deaminase
Answer: A. It occupies the ATP-binding site of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase
Why this is correct: CML is defined by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) and BCR-ABL1 fusion. It's separated from a leukemoid reaction by a low LAP score and basophilia. Imatinib and related TKIs occupy the ATP-binding site of BCR-ABL, blocking downstream phosphorylation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It kills all rapidly dividing cells: That's traditional chemotherapy, not targeted therapy.
C. It inhibits JAK2: JAK inhibitors are used in some MPNs like PMF.
D. It induces degradation of PML-RARA: That's ATRA in APL.
E. It inhibits adenosine deaminase: That's cladribine in hairy cell leukemia.

Question 48
A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, weight loss, and early fullness when eating. He takes metformin for diabetes. His spleen is massively enlarged, reaching his pelvis. His WBC is 14,000/mm³, and platelets are 90,000/mm³. His LDH is elevated. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL, and his smear is shown, along with nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes. A bone marrow aspiration yields no cells. Which finding on marrow biopsy is expected? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Teardrop_Cells_smear_2009-09-22.JPG)
A. Sheets of lymphoblasts that are TdT positive
B. Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue
C. Marrow fibrosis on reticulin stain
D. Large staghorn megakaryocytes with normal cellularity
E. Clonal plasma cells over 10%
Answer: C. Marrow fibrosis on reticulin stain
Why this is correct: Primary myelofibrosis is a JAK2-associated MPN that causes a myelophthisic smear with teardrop cells (dacrocytes), nucleated red cells, and immature granulocytes, massive splenomegaly, and a dry tap on aspiration confirmed by reticulin stain on biopsy.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Sheets of lymphoblasts that are TdT positive: That's ALL.
B. Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue: That's sideroblastic anemia or MDS.
D. Large staghorn megakaryocytes with normal cellularity: That's essential thrombocythemia.
E. Clonal plasma cells over 10%: That's multiple myeloma.

Question 49
A 3-year-old boy with Down syndrome is brought to the physician because of fatigue, pallor, and bruising for 2 weeks. He had surgery for a heart defect as an infant. He has petechiae on his chest. Question 50
A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, fevers, and gum bleeding for 3 weeks. She had chemotherapy for breast cancer 5 years ago. She has petechiae and pale conjunctivae. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, platelets are 24,000/mm³, and her marrow has 35% blasts. Her WBC is 22,000/mm³, and her PT and PTT are normal. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Her smear is shown. What threshold defines acute myeloid leukemia? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/Myeloblast_with_Auer_Rod_smear_2009-11-23_cropped.jpg)
A. At least 20% myeloid blasts in blood or marrow
B. At least 5% blasts
C. At least 10% blasts
D. Any blasts at all
E. At least 50% blasts
Answer: A. At least 20% myeloid blasts in blood or marrow
Why this is correct: AML is defined by 20% or more myeloid blasts in blood or marrow and presents with marrow-failure symptoms. MDS has fewer than 20%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. At least 5% blasts: That's below the AML threshold.
C. At least 10% blasts: That's below the AML threshold.
D. Any blasts at all: Small numbers of blasts can occur in MDS.
E. At least 50% blasts: The threshold is 20%.

Question 51
A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because his gums have become swollen and bleed easily. He also has fatigue and fevers. His gums are hypertrophied, and his liver and spleen are enlarged. WBC is 68,000/mm³ with many blasts, some monocytic. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, and platelets are 34,000/mm³. His PT and PTT are normal. His smear is shown. What does his gum swelling suggest? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/Myeloblast_with_Auer_Rod_smear_2009-11-23_cropped.jpg)
A. Acute promyelocytic leukemia
B. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
C. AML with monocytic differentiation
D. Hairy cell leukemia
E. Scurvy
Answer: C. AML with monocytic differentiation
Why this is correct: Gingival hyperplasia with organomegaly in AML points to monocytic differentiation, seen with inv(16)/AML-M4Eo or 11q23/KMT2A rearrangement.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Acute promyelocytic leukemia: APL presents with DIC.
B. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: CLL is mature lymphocytes.
D. Hairy cell leukemia: Hairy cell causes splenomegaly and a dry tap.
E. Scurvy: His smear shows leukemia.

Question 52
A 36-year-old woman with acute promyelocytic leukemia is started on ATRA. On day 9 she develops fever, shortness of breath, weight gain, and bilateral lung infiltrates. Her blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air, and her creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.6 mg/dL. Her WBC has risen to 34,000/mm³. Her smear at diagnosis is shown. What is happening, and how is it treated? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Faggot_cell_in_AML-M3.jpg)
A. DIC; start heparin
B. Tumor lysis syndrome; give fluids only
C. TTP; start plasma exchange
D. Pneumonia; stop ATRA permanently
E. Differentiation syndrome; start dexamethasone
Answer: E. Differentiation syndrome; start dexamethasone
Why this is correct: Differentiation syndrome is a capillary leak syndrome from cytokines released by differentiating promyelocytes, starting days to weeks after ATRA or arsenic trioxide. It's treated with dexamethasone, holding ATRA only if severe.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. DIC; start heparin: The timing and lung findings point to differentiation syndrome.
B. Tumor lysis syndrome; give fluids only: Her findings are capillary leak after ATRA.
C. TTP; start plasma exchange: That isn't the complication.
D. Pneumonia; stop ATRA permanently: ATRA is held only if severe.

Question 53
A 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department with nosebleeds and bruises. His PT and PTT are elevated, and fibrinogen is low. He takes no medications. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, platelets are 38,000/mm³, and WBC is 3,800/mm³. Haptoglobin is low, and D-dimer is high. His smear is shown, with atypical promyelocytes stuffed with granules and bundled Auer rods. Flow cytometry is CD34-negative and HLA-DR-negative with strong MPO. Which genetic change is expected? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Faggot_cell_in_AML-M3.jpg)
A. t(8;14) involving MYC
B. t(15;17) producing PML-RARA
C. BRAF V600E
D. t(9;22) producing BCR-ABL
E. t(14;18) involving BCL2
Answer: B. t(15;17) producing PML-RARA
Why this is correct: APL is t(15;17) PML-RARA. Its flow pattern (CD34-negative, HLA-DR-negative, strong MPO) is essentially unique among AMLs, and it presents with DIC.

A. t(8;14) involving MYC: That's Burkitt lymphoma.
C. BRAF V600E: That's hairy cell leukemia.
D. t(9;22) producing BCR-ABL: That's CML.

Question 54
A 70-year-old woman with myelodysplastic syndrome comes for follow-up and asks why her marrow is full of cells but her blood counts are low. Her B12 and folate are normal, and her reticulocyte count is low. She takes no medications and has no lead exposure. Her smear is shown, with hypogranular bilobed neutrophils. Her marrow is hypercellular with 7% blasts. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL and platelets are 72,000/mm³. What explains this contradiction? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/02/Hypogranular_neutrophil_with_a_pseudo-Pelger-Huet_nucleus_in_MDS.jpg)
A. She has AML
B. The spleen destroys the cells
C. She has iron deficiency
D. Ineffective hematopoiesis: dysplastic cells are made but fail to mature and leave the marrow
E. The marrow is actually hypocellular
Answer: D. Ineffective hematopoiesis: dysplastic cells are made but fail to mature and leave the marrow
Why this is correct: MDS is dysplastic, ineffective hematopoiesis. The marrow is hypercellular, but the dysplastic cells don't mature and exit normally, causing peripheral cytopenias.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. She has AML: She has fewer than 20% blasts.
B. The spleen destroys the cells: That isn't the mechanism.
C. She has iron deficiency: That doesn't cause dysplastic neutrophils.
E. The marrow is actually hypocellular: MDS marrow is usually hypercellular.

Question 55

Week 7: Hematology / Lymphoid Neoplasms

Question 61
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of bone pain, fever, and bruising for 3 weeks. She has refused to walk for several days. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). She has enlarged lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, and petechiae. WBC is 52,000/mm³, hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL, and platelets are 30,000/mm³. Her LDH and uric acid are elevated. Chest x-ray shows no mediastinal mass. Her smear is shown, with blasts that have scant cytoplasm and no Auer rods. Which marker confirms these are lymphoblasts? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/Acute_leukemia-ALL.jpg)
A. CD5 and CD23
B. TdT
C. Myeloperoxidase
D. TRAP
E. CD15 and CD30
Answer: B. TdT
Why this is correct: TdT is the gold-standard marker for lymphoblasts. It's a DNA polymerase used early in V(D)J recombination and marks lymphoblasts of either B or T lineage. B-ALL is also CD19+ and CD10+.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD5 and CD23: These mark CLL.
C. Myeloperoxidase: MPO marks myeloid cells.
D. TRAP: TRAP marks hairy cell leukemia.
E. CD15 and CD30: These mark Reed-Sternberg cells.

Question 62
A 71-year-old man is found to have a high white count at a routine visit. He feels well and has no fevers or weight loss. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. He has small, painless lymph nodes in his neck and armpits. WBC is 48,000/mm³ with 90% small, mature-looking lymphocytes. Hemoglobin is 13.2 g/dL, and platelets are 180,000/mm³. C. CD15+ and CD30+

E. TdT+ blasts
Answer: D. CD5+ and CD23+ B cells
Why this is correct: CLL/SLL is a mature B-cell neoplasm that's CD5+ and CD23+, with smudge cells (fragile cells that break during smear preparation).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CD11c+, CD103+, and TRAP+: That's hairy cell leukemia.
B. CD34-negative, HLA-DR-negative, strong MPO: That's APL.
C. CD15+ and CD30+: That's Reed-Sternberg cells.
E. TdT+ blasts: TdT marks lymphoblasts in ALL.

Question 63
A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and fullness in his left upper abdomen for 4 months. He has had two bouts of pneumonia this year. He takes no medications. His spleen is massively enlarged, with no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL, WBC is 2,100/mm³, and platelets are 70,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspiration is a dry tap. He has no night sweats. His LDH is normal. His smear is shown. What is the treatment? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Hairy_cell_leukemia_smear_2009-08-20.JPG)
A. Radiation to the spleen
B. ATRA
C. Watchful waiting only
D. Cladribine
E. Imatinib
Answer: D. Cladribine
Why this is correct: Hairy cell leukemia shows B cells with fine hair-like projections, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and a dry tap from marrow fibrosis. It's TRAP positive and carries BRAF V600E. It's treated with cladribine, an adenosine deaminase inhibitor, and has an excellent prognosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Radiation to the spleen: That isn't the listed treatment.
B. ATRA: That's for APL.

Question 64
A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in her neck for 2 months. She has had night sweats, and her neck hurts after drinking alcohol. She takes an oral contraceptive. She has a firm 3-cm supraclavicular node. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. A. CD34 and MPO

Answer: B. CD15 and CD30, and it's CD45-negative

Question 65
A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of back pain for 3 months and fatigue. He has had two pneumonias this year. He takes ibuprofen for the pain. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, calcium is 11.9 mg/dL, and creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL. X-rays show lytic lesions in his spine and skull. Serum electrophoresis shows an M-spike. His marrow aspirate is shown, with 30% plasma cells that have eccentric nuclei. What separates this from MGUS? ![Bone marrow aspirate](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f9/Plasma_Cells_in_a_Marrow_film_on_a_Myeloma_patient.jpg)
A. A positive TdT stain
B. Reed-Sternberg cells
C. The presence of an M-spike
D. Any number of marrow plasma cells
E. The presence of CRAB features
Answer: E. The presence of CRAB features
Why this is correct: Multiple myeloma is a clonal proliferation of plasma cells making a monoclonal immunoglobulin. Myeloma is CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone lesions) plus an M-spike. MGUS has no CRAB, fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells, and progresses at about 1% per year.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A positive TdT stain: TdT marks lymphoblasts.
B. Reed-Sternberg cells: Those define Hodgkin lymphoma.
C. The presence of an M-spike: MGUS also has an M-spike.
D. Any number of marrow plasma cells: MGUS has under 10%.

Question 66
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue and bone pain. She has osteoporosis and takes calcium. Her ESR is 110 mm/h, total protein is 10.2 g/dL, and albumin is 3.2 g/dL. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, and calcium is 11.2 mg/dL. Her creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. X-rays show lytic lesions in her skull, and serum electrophoresis shows an M-spike. Her peripheral smear is shown, with red cells stacked like coins. Why do the red cells stack this way? ![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b1/Rouleaux_formation.jpg)
A. Spectrin defects make the cells spherical
B. IgM binds red cells in the cold and fixes complement
C. High serum protein reduces the charge repulsion that normally keeps red cells apart
D. HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated
E. Microthrombi fragment the cells
Answer: C. High serum protein reduces the charge repulsion that normally keeps red cells apart
Why this is correct: Rouleaux formation, red cells stacked like poker chips, is seen in multiple myeloma because the high serum protein reduces the charge repulsion between red cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. IgM binds red cells in the cold and fixes complement: That's cold AIHA agglutination.
D. HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated: That's sickle cell disease.
E. Microthrombi fragment the cells: That's schistocytes in TTP.

Question 71
A 72-year-old man has had CLL for 8 years with stable counts and small lymph nodes. He takes allopurinol and has never needed treatment for CLL. He has lost 4 kg this month. Question 72

Answer: D. SLL and CLL are the same disease, named by whether it presents as a mass or in the blood
Why this is correct: Leukemia versus lymphoma is a clinical distinction. SLL (a mass) and CLL (circulating cells over 5,000) are the same tumor, both CD5+ and CD23+.

A. SLL is Hodgkin lymphoma: SLL is non-Hodgkin.
B. SLL is always aggressive: SLL is indolent like CLL.
C. They have different translocations: Both are defined by deletions, not translocations.
E. SLL is a T-cell disease: Both are B-cell neoplasms.

E. Plasma cells
Answer: D. Tingible-body macrophages
Why this is correct: The starry-sky pattern of Burkitt lymphoma comes from tingible-body macrophages scattered among sheets of tumor cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Germinal centers: Burkitt doesn't form follicles.
B. Hassall's corpuscles: Those are in the thymus.
C. Reed-Sternberg cells: Those define Hodgkin lymphoma.
E. Plasma cells: Those are myeloma cells.
Image credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Question 83
A 7-year-old girl in Kenya has a swelling of her jaw that has doubled in size in 2 weeks. She was previously healthy. Her teeth on that side have become loose. She has no fever. Her LDH is very high, and her HIV test is negative. Her abdomen is soft. A touch prep of the tumor is shown, with deep blue cells containing cytoplasmic vacuoles. Which virus is associated with this endemic form of her disease? ![Tumor biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/Burkitt_lymphoma%2C_touch_prep%2C_Wright_stain.jpg)
A. HHV-8
B. Epstein-Barr virus
C. Hepatitis C
D. Parvovirus
E. HIV
Answer: B. Epstein-Barr virus
Why this is correct: Endemic African Burkitt lymphoma presents as a jaw or facial mass and is associated with EBV.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. HHV-8: HHV-8 isn't linked here.
C. Hepatitis C: Hepatitis C is linked to PCT.
D. Parvovirus: Parvovirus isn't linked.

Question 84
A 62-year-old woman with follicular lymphoma that waxed and waned for 8 years develops a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass and fevers. She takes no medications and has been on watchful waiting. Her pulse is 104/min. Her LDH is high, and she has lost 5 kg. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Her old biopsy showed t(14;18). A biopsy is shown, with sheets of large cells. Which prognosis marker separates subtypes of her new lymphoma? ![Lymph node biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Diffuse_large_B-cell_lymphoma_%28DLBCL%29%2C_high_mag.jpg)
A. A high LAP score
B. BRAF V600E
C. TdT positivity
D. CD15 and CD30
E. Germinal center B-cell subtype has a better prognosis than activated B-cell subtype
Answer: E. Germinal center B-cell subtype has a better prognosis than activated B-cell subtype
Why this is correct: DLBCL arises de novo or by transformation from a low-grade lymphoma such as CLL or follicular lymphoma. Its subtypes are germinal center B-cell (better prognosis) and activated B-cell (worse prognosis).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A high LAP score: That's used for CML.
B. BRAF V600E: That's hairy cell leukemia.
C. TdT positivity: TdT marks lymphoblasts.
D. CD15 and CD30: Those mark Reed-Sternberg cells.

Question 85
A 56-year-old man has had painless, generalized lymphadenopathy that came and went for years. He has never been treated because his disease was slow. His vital signs are normal, and he has lost 3 kg. A node biopsy showed back-to-back follicles of centrocytes and centroblasts that were BCL2-positive. He takes no medications. His LDH is now high, and he has night sweats. Now a new biopsy of a rapidly growing node is shown. What has happened? ![Lymph node biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Diffuse_large_B-cell_lymphoma_%28DLBCL%29%2C_high_mag.jpg)
A. It became Burkitt lymphoma
B. It became Hodgkin lymphoma
C. Follicular lymphoma has transformed to DLBCL
D. It regressed
E. It became CLL
Answer: C. Follicular lymphoma has transformed to DLBCL
Why this is correct: Follicular lymphoma is indolent and waxes and wanes, with t(14;18) and BCL2 overexpression. It may transform to DLBCL, which shows sheets of large cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It became Burkitt lymphoma: Transformation to DLBCL is the listed course.
B. It became Hodgkin lymphoma: There are no Reed-Sternberg cells.
D. It regressed: The node is growing.
E. It became CLL: CLL is small lymphocytes.

Question 86
A 21-year-old woman has a cough and a painless mass in her neck. She is a college student and takes an oral contraceptive. Her pulse is 88/min. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. She has night sweats and itching. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Her CBC is normal. A node biopsy is shown, with bands of collagen and large cells sitting in clear spaces. Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is this? ![Lymph node biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/Hodgkin_disease%2C_nodular_sclerosis_type_Case_236_%287493491670%29.jpg)
A. Nodular sclerosis
B. Lymphocyte depleted
C. Follicular lymphoma
D. Mixed cellularity
E. Lymphocyte rich
Answer: A. Nodular sclerosis
Why this is correct: Nodular sclerosis is the most common Hodgkin subtype, favors young women with a mediastinal mass, and shows collagen bands and lacunar cells (RS cells sitting in empty spaces).
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Lymphocyte depleted: That occurs with HIV and in the elderly.
C. Follicular lymphoma: That's non-Hodgkin.
D. Mixed cellularity: That's EBV-associated with many eosinophils.
E. Lymphocyte rich: That has the best prognosis.

Week 7: Hematology / Protozoan Parasites of the Blood

Question 87
A 30-year-old man comes to the emergency department with fever, headache, and confusion 2 weeks after returning from a trip to Nigeria, where he didn't take prophylaxis. Temperature is 39.9°C (103.8°F), and he is jaundiced. His glucose is 52 mg/dL, and 10% of his red cells are parasitized. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, and his creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL. His platelets are 60,000/mm³. His thin smear is shown. Why are schizonts rarely seen on this species' peripheral smear? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Plasmodium_falciparum_gametocyte.jpg)
A. The parasite only infects reticulocytes
B. Heavily infected red cells stick to and sequester in deep capillaries
C. Schizonts dissolve on staining
D. P. falciparum doesn't undergo schizogony
E. Schizonts only form in the liver
Answer: B. Heavily infected red cells stick to and sequester in deep capillaries
Why this is correct: P. falciparum infects red cells of any age, allowing high parasitemia, and makes PfEMP1 knobs that cause cytoadherence. Heavily parasitized cells sequester in deep capillary beds, so the smear shows rings and crescent gametocytes but rarely schizonts. Severe disease is treated with IV artesunate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The parasite only infects reticulocytes: That's P. vivax and P. ovale.
C. Schizonts dissolve on staining: The absence reflects sequestration.
D. P. falciparum doesn't undergo schizogony: It does; the schizonts are sequestered.
E. Schizonts only form in the liver: Blood-stage schizonts form in red cells.
Image credit: Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 88
A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever every other day for a week. He returned from a year of volunteer work in Papua New Guinea 8 months ago and was treated for malaria there. He hasn't traveled since and takes no medications. Temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), and his spleen is palpable. His thin smear is shown, with an enlarged infected red cell containing fine dots. What must be added to blood-stage treatment to prevent another relapse? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/P_vivax_gametocyte3.jpg)
A. IV artesunate
B. No additional drug is needed
C. Benznidazole
D. Primaquine or tafenoquine, after checking G6PD status
E. Atovaquone plus azithromycin
Answer: D. Primaquine or tafenoquine, after checking G6PD status
Why this is correct: P. vivax infects reticulocytes, enlarges the red cell, and shows Schüffner's dots. It forms hypnozoites in the liver that cause relapse months later, so chloroquine must be followed by primaquine or tafenoquine. G6PD must be checked first because these drugs can cause severe hemolysis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IV artesunate: That's for severe malaria.
B. No additional drug is needed: Without hypnozoite therapy he'll relapse again.
C. Benznidazole: That's for Chagas disease.
E. Atovaquone plus azithromycin: That's for babesiosis.

Question 89
A 68-year-old man from Massachusetts comes to the emergency department in July with fever, fatigue, and dark urine for a week. He had his spleen removed after a car accident years ago. He gardens and hikes but doesn't recall a tick bite. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F). Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, platelets are low, and LDH and bilirubin are high. His thin smear is shown, with intracellular forms arranged in a tetrad. What is the treatment for mild to moderate disease? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Blood_smear_of_Babesia_microti%2C_original.png)
A. Benznidazole
B. Chloroquine plus primaquine
C. Doxycycline alone
D. Atovaquone plus azithromycin
E. IV artesunate
Answer: D. Atovaquone plus azithromycin
Why this is correct: Babesia microti is carried by Ixodes ticks, invades red cells directly without a liver stage, and forms a Maltese cross tetrad, which Plasmodium never does. Asplenia raises the risk of severe disease. Mild to moderate disease is treated with atovaquone plus azithromycin, and severe disease with clindamycin plus quinine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Benznidazole: That's for Chagas disease.
B. Chloroquine plus primaquine: That's for P. vivax.
C. Doxycycline alone: That isn't the listed regimen.
E. IV artesunate: That's for severe malaria.

Question 90
A 7-year-old boy in rural Bolivia is brought to a clinic because of fever and swelling around his right eye for a week. His family lives in a mud-brick house with a thatched roof. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). He has painless swelling of the right eyelid, enlarged lymph nodes, and hepatosplenomegaly. His hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. A thick smear is also positive. His blood smear is shown, with flagellated organisms outside the red cells. How was this infection transmitted? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/T._cruzi_trypomastigotes_in_peripheral_blood_smear.jpg)
A. An Ixodes tick bite
B. Triatomine bug feces rubbed into the bite or mucous membranes
C. Eating undercooked meat
D. The bite of a female Anopheles mosquito
E. Blood transfusion only
Answer: B. Triatomine bug feces rubbed into the bite or mucous membranes
Why this is correct: Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease. The kissing bug doesn't inject the parasite; its feces contain trypomastigotes that are rubbed into the bite or eye. Acute infection can show circulating trypomastigotes and Romaña sign (unilateral periorbital swelling). Early treatment is benznidazole or nifurtimox.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An Ixodes tick bite: That transmits Babesia.
C. Eating undercooked meat: That transmits Toxoplasma.
D. The bite of a female Anopheles mosquito: That transmits malaria.
E. Blood transfusion only: The eye swelling points to bug exposure near the eye.

Question 91
A 26-year-old woman develops fever and chills 10 days after returning from Kenya. She didn't take prophylaxis. She is alert and can eat. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). Parasitemia is 1%, and her creatinine and glucose are normal. Pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. She is not pregnant. Her platelets are 110,000/mm³. Her smear is shown with crescent-shaped gametocytes. Which treatment is appropriate for uncomplicated disease? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Plasmodium_falciparum_gametocyte.jpg)
A. Atovaquone plus azithromycin
B. Chloroquine plus primaquine
C. Chloroquine alone
D. Artemether-lumefantrine or atovaquone-proguanil
E. IV artesunate
Answer: D. Artemether-lumefantrine or atovaquone-proguanil
Why this is correct: Uncomplicated P. falciparum outside the Caribbean is treated with artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) or atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone). It must be treated as chloroquine-resistant in most of the world and needs no anti-relapse therapy because it has no hypnozoites.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Atovaquone plus azithromycin: That's for babesiosis.
B. Chloroquine plus primaquine: That's for vivax, ovale, or malariae.
C. Chloroquine alone: That's only for Caribbean infections.
E. IV artesunate: That's for severe malaria.

Question 92
A 35-year-old man is treated for falciparum malaria after a trip to Mozambique. He had fever and chills for 3 days and is alert. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), parasitemia is 1.5%, and his creatinine and glucose are normal. He has no allergies. His platelets are 120,000/mm³. His smear is shown. He's started on artemether combined with lumefantrine and asks why he needs two drugs. What is the reason? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Plasmodium_falciparum_gametocyte.jpg)
A. They collapse the parasite ETC
B. They inhibit parasite DHFR
C. They only kill hypnozoites
D. They act through a different, ROS-generating mechanism and are paired rather than used alone
E. They block heme polymerase like chloroquine
Answer: D. They act through a different, ROS-generating mechanism and are paired rather than used alone
Why this is correct: Artemisinins have an endoperoxide bridge that generates reactive oxygen species and damages many parasite pathways. Because their mechanism differs from the heme-detoxification blockers, they're combined with a partner drug rather than used alone.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. They collapse the parasite ETC: That's atovaquone.
B. They inhibit parasite DHFR: That's proguanil.
C. They only kill hypnozoites: That's primaquine and tafenoquine.
E. They block heme polymerase like chloroquine: That's the quinoline mechanism.

Question 93
A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with malaria after returning from India. She has fever every 48 hours. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and her parasitemia is 0.5%. Her G6PD level is normal. Her creatinine and glucose are normal. Her smear is shown, with enlarged red cells containing fine dots. She's treated with chloroquine for the blood stage. Why is primaquine not given now? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/P_vivax_gametocyte3.jpg)
A. She should get IV artesunate
B. Primaquine and tafenoquine are contraindicated in pregnancy
C. P. vivax has no hypnozoites
D. Primaquine only works on P. falciparum
E. Chloroquine already kills hypnozoites
Answer: B. Primaquine and tafenoquine are contraindicated in pregnancy
Why this is correct: P. vivax needs hypnozoite-directed therapy with primaquine or tafenoquine, but these are contraindicated in pregnancy, and G6PD status must be checked first.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. She should get IV artesunate: She doesn't have severe malaria.
C. P. vivax has no hypnozoites: P. vivax forms hypnozoites.
D. Primaquine only works on P. falciparum: It targets hypnozoites.
E. Chloroquine already kills hypnozoites: It only acts on blood forms.

Question 94
A 31-year-old man has fever every 48 hours after a trip to Central America. He works as a teacher and took no prophylaxis. He has no cough or rash. His parasitemia is below 1%. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). His spleen is palpable, and his hemoglobin is 11.6 g/dL. His creatinine is normal. His smear is shown, with infected red cells larger than their neighbors. Why does this species rarely cause the very high parasitemia seen with P. falciparum? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/P_vivax_gametocyte3.jpg)
A. It only invades senescent red cells
B. It is killed by the spleen
C. It has no blood stage
D. It invades any red cell
E. It only invades reticulocytes
Answer: E. It only invades reticulocytes
Why this is correct: RBC tropism determines severity. P. falciparum invades any red cell, allowing very high parasitemia. P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. knowlesi are reticulocyte-restricted, which caps parasitemia, and P. malariae only invades senescent cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It only invades senescent red cells: That's P. malariae.
B. It is killed by the spleen: That isn't the explanation.
C. It has no blood stage: It does have a blood stage.
D. It invades any red cell: That's P. falciparum.

Question 95
A 55-year-old woman from Connecticut develops fever and hemolysis 4 weeks after a blood transfusion during hip surgery. She takes aspirin and a statin. She has no rash or joint pain. She hasn't been outdoors much. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). Her hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL, platelets are low, and LDH and bilirubin are high. Her smear is shown, with a tetrad of organisms in one red cell. Which feature of this parasite's life cycle differs from Plasmodium? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Blood_smear_of_Babesia_microti%2C_original.png)
A. It multiplies by schizogony
B. It forms hypnozoites in the liver
C. It invades red cells directly with no liver stage
D. It forms crescent gametocytes
E. It's spread by Anopheles mosquitoes
Answer: C. It invades red cells directly with no liver stage
Why this is correct: Babesia sporozoites invade red cells directly with no liver stage and multiply by merogony (binary fission), not schizogony. Transfusion within 6 months is a risk factor. The Maltese cross tetrad is pathognomonic.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It multiplies by schizogony: Babesia uses merogony.
B. It forms hypnozoites in the liver: That's P. vivax and P. ovale.
D. It forms crescent gametocytes: That's P. falciparum.
E. It's spread by Anopheles mosquitoes: Babesia is spread by Ixodes ticks.

Question 96
A 74-year-old man without a spleen is admitted from Nantucket with high fever, dark urine, and shortness of breath. He had his spleen removed after a car crash 20 years ago. Question 97
A 48-year-old man who grew up in rural Bolivia comes to the physician because of trouble swallowing solids and liquids and severe constipation. As a child he had swelling around one eye. His echocardiogram shows a dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm. He has lived in the United States for 20 years. His ELISA for anti-T. cruzi IgG is positive. Question 98
A 5-year-old girl in rural Argentina has fever, swelling at a bite site on her cheek, and an enlarged liver and spleen. She has no heart murmur, and her stools are normal. Her pulse is 128/min. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Her mother has positive Chagas serology. The family lives in a mud-walled home. Her smear is shown. She's started on benznidazole. How does this drug kill the parasite? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/T._cruzi_trypomastigotes_in_peripheral_blood_smear.jpg)

Answer: C. The parasite's nitroreductase converts it into metabolites toxic to its DNA, RNA, and proteins
Why this is correct: Benznidazole and nifurtimox are converted by parasite nitroreductase into metabolites that damage the organism's DNA, RNA, and proteins. They're used for acute, congenital, and some chronic infections.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. It blocks heme polymerase: That's chloroquine.

E. It generates ROS through an endoperoxide bridge: That's artemisinin.

Question 99
A 40-year-old man returns from Ghana with fever, confusion, and seizures. He works as an engineer and has no medical history. His parasitemia is 8%. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F). Blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, and his glucose is 48 mg/dL. His creatinine is 3.0 mg/dL. He didn't take prophylaxis. His parasitemia is 8%, and his smear is shown with many small ring forms. Why can this species reach such high parasitemia and cause cerebral malaria? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/P._falciparum_thin_smear_with_ring_forms.jpg)
A. It only invades reticulocytes
B. It has no liver stage
C. It only invades senescent cells
D. It invades red cells of any age
E. It forms hypnozoites
Answer: D. It invades red cells of any age
Why this is correct: P. falciparum invades any red cell, allowing unlimited parasitemia, and it's the only species that causes cerebral malaria. Severe malaria is treated with IV artesunate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It only invades reticulocytes: That's vivax, ovale, and knowlesi, which caps parasitemia.
B. It has no liver stage: That's Babesia.
C. It only invades senescent cells: That's P. malariae.
E. It forms hypnozoites: That causes relapse, not high parasitemia.

Question 100
A 60-year-old woman originally from Nigeria has fevers that recur every 72 hours. She moved to the United States 20 years ago. Her parasitemia is very low. She hasn't traveled back to Africa since. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), and her spleen is mildly enlarged. Her hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. Her smear is shown, with a schizont whose merozoites are arranged in a rosette. Which species is this? ![Thin blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/02/Mature_Plasmodium_malariae_schizont_PHIL_2715_lores.jpg)
A. Babesia microti
B. Plasmodium malariae
C. Plasmodium vivax
D. Plasmodium falciparum
E. Plasmodium ovale
Answer: B. Plasmodium malariae
Why this is correct: P. malariae invades only senescent red cells, so it has the lowest parasite burden. It has a 72-hour (quartan) fever cycle and shows band-form trophozoites and rosette schizonts. It doesn't form hypnozoites.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Babesia microti: Babesia forms a Maltese cross.
C. Plasmodium vivax: Vivax has a 48-hour cycle and Schüffner's dots.
D. Plasmodium falciparum: Schizonts are rare on falciparum smears.
E. Plasmodium ovale: Ovale has fimbriated cells and a 48-hour cycle.

Week 8: Virology & Cell Injury / Viral Structure & Pathogenesis

Question 1
A 6-year-old boy and 14 classmates develop vomiting and watery diarrhea within 2 days of one another. The school uses hand sanitizer at every door, but the outbreak spreads anyway. He takes no medications and has no other medical problems. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 118/min, and his mucous membranes are dry. Stool testing identifies a virus without a lipid envelope. Why was this virus able to spread by the fecal-oral route despite sanitizer use?
A. Naked viruses resist acid, detergents, and heat
B. Its envelope protects it from stomach acid
C. It replicates only in the nucleus
D. It uses reverse transcriptase
E. It has a segmented genome
Answer: A. Naked viruses resist acid, detergents, and heat
Why this is correct: Naked (non-enveloped) viruses are released by lysis and are stable, resisting acid, detergents, and heat, so they can be transmitted by the fecal-oral route. Enveloped viruses are fragile, sensitive to stomach acid and bile, and aren't spread fecal-orally.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Its envelope protects it from stomach acid: Envelopes make viruses fragile and acid-sensitive.
C. It replicates only in the nucleus: Replication site doesn't explain environmental stability.
D. It uses reverse transcriptase: That's retroviruses and HBV.
E. It has a segmented genome: Segmentation affects reassortment, not stability.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 2
A 30-year-old nurse asks why the influenza virus doesn't spread through contaminated food the way norovirus does. She works on a pediatric unit and received this year's flu vaccine. Her vital signs are normal. Her physician explains that influenza carries a lipid layer taken from the host cell membrane, studded with glycoprotein spikes. She asks because a coworker got sick after sharing a lunch with a child who had norovirus. She washes her hands often and uses alcohol sanitizer. Which statement about viruses with this structure is correct?
A. They're resistant to detergents
B. Their envelope is made by viral enzymes from scratch
C. They're fragile and spread through bodily fluids, not the fecal-oral route
D. They're released only by lysis
E. They survive stomach acid
Answer: C. They're fragile and spread through bodily fluids, not the fecal-oral route
Why this is correct: Enveloped viruses carry a portion of the host cell membrane with protein/glycoprotein spikes that bind host cells. They're released by budding or lysis, are sensitive to acid, detergents, heat, and bile, and spread through bodily fluids rather than the fecal-oral route.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. They're resistant to detergents: Enveloped viruses are detergent-sensitive.
B. Their envelope is made by viral enzymes from scratch: It comes from host membrane.
D. They're released only by lysis: They can bud or lyse.
E. They survive stomach acid: Enveloped viruses are acid-sensitive.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 3
A 22-year-old woman develops sore throat, fever, and a runny nose. She works at a daycare and takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Her physician explains that the virus causing her illness first had to recognize and bind specific molecules on her respiratory epithelial cells before it could enter. Her pulse is 96/min, and her throat is red without exudates. Her rapid strep test is negative. She asks why some viruses infect the throat but not other organs. What determines which host and tissue a virus infects?
A. The viral polymerase
B. The prodromal period
C. Uncoating
D. Chromatin margination
E. Viral attachment proteins binding specific host receptors
Answer: E. Viral attachment proteins binding specific host receptors
Why this is correct: Attachment is the first step of the viral life cycle. Viral attachment proteins (VAPs) recognize and bind host cell receptors and determine host and tissue specificity.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The viral polymerase: The polymerase copies the genome.
B. The prodromal period: That's a clinical phase.
C. Uncoating: Uncoating follows entry.
D. Chromatin margination: That's a histologic finding in parvovirus B19.

Question 4
A 41-year-old man with fever and cough has a respiratory virus grown in the hospital lab to guide his care. He has asthma and uses an albuterol inhaler. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). The microbiologist explains that the virus has attached to and entered his cells, but it hasn't yet released its genome from the protein capsid. His oxygen saturation is 95%, and his chest x-ray is clear. The lab is studying how the virus moves through the steps of infection inside cells. Which step of the viral life cycle comes next?
A. Release
B. Uncoating
C. Attachment
D. Assembly
E. Replication
Answer: B. Uncoating
Why this is correct: The general stages are attachment, entry, uncoating, replication, assembly/maturation, and release.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Release: That's the last step.
C. Attachment: That comes first.
D. Assembly: That follows replication.
E. Replication: Uncoating must happen first.

Question 5
A 45-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and newly diagnosed HIV is started on antiviral therapy. He has a history of injection drug use and takes methadone. His HBV DNA and HIV RNA are both detectable. His physician chooses a drug that works against both viruses because both copy an RNA intermediate back into DNA. His ALT is 110 U/L, and his CD4 count is 340/μL. He has no cirrhosis on ultrasound. He wants as few pills as possible. Which drug is this?
A. Enfuvirtide
B. Maraviroc
C. Ganciclovir
D. Lamivudine
E. Acyclovir
Answer: D. Lamivudine
Why this is correct: DNA viruses usually replicate in the nucleus, except poxvirus and hepatitis B, which copy an RNA intermediate back into DNA using reverse transcriptase. Lamivudine inhibits reverse transcriptase and is effective against both HIV and HBV.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Enfuvirtide: Enfuvirtide blocks HIV fusion.
B. Maraviroc: Maraviroc blocks CCR5 and doesn't treat HBV.
C. Ganciclovir: Ganciclovir treats CMV.
E. Acyclovir: Acyclovir treats HSV and VZV.

Question 6
A 33-year-old woman with influenza asks why the virus is described as unusual among RNA viruses. She is a teacher and takes no medications. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Her physician explains that most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, but influenza and HIV are exceptions. Her pulse is 102/min, and she has muscle aches and a dry cough. Her rapid influenza test is positive. She is a biology teacher and wants to explain it to her students. What is the exception?
A. They're naked viruses
B. They use DNA polymerase
C. They have no capsid
D. They replicate in the nucleus
E. They replicate in mitochondria
Answer: D. They replicate in the nucleus
Why this is correct: RNA viruses usually replicate in the cytoplasm with RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Influenza and HIV are exceptions and replicate in the nucleus.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. They're naked viruses: Both are enveloped.
B. They use DNA polymerase: Influenza doesn't use DNA polymerase.
C. They have no capsid: Both have capsids.
E. They replicate in mitochondria: That isn't described.

Question 7
A new influenza A strain emerges in a region where pig farms and poultry farms sit side by side. Within a year, a pandemic spreads worldwide. A 50-year-old farmer is among the first patients; he has diabetes and takes metformin. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). Genetic analysis shows the new strain combined gene segments from two different viruses. His oxygen saturation is 88%, and chest x-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Local health officials notice that few people had any immunity to the new strain. What is this process called?
A. Latency
B. Antigenic shift from reassortment of the segmented genome
C. Antigenic drift
D. Syncytium formation
E. Reverse transcription
Answer: B. Antigenic shift from reassortment of the segmented genome
Why this is correct: Influenza's genome has 8 segments. Antigenic drift causes slow changes and yearly outbreaks, while antigenic shift comes from reassortment of genome segments.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Latency: That's a herpesvirus feature.
C. Antigenic drift: Drift is gradual point mutation.
D. Syncytium formation: That's cell fusion.
E. Reverse transcription: That's retroviruses.

Question 12
A 7-month-old girl has fever and rhinorrhea for 3 days followed by wheezing and increased work of breathing. She was born at 34 weeks and attends daycare. Respiratory rate is 62/min, and oxygen saturation is 91%. Her physician mentions that this virus causes infected cells to fuse into large multinucleated cells. Her older brother has a cold. She has intercostal retractions and diffuse wheezes. Rapid antigen testing is positive for RSV. What causes this finding?
A. Negri bodies form
B. Chromatin marginates to the nuclear edge
C. Viral glycoproteins on the cell surface promote cell fusion (syncytium)
D. Koilocytosis
E. Viral DNA integrates into the host
Answer: C. Viral glycoproteins on the cell surface promote cell fusion (syncytium)
Why this is correct: Syncytium formation occurs when viral glycoprotein on the cell surface promotes fusion of cells, generating multinucleated giant cells. This helps cell-to-cell spread and disguises the virus. RSV is associated with syncytium formation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Negri bodies form: That's rabies.
B. Chromatin marginates to the nuclear edge: That's parvovirus B19.
D. Koilocytosis: That's HPV.
E. Viral DNA integrates into the host: That's retroviruses.

Question 13
A 30-year-old man develops fever and muscle aches for 2 days before his specific illness becomes clear. He had a viral exposure 10 days ago at work. His pulse is 98/min, and his exam is otherwise normal. He asks why he feels sick before any specific symptoms appear. What is the phase with nonspecific fever, chills, and body aches called?
A. Acquisition
B. Convalescence
C. Contagion
D. The incubation period
E. The prodromal period
Answer: E. The prodromal period
Why this is correct: Viral progression moves through acquisition, incubation (amplification and spread), the prodromal period (nonspecific symptoms like fever, chills, and aches), replication with specific manifestations, contagion, and convalescence.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Acquisition: That's initiation at the primary site.
B. Convalescence: That's resolution.
C. Contagion: That's release of virus from tissue.
D. The incubation period: That's amplification before symptoms.

Question 14
A 64-year-old man is admitted with COVID-19 pneumonia. He has hypertension and diabetes and takes lisinopril and metformin. Oxygen saturation is 86%, and his D-dimer is elevated. His physician explains that the virus binds a host peptidase and causes loss of its function. His blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg, and chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. His platelets are normal. What is the downstream effect?
A. Increased ACE2 activity
B. Increased angiotensin II, causing vasoconstriction and coagulopathy
C. Decreased angiotensin II
D. Integration into the host genome
E. Syncytium in the gut only
Answer: B. Increased angiotensin II, causing vasoconstriction and coagulopathy
Why this is correct: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2, a peptidase that cleaves angiotensin II. Binding causes loss of ACE2 function, raising angiotensin II, which leads to vasoconstriction, coagulopathy, and other effects.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Increased ACE2 activity: Binding causes loss of function.
C. Decreased angiotensin II: Loss of ACE2 raises Ang II.
D. Integration into the host genome: SARS-CoV-2 doesn't integrate.
E. Syncytium in the gut only: That isn't the mechanism described.

Question 15
A 48-year-old man is diagnosed with HTLV-1 after workup for an abnormal white count. He was born in southern Japan and takes no medications. His physician explains that his virus has a (+) RNA genome that is copied into DNA and inserted into his cells' chromosomes. His lymphocyte count is elevated, and his calcium is high. He has no medical problems otherwise. His mother also has HTLV-1. Why does this family of viruses carry oncogenic potential?
A. They cause koilocytosis
B. They replicate only in the cytoplasm
C. They have segmented genomes
D. The viral DNA is integrated into the host genome
E. They're naked viruses
Answer: D. The viral DNA is integrated into the host genome
Why this is correct: Retroviruses have a (+) RNA genome converted into DNA that is integrated into the host genome, giving them oncogenic potential. They use reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) to make dsDNA from (+) ssRNA.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. They cause koilocytosis: That's HPV.
B. They replicate only in the cytoplasm: HIV replicates in the nucleus.
C. They have segmented genomes: That's influenza and rotavirus.
E. They're naked viruses: Retroviruses are enveloped.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 19
A 26-year-old woman asks why her cold sores keep returning. She had her first outbreak as a child. She takes an oral contraceptive. Her physician explains that her virus is a double-stranded DNA virus with a lipid envelope, an icosahedral nucleocapsid, and a layer of proteins between them that helps it replicate. She takes no medications and works as a nurse. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. She read that herpesviruses have four structural layers. What is that middle layer called?
A. The peplomer
B. The matrix of the envelope
C. The tegument
D. The core
E. The capsid
Answer: C. The tegument
Why this is correct: Herpesviruses have four structural features: an outer lipid envelope, the tegument (proteins that aid replication and reactivation), an icosahedral nucleocapsid, and an inner double-stranded linear DNA core.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The peplomer: That's a surface glycoprotein spike.
B. The matrix of the envelope: That isn't the term used.
D. The core: The core holds the DNA.
E. The capsid: The capsid is the icosahedral cage.

Question 25
A 4-year-old girl with poorly controlled atopic dermatitis suddenly develops fever and clusters of punched-out, crusted erosions over her eczema patches on her face and neck. She uses topical steroids. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Her pulse is 128/min, and she is irritable. Her mother has a cold sore. She attends preschool. What is the diagnosis?
A. Chickenpox
B. Shingles
C. Impetigo
D. Eczema herpeticum
E. Herpes gladiatorum
Answer: D. Eczema herpeticum
Why this is correct: Eczema herpeticum is HSV occurring in the setting of active skin disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chickenpox: Chickenpox is pruritic and starts on the trunk.
B. Shingles: Shingles is dermatomal.
C. Impetigo: The Tzanck smear points to herpes.
E. Herpes gladiatorum: That's HSV in wrestlers.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 26
A 34-year-old woman is exposed to her nephew's chickenpox. She has no memory of having had it and never received the vaccine. Five days after delivering her son, she develops a vesicular rash. Her newborn is exposed. She has asthma and takes an inhaled steroid. Her son was born at 39 weeks and is feeding well. Her physician explains treatment for the baby. Which treatment is recommended for the neonate?
A. Supportive care only
B. Acyclovir alone
C. Shingrix
D. Varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) and acyclovir
E. Ganciclovir
Answer: D. Varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) and acyclovir
Why this is correct: Primary varicella is spread by respiratory transmission or lesion contact. Neonates receive VZIG and acyclovir, and adults receive acyclovir. VARIVAX is the childhood vaccine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Supportive care only: Neonates need VZIG and acyclovir.
B. Acyclovir alone: Neonates also get VZIG.
C. Shingrix: Shingrix prevents zoster in adults.
E. Ganciclovir: That treats CMV.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 27
A 7-year-old boy is kept home from school with an itchy vesicular rash that began on his trunk 4 days ago. Some lesions are vesicles, some are pustules, and some are crusted. He was never vaccinated. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). His mother asks when he can return to school. His sister is 2 and also unvaccinated. His pulse is 104/min, and he is scratching constantly. His lungs are clear. What is the answer?
A. After 24 hours of antibiotics
B. When all lesions have crusted
C. When the fever resolves
D. Immediately, since chickenpox isn't contagious
E. Only after a negative PCR
Answer: B. When all lesions have crusted
Why this is correct: Chickenpox usually begins on the trunk, is almost always pruritic, and progresses from vesicle to pustule to crusted ulcer. It's contagious until all lesions have crusted.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. After 24 hours of antibiotics: It's viral.
C. When the fever resolves: He's contagious until lesions crust.
D. Immediately, since chickenpox isn't contagious: It's contagious.
E. Only after a negative PCR: That isn't the listed criterion.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 28
A 74-year-old man had a painful band-like rash on his left chest 3 months ago that has healed, but he still has burning pain in the same area that keeps him awake. He has hypertension and takes amlodipine. His skin looks normal. He never received a shingles vaccine. His blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. The rash was treated late with an antiviral. What is this condition, and what might have reduced its risk?
A. Eczema herpeticum; steroids
B. Recurrent chickenpox; VZIG
C. Herpes encephalitis; acyclovir
D. Disseminated zoster; ganciclovir
E. Post-herpetic neuralgia; early antiviral treatment of the shingles
Answer: E. Post-herpetic neuralgia; early antiviral treatment of the shingles
Why this is correct: Shingles is reactivation of latent varicella from a sensory ganglion, usually in thoracic or lumbar dermatomes. Post-herpetic neuralgia is persistent pain in the dermatome after the rash resolves, common in the elderly from nerve damage. Early treatment may reduce its occurrence and duration. Shingles is treated with famciclovir or valacyclovir.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Eczema herpeticum; steroids: That's HSV in active skin disease.
B. Recurrent chickenpox; VZIG: This is zoster, not primary varicella.
C. Herpes encephalitis; acyclovir: He has no CNS symptoms.
D. Disseminated zoster; ganciclovir: His rash was dermatomal.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 30
A 17-year-old boy has fever, severe sore throat, and fatigue for a week. He recently started dating someone. Question 31
A 24-year-old graduate student has fever, malaise, and enlarged lymph nodes for 2 weeks. He has no sore throat. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). His blood shows atypical lymphocytes, but his heterophile antibody test is negative on two occasions. CMV IgM is positive. He has no rash, and his throat is normal. A. CMV mononucleosis syndrome
B. HHV-6 infection
C. Toxoplasmosis
D. EBV mononucleosis
E. Acute HIV
Answer: A. CMV mononucleosis syndrome
Why this is correct: CMV mononucleosis affects healthy young adults with fever, malaise, adenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. It clinically mimics EBV mono, and the biggest difference is a negative heterophile antibody. Positive CMV IgM suggests active disease.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. HHV-6 infection: That causes roseola in children.
C. Toxoplasmosis: That isn't a heterophile-negative herpesvirus.

Question 34
A 10-month-old girl had 3 days of high fever up to 40°C (104°F), during which she seemed surprisingly well. When the fever broke, a pink, blanching rash appeared on her trunk. She had a brief febrile seizure on day 2. Her vaccines are up to date. She attends daycare and has an older brother. Her pulse is 128/min, and she is playing normally now. B. HHV-6 (exanthem subitum)
C. VZV
D. EBV

Answer: B. HHV-6 (exanthem subitum)
Why this is correct: HHV-6 causes exanthem subitum (roseola infantum), a rash and fever in a child, and febrile syndromes. Seroprevalence is over 80% by age 2. HHV-7 causes a very similar illness, including seizures.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Parvovirus B19: Fifth disease causes slapped cheeks.
C. VZV: Chickenpox is pruritic and vesicular.

Question 35
A 32-year-old woman has had cold sores several times a year since childhood. She notices they appear after sunburns, stressful exams, and when she has a fever. She takes no medications. She asks where the virus hides between outbreaks and what happens during one. Her vital signs are normal. She asks what triggers the outbreaks and where the virus goes. Which statement is correct?
A. It's cleared completely after each outbreak
B. It integrates into skin cell DNA
C. It lies latent in endothelial cells
D. It lies latent in sensory ganglia and travels along the axon to the skin when reactivated
E. It lives in B cells and reactivates in the blood
Answer: D. It lies latent in sensory ganglia and travels along the axon to the skin when reactivated
Why this is correct: HSV-1 establishes latency in sensory ganglia, where no infectious virions are made. Reactivation (provoked by fever, stress, sun, trauma, decreased immunity, and steroids) spreads virus from the neuron along the axon to the skin, causing blisters and cold sores.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It's cleared completely after each outbreak: It persists in latency.
B. It integrates into skin cell DNA: Herpesviruses don't integrate this way.
C. It lies latent in endothelial cells: That's HHV-8.
E. It lives in B cells and reactivates in the blood: That's EBV latency.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 36
A 28-year-old man has blood drawn during a workup for fatigue. He is otherwise healthy. His physician explains the serologic pattern for his herpesvirus results: one antibody class suggests acute infection, and another shows prior exposure. His vital signs are normal, and his exam shows no rash. His physician ordered antibodies to several herpesviruses. He asks what the results mean. Which pairing is correct?

B. IgA suggests acute infection
