D. IgM suggests acute infection, and IgG indicates prior exposure
E. IgG suggests acute infection, and IgM indicates prior exposure
Answer: D. IgM suggests acute infection, and IgG indicates prior exposure
Why this is correct: Herpesvirus diagnostics include culture, antigen detection (ELISA, IF), PCR, serology (IgM for acute infection, IgG for prior exposure), and histopathology such as the Tzanck smear.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Serology can't be used for herpesviruses: Serology is listed.
B. IgA suggests acute infection: That isn't the listed marker.
C. IgE indicates prior exposure: That isn't the listed marker.
E. IgG suggests acute infection, and IgM indicates prior exposure: This is reversed.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 38

Question 39
A 23-year-old woman has painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her labia. She has a new partner. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). She has tender inguinal nodes. Her HIV test is negative. Question 40

Question 46

Question 47
A 19-year-old man has fever, sore throat, and fatigue. His spleen is mildly enlarged. His liver enzymes are elevated. He has tender posterior cervical nodes. Week 8: Virology & Cell Injury / HIV Pathogenesis & Opportunistic Infections

Question 48
A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV after a routine screening. He feels well and takes no medications. His CD4 count is 520/μL. He asks how the virus gets into his cells. His physician explains that binding CD4 alone isn't enough, and that the virus needs a second receptor to trigger entry. He works as a paramedic and has no other medical problems. His viral load is 38,000 copies/mL. He asks why the virus targets only certain cells. What happens after gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor?
A. The virus enters by lysis
B. gp41 binds MHC class II
C. gp120 integrates into the membrane
D. CD4 alone triggers endocytosis
E. gp120 and gp41 change shape, and gp41 exposes a hydrophobic domain that fuses the viral and cell membranes
Answer: E. gp120 and gp41 change shape, and gp41 exposes a hydrophobic domain that fuses the viral and cell membranes
Why this is correct: HIV binds CD4 on helper T cells, but CD4 alone allows binding, not entry. Binding a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) triggers conformational changes in gp120 and gp41, and gp41 exposes its hydrophobic domain to induce fusion. The primary target is the memory T cell.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The virus enters by lysis: Entry is by fusion.
B. gp41 binds MHC class II: That isn't the mechanism.
C. gp120 integrates into the membrane: gp41 mediates fusion.
D. CD4 alone triggers endocytosis: CD4 isn't enough for entry.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 49
A 36-year-old man has had repeated sexual exposures to partners with HIV but has never been infected. He takes no medications and is healthy. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for a truncated co-receptor. His brother, who is heterozygous for the same variant, has HIV. He works as a sex educator and uses condoms inconsistently. His vital signs are normal. His HIV antibody and RNA tests have always been negative. What explains the difference?
A. CXCR4 Δ32 causes resistance
B. CCR5 Δ32 prevents CD4 expression
C. Homozygous CCR5 Δ32 confers resistance, while heterozygotes are susceptible but may progress slower
D. Heterozygotes are fully resistant
E. The brother has an elite controller genotype
Answer: C. Homozygous CCR5 Δ32 confers resistance, while heterozygotes are susceptible but may progress slower
Why this is correct: CCR5 normally binds pro-inflammatory cytokines. The CCR5 Δ32 mutation truncates the receptor without harming the inflammatory response. Homozygotes are resistant to HIV, while heterozygotes are susceptible but may progress more slowly.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. CXCR4 Δ32 causes resistance: The variant is CCR5.
B. CCR5 Δ32 prevents CD4 expression: It affects the co-receptor.
D. Heterozygotes are fully resistant: Heterozygotes are susceptible.
E. The brother has an elite controller genotype: That isn't what's described.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 50
A 42-year-old woman has been HIV positive for 6 years and has never taken antiretrovirals. She feels well. Her HIV RNA has stayed detectable but below 200 copies/mL for 3 years, and her CD4 count is 780/μL. She is heterozygous for CCR5 Δ32. She works as an accountant and takes no medications. She has no opportunistic infections. She asks whether she can still infect a partner. How is she best classified?
A. An elite controller
B. She can't transmit the virus
C. She is HIV resistant
D. She has AIDS
E. She has acute HIV
Answer: A. An elite controller
Why this is correct: Elite controllers (1.5–2% of people with HIV) maintain undetectable or very low viral loads (under 200 and always under 500 copies/mL) for at least 12 months without therapy, with CD4 counts above 500. CCR5 Δ32 heterozygosity can't be the only explanation, and they can still transmit virus.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. She can't transmit the virus: The virus can infect others normally.
C. She is HIV resistant: She's infected.
D. She has AIDS: Her CD4 is above 200 without OIs.
E. She has acute HIV: Her infection is years old.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 54
A 37-year-old man with AIDS has headache, fever, and confusion that developed over 2 weeks. His CD4 count is 40/μL. C. Bone marrow toxicity of fluconazole: Flucytosine is marrow toxic.
D. Bacterial superinfection: That isn't the listed cause.

Question 58
A 32-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He has no symptoms and no opportunistic infections. His CD4 count is 170/μL. He asks whether this means he has AIDS. He works as a mechanic and has no medical problems. His viral load is 64,000 copies/mL. His vital signs are normal, and he has no thrush or weight loss. What is the answer?

E. Yes, because his CD4 count is below 200

Why this is correct: AIDS is defined by an opportunistic infection, malignancy, or a CD4 count below 200. HIV is a continuum, and worsening CD4 decline means worsening immunosuppression.

B. It can't be decided without a viral load: Viral load isn't part of the definition.

Question 60
A 33-year-old man with HIV asks which of his immune cells the virus prefers. His CD4 count is 410/μL, and he takes a single-pill regimen. Week 8: Virology & Cell Injury / Oncogenic Viruses

Question 67
A 28-year-old woman asks how a virus can cause cancer. She has had abnormal Pap smears. She smokes and takes an oral contraceptive. Her physician explains that some viruses insert into the host genome and turn a normal growth gene into a cancer-driving gene, while others disable genes that normally stop growth. Her last Pap smear showed a low-grade lesion. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. She asks whether the virus that causes warts could cause cancer too. Which pair of terms describes these two mechanisms?
A. Latency and reactivation
B. Activating oncogenes and interfering with tumor suppressor genes
C. Budding and lysis
D. Antigenic drift and shift
E. Syncytium and koilocytosis
Answer: B. Activating oncogenes and interfering with tumor suppressor genes
Why this is correct: Persistent infections cause uncontrolled growth that can lead to malignant transformation. Some viruses insert into the host and convert proto-oncogenes into oncogenes, and some interfere with tumor suppressor genes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Latency and reactivation: Those describe herpesvirus behavior.
C. Budding and lysis: Those describe viral release.
D. Antigenic drift and shift: Those describe influenza.
E. Syncytium and koilocytosis: Those are histologic findings.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 68
A 10-year-old boy in Uganda has a rapidly growing jaw mass. He lives in a region with high rates of malaria. Biopsy shows a high-grade B-cell lymphoma, and the tumor cells carry EBV genomes. His physician explains how the virus sets the stage for the translocation. His WBC is 14,000/mm³, and his LDH is very high. His HIV test is negative. The mass has doubled in size in 3 weeks. What is EBV's role?
A. It integrates at the MYC locus
B. It inactivates p53 with E6
C. It produces viral IL-6 in endothelial cells
D. It causes koilocytosis
E. It acts as a polyclonal B-cell mitogen, setting the stage for t(8;14)
Answer: E. It acts as a polyclonal B-cell mitogen, setting the stage for t(8;14)
Why this is correct: Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm prevalent along the malaria belt; over 90% of African tumors carry EBV. EBV acts as a polyclonal B-cell mitogen, setting the stage for the t(8;14) MYC translocation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It integrates at the MYC locus: EBV doesn't cause the translocation by integration.
B. It inactivates p53 with E6: That's HPV.
C. It produces viral IL-6 in endothelial cells: That's HHV-8.
D. It causes koilocytosis: That's HPV.

Question 69
A 20-year-old man with EBV mononucleosis asks how the virus could ever cause cancer. He is otherwise healthy. His physician explains that an EBV latent protein acts like a constitutively active CD40 receptor, driving B-cell growth and activating BCL2. His spleen is mildly enlarged, and his liver enzymes are elevated. He takes no medications. His heterophile test is positive. Which protein is this?
A. LANA-1
B. vIL-10
C. LMP-1
D. EBNA-2
E. E6
Answer: C. LMP-1
Why this is correct: LMP-1 is an oncogene that acts as a constitutively active CD40 receptor, causing B-cell growth and preventing apoptosis by activating BCL2. EBNA-2 transactivates host genes like cyclin D and immortalizes B cells, and vIL-10 prevents macrophages from activating T cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. LANA-1: LANA-1 is an HHV-8 protein.
B. vIL-10: vIL-10 prevents T-cell activation.
D. EBNA-2: EBNA-2 transactivates cyclin D.
E. E6: E6 is an HPV protein.
Objective: Explain the mechanisms of viral pathogenesis, including cytopathic effect and immunopathogenesis (CBO 1.2)

Question 71
A 38-year-old woman has a cervical biopsy showing invasive squamous cell carcinoma. She never received the HPV vaccine. Testing shows HPV 16. Her pelvic exam shows a friable cervical mass. Which proteins do E6 and E7 inactivate?

C. Both mimic CD40
D. E6 inactivates Rb, and E7 inactivates p53
E. Both block ACE2
Answer: A. E6 inactivates p53, and E7 inactivates Rb
Why this is correct: HPV infects squamous epithelium and integrates into the host genome. E6 and E7 inactivate the tumor suppressors p53 and Rb. E6 also increases telomerase (TERT) expression, and E7 inhibits p21.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Both activate MYC: That isn't the mechanism.
C. Both mimic CD40: That's EBV LMP-1.
D. E6 inactivates Rb, and E7 inactivates p53: It's the reverse.
E. Both block ACE2: That's SARS-CoV-2.

Question 78
A 34-year-old man with multidrug-resistant HIV is started on an injectable drug that resembles the C-helix of gp41 and blocks the conformational change needed for fusion. He has had HIV for 15 years. After a week, he has red, itchy nodules where he injects it. His CD4 count is 180/μL, and his viral load is 60,000 copies/mL. He has tried many regimens. His blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Which drug is this?
A. Ritonavir
B. Abacavir
C. Dolutegravir
D. Maraviroc
E. Enfuvirtide
Answer: E. Enfuvirtide
Why this is correct: Enfuvirtide is a fusion inhibitor resembling the C-helix of gp41 that blocks the conformational change required for fusion. It's used in multidrug-resistant HIV and causes injection-site reactions, hypersensitivity, hypotension, GI intolerance, pruritus, and myalgia.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ritonavir: That's a protease inhibitor.
B. Abacavir: That's an NRTI.
C. Dolutegravir: That's an integrase inhibitor.
D. Maraviroc: Maraviroc blocks CCR5.

Question 80
A 30-year-old man with HIV is started on a regimen that includes zidovudine. He has hepatitis C. His physician explains that the drug is a thymidine analog whose 3' hydroxyl is replaced by an azido group, so it acts as a chain terminator. After a month, his hemoglobin falls and his neutrophil count drops. His CD4 count is 290/μL. His blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, and he has no bleeding. His MCV is elevated. Which toxicity is this?
A. Bone marrow suppression
B. Bone density loss
C. Injection-site reactions
D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
E. Hypersensitivity
Answer: A. Bone marrow suppression
Why this is correct: NRTIs function as chain terminators. Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine analog lacking the 3' OH and causes bone marrow suppression. Abacavir causes hypersensitivity, and tenofovir (TDF) causes bone density loss.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Bone density loss: That's tenofovir TDF.
C. Injection-site reactions: That's enfuvirtide.
D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome: That's NNRTIs.
E. Hypersensitivity: That's abacavir.

Week 8: Virology & Cell Injury / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death

Question 90
A 55-year-old man has chest pain from a coronary blockage that resolves after 10 minutes of rest. He has hypertension and smokes. His troponin stays normal. His physician explains how brief ischemia injures cells. His ECG during pain showed ST depression that resolved. His blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. He asks what happens inside heart cells when blood flow drops. What is the earliest consequence of decreased mitochondrial activity?
A. Inadequate ATP production, causing failure of membrane pumps
B. Fibrin deposition in vessels
C. Koilocytosis
D. Caseous necrosis
E. Immediate karyolysis
Answer: A. Inadequate ATP production, causing failure of membrane pumps
Why this is correct: The main targets of cell injury are mitochondria, cell membrane, cytoskeleton, and DNA/protein synthesis. Decreased mitochondrial activity causes inadequate ATP and failure of membrane pumps; rising intracellular calcium damages membranes and mitochondria, and oxygen metabolites cause further damage.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Fibrin deposition in vessels: That's fibrinoid necrosis.
C. Koilocytosis: That's HPV.
D. Caseous necrosis: That's typical of TB.
E. Immediate karyolysis: That's a late irreversible change.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 91
A pathologist reviews an electron micrograph of heart muscle from a patient who had a brief episode of ischemia but recovered fully. The patient is a 50-year-old man with diabetes. The patient's episode lasted 15 minutes, and his troponin stayed normal. His heart function is normal on echocardiogram. The micrograph was taken from a biopsy during unrelated surgery. Which ultrastructural findings are characteristic of reversible injury?
A. Ribosomes detached from rough ER with preserved mitochondrial cristae
B. Karyorrhexis
C. Severe mitochondrial swelling with destroyed cristae
D. Lysosomal enzyme leakage
E. Extensive plasma membrane damage
Answer: A. Ribosomes detached from rough ER with preserved mitochondrial cristae
Why this is correct: Reversible injury by EM shows ribosome detachment from rough ER and preserved mitochondrial cristae. Later, light microscopy shows cellular swelling, hydropic degeneration, and fatty change.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Karyorrhexis: That's a necrotic nuclear change.
C. Severe mitochondrial swelling with destroyed cristae: That's irreversible injury.
D. Lysosomal enzyme leakage: That's irreversible.
E. Extensive plasma membrane damage: That's irreversible.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 92
A 70-year-old woman dies 3 days after a large heart attack. She had diabetes and hypertension. At autopsy, heart muscle cells show small, dense, shrunken nuclei; others show fragmented nuclei; and some have no nuclei at all. Her troponin had peaked at a very high level. She had no fever. Her coronary arteries show a fresh clot. What is the correct order of these nuclear changes?
A. Karyorrhexis, then pyknosis, then karyolysis
B. Koilocytosis, then syncytium
C. Pyknosis, then karyorrhexis, then karyolysis
D. Karyolysis, then pyknosis, then karyorrhexis
E. Hydropic degeneration, then fatty change
Answer: C. Pyknosis, then karyorrhexis, then karyolysis
Why this is correct: Irreversible injury by light microscopy shows pyknosis (shrinkage and condensation), karyorrhexis (fragmentation), and karyolysis (dissolution). Cytoplasmic proteins denature and take up eosin, turning deep pink.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Karyorrhexis, then pyknosis, then karyolysis: The order is wrong.
B. Koilocytosis, then syncytium: Those are viral changes.
D. Karyolysis, then pyknosis, then karyorrhexis: The order is wrong.
E. Hydropic degeneration, then fatty change: Those are reversible changes.

Question 93
A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation stopped his anticoagulant and developed a sudden left-sided weakness. He dies 2 weeks later, and autopsy shows a cystic, liquefied area in the right hemisphere where the tissue architecture is lost. His blood pressure was 168/96 mm Hg at admission. He had no fever. CT at the time showed a large right-sided infarct. Why does ischemia in this organ produce this pattern rather than coagulative necrosis?
A. Brain cells have no lysosomes
B. Intracellular acidosis preserves the architecture
C. Fat saponification
D. Granulomas form
E. In the brain, lysosomal digestion outpaces protein denaturation
Answer: E. In the brain, lysosomal digestion outpaces protein denaturation
Why this is correct: Liquefactive necrosis occurs when digestion by lysosomal enzymes exceeds protein denaturation, causing rapid loss of architecture and liquefaction. Arterial occlusion in the brain produces liquefactive necrosis, while the heart, kidney, liver, and spleen show coagulative necrosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Brain cells have no lysosomes: They do.
B. Intracellular acidosis preserves the architecture: That's coagulative necrosis.
C. Fat saponification: That's fat necrosis.
D. Granulomas form: That's caseous necrosis.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 94

C. Fat necrosis
D. Liquefactive necrosis
E. Coagulative necrosis
Answer: B. Fibrinoid necrosis
Why this is correct: Fibrinoid necrosis is associated with vasculitis and hypertension, damaging the arterial intima and depositing fibrin in the necrotic vessel wall.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Caseous necrosis: That's typical of TB.

D. Liquefactive necrosis: That's typical of the brain.
E. Coagulative necrosis: That preserves architecture.

Question 95
A 30-year-old man with sudden kidney pain has a renal infarct from a clot. He has a patent foramen ovale. A biopsy 2 days later shows cells without nuclei, but the outlines of tubules are still visible and deeply pink. His creatinine is mildly elevated. His urinalysis shows blood. He had a recent long flight. What explains why the architecture is preserved?
A. Fibrin coats the vessels
B. Granulomas wall off the area
C. Lysosomal enzymes digest the tissue
D. Intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, including enzymes, early in the process
E. Lipase saponifies fat
Answer: D. Intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, including enzymes, early in the process
Why this is correct: In coagulative necrosis, the cell outline and tissue architecture are identifiable early even as cells die. Intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, increasing eosin affinity. It follows arterial occlusion in the heart, kidney, liver, and spleen.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fibrin coats the vessels: That's fibrinoid necrosis.
B. Granulomas wall off the area: That's caseous necrosis.
C. Lysosomal enzymes digest the tissue: That's liquefactive necrosis.
E. Lipase saponifies fat: That's fat necrosis.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 96
A 45-year-old man with heavy alcohol use has an enlarged liver. His liver biopsy shows many cells with clear cytoplasmic droplets and others with pale, swollen cytoplasm full of water. He stops drinking, and his liver enzymes normalize. He drinks a liter of vodka daily. His ALT and AST are elevated. His albumin is normal. How are these changes classified?
A. Irreversible injury with karyolysis
B. Coagulative necrosis
C. Fibrinoid necrosis
D. Reversible injury seen by light microscopy (fatty change and hydropic degeneration)
E. Caseous necrosis
Answer: D. Reversible injury seen by light microscopy (fatty change and hydropic degeneration)
Why this is correct: Reversible injury by light microscopy shows organelle and cellular swelling, hydropic degeneration (water droplets), and fatty change (lipid droplets). The earliest findings are EM changes in mitochondria and rough ER.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Irreversible injury with karyolysis: The cells recovered.
B. Coagulative necrosis: That's irreversible.
C. Fibrinoid necrosis: That's vascular.
E. Caseous necrosis: That's TB.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 97
A 60-year-old woman has a prolonged cardiac arrest before resuscitation and later develops heart failure. Her heart shows extensive muscle cell death. Her physician explains what happens once injury becomes irreversible. She had no pulse for 25 minutes. Her troponin is very high. Her ejection fraction is 25% afterward. Which process leads to enzymatic digestion of tissue and necrosis?
A. Koilocytosis
B. Calcium influx and release of lysosomal enzymes after membrane damage
C. Ribosome detachment from rough ER
D. Fatty change
E. Preservation of mitochondrial cristae
Answer: B. Calcium influx and release of lysosomal enzymes after membrane damage
Why this is correct: Irreversible injury causes ATP depletion and membrane damage. Lysosomal enzymes are released inside cells, breaking down chromatin and denaturing protein, and membrane injury allows calcium influx and release of enzymes into tissue, digesting it and causing necrosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Koilocytosis: That's HPV.
C. Ribosome detachment from rough ER: That's reversible injury.
D. Fatty change: That's reversible.
E. Preservation of mitochondrial cristae: That's reversible.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 98
A 58-year-old man from Haiti dies of an unrelated cause. He had lived in the United States for 20 years. He had no history of cough or weight loss. His chest x-ray years ago showed a small calcified nodule. At autopsy, the lung has the subpleural lesion shown, with soft, white, cheese-like dead tissue. Histology shows amorphous pink debris with no tissue architecture, surrounded by granulomas. Which infection is classically associated with this necrosis? ![Gross specimen](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b5/Tuberculosis_-_Sub-pleural_primary_%28Ghon%29_focus_%286596011395%29.jpg)
A. Stroke
B. Pancreatitis
C. Hypertension
D. Myocardial infarction
E. Tuberculosis
Answer: E. Tuberculosis
Why this is correct: Caseous necrosis produces soft, white, cheese-like dead tissue that forms an amorphous proteinaceous mass with no original architecture. It's commonly associated with tuberculosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stroke: That causes liquefactive necrosis.
B. Pancreatitis: That causes fat necrosis.
C. Hypertension: That causes fibrinoid necrosis.
D. Myocardial infarction: That causes coagulative necrosis.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Question 99
A 64-year-old man dies 2 days after a large myocardial infarction. He had diabetes and smoked. His troponin had peaked at a very high level. He had a left anterior descending occlusion. He had no fever. A section of his heart is shown, with deeply eosinophilic muscle fibers that have lost their nuclei but keep their outlines. What type of necrosis is this? ![Histology section](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Histopathology_of_coagulative_necrosis_of_cardiomyocytes.jpg)
A. Liquefactive necrosis
B. Fat necrosis
C. Coagulative necrosis
D. Fibrinoid necrosis
E. Caseous necrosis
Answer: C. Coagulative necrosis
Why this is correct: Coagulative necrosis keeps the cell outline and tissue architecture early even as cells die, from intracellular acidosis that denatures proteins and raises eosin affinity. It follows arterial occlusion in the heart, kidney, liver, and spleen.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Liquefactive necrosis: That occurs in the brain.
B. Fat necrosis: That occurs around the pancreas.
D. Fibrinoid necrosis: That's in vessel walls.
E. Caseous necrosis: That's typical of TB.

Question 100
A 45-year-old man with malignant hypertension has a blood pressure of 230/140 mm Hg and rising creatinine. He has headaches and blurred vision. His fundoscopic exam shows hemorrhages and papilledema. He stopped his antihypertensive pills months ago. His kidney biopsy is shown, with bright pink material in the damaged wall of a small vessel at the arrow. What type of necrosis is this, and which conditions cause it? ![Kidney biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Fibrinoid_necrosis.jpg)
A. Fibrinoid necrosis; vasculitis and hypertension
B. Coagulative necrosis; infarction
C. Caseous necrosis; tuberculosis
D. Liquefactive necrosis; stroke
E. Fat necrosis; pancreatitis
Answer: A. Fibrinoid necrosis; vasculitis and hypertension
Why this is correct: Fibrinoid necrosis is associated with vasculitis and hypertension, damaging the arterial intima and depositing fibrin in the necrotic vessel wall.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Coagulative necrosis; infarction: That preserves tissue architecture.
C. Caseous necrosis; tuberculosis: That's cheese-like tissue.
D. Liquefactive necrosis; stroke: That's in the brain.
E. Fat necrosis; pancreatitis: That's around the pancreas.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Week 9: Bacteria & Antibiotics / Gram-Positive Cocci

Question 1
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with fever, vomiting, and a diffuse red rash that started yesterday. She is on the third day of her period and has been using high-absorbency tampons. She takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 132/min, and blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg. She has a sunburn-like rash over her trunk and palms. Blood cultures are negative, but a vaginal swab grows the organism shown in the Gram stain below, which is coagulase positive. How does this organism's toxin cause her shock? ![Gram stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/24/Gram_Positive_Cocci_in_singles%2C_pairs_and_clusters.jpg)
A. The toxin inactivates elongation factor 2
B. The toxin raises cGMP in the gut
C. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release
D. The toxin is lipooligosaccharide from the outer membrane
E. The toxin is a superantigen that binds MHC II and raises IL-2
Answer: E. The toxin is a superantigen that binds MHC II and raises IL-2
Why this is correct: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by TSST-1, a superantigen toxin of Staphylococcus aureus, a coagulase-positive gram-positive coccus in clusters. The toxin binds MHC II and increases IL-2.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The toxin inactivates elongation factor 2: That's diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
B. The toxin raises cGMP in the gut: That's the heat-stable toxin of B. cereus.
C. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release: That's botulinum toxin.
D. The toxin is lipooligosaccharide from the outer membrane: LOS is a gram-negative component; this organism is gram positive.
Image credit: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 2
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a sore throat and fever for 2 days. He has no cough or runny nose. He is in the fourth grade, and several classmates have been sick. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). His tonsils are red and swollen with exudates, and he has tender anterior cervical nodes. A throat culture grows beta-hemolytic colonies, and the Gram stain of the colonies is shown below. What is this organism's major virulence factor? ![Gram stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/Gram_stain_of_Streptococcus_pyogenes.jpg)
A. Exotoxin A
B. Pneumolysin
C. M protein
D. Granadaene
E. TSST-1
Answer: C. M protein
Why this is correct: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep) is a gram-positive coccus in chains that causes pharyngitis, erysipelas, cellulitis, and scarlet fever. M protein is its major virulence factor.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Exotoxin A: Exotoxin A belongs to Pseudomonas.
B. Pneumolysin: Pneumolysin belongs to S. pneumoniae.
D. Granadaene: Granadaene is the hemolytic pigment of group B strep.
E. TSST-1: TSST-1 is a Staphylococcus aureus toxin.
Image credit: Gary E. Kaiser, Ph.D., CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 3
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever, sore throat, and a rash that began on her neck and spread to her trunk. She has no allergies and takes no medications. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Her throat is red with exudates, and her skin has a fine, sandpaper-like rash that blanches, with red lines in the folds of her elbows. Her tongue is shown below. Throat culture grows group A strep. Which condition does she have? ![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/72/Strep_throat_with_white_strawberry_tongue.jpg)
A. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
B. Rocky Mountain spotted fever
C. Diphtheria
D. Toxic shock syndrome
E. Scarlet fever
Answer: E. Scarlet fever
Why this is correct: Scarlet fever from Streptococcus pyogenes causes a strawberry tongue, Pastia's lines, and a blanching rash.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: SSSS causes skin peeling from exfoliative toxins.
B. Rocky Mountain spotted fever: RMSF causes a rash that starts at the wrists and ankles after a tick bite.
C. Diphtheria: Diphtheria causes pharyngitis with a bull neck.
D. Toxic shock syndrome: TSS causes shock with a sunburn-like rash from S. aureus.
Image credit: Whispyhistory, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Question 4
A 6-year-old boy has a sore throat, and a throat swab is plated on blood agar. He has had fever and painful swallowing for 2 days. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), and he has tonsillar exudates. After 24 hours the colonies look like the image below, with complete clearing of the agar around each colony. His physician explains that this organism can later cause joint pain, carditis, and involuntary jerking movements if untreated. Which organism is this? ![Blood agar plate](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/Streptococcus_pyogenes_%28Lancefield_Group_A%29_on_Columbia_Horse_Blood_Agar_-_Detail.jpg)
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Enterococcus faecalis
C. Staphylococcus saprophyticus
D. Viridans streptococci
E. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Answer: E. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Why this is correct: The clear zones are beta hemolysis. Group A strep causes pharyngitis and can lead to rheumatic fever and Sydenham chorea.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae: S. pneumoniae is alpha hemolytic.
B. Enterococcus faecalis: Enterococcus is gamma hemolytic.
C. Staphylococcus saprophyticus: S. saprophyticus causes UTIs and grows in clusters.
D. Viridans streptococci: Viridans strep are alpha hemolytic.

Question 5
A 3-day-old boy develops fever, poor feeding, and lethargy. He was born at 38 weeks by vaginal delivery after 20 hours of ruptured membranes. His mother had no prenatal care in the third trimester. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 182/min, and his fontanelle is full. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains. The lab performs the test shown below, which produces an arrowhead-shaped zone of enhanced hemolysis. His WBC is 4,200/mm³ with many bands. CSF shows neutrophils and a low glucose. Which organism is this? ![Blood agar plate](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d9/CAMP_test.JPG)
A. Streptococcus agalactiae (group B)
B. Streptococcus pyogenes
C. Listeria monocytogenes
D. Enterococcus faecalis
E. Staphylococcus aureus
Answer: A. Streptococcus agalactiae (group B)
Why this is correct: Group B strep colonizes the GI and GU tracts and is transmitted to babies at birth, causing neonatal sepsis. It's weakly beta or alpha hemolytic and encapsulated, and the CAMP test produces an arrowhead-shaped zone of hemolysis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A strep isn't identified by a positive CAMP test.
C. Listeria monocytogenes: Listeria is a gram-positive rod.
D. Enterococcus faecalis: Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and is gamma hemolytic.
E. Staphylococcus aureus: S. aureus grows in clusters.

Question 6
A 70-year-old man is admitted with fever, chills, and a cough producing rust-colored sputum for 2 days. He has COPD and smokes. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), respiratory rate is 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 88%. Chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Sputum grows alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci. The plate below shows a zone of no growth around a disk. He lives alone and had influenza last week. His WBC is 18,000/mm³. A. Pneumolysin
B. M protein
C. Lecithinase (alpha toxin)
D. TSST-1

Why the other answers are wrong:
B. M protein: M protein is the virulence factor of group A strep.
C. Lecithinase (alpha toxin): That's C. perfringens.
D. TSST-1: TSST-1 comes from S. aureus.
E. Exoenzyme S: That's Pseudomonas.

Question 7
A 78-year-old woman in a nursing home develops fever and suprapubic pain. She has had a urinary catheter for 6 months. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Urine culture grows gamma-hemolytic gram-positive cocci that grow in 6.5% NaCl broth. On bile esculin agar, the organism produces the result shown below. She has dementia and hypertension and takes donepezil and amlodipine. Pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Her WBC is 13,600/mm³, and urinalysis shows many white cells. A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Proteus mirabilis
C. Enterococcus faecalis
D. Streptococcus agalactiae
E. Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Answer: C. Enterococcus faecalis
Why this is correct: Enterococcus (group D strep) lives in the GI, GU, and biliary tracts. It reacts with iron to turn black on bile esculin agar, is gamma hemolytic, and grows (turbidity) in 6.5% NaCl.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae: Pneumococcus is optochin sensitive and alpha hemolytic.
B. Proteus mirabilis: Proteus is a gram-negative rod that swarms.
D. Streptococcus agalactiae: Group B strep is identified by the CAMP test.
E. Staphylococcus saprophyticus: S. saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative staph that causes UTIs in young women.

Question 8

Question 10
A 45-year-old man with a skin abscess has pus sent for culture. He injects heroin into his arm. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and there is a 4-cm fluctuant, tender mass on his forearm. The lab finds gram-positive cocci in clusters and needs to separate Staphylococcus aureus from the coagulase-negative staph like S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus. His HIV test is negative, and his glucose is normal. Blood cultures are drawn. Which test distinguishes them?
A. The oxidase test
B. The CAMP test
C. The coagulase test
D. Growth in 6.5% NaCl
E. The optochin test
Answer: C. The coagulase test
Why this is correct: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive, while S. saprophyticus and S. epidermidis are coagulase negative.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. The CAMP test: CAMP identifies group B strep.
D. Growth in 6.5% NaCl: That identifies Enterococcus.
E. The optochin test: Optochin identifies S. pneumoniae.

Question 11
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever and red, tender skin that has begun peeling in large sheets around his mouth, neck, and armpits. D. TSST-1: TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome.
E. M protein: M protein is a group A strep virulence factor.

Question 12
A 10-year-old girl comes to the physician because of joint pain that moves from her knees to her wrists and odd, jerky movements of her arms and face. Her mother says she had a sore throat about a month ago that wasn't treated. She takes no medications. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). She has a new heart murmur and swollen, tender wrists, and her movements are purposeless and quick. What are her jerky movements called, and which organism started this illness?

B. Tetanus from Clostridium tetani
C. Sydenham chorea from Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Sydenham chorea from Streptococcus pyogenes
E. Neurobrucellosis from Brucella
Answer: D. Sydenham chorea from Streptococcus pyogenes

B. Tetanus from Clostridium tetani: Tetanus causes spastic paralysis.
C. Sydenham chorea from Streptococcus pneumoniae: Pneumococcus doesn't cause rheumatic fever.
E. Neurobrucellosis from Brucella: Neurobrucellosis causes cranial nerve palsies and personality change.

Question 13
A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, fatigue, and night sweats for 3 weeks. He had several teeth extracted a month ago and has a history of rheumatic heart disease. He has many dental caries. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and a new holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci that aren't typeable by Lancefield grouping and are optochin resistant. His WBC is 12,600/mm³, and his ESR is elevated. He has small painful nodules on his fingertips. Which organism is most likely?
A. Viridans streptococci
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Staphylococcus epidermidis
D. Enterococcus faecalis
E. Streptococcus pyogenes
Answer: A. Viridans streptococci
Why this is correct: Viridans streptococci are alpha hemolytic and not Lancefield typeable. They cause dental caries through sugar-driven acidification and demineralization and infective endocarditis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae: Pneumococcus is optochin sensitive.
C. Staphylococcus epidermidis: S. epidermidis is a staph in clusters.
D. Enterococcus faecalis: Enterococcus is gamma hemolytic.
E. Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A strep is beta hemolytic.
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Week 9: Bacteria & Antibiotics / Gram-Positive Bacilli

Question 14
A 50-year-old man who works in a wool processing plant comes to the emergency department with fever, cough, and chest discomfort. His symptoms began like the flu 5 days ago, improved briefly, and then worsened with severe shortness of breath and confusion. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and oxygen saturation is 84%. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Blood culture grows non-motile, non-hemolytic, spore-forming gram-positive rods in long chains, shown below. What is the diagnosis? ![Stained smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Bacillus_anthracis.png)
A. Bacillus cereus food poisoning
B. Gastrointestinal anthrax
C. Q fever
D. Cutaneous anthrax
E. Inhalational anthrax
Answer: E. Inhalational anthrax
Why this is correct: Bacillus anthracis is a spore-forming gram-positive rod that forms bamboo-like chains and medusa-head colonies and is non-motile and non-hemolytic. Inhalational anthrax causes a biphasic respiratory illness with a widened mediastinum.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bacillus cereus food poisoning: B. cereus is a motile, beta-hemolytic rod linked to fried rice.
B. Gastrointestinal anthrax: GI anthrax causes intestinal ulcers and bloody diarrhea.
C. Q fever: Q fever is caused by Coxiella, a gram-negative coccobacillus.
D. Cutaneous anthrax: Cutaneous anthrax causes a malignant pustule.
Image credit: CDC, uploaded by en:User:MarcoTolo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 15
A 42-year-old rancher comes to the physician because of a sore on his forearm that started as a small bump 6 days ago. He recently skinned a cow that had died suddenly. He takes no medications. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). The lesion is shown below, with swelling around it and painful enlarged lymph nodes in his armpit. His vaccines are up to date, and he has no other medical problems. Which toxin component helps this organism's other toxins enter cells? ![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/Anthrax_PHIL_2033.png)
A. Lethal factor alone
B. Protective antigen
C. Pneumolysin
D. Exfoliative toxin
E. TSST-1
Answer: B. Protective antigen
Why this is correct: Cutaneous anthrax comes from contact with infected animal tissue and causes a malignant pustule with painful adenopathy. B. anthracis makes edema toxin and lethal toxin, which enter cells with protective antigen (PA). Edema toxin lowers ATP and causes fluid, and lethal toxin causes cell leakage and lysis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lethal factor alone: Lethal toxin needs PA to enter cells.
C. Pneumolysin: That's a pneumococcal toxin.
D. Exfoliative toxin: That's the cause of SSSS.
E. TSST-1: That's a staph superantigen.

Question 16
A 72-year-old woman is admitted with 12 watery stools a day, cramping, and fever. Two weeks ago she finished a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. She lives in a nursing home and has hypertension. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and WBC is 24,000/mm³. Colonoscopy shows the appearance below. Question 17
A 20-year-old college student comes to the emergency department with intense vomiting that started 2 hours after eating leftover fried rice from a restaurant. His roommate who ate the same rice is also sick. He has no fever or diarrhea. Pulse is 104/min, and his mucous membranes are dry. The rice grows a large, motile, beta-hemolytic gram-positive rod. B. A toxin inactivates elongation factor 2
C. A toxin blocks acetylcholine release
D. A heat-stable toxin raises cGMP
E. A superantigen binds MHC II
Answer: D. A heat-stable toxin raises cGMP
Why this is correct: Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning linked to fried rice. Its heat-stable toxin causes vomiting and raises cGMP, and its heat-labile toxin causes diarrhea and raises cAMP.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. A toxin inactivates elongation factor 2: That's diphtheria toxin.
C. A toxin blocks acetylcholine release: That's botulinum toxin.
E. A superantigen binds MHC II: That's TSST-1.

Question 18
A 34-year-old construction worker comes to the emergency department with severe pain in his leg 2 days after a deep, dirty laceration. E. Exotoxin A of Pseudomonas
Answer: C. Alpha toxin (lecithinase) of Clostridium perfringens

Question 19
A 5-day-old boy born at 29 weeks is in the neonatal ICU when he develops abdominal distension, vomiting, and bloody stools. He is fed formula by tube. Question 20

Question 21
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of constipation for 5 days, a weak cry, and poor feeding. His parents have been putting honey on his pacifier to calm him. He was born at term. He is afebrile, has drooping eyelids, and is floppy with poor head control. His blood glucose and electrolytes are normal. He has a weak suck and poor gag. Which tests confirm the diagnosis, and how does the toxin work?
A. Stool culture; the toxin raises cAMP
B. CAMP test; the toxin lyses red cells
C. Blood culture; the toxin inhibits glycine release
D. Stool culture and toxin assay; the toxin blocks acetylcholine release
E. Loeffler medium culture; the toxin inactivates EF-2
Answer: D. Stool culture and toxin assay; the toxin blocks acetylcholine release
Why this is correct: Clostridium botulinum spores are found in honey, corn syrup, soil, and canned food. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis. Infant botulism (floppy baby syndrome) is confirmed by positive stool culture and toxin assay.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stool culture; the toxin raises cAMP: That describes enterotoxins causing diarrhea.
B. CAMP test; the toxin lyses red cells: That's group B strep.
C. Blood culture; the toxin inhibits glycine release: Glycine inhibition is tetanus.
E. Loeffler medium culture; the toxin inactivates EF-2: That's diphtheria.

Question 22
A 7-year-old boy who recently arrived from a country with low vaccination rates has a sore throat, fever, and a swollen neck. He hasn't received any vaccines. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). He has a gray membrane over his tonsils and massive neck swelling. A week later he has a new arrhythmia. E. Doxycycline alone
Answer: C. Penicillin or erythromycin plus diphtheria antitoxin
Why this is correct: Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes pharyngitis, bull neck, myocarditis, and cranial neuropathy. Its toxin inactivates elongation factor 2. It's treated with penicillin or erythromycin plus antitoxin, and prevented with Tdap.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Supportive care only: The toxin must be neutralized.
B. Rifampin prophylaxis alone: That's used for meningococcal contacts.
D. Vancomycin alone: That doesn't address the toxin.
E. Doxycycline alone: That treats rickettsial infections.

Question 23
A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of fever, muscle aches, and fatigue for 3 days. She ate deli meats and soft cheese last week. Question 24
A 35-year-old man in a rural village where several animals recently died develops fever, chills, sore throat, and trouble swallowing. He ate undercooked meat from one of the animals 3 days ago. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), and pulse is 124/min. He has neck swelling and bloody diarrhea. CT shows enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Blood cultures grow spore-forming gram-positive rods in chains. He has no cough or skin lesions. His chest x-ray is normal. What is the diagnosis?
A. Bacillus cereus food poisoning
B. Injectional anthrax
C. Cutaneous anthrax
D. Gastrointestinal anthrax
E. Inhalational anthrax
Answer: D. Gastrointestinal anthrax
Why this is correct: Gastrointestinal anthrax causes intestinal ulcers, mesenteric adenopathy, neck and chest swelling, dysphagia, fever and chills, bloody diarrhea, and sepsis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bacillus cereus food poisoning: B. cereus is motile and causes food poisoning without sepsis.
B. Injectional anthrax: That causes cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis at an injection site.
C. Cutaneous anthrax: That causes a malignant pustule.
E. Inhalational anthrax: That causes a widened mediastinum.

Question 25
A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe left flank pain radiating to her groin. She has had four urinary tract infections this year. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Urine pH is 8.0, and CT shows a large branching kidney stone. Her urine culture grows a gram-negative rod that is urease positive and oxidase negative, and it spreads across the plate as shown below. She takes no medications and has no other medical problems. Her WBC is 12,800/mm³. Which organism is this? ![Blood agar plate](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ad/Proteus_swarming_on_blood_agar.jpg)
A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
B. Shigella
C. Enterococcus faecalis
D. Proteus mirabilis
E. Klebsiella pneumoniae
Answer: D. Proteus mirabilis
Why this is correct: Proteus mirabilis causes kidney stones, is urease positive and oxidase negative, and has swarming motility that makes the agar look like a target with ripples.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Pseudomonas is oxidase positive.
B. Shigella: Shigella is non-motile.
C. Enterococcus faecalis: Enterococcus is a gram-positive coccus.
E. Klebsiella pneumoniae: Klebsiella is non-motile with a thick capsule.

Question 26
A 60-year-old woman with pyelonephritis has a urine sample plated on selective media. She has type 2 diabetes. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and she has left flank tenderness. Gram-positive organisms don't grow on the plate, and the gram-negative colonies turn pink-red as shown below. She takes metformin and has had two urinary infections this year. Her WBC is 15,200/mm³, and urinalysis shows nitrites. What does the pink color indicate? ![MacConkey agar plate](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/05/Raoultella_planticola_MacConkey_colonies_32.jpg)
A. The organism is oxidase positive
B. The organism ferments lactose, dropping the pH below 6.8
C. The organism produces urease
D. The organism is gram positive
E. The organism raised the pH above 6.8
Answer: B. The organism ferments lactose, dropping the pH below 6.8
Why this is correct: MacConkey agar is selective media with lactose as the sole carbohydrate. Bile salts and crystal violet prevent gram-positive growth. Lactose fermentation drops the pH below 6.8, turning colonies red; above 6.8 there's no color.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The organism is oxidase positive: Oxidase isn't what MacConkey measures.
C. The organism produces urease: Urease isn't measured by MacConkey.
D. The organism is gram positive: Crystal violet and bile salts stop gram-positive growth.
E. The organism raised the pH above 6.8: A pH above 6.8 gives no color.
Image credit: A doubt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 27
A 62-year-old man is admitted with fever and hypotension from a urinary source. He has diabetes and takes insulin. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), and blood pressure is 80/44 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that ferments glucose, reduces nitrate to nitrite, and is oxidase negative. His lactate is 5.4 mmol/L, and his WBC is 21,000/mm³. Urinalysis shows many white cells. Which component of this organism mainly drives his shock?
A. M protein
B. Pneumolysin
C. TSST-1
D. Exotoxin A
E. Endotoxin
Answer: E. Endotoxin
Why this is correct: Enterobacteriaceae (including E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Serratia, Enterobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia) are facultative anaerobes that ferment glucose, reduce nitrate, and lack cytochrome c oxidase. Endotoxin, released more during rapid growth and lysis, is the major cause of septic shock.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. M protein: That's a group A strep factor.
B. Pneumolysin: That's a pneumococcal toxin.
C. TSST-1: That's a staph superantigen.
D. Exotoxin A: That's a Pseudomonas toxin; Pseudomonas is oxidase positive.
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 28

Question 31
A 45-year-old man is admitted with fever and abdominal pain 10 days after surgery for a perforated appendix. He has hypertension. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), and CT shows a pelvic abscess. The drained pus smells foul, and Gram stain shows mixed organisms. Culture grows an anaerobic gram-negative rod that contains endotoxin and makes beta-lactamase. His WBC is 18,200/mm³. He received cefazolin at surgery. Which features point to an anaerobic infection?
A. A positive CAMP test
B. Coagulase-positive cocci
C. Infection near a mucosal surface with mixed flora, foul odor, and tissue gas
D. Growth only on MacConkey agar
E. A single organism with no odor
Answer: C. Infection near a mucosal surface with mixed flora, foul odor, and tissue gas
Why this is correct: Anaerobic infections occur near mucosa and show mixed flora on Gram stain, a malodorous infection, and tissue gas. Bacteroidetes are anaerobes that contain endotoxin and make beta-lactamase.

B. Coagulase-positive cocci: That's S. aureus.

E. A single organism with no odor: That doesn't fit anaerobic infection.

Question 32
A 40-year-old man is admitted with burns over 35% of his body after a house fire. On day 8, his burn wounds develop a blue-green exudate with a sweet, grape-like odor. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). Culture grows an aerobic gram-negative rod that is oxidase positive. He is on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Why this is correct: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod from soil and water with a blue-green pigment and grape-like odor. Exotoxin A inactivates EF-2, elastase and alkaline protease destroy the cornea, and exoenzyme S impairs phagocytosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Elastase: Elastase is a protease that can destroy the cornea.
B. Exoenzyme S: Exoenzyme S impairs phagocytosis.
C. TSST-1: That's a staph toxin.
D. Heat-stable toxin: That's from B. cereus or ETEC.

Question 33
A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of burning with urination and a thick yellow discharge from his penis for 3 days. He had a new sexual partner 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). A Gram stain of the discharge looks like the image below, and the organism ferments glucose but not maltose. He has no rash or joint pain, and HIV testing is negative. His urinalysis shows many white cells. Which treatment is recommended? ![Gram stain of urethral discharge](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Neisseria_gonorrhoeae_PHIL_3693_lores.jpg)
A. Parenteral ceftriaxone
B. Oral tetracycline
C. Vancomycin
D. Oral ciprofloxacin
E. Rifampin prophylaxis
Answer: A. Parenteral ceftriaxone
Why this is correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose only and has LOS and pili but no capsule. It's treated with parenteral ceftriaxone, and it has chromosomal resistance to other drugs.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Oral tetracycline: Efflux pumps give resistance to tetracyclines.
C. Vancomycin: Vancomycin only covers gram-positive organisms.
D. Oral ciprofloxacin: Mutations in porins and DNA gyrase give fluoroquinolone resistance.
E. Rifampin prophylaxis: Rifampin is used for meningococcal contacts.

Question 34
An 18-year-old college freshman is brought to the emergency department with fever, headache, and a spreading purple rash that began this morning. He lives in a dormitory. Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hemolytic uremic syndrome: That's from Shiga toxin.
B. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: That's from staph exfoliative toxins.
D. Weil disease: That's severe leptospirosis.
E. Toxic shock syndrome: That's from staph TSST-1.

Question 35
The roommate of an 18-year-old college student with meningococcal meningitis comes to the physician. He feels well and has no fever or headache. He takes no medications. His vital signs and exam are normal. He needs chemoprophylaxis. He shared a room with the patient for 3 weeks. Which option is appropriate, and what should he know about one of the choices?
A. No prophylaxis is needed for close contacts
B. Doxycycline; it causes photosensitivity
C. Vancomycin; it causes red man syndrome
D. Rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin; rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer
E. Metronidazole; it causes a disulfiram reaction
Answer: D. Rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin; rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer
Why this is correct: Close contacts of meningococcal disease get chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin. Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer, which matters for drug interactions.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. No prophylaxis is needed for close contacts: All close contacts need prophylaxis.
B. Doxycycline; it causes photosensitivity: Doxycycline isn't the listed prophylaxis.
C. Vancomycin; it causes red man syndrome: Vancomycin isn't used for prophylaxis.
E. Metronidazole; it causes a disulfiram reaction: Metronidazole isn't used here.

Question 36
A 19-year-old woman is starting college in the fall and will live in a dormitory. She received the quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine at 16. She is healthy and takes no medications. Her physician recommends an additional vaccine for short-term protection against one serogroup not covered by her first vaccine. Her vital signs are normal. Her other childhood vaccines are up to date. Which serogroup is this?
A. Serogroup B
B. Serogroup W
C. Serogroup Y
D. Serogroup C
E. Serogroup A
Answer: A. Serogroup B
Why this is correct: The quadrivalent polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine covers serogroups A, C, Y, and W. Serogroup B vaccine is given at ages 18 to 23 for short-term protection in groups like military recruits and college students, and a pentavalent vaccine covers A, B, C, Y, and W.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Serogroup W: W is covered by the quadrivalent vaccine.
C. Serogroup Y: Y is covered by the quadrivalent vaccine.
D. Serogroup C: C is covered by the quadrivalent vaccine.
E. Serogroup A: A is covered by the quadrivalent vaccine.

Question 37
A 3-day-old boy has red, swollen eyelids and a thick purulent discharge from both eyes. He was born vaginally to a mother who had no prenatal care. He is otherwise feeding well. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F). Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci that ferment glucose only and have no capsule. His mother had a vaginal discharge late in pregnancy that wasn't treated. Why isn't a tetracycline or fluoroquinolone used for this organism?
A. Chromosomal resistance from efflux pumps (tetracyclines) and porin and DNA gyrase changes (fluoroquinolones)
B. It's a gram-positive organism
C. It lacks a cell wall
D. It has a thick capsule that blocks the drugs
E. It lives inside host cell vacuoles
Answer: A. Chromosomal resistance from efflux pumps (tetracyclines) and porin and DNA gyrase changes (fluoroquinolones)
Why this is correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum). It has chromosomal resistance: efflux pumps affect tetracyclines, PenA mutations change PCN-binding proteins, and PenB porin and DNA gyrase changes affect fluoroquinolones. It's treated with parenteral ceftriaxone.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. It's a gram-positive organism: It's a gram-negative diplococcus.
C. It lacks a cell wall: Neisseria has a cell wall.
D. It has a thick capsule that blocks the drugs: N. gonorrhoeae has no capsule.
E. It lives inside host cell vacuoles: That describes Ehrlichia and Anaplasma.

Question 38

Question 41
A 3-month-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the emergency department because of coughing fits that end with a high-pitched whoop and vomiting. She had a runny nose for a week before the cough started. Between spells she looks well. During a spell she turns blue. WBC is 40,000/mm³ with 70% lymphocytes. The organism is grown on Regan-Lowe medium. Her oxygen saturation is 97% between spells. How does its toxin work?
A. It inactivates elongation factor 2
B. It binds MHC II as a superantigen
C. It blocks acetylcholine release
D. It raises cGMP
E. It ADP-ribosylates the Gαi protein, raising cAMP
Answer: E. It ADP-ribosylates the Gαi protein, raising cAMP
Why this is correct: Bordetella pertussis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative coccobacillus spread by aerosol. It goes through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages. Its toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαi, raising cAMP, and it causes a very high WBC with lymphocytosis. It's cultured on Regan-Lowe, treated with erythromycin, and prevented with Tdap.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. It inactivates elongation factor 2: That's diphtheria toxin.
B. It binds MHC II as a superantigen: That's TSST-1.
C. It blocks acetylcholine release: That's botulinum toxin.
D. It raises cGMP: That's the B. cereus heat-stable toxin.

Question 42

Question 43
A 20-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he refuses to walk and his right knee is swollen and warm. He had a cold with mouth sores last week. He attends daycare. Question 44
A 36-year-old man with AIDS comes to the physician because of fever, night sweats, diarrhea, and a 9-kg weight loss. He stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago. His CD4 count is 30/μL. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), and he has an enlarged liver and spleen and anemia. Blood cultures grow slow-growing organisms that are non-chromogens. A stain of the organisms is shown below. He has no cough, and chest x-ray is clear. What is the recommended treatment? ![Acid-fast stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d1/Acid_fast_bacilli.jpg)
A. Clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol
B. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
C. Amphotericin B and flucytosine
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone
E. Doxycycline alone
Answer: A. Clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol
Why this is correct: Mycobacterium avium complex causes disseminated infection in AIDS with CD4 under 50, with fever, night sweats, diarrhea, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia. It's a slow-growing non-chromogen. Treatment is clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol, adding rifabutin if severe.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine: That's the regimen for leprosy.
C. Amphotericin B and flucytosine: That's for cryptococcal meningitis.
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone: That's for PCP and Nocardia.
E. Doxycycline alone: That's used for rickettsial infections.

Question 45
A 55-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 2 years ago develops cough and fever for 3 weeks, followed by headache and new weakness in his right arm. He takes tacrolimus and prednisone. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Chest CT shows a lung nodule, and brain MRI shows an abscess. Sputum shows weakly acid-fast, filamentous branching organisms, shown below. Biopsy shows no granulomas. His WBC is 12,400/mm³, and blood cultures are negative. What is the most likely organism? ![Gram stain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a9/Norcardia_Bacteria_under_the_Microscope.jpg)
A. Toxoplasma gondii
B. Mycobacterium avium complex
C. Nocardia asteroides
D. Mycobacterium kansasii
E. Cryptococcus neoformans
Answer: C. Nocardia asteroides
Why this is correct: Nocardia is a gram-positive, weakly acid-fast organism with branching filaments. N. asteroides causes lung infections in immunocompromised patients and can spread to the brain as an abscess. It prevents phagosome acidification and fusion and doesn't form granulomas.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Toxoplasma gondii: Toxoplasma is a parasite, not a branching bacterium.
B. Mycobacterium avium complex: MAC is fully acid fast and not filamentous.
D. Mycobacterium kansasii: M. kansasii causes TB-like cavitary lung disease without brain abscess.
E. Cryptococcus neoformans: Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast.

Question 46
A 60-year-old man who smokes comes to the physician because of a chronic cough and weight loss for 4 months. He isn't immunocompromised and has no TB exposure. Chest CT shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe that looks like TB. Sputum grows a slow-growing mycobacterium that makes pigment only after exposure to light and is consistently isolated from tap water. His HIV test is negative. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F). Which organism is this?
A. Mycobacterium kansasii
B. Mycobacterium abscessus
C. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum
D. Mycobacterium gordonae
E. Mycobacterium avium complex
Answer: A. Mycobacterium kansasii
Why this is correct: M. kansasii causes TB-like lung disease with cavitation and a right upper lobe predilection. It prevents phagolysosome fusion, is consistently isolated from tap water, and is a slow-growing photochromogen.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Mycobacterium abscessus: It's a rapid grower that's non-pigmented.
C. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum: It's a scotochromogen that makes pigment in the dark.
D. Mycobacterium gordonae: It's a scotochromogen.
E. Mycobacterium avium complex: MAC is a non-chromogen.
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 47
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a painless, enlarging lump in her neck for 6 weeks. She is healthy otherwise, and her vaccines are up to date. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and there's a firm 3-cm node in her neck. Culture of the node grows a slow-growing mycobacterium that makes yellow pigment even when grown in the dark. She has no fever, cough, or TB exposure. Her chest x-ray is normal. How is this organism classified?
A. A non-grower
B. A scotochromogen
C. A rapid grower
D. A photochromogen
E. A non-chromogen
Answer: B. A scotochromogen
Why this is correct: Scotochromogens, like M. scrofulaceum and M. gordonae, make pigment in the dark and are slow growers. Photochromogens, like M. kansasii and M. marinum, make pigment only with light.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A non-grower: M. leprae is the non-grower.
C. A rapid grower: M. scrofulaceum is a slow grower.
D. A photochromogen: Photochromogens need light to make pigment.
E. A non-chromogen: Non-chromogens like MAC don't make pigment.
Objective: Explain bacterial cell wall structures and associated properties (Gram positive/negative cell wall, staining, peptidoglycan, LPS, role in pathogenesis, and targets of antibiotics) (CBO 1.1)

Question 48
A 22-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis has worsening cough and weight loss despite her usual treatments. Her FEV1 has fallen to 48% of predicted. Chest CT shows nodules and bronchiectasis that resemble MAC disease. Sputum grows a mycobacterium that forms non-pigmented colonies within a week. B. Mycobacterium abscessus
C. Mycobacterium marinum
D. Mycobacterium kansasii

Why this is correct: M. abscessus resembles MAC disease, comes from soil, dust, water, and animals, and is a non-pigmented rapid grower. Rapid growers also include M. chelonae and M. fortuitum.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Mycobacterium avium complex: MAC is a slow grower.
C. Mycobacterium marinum: M. marinum is a slow-growing photochromogen.
D. Mycobacterium kansasii: M. kansasii is a slow-growing photochromogen.
E. Mycobacterium leprae: M. leprae doesn't grow in culture.

Question 49
A 38-year-old man from Brazil comes to the physician because of a few pale, numb skin patches on his arm and trunk. He burned his hand on a stove without feeling it. He has thickened nerves at his elbow. Biopsy shows granulomas with very few acid-fast bacilli. His family has lived for generations in a rural area where armadillos are common. He has no fever. Which immune response explains this form of his disease?
A. An IgE-mediated response
B. No immune response
C. A weak TH1 and strong TH2 response
D. A complement deficiency
E. A strong TH1 response with IL-2 and IFN-γ
Answer: E. A strong TH1 response with IL-2 and IFN-γ
Why this is correct: Tuberculoid (paucibacillary) leprosy reflects a strong TH1 response with IL-2 and IFN-γ, causing granulomatous infection, nerve damage, and autoamputation. It's treated with dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. An IgE-mediated response: That isn't the leprosy mechanism.
B. No immune response: The strong TH1 response creates granulomas.
C. A weak TH1 and strong TH2 response: That's lepromatous leprosy.
D. A complement deficiency: That isn't the mechanism.

Question 50
A 52-year-old man from rural India comes to the physician because of numb hands and feet and many skin nodules on his face and ears. He has lost his eyebrows, and his face looks thickened. Biopsy shows many acid-fast bacilli clustered in globi. He has no fever, and his CBC is normal. He has lost sensation in several fingers. Which immune response and treatment fit this form?
A. A strong TH2 response; amphotericin B
B. A strong TH1 response; clarithromycin and ethambutol
C. A strong TH1 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
D. A strong TH2 response; doxycycline alone
E. A strong TH2 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
Answer: E. A strong TH2 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
Why this is correct: Lepromatous (multibacillary) leprosy reflects a weak TH1 and strong TH2 response, with globi of acid-fast bacilli. It's treated with the triple regimen of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. M. leprae is found in armadillos.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A strong TH2 response; amphotericin B: That's for fungal infections.
B. A strong TH1 response; clarithromycin and ethambutol: That's MAC treatment.
C. A strong TH1 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine: A strong TH1 response is tuberculoid leprosy.
D. A strong TH2 response; doxycycline alone: The regimen is the triple drug combination.

Week 9: Bacteria & Antibiotics / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections

Question 52
A 6-year-old girl from North Carolina is brought to the emergency department in June because of fever, headache, and a rash for 3 days. Her family went camping 10 days ago, and her mother removed a tick from her scalp. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F). The rash began on her wrists and ankles and spread to her trunk, as shown below. Platelets are 82,000/mm³, and ALT and AST are elevated. What is the most appropriate treatment? ![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d2/Rocky_Mountain_spotted_fever_PHIL_1962_lores.jpg)
A. Penicillin
B. Doxycycline
C. Supportive care only
D. Vancomycin
E. Ceftriaxone
Answer: B. Doxycycline
Why this is correct: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia, obligate intracellular bacteria spread by ticks in spring and summer. The rash starts at the wrists and ankles and moves to the trunk, with thrombocytopenia and raised liver enzymes. Delay raises fatality, and treatment is doxycycline.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Penicillin: Penicillin doesn't cover Rickettsia.
C. Supportive care only: Treatment shouldn't be delayed.
D. Vancomycin: Vancomycin only covers gram-positive organisms.
E. Ceftriaxone: Ceftriaxone isn't the treatment for RMSF.

Question 53
A 45-year-old man who raises goats and drinks unpasteurized milk comes to the physician because of fevers that come and go over 6 weeks, drenching foul-smelling sweats, and lower back pain. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and his liver and spleen are enlarged. He has tenderness over his sacroiliac joints. Blood and marrow cultures grow a gram-negative coccobacillus, and a Rose Bengal test is positive. His WBC is normal, and his ALT is mildly elevated. What is the treatment?
A. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
B. Penicillin G
C. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
D. Supportive care only
E. Doxycycline alone
Answer: A. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
Why this is correct: Brucellosis comes from infected animals, animal-derived food, inhalation, or skin abrasions. It causes undulating fever, night sweats, malodorous sweat, hepatosplenomegaly, sacroiliitis, and spondylitis. It's diagnosed by blood and marrow culture and the Rose Bengal test and treated with doxycycline plus gentamicin or doxycycline, rifampin, and ceftriaxone.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Penicillin G: That's used for leptospirosis.
C. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine: That's for leprosy.
D. Supportive care only: Brucellosis needs antibiotics.
E. Doxycycline alone: The recommended regimens combine drugs.

Question 54

C. Rocky Mountain spotted fever: RMSF causes fever and a rash after a tick bite.

Question 55
A 55-year-old man from Missouri comes to the physician because of fever, headache, and muscle aches for 5 days. He removed a tick after hiking 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). He has a faint petechial rash on his trunk. WBC is 2,800/mm³, platelets are 90,000/mm³, and liver enzymes are elevated. A blood smear shows clusters of organisms inside vacuoles of monocytes. He has no joint pain. His CSF is normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
A. Q fever; hydroxychloroquine alone
B. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis; doxycycline
C. Brucellosis; doxycycline and gentamicin
D. Rocky Mountain spotted fever; penicillin
E. Human monocytic ehrlichiosis; doxycycline
Answer: E. Human monocytic ehrlichiosis; doxycycline
Why this is correct: Ehrlichia chaffeensis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that replicates in host cell vacuoles (Anaplasmataceae). It causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis with nonspecific symptoms, rare vasculitis, and a rash in about a third. It's treated with doxycycline.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Q fever; hydroxychloroquine alone: Coxiella causes Q fever.
B. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis; doxycycline: Anaplasma infects granulocytes.
C. Brucellosis; doxycycline and gentamicin: Brucella doesn't form clusters in monocytes.
D. Rocky Mountain spotted fever; penicillin: RMSF organisms grow freely in the cytoplasm, and treatment is doxycycline.
